intro.title: Introduction
paras: The Second Thirumurai is one of the great books of Ramalinga Adigal's early songs: 113 poems and 1,228 verses. Most of them were sung at Otriyur, the old temple town by the sea at the northern edge of Chennai, to Siva as Thyagar, the Lord who gives. As a young man in Chennai, Vallalar went there day after day, and these poems carry the road, the temple and the sea in them. A few are sung at Chidambaram, the golden hall of the dance, and at other shrines; some are general poems, not tied to one place.

The book opens with the holy ash and the sacred name, Namasivaya. To wear the ash and say the name, Vallalar tells his own heart, is to want for nothing: “Do not fear. I swear this upon myself.” Then come dozens of poems in which he speaks to his heart and his mind. He coaxes them, scolds them, comforts them, and asks them to come with him to Otriyur. He calls greed and lust by name and promises to cut them down with the sword of grace.

At the heart of the book stand the petitions and the laments. Vallalar calls himself the lowest of the low, a dog at the Lord's door, and pleads. The Lord's very name means the Giver, yet he stays silent: “If you give nothing to those who beg, why did you take this name?” If he will not take him as his own, let him keep him as a pledge at his feet. Nothing in these verses is held back: the shame, the fear of death, the days wasted, the longing to see the golden face once again.

And there is the joy of grace received: the vision of the dance in the golden hall, the bliss that melts stone, and at the end of the book songs of village dance and of the white moon, a young woman who was garlanded by the Lord in her childhood, and the Lord praised as the one true medicine.

One verse of this book says plainly where all of it leads. Even a master who could turn a man into a woman and back, and raise the dead, if he lacks compassion and kills living beings to eat their bodies, can never be called one who knows God. This is Jeevakarunyam, compassion for every living being, which Vallalar later taught as the one path to ArutPerunJothi, the Vast Grace Light, open to all.

Each verse is given in four layers: the original Tamil, an ISO 15919 transliteration, a translation and a short commentary. Editor's notes under the titles give the place of a poem where it is not Otriyur and explain the word puzzles and the variant readings. A glossary explains the Tamil terms. The Tamil has been checked against the 1896 printed edition.

intro.title: A Note on Context
paras: These are among Vallalar's early songs. They come from the years when he worshipped God through the forms of the Saiva tradition. Most of them were sung at Otriyur, to Siva as Thyagar, the Lord who gives, and a few at Chidambaram and other shrines. Again and again he asks his mind to come with him to the temple and to repeat the sacred names: “Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on the rising mantra ‘Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya’.”

He did not stay there. In the Great Teaching (Perupadesam) of 1873 he told those gathered to place no aim in the religions, Saivism among them, and he named himself as the witness. His hold on the Saiva religion had once been beyond measure. For proof he pointed to this very collection: “The hymns I have sung, gathered in the Thiru Arutpa, are enough.” Why had he held to it so firmly? He answered:
அப்போது எனக்கு அவ்வளவு கொஞ்சம் அற்ப அறிவாக இருந்தது.
“Because at that time I had only so little, such petty knowledge.”

In that same teaching he gave one mantra to all: Arutperunjothi Arutperunjothi, Thanipperunkarunai Arutperunjothi (Vast Grace-Light, Vast Grace-Light, Unique Vast Compassion, Vast Grace-Light). From then on he taught the worship of Arutperunjothi, the Vast Grace-Light, alone. His late songs in the Sixth Thirumurai sing of that Light.

So these poems are an early stage of one journey, and a sincere one. The longing in them is real, and so is the shame at his own faults. Compassion is already the measure: one verse of this book says that a master who kills living beings to eat their bodies can never be called one who knows God. Read them as the first steps of the man who later expanded and evolved even further up until the full realization of the Vast Grace-Light.

note: Editor's note: a general poem (potu, பொது), not tied to one temple.
tamil: பாடற் கினிய வாக்களிக்கும் பாலும் சோறும் பரிந்தளிக்கும்
கூடற் கினிய அடியவர்தம் கூட்டம் அளிக்கும் குணம்அளிக்கும்
ஆடற் கினிய நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
தேடற் கினிய சீர் அளிக்கும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: pāṭaṟ kiṉiya vākkaḷikkum pālum cōṟum parintaḷikkum kūṭaṟ kiṉiya aṭiyavartam kūṭṭam aḷikkum kuṇamaḷikkum āṭaṟ kiṉiya neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy tēṭaṟ kiṉiya cīr aḷikkum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama" gives a sweet voice for singing. It lovingly provides milk and rice. It grants the sweet company of devotees and bestows good character. O wavering heart, do not fear. I swear this upon myself. This holy ash provides the sought-after wealth of greatness.
commentary: Vallalar addresses his anxious heart directly, promising that chanting the sacred mantra "Sivaya Nama" while wearing holy ash brings protection. He swears a personal oath that this devotion will provide worldly needs like food and good company while granting spiritual greatness.

tamil: கருமால் அகற்றும் இறப்பதனைக் களையு நெறியும் காட்டுவிக்கும்
பெருமால் அதனால் மயக்குகின்ற பேதை மடவார் நசைஅறுக்கும்
அருமால் உழந்த நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
திருமால் அயனும் தொழுதேத்தும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: karumāl akaṟṟum iṟappataṉaik kaḷaiyu neṟiyum kāṭṭuvikkum perumāl ataṉāl mayakkukiṉṟa pētai maṭavār nacai-aṟukkum arumāl uḻanta neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy tirumāl ayaṉum toḻutēttum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", which Vishnu and Brahma worship and praise, removes dark delusion. It shows the path to conquer death. It severs the desire for foolish women who bewilder the mind with great lust. O heart suffering in deep delusion, do not fear. I swear this upon myself.
commentary: This sacred practice clears dark mental confusion and cuts the ties of worldly lust. Brahma and Vishnu worship this ash because it reveals the path to overcoming death.

tamil: வெய்ய வினையின் வேர்அறுக்கும் மெய்ம்மை ஞான வீட்டிலடைந்
துய்ய அமல நெறிகாட்டும் உன்னற் கரிய உணர்வளிக்கும்
ஐயம் அடைந்த நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
செய்ய மலர்க்கண் மால்போற்றும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: veyya viṉaiyiṉ vēraṟukkum meymmai ñāṉa vīṭṭilaṭain tuyya amala neṟikāṭṭum uṉṉaṟ kariya uṇarvaḷikkum aiyam aṭainta neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy ceyya malarkkaṇ mālpōṟṟum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", praised by the red-lotus-eyed Vishnu, severs the root of cruel karma. It shows the pure path to attain the home of true wisdom and find salvation. It grants realization that is hard to conceive. O heart filled with doubt, do not fear. I swear this upon myself.
commentary: Chanting the divine name severs the root of cruel karma, the cycle of past actions and their consequences. It guides the doubting mind toward a pure path of wisdom and a realization of the divine that is impossible to grasp.

tamil: கோல மலர்த்தாள் துணைவழுத்தும் குலத்தொண் டடையக் கூட்டுவிக்கும்
நீல மணிகண் டப்பெருமான் நிலையை அறிவித் தருளளிக்கும்
ஆல வினையால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
சீலம் அளிக்கும் திருஅளிக்கும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: kōla malarttāḷ tuṇaivaḻuttum kulattoṇ ṭaṭaiyak kūṭṭuvikkum nīla maṇikaṇ ṭapperumāṉ nilaiyai aṟivit taruḷaḷikkum āla viṉaiyāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy cīlam aḷikkum tiru-aḷikkum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama" unites one with the noble service of praising the Lord's beautiful lotus feet. It reveals the state of the blue-gem-throated Lord and grants His grace. O heart troubled by poisonous karma, do not fear. I swear this upon myself. This holy ash grants virtue and divine wealth.
commentary: Siva is the blue-throated Lord who drank poison to save the world. Vallalar assures his troubled heart that wearing holy ash and chanting the sacred name draws the soul into a life of noble service and divine grace.

tamil: வஞ்சப் புலக்கா டெறியஅருள் வாளும் அளிக்கும் மகிழ்வளிக்கும்
கஞ்சத் தவனும் கரியவனும் காணற் கரிய கழல்அளிக்கும்
அஞ்சில் புகுந்த நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
செஞ்சொல் புலவர் புகழ்ந்தேத்தும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: vañcap pulakkā ṭeṟiya-aruḷ vāḷum aḷikkum makiḻvaḷikkum kañcat tavaṉum kariyavaṉum kāṇaṟ kariya kaḻalaḷikkum añcil pukunta neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy ceñcol pulavar pukaḻntēttum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", praised and extolled by poets of refined words, grants the sword of grace to cut down the deceitful forest of the senses. It grants joy. It grants the holy feet that are hard to see even for the lotus-born Brahma and the dark-hued Vishnu. O heart entangled in the five senses, do not fear. I swear this upon myself.
commentary: Vallalar describes the physical senses as a deceitful forest that traps the mind. He promises that the sacred ash grants a sword of divine grace to cut through these distractions, bringing the seeker directly to a state of joy and realization.

tamil: கண்கொள் மணியை முக்கனியைக் கரும்பைக் கரும்பின் கட்டிதனை
விண்கொள் அமுதை நம்அரசை விடைமேல் நமக்குத் தோற்றுவிக்கும்
அண்கொள் வினையால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
திண்கொள் முனிவர் சுரர்புகழும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: kaṇkoḷ maṇiyai mukkaṉiyaik karumpaik karumpiṉ kaṭṭitaṉai viṇkoḷ amutai namaracai viṭaimēl namakkut tōṟṟuvikkum aṇkoḷ viṉaiyāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy tiṇkoḷ muṉivar curarpukaḻum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: O heart, do not fear the approaching karma. I swear upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", praised by steadfast sages and celestials, will reveal our King to us on his bull mount. He is the gem of the eye, the three sweet fruits, the sugarcane, the crystallized sugar, and the heavenly nectar.
commentary: He promises that chanting the sacred syllables "Sivaya Nama" (homage to Siva) and wearing holy ash will summon the divine King. God is described as the most satisfying things he can name: the pupil of the eye, sweet fruit, sugarcane, and heavenly nectar. By swearing an oath on himself, Vallalar gives assurance that this divine presence will overcome any past burden.

tamil: நோயை அறுக்கும் பெருமருந்தை நோக்கற் கரிய நுண்மைதனைத்
தூய விடைமேல் வரும்நமது சொந்தத் துணையைத் தோற்றுவிக்கும்
ஆய வினையால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
சேய அயன்மால் நாடரிதாம் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: nōyai aṟukkum perumaruntai nōkkaṟ kariya nuṇmaitaṉait tūya viṭaimēl varumnamatu contat tuṇaiyait tōṟṟuvikkum āya viṉaiyāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy cēya ayaṉmāl nāṭaritām civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: O heart, do not fear the accumulated karma. I swear upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", which is difficult for Brahma and Vishnu to comprehend, will reveal our true companion arriving on the pure bull mount. He is the great medicine that destroys disease and the subtlety that is hard to perceive.
commentary: The divine is the great medicine that destroys disease. Vallalar assures his heart that chanting the holy name and applying sacred ash will bring this cure, revealing a God who is both subtle and a personal companion. This reality is hard even for Brahma and Vishnu to comprehend, yet it remains freely available to the sincere seeker.

tamil: எண்ண இனிய இன்னமுதை இன்பக் கருணைப் பெருங்கடலை
உண்ண முடியாச் செழுந்தேனை ஒருமால் விடைமேல் காட்டுவிக்கும்
அண்ண வினையால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
திண்ண மளிக்கும் திறம்அளிக்கும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: eṇṇa iṉiya iṉṉamutai iṉpak karuṇaip peruṅkaṭalai uṇṇa muṭiyāc ceḻuntēṉai orumāl viṭaimēl kāṭṭuvikkum aṇṇa viṉaiyāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy tiṇṇa maḷikkum tiṟamaḷikkum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: O heart, do not fear the approaching karma. I swear upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", which grants certainty and ability, will show him to us on the great bull mount. He is the sweet nectar pleasant to contemplate, the great ocean of blissful compassion, and the rich honey that cannot be exhausted.
commentary: Divine grace is described as an inexhaustible ocean of blissful compassion and rich honey. Vallalar reassures his heart that calling on God through the sacred chant grants certainty and inner ability. Anchored in this compassionate presence, the fear of approaching karma dissolves.

tamil: சிந்தா மணியை நாம்பலநாள் தேடி எடுத்த செல்வமதை
இந்தார் வேணி முடிக்கனியை இன்றே விடைமேல் வரச்செயும்காண்
அந்தோ வினையால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
செந்தா மரையோன் தொழுதேத்தும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: cintā maṇiyai nāmpalanāḷ tēṭi eṭutta celvamatai intār vēṇi muṭikkaṉiyai iṉṟē viṭaimēl varacceyumkāṇ antō viṉaiyāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy centā maraiyōṉ toḻutēttum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: Alas, O heart, do not fear the karma. I swear upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", worshipped and praised by Brahma on the red lotus, will make him come to us today on the bull mount. He is the wish-fulfilling gem, the wealth we sought and found over many days, and the supreme fruit with a moon-adorned crown of matted hair.
commentary: The divine presence is a wish-fulfilling gem and the wealth the soul has sought for a long time. Vallalar insists that grace is not a distant promise, but a reality that will arrive this very day. He pictures the divine wearing a crown of matted hair adorned with the moon, a traditional image of Siva. Even Brahma, seated on a red lotus, praises this practice of chanting the holy name.

tamil: உள்ளத் தெழுந்த மகிழ்வைநமக் குற்ற துணையை உள்உறவைக்
கொள்ளக் கிடையா மாணிக்கக் கொழுந்தை விடைமேல் கூட்டுவிக்கும்
அள்ளல் துயரால் நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
தெள்ளக் கடலான் புகழ்ந்தேத்தும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: uḷḷat teḻunta makiḻvainamak kuṟṟa tuṇaiyai uḷuṟavaik koḷḷak kiṭaiyā māṇikkak koḻuntai viṭaimēl kūṭṭuvikkum aḷḷal tuyarāl neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy teḷḷak kaṭalāṉ pukaḻntēttum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: O heart, do not fear the sorrow of this worldly mire. I swear upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama", praised and worshipped by Vishnu on the clear ocean, will unite us with him on the bull mount. He is the joy that rises in the heart, our fitting companion, our inner kinship, and the tender ruby shoot that is hard to attain.
commentary: Vallalar tells his heart not to fear the immediate sorrows of worldly life. He describes God as the joy rising from within and our inner kinship. The divine is a rare ruby shoot, delicate and precious. Vishnu, resting on the clear ocean, praises this path, which promises to unite the seeker with their divine companion.

tamil: உற்ற இடத்தில் உதவநமக் குடையோர் வைத்த வைப்பதனைக்
கற்ற மனத்தில் புகுங்கருணைக் கனியை விடைமேல் காட்டுவிக்கும்
அற்றம் அடைந்த நெஞ்சேநீ அஞ்சேல் என்மேல் ஆணைகண்டாய்
செற்றம் அகற்றித் திறல் அளிக்கும் சிவாய நமஎன் றிடுநீறே.
translit: uṟṟa iṭattil utavanamak kuṭaiyōr vaitta vaippataṉaik kaṟṟa maṉattil pukuṅkaruṇaik kaṉiyai viṭaimēl kāṭṭuvikkum aṟṟam aṭainta neñcēnī añcēl eṉmēl āṇaikaṇṭāy ceṟṟam akaṟṟit tiṟal aḷikkum civāya nama-eṉ ṟiṭunīṟē.
translation: O vulnerable heart, do not fear. I swear this upon myself. The holy ash worn while chanting "Sivaya Nama" dispels anger and grants strength. It is the treasure our Master stored away to help us in our time of need. It reveals the fruit of grace that enters the learned mind, appearing upon the sacred bull.
commentary: The sacred ash acts as a divine safeguard for times of trouble. God left this ash as a hidden treasure to wipe away inner anger and provide spiritual strength. By trusting in it, the mind prepares to receive the sweetness of divine grace, pictured here as the Lord arriving on his sacred bull.

sections.title: The Light of the Name of Grace

translit: vāṅku vilnutal maṅkaiyar viḻiyāl mayaṅki vañcarpāl varuntināḷ tōṟum ēṅku kiṉṟatil eṉpayaṉ kaṇṭāy eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu tēṅku lāvuceṅ karumpiṉum iṉitāyt tittit taṉpartam cittattuḷ ūṟi ōṅkum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: O mind, what do you gain by constantly pining, bewildered by the eyes of women with foreheads like bent bows and suffering among deceitful people? Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on the rising mantra "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". It tastes sweeter than rich red sugarcane and wells up within the minds of devotees.
commentary: Worldly attractions and deceitful people only bring suffering. Vallalar urges his mind to leave them behind, visit the holy town of Otriyur, and meditate on a mantra (a sacred chant) combining the names of Siva and Shanmuka (Siva's son Murugan).

translit: tavama tiṉṟivaṉ maṅkaiyar muyakkāl tarumam iṉṟuvañ cakarkaṭuñ cārvāl ivakai yālmika varuntuṟil eṉṉām eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu pavama tōṭṭinal āṉanta uruvām pāṅku kāṭṭinal patantarum aṭiyār uvakai ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: Penance is lost through the embrace of women. Righteousness is lost through harsh association with deceitful people. What will come of suffering so greatly in these ways? Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". It is the joy of the devotees, driving away worldly existence, revealing the true form of bliss, and granting the exalted state.
commentary: Chasing worldly desires destroys spiritual discipline, and keeping bad company ruins righteousness. Chanting this mantra ends the cycle of birth and death, revealing bliss and granting the soul the highest spiritual state.

translit: miṉṉum nuṇṇiṭaip peṇperum pēykaḷ veyya nīrkkuḻi viḻuntatu pōka iṉṉum vīḻkalai uṉakkoṉṟu colvēṉ eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu poṉu lāviya puyam uṭai yāṉum pukaḻu lāviya pū-uṭai yāṉum uṉṉum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: Let your past falls into the cruel watery pits of great female demons with waists thin as lightning be gone. Do not fall anymore. I will tell you one thing. Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". This is meditated upon by the Lord with golden shoulders and the Lord seated on the glorious flower.
commentary: Physical temptations drag the soul down. Vallalar urges his mind to stop repeating the same errors and points to the supreme power of this mantra. Even the greatest gods meditate on it: the Lord with golden shoulders is Vishnu, and the Lord seated on the glorious flower is Brahma.

translit: poṉṟum vāḻkkaiyai nilai-eṉa niṉaintē pulaiya maṅkaiyar puḻuneḷi aḷaṟṟil eṉṟum vīḻntuḻal maṭamaiyai viṭuttē eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu tuṉṟu tīmpalāc cuḷaiyiṉum iṉippāyt toṇṭar taṅkaḷnāc cuvaipeṟa ūṟi oṉṟum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: You consider this perishing life to be permanent and constantly fall and wallow in the worm-infested mire of wretched women. Abandon this foolishness. Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". It tastes sweeter than dense sweet jackfruit segments and wells up to grace the tongues of devotees who merge with it.
commentary: People treat this temporary physical life as if it will last forever. Vallalar tells his mind to abandon the dirt of worldly attachments and taste something far better, surrendering to the chant that wells up on the tongues of devotees.

translit: varaikku nērmulai maṅkaiyar mayalāl mayaṅki vañcarāl varuttamuṟ ṟañarām iraikkum mākkaṭal iṭaiviḻun tayarēl eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu karaikkum teḷḷiya amutamō tēṉō kaṉiko lō-eṉak kaṉivuṭaṉ uyarntōr uraikkum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: Do not become exhausted falling into the roaring great ocean of sorrow, bewildered by the delusion of women with mountain-like breasts and tormented by deceitful people. Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". Exalted ones speak of it with deep affection, wondering whether it is melting clear nectar, sweet honey, or ripe fruit.
commentary: Worldly delusion pulls the mind into a roaring ocean of sorrow. Vallalar tells his mind not to drown in it. Wise souls who have experienced the chant cannot even decide how to describe its sweetness.

translit: vātu ceymmaṭa vārtamai viḻaintāy maṟali vantuṉai vā-eṉa aḻaikkil ētu ceyvaiyō ēḻainī antō eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu pōtu vaikiya nāṉmukaṉ makavāṉ puṇari vaikiya pūmakaḷ koḻunaṉ ōtum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: You desired quarrelsome women. If the god of death comes and calls you, what will you do, poor one? Alas, come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya", the mantra chanted by the lotus-seated four-faced Brahma, Indra, and Vishnu, the husband of the ocean-born goddess.
commentary: Death can arrive at any moment while the mind is distracted by worldly lust. Vallalar urges his mind to travel to Otriyur, a temple town in present-day Chennai, to seek refuge in the divine name.

translit: naṇṇum maṅkaiyar puḻumalak kuḻiyil nāḷum vīḻvuṟṟu nalintiṭēl nitamāy eṇṇum eṉmoḻi kurumoḻi āka eṇṇi oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu paṇṇum iṉcuvai amutiṉum iṉitāyp pattar nāḷtoṟum cittamuḷ ḷūṟa uṇṇum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: Do not fall and suffer every day in the pit of worms and feces of the women you approach. Consider my daily words as the words of the guru. Come with me to Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya". It is sweeter than sweet ambrosia, and devotees consume it daily as it wells up within their minds.
commentary: The physical body is a vessel of waste and decay, yet human beings obsess over it through sexual infatuation. To break this destructive habit, Vallalar commands his mind to accept his own inner wisdom as a spiritual teacher (guru). Repeating the divine name brings a sweetness far greater than the mythical nectar of immortality (ambrosia).

translit: panta vaṇṇamām maṭantaiyar mayakkāl pacaiyil neñcarāl parivuṟu kiṉṟāy enta vaṇṇanī uyvaṇam antō eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu canta māmpukaḻ aṭiyaril kūṭic caṉaṉam eṉṉumōr cākaram nīnti unta ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: Confused by your infatuation with worldly women, you suffer at the hands of people with affectionless hearts. Alas, how will you find salvation? Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. Join the devotees of beautiful fame to swim across the ocean of birth and push forward. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya".
commentary: Worldly attachments lead a person to seek favors from cold, uncaring people. The only way to cross the painful ocean of repeated birth and death is to abandon worldly pursuits and join the company of true devotees.

translit: maṭṭiṉ maṅkaiyar koṅkaiyai viḻaintāy maṭṭi lātatōr vaṉtuyar aṭaintāy eṭṭi aṉṉarpāl irantalai kiṉṟāy eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu taṭṭi lātanal tavattavar vāṉōr cārntum kāṇkilāt taṟparam poruḷai oṭṭi ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: You desired the breasts of foolish women and attained boundless, harsh sorrow. You wander and beg from people who are as bitter as the Etti tree. Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. To unite with the supreme reality that even flawless ascetics and celestials cannot see when they approach, O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya".
commentary: Lust destroys a person's dignity and reduces them to begging for help from people as toxic as the poisonous Etti tree. Chanting the divine name is the direct path to the supreme reality. This truth remains hidden even from heavenly beings and strict ascetics, yet it is available through sincere devotion.

translit: nilavum oṇmati mukattiyark kuḻaṉṟāy nīca neñcartam neṭuṅkaṭai taṉiṟpōy ilavu kāttaṉai eṉṉainiṉ matiyō eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūrk keṉṉuṭaṉ pōntu palavum āyntunaṉ kuṇmaiyai uṇarnta pattar uḷḷakap patumaṅkaḷ tōṟum ulavum ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm ōmci vāya-eṉ ṟuṉṉuti maṉaṉē.
translation: You roamed after women with bright moon-like faces. You went to the tall gates of vile-hearted men and waited in vain like a parrot expecting a barren cotton pod to yield sweet fruit. What kind of intelligence is yours? Come with me to beautiful Otriyur. O mind, meditate on "Om Siva Shanmuka Siva Om, Om Sivaya", which strolls in the lotus hearts of devotees who have examined many things and realized the truth.
commentary: Relying on the wealthy and corrupt is a foolish illusion. Vallalar compares it to a hungry parrot waiting for a dry cotton pod to turn into sweet fruit. True wisdom means abandoning this futile wait and seeking the divine name, which lives permanently in the hearts of those who have realized the truth.

sections.title: The Ecstatic Wave of Chanting the Names of Sri Siva Shanmukha

translit: paḻutu nērkiṉṟa vañcakar kaṭaivāyp paṟṟi niṉṟatil payaṉetu kaṇṭāy poḻutu pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē poḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyam puritaṉak kēkit toḻutu caṇmuka civaciva eṉanam tōṉṟa lārtamait tutittavar tirumuṉ paḻutu collutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: What benefit have you found by standing at the doorways of deceivers who cause only ruin? Time is passing. Rise, my heart! Let us go to Otriyur, a place surrounded by groves. Let us bow down and praise our Lord, calling out, "Shanmuka! Siva! Siva!" Before His holy presence, we will confess our faults. Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Seeking help from worldly deceivers wastes a short life. Vallalar urges his heart to abandon this effort and turn to Otriyur, a historic temple town near Chennai. By chanting the holy names and honestly confessing all faults, grace is guaranteed.

translit: cūtu nērkiṉṟa mulaicciyar poruṭṭāc cuṟṟi niṉṟatil cukametu kaṇṭāy pōtu pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē poḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyam puritaṉak kēki ōtu caṇmuka civaciva eṉavē uṉṉi nekkuviṭ ṭurukinam tuyarām ātu collutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: What happiness have you found by wandering around for the sake of deceitful women? Time is passing. Rise, my heart! Let us go to Otriyur, a place surrounded by groves, and chant, "Shanmuka! Siva! Siva!" Melting with a broken heart as we think of Him, we will speak of our sorrowful destitution. Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Worldly desires and infatuations offer no lasting happiness. As time slips away, the only meaningful action is to approach the divine with a melting, humble heart and openly share our sorrows.

translit: ñālam celkiṉṟa vañcakar kaṭaivāy naṇṇi niṉṟatil nalametu kaṇṭāy kālam celkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē karutum oṟṟiyam kaṭinakark kēkik kōlam ceyaruḷ caṇmuka civa-ōm kuḻaka vō-eṉak kūvinam tuyarām ālam collutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: What good have you found by approaching the doorways of worldly deceivers? Time is passing. Rise, my heart! Let us go to the esteemed city of Otriyur. We will cry out, "O beautiful, graceful Shanmuka! Siva! Om! O youthful Lord!" and speak of the poison of our sorrow. Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: The sorrow of worldly life is a poison brought on by relying on unreliable people. Healing comes from crying out sacred syllables like Om and the names of the youthful Lord, trusting in divine relief.

translit: maruṭṭi vañcakam matittiṭum koṭiyār vāyal kāttiṉṉum varuntileṉ payaṉō iruṭṭip pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūr eṉumtalat tēkit teruṭṭi ṟañceyum caṇmuka civa-ōm civana mā-eṉac ceppinam tuyarām ariṭṭai ōtutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: What is the use of suffering any longer by waiting at the doors of cruel people who plot delusion and deceit? It is getting dark. Rise, my heart! Let us go to the beautiful place called Otriyur and call out, "Shanmuka, who grants clarity! Siva! Om! Siva Nama!" We will tell Him of our disastrous sorrow. Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Waiting for favors from manipulative people brings only suffering, and the darkness of life's end is fast approaching. The divine presence grants clarity, wiping away the confusion of the world and the disasters it causes.

translit: illai eṉpatē poruḷeṉak koṇṭōr īṉa vāyilil iṭarppaṭu kiṉṟāy ellai celkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūr eṉumtalat tēkit tollai ōmciva caṇmuka civa-ōm tūya eṉṟaṭi toḻutunām uṟṟa allal ōtutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: You suffer at the lowly doors of miserly people who treat the word "No" as their greatest wealth. Our time is running out. Rise, my heart! Let us go to the beautiful place called Otriyur. We will bow at His feet, calling out, "Ancient One! Om Siva Shanmuka! Siva Om! Pure One!" We will speak of the afflictions we have endured. Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Worldly wealth is guarded by misers whose favorite word is a flat refusal. Instead of suffering humiliation at their doors, we can take our burdens to the pure, ancient divine source, which never turns away a sincere seeker.

translit: karavu neñciṉar kaṭaittalaik kuḻaṉṟāy kalaṅki iṉṉumnī kaluḻntiṭil kaṭitē iravu pōntiṭum eḻuti-eṉ neñcē eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūr eṉumtalat tēkip paravu caṇmuka civaciva civa-ōm paracu yampucaṅ karacampu nama-ōm ara-eṉ ṟēttutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: You wandered at the doors of those with deceitful hearts. If you stay confused and weep any longer, night will fall swiftly. Arise, my heart! Let us go to the beautiful place called Otriyur and praise Him, chanting: "Shanmuga, Siva Siva Siva Om! Supreme Swayambhu, Sankara, Sambhu, Nama Om! Hara!" Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: The mind often wastes its energy seeking help from worldly patrons who make empty promises. Because human life is so short, the heart must wake up and turn directly to God, whose grace is certain.

translit: ēyntu vañcakar kaṭaittalai varunti irukkiṉ ṟāyiṉi icciṟu poḻutum cāyntu pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē takaikoḷ oṟṟiyam talattiṉuk kēki vāyntu caṇmuka namaciva civa-ōm varacu yampucaṅ karacampu eṉavē āyntu pōṟṟutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: You stay and suffer at the doors of deceitful people. Even this brief time is slipping away. Arise, my heart! Let us go to the great place of Otriyur. Let us praise Him purposefully, chanting: "Shanmuga, Nama Siva Siva Om! Supreme Swayambhu, Sankara, Sambhu!" Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Relying on deceitful people brings only suffering and drains away the brief span of human life. True security lies in focusing the mind on the Divine, calling upon the Lord through sacred names like Shanmuga and Siva.

translit: īrnta neñciṉar iṭantaṉil iruntē iṭarkoṇ ṭāyiṉi icciṟu poḻutum pērntu pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē piṟaṅkum oṟṟiyam perunakark kēki orntu caṇmuka caravaṇa pava-ōm ōmcu yampucaṅ karacampu eṉavē ārntu pōṟṟutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: You suffered by staying at the places of those with cruel hearts. Even this brief time is passing away. Arise, my heart! Let us go to the shining great city of Otriyur. Let us focus our minds and praise Him fully, chanting: "Shanmuga, Saravana Bhava Om! Om Swayambhu, Sankara, Sambhu!" Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Cruelty is the opposite of compassion, the natural state of the soul. Waiting on cruel-hearted people only brings distress. Because life is fleeting, the seeker must hurry to the divine presence and chant sacred syllables like Om to attain grace.

translit: kamaippiṉ īkilā vañcakar kaṭaiyaik kātti rukkalai kaṭuki-ip poḻutum imaippil pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē eḻilkoḷ oṟṟiyūr eṉumtalat tēki emaippu rantacaṇ mukaciva civa-ōm iṟaiva caṅkara arakara eṉavē amaippiṉ ēttutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: Do not wait at the doors of deceitful people who refuse to give even the slightest thing. Even this moment is vanishing swiftly in the blink of an eye. Arise, my heart! Let us go to the beautiful place called Otriyur and praise Him properly, chanting: "Shanmuga who protects us, Siva Siva Om! Lord, Sankara, Hara Hara!" Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Worldly patrons often refuse to give even the smallest help to those in need. Rather than lingering on their doorsteps while precious time vanishes in the blink of an eye, the seeker must trust in the Lord who protects.

translit: uṟaintu vañcarpāl kuṟaiyiran tavamē uḻalkiṉ ṟāyiṉi uraikkumip poḻutum kuṟaintu pōkiṉṟa teḻuti-eṉ neñcē kulavum oṟṟiyam kōnakark kēki niṟainta caṇmuka kurunama civa-ōm nimala ciṟpara arakara eṉavē aṟaintu pōṟṟutum aiyuṟal eṉmēl āṇai kāṇavar aruḷpeṟal āmē.
translation: You stay with deceitful people, begging them for your needs and wandering in vain. Even the time we spend speaking now is running out. Arise, my heart! Let us go to the celebrated great city of Otriyur. Let us proclaim and praise Him, chanting: "All-pervading Shanmuga, Guru, Nama Siva Om! Pure One, Supreme Consciousness, Hara Hara!" Do not doubt. I swear upon myself, we will surely receive His grace.
commentary: Begging from worldly people is a vain pursuit that achieves nothing. Even the time spent talking about it is a loss of precious moments that should be spent calling upon God, the teacher (Guru) and pure consciousness.

note: Editor's note: sung at Otriyur and at Thillai (Chidambaram) (tiruvoṟṟiyūrum tiruttillaiyum, திருவொற்றியூரும் திருத்தில்லையும்).
translit: cola vāviya toṇṭartam maṉattil cutanta raṅkoṭu tōṉṟiya tuṇaiyaik kala vāviya ēḻaiyēṉ neñcum karaintu vantiṭak kalantiṭum kaḷippaic cela vāviya poḻiltiru voṟṟit tēṉait tillaicciṟ ṟampalat tāṭum nalla vāḻviṉai nāṉmaṟaip poruḷai namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: I will never forget Namasivaya, the companion who freely appears in the minds of devotees longing to sing His praise, the rapture that merges to melt the stony heart of this poor wretch, the honey of sacred Otriyur ringed by flourishing groves, the good life dancing in the little hall of Thillai, the meaning of the four Vedas.
commentary: The sacred chant is a living companion appearing in the minds of true seekers. Vallalar marvels at how this divine presence softens his heart, melting it like stone turning to water. He experiences this sweet grace locally in Otriyur and universally in the cosmic dance hall of Thillai.

translit: aṭṭa mūrttama tākiya poruḷai aṇṭar ātiyōr aṟikilāt tiṟattai viṭṭa vēṭkaiyark kaṅkaiyil kaṉiyai vēta mūlattai vittaka viḷaivai eṭṭa rumpara māṉanta niṟaivai eṅkum ākiniṉ ṟilaṅkiya oḷiyai naṭṭam āṭiya naṭaṉanā yakattai namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: I will never forget Namasivaya, the reality manifesting as the eight forms, the greatness unknown to the gods and others, the fruit in the palm for those who have shed all desires, the root of the Vedas, the miraculous harvest, the boundless fullness of supreme bliss, the light that shines becoming all things everywhere, the Lord of the cosmic dance.
commentary: The divine reality takes the form of everything in the universe, yet remains hidden from the lesser gods. While celestial beings cannot grasp this supreme light, it rests easily like fruit in the hands of those who have let go of worldly desires. To chant the holy name is to hold the boundless light that has become all things.

translit: umpar vāṉtuyar oḻittaruḷ civattai ulake lāmpukaḻ uttamap poruḷait tampa māyaki lāṇṭamum tāṅkum campu vaicciva tarumattiṉ payaṉaip pampu cīraruḷ poḻitaru mukilaip parama ñāṉattaip paramaciṟ cukattai nampi ṉōrkaḷai vāḻvikkum nalattai namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: I will never forget Namasivaya, the Sivam who dispelled the great sorrow of the celestials, the supreme reality praised by all the worlds, Shambhu who supports all universes like a pillar, the fruit of righteous action, the cloud pouring down abundant grace, the supreme wisdom, the supreme conscious bliss, the goodness that uplifts those who trust Him.
commentary: The divine presence stands as a massive pillar holding up all universes. Calling God Shambhu (the source of happiness), Vallalar compares this force to a raincloud pouring down pure grace. He promises that this conscious bliss lifts up anyone who trusts in it.

translit: māliṉ uccimēl vatintamā maṇiyai vaḻuttum nā-akam maṇakkumnaṉ malaraip pāliṉ uḷiṉit tōṅkiya cuvaiyaip pattar tamuḷam paricikkum paḻattai āliṉ ōṅkiya āṉantak kaṭalai ampa lattilām amutaivē taṅkaḷ nāliṉ oṟṟiyūr amarntiṭum civattai namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: I will never forget Namasivaya, the great gem resting on the crown of Vishnu, the fine flower that fragrances the praising tongue and heart, the sweet exalted essence within milk, the fruit tasted by the hearts of devotees, the ocean of bliss surging beneath the banyan tree, the nectar in the cosmic hall, the Sivam seated in sacred Otriyur of the four Vedas.
commentary: The holy chant is a sensation of sweetness and fragrance transforming the praising tongue and heart. It is the hidden sweetness inside milk and a vast ocean of bliss under the banyan tree. By naming it the gem on the crown of Vishnu, Vallalar places this pure reality above all other deities.

translit: uṇṇi ṟainteṉai oḷittiṭum oḷiyai uṇṇa uṇṇamēl uvaṭṭuṟā naṟavaik kaṇṇi ṟaintatōr kāṭciyai yāvum kaṭanta mēlavar kalantiṭum uṟavai eṇṇi ṟaintamāl ayaṉmutal tēvar yārum kāṇkilā iṉpattiṉ niṟaivai naṇṇi oṟṟiyūr amarntaruḷ civattai namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: I will never forget Namasivaya, the light that fills my inner being and conceals me, the nectar that never cloys no matter how much it is drunk, the vision filling the eyes, the kinship uniting those exalted ones who have transcended all things, the fullness of joy unseen by the countless gods beginning with Vishnu and Brahma, the Sivam graciously seated in sacred Otriyur.
commentary: When this supreme light floods the inner being, it hides the individual ego. It acts as a sweet nectar that never sickens, no matter how much is drunk. Vallalar repeats a central theme: this absolute joy unites those who have given up worldly attachments, while remaining invisible to conventional gods like Vishnu and Brahma.

translit: tikku māṟiṉum eḻukaṭal puvimēl ceṉṟu māṟiṉum cēṇviḷaṅ koḷikaḷ ukku māṟiṉum peyaliṉṟi ulakil uṇavu māṟiṉum puvikaḷōr ēḻum mikku māṟiṉum aṇṭaṅkaḷ ellām viḻuntu māṟiṉum vētaṅkaḷ uṇarā nakkaṉ empirāṉ aruḷtirup peyarām namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: Even if the directions reverse, even if the seven seas rise over the earth and engulf it, even if the shining lights of the high heavens fall and vanish, even if rain fails and food disappears from the world, even if the seven worlds expand and transform, even if all the universes collapse and perish, I will never forget Namasivaya, the gracious holy name of our naked Lord whom the Vedas cannot comprehend.
commentary: True devotion outlasts the destruction of the universe. Even if the stars fall and the world is swallowed by the sea, Vallalar pledges to hold fast to the divine name Namaccivaya (a sacred mantra meaning adoration to Lord Siva). This reality is so deep that even the ancient scriptures cannot grasp it.

translit: peṟṟa tāytaṉai makamaṟan tālum piḷḷai yaippeṟum tāymaṟan tālum uṟṟa tēkattai uyirmaṟan tālum uyirai mēviya uṭalmaṟan tālum kaṟṟa neñcakam kalaimaṟan tālum kaṇkaḷ niṉṟimaip patumaṟan tālum naṟṟa vattavar uḷḷirun tōṅkum namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: Even if a child forgets the mother who bore him, even if a mother forgets her own child, even if the life-breath forgets the body it inhabits, even if the body forgets the life-breath within it, even if a learned heart forgets all its knowledge, even if the eyes forget to blink, I will never forget Namasivaya, which rises high within the hearts of those who perform great penance.
commentary: The bond with the divine is deeper than the fundamental instincts of nature. A mother's love and the blinking of eyes are basic laws of life. Even if these absolute laws fail, the steady remembrance of God's name remains unbroken in the hearts of the devoted.

translit: uṭai-u ṭuttiṭa iṭaimaṟan tālum ulaku ḷōrpacik kuṇamaṟan tālum paṭaiye ṭuttavar paṭaimaṟan tālum paravai tāṉalaip patumaṟan tālum puṭai-a ṭuttavar tamaimaṟan tālum poṉṉai vaitta-ap putaimaṟan tālum naṭai-a ṭuttavar vaḻimaṟan tālum namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: Even if the waist forgets to wear clothing, even if the people of the world forget the sensation of hunger, even if warriors forget their weapons, even if the ocean forgets to make waves, even if those standing close by forget themselves, even if one forgets a buried treasure of gold, even if travelers forget their path, I will never forget Namasivaya.
commentary: Remembering the divine name takes priority over basic human needs and natural functions. Feeling hunger, getting dressed, and finding one's way are things done without thinking. Even if humanity forgets these automatic habits, or the ocean forgets to make waves, the mind will never let go of God.

translit: vaṉmai ceytiṭum vaṟumaivan tālum makiḻvu ceyperu vāḻvuvan tālum puṉmai maṅkaiyar puṇarccinērn tālum porunti ṉālumniṉ ṟālumceṉ ṟālum taṉmai illavar cārpirun tālum cāṉṟa mēlavar tamai-aṭain tālum naṉmai eṉpaṉa yāvaiyum aḷikkum namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: Even if cruel poverty strikes, even if a grand and joyful life arrives, even if union with base women occurs, whether resting, standing, or walking, even if I am in the company of people without character, even if I reach the presence of noble and exalted souls, I will never forget Namasivaya, which grants all things that are good.
commentary: Outer circumstances have no power to alter inner devotion. Whether facing bitter poverty or great wealth, and surrounded by the corrupt or the wise, connection to the divine remains constant. The sacred name grants all good things and stands steady through every change in fortune.

translit: iṉṉum paṟpala nāḷirun tālum ikka ṇantaṉi lē-iṟan tālum tuṉṉum vāṉkatik kēpukun tālum cōrntu mānara kattuḻaṉ ṟālum eṉṉa mēlumiṅ keṉakkuvan tālum empi rāṉeṉakku yātucey tālum naṉṉar neñcakam nāṭiniṉ ṟōṅkum namacci vāyattai nāṉmaṟa vēṉē.
translation: Even if I live for many more days, even if I die this very moment, even if I enter the heavenly realm, even if I fall exhausted and suffer in the vast hell, whatever else may come to me here, whatever my Lord may do to me, I will never forget Namasivaya, which rises steadily within the seeking hearts of the good.
commentary: True love for God demands nothing and accepts whatever fate brings. Whether the future holds long life, instant death, the joys of heaven, or the agonies of hell, the mind stays anchored in the divine. Vallalar accepts whatever the Lord chooses, keeping the holy name alive in the seeking heart.

sections.title: The Light of the True Companion

translit: eñca vēṇṭiya aimpulap pakaiyāl iṭarkoṇ ṭōyntaṉai eṉṉiṉum iṉinī añca vēṇṭiya teṉṉai-eṉ neñcē añcal añcalkāṇ arumaṟai nāṉkum viñca vēṇṭiyum mālavaṉ malarōṉ viḷaṅka vēṇṭiyum miṭaṟṟiṉkaṇ amutā nañcai vēṇṭiya nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: Even if you are exhausted from the affliction caused by the five hostile senses that must be overcome, why should you fear anymore, my heart? Fear not, fear not! Desiring the four precious Vedas to excel, and desiring Vishnu and Brahma to flourish, the Lord willingly took the poison into his throat as nectar. His name is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The five senses pull the mind in every direction and exhaust the soul, yet there is no need to fear. To save the Vedas (ancient Hindu scriptures) alongside the creator deity Brahma and the preserver deity Vishnu, the Lord willingly swallowed deadly poison as if it were nectar. His sacred name, Namasivaya, is all the protection we need.

translit: kāviṉ maṉṉavaṉ etirkkiṉum kāmaṉ kaṇaikaṉ ēviṉum kālaṉē variṉum pūviṉ maṉṉavaṉ cīṟiṉum tirumāl pōrkku nēriṉum poruḷala neñcē ōvil mātuyar eṟṟiṉuk kaṭaintāy oṉṟum añcalnī uḷavaṟin tilaiyō nāviṉ maṉṉaraik karaitaṉil cērtta namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: Even if Indra opposes you, even if Kaman shoots his arrows, even if Death himself comes, even if Brahma is enraged, even if Vishnu comes to fight, they matter not, my heart. Why do you suffer this unceasing great sorrow? Fear nothing. Do you not know the truth? The name that brought the king of speech safely to the shore is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The anger of the greatest celestial deities means nothing when the soul holds fast to the divine name. This same name rescued the king of speech (the saint Appar), allowing him to float safely to shore when enemies threw him into the sea tied to a heavy stone.

translit: nīṭṭam uṟṟatōr vañcaka maṭavār neṭuṅkaṇ vēlpaṭa nilaiyatu kalaṅki vāṭṭam uṟṟaṉai āyiṉum añcēl vāḻi neñcamē malarkkaṇai toṭuppāṉ kōṭṭam uṟṟatōr nilaiyoṭu niṉṟa koṭiya kāmaṉaik koḷuviya nutaltī nāṭṭam uṟṟatōr nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: Even if you are pierced by the spear-like long eyes of deceitful women, and you wither in confusion, do not fear. May you prosper, my heart! The Lord's eye of fire on his forehead consumed the cruel Kaman who proudly aimed his flower arrows. The name of that Lord is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: Romantic and sexual desire can leave the mind confused, yet the sacred name offers a shield against this weakness. When Kaman proudly aimed his arrows of lust at the Lord, a fierce fire from the Lord's third eye burned him to ashes. Remembering this power frees the heart from worldly distraction.

translit: emmai vāṭṭumip paciyiṉuk kevarpāl ēku vōmeṉa eṇṇalai neñcē amma oṉṟunī aṟintilai pōlum ālak kōyiluḷ aṉṟucun tararkkāyc cemmai māmalarp pataṅkaḷnon tiṭavē ceṉṟu cōṟiran taḷittaruḷ ceytōṉ nammai āḷuṭai nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: Do not worry, my heart, wondering to whom we shall go to relieve this withering hunger. Alas, it seems you do not know this truth. On that day at the Alakkoil temple, his perfect lotus feet aching, he walked and begged for food to graciously feed Sundarar. The name of the Lord who rules us is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: Physical hunger brings terrible anxiety. Yet the Lord once felt such compassion for his devotee Sundarar (a revered Tamil saint) that he walked the streets begging for food to relieve the saint's hunger until his own feet ached. The God who provides for his devotees with such love is the companion we keep when we chant his name.

translit: ōṭu kiṉṟaṉaṉ katiravaṉ avaṉpiṉ ōṭu kiṉṟaṉa ovvoru nāḷāy vīṭu kiṉṟaṉa eṉceyvōm iṉi-av veyya kūṟṟuvaṉ vekuṇṭiṭil eṉṟē vāṭu kiṉṟaṉai añcalai neñcē mārkkaṇ ṭēyartam māṇpaṟin tilaiyō nāṭu kiṉṟavar nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: The sun races on. Following it, the days race by one by one and perish. You wither away, asking what we shall do if the cruel God of Death grows angry. Do not fear, my heart! Do you not know the glory of Markandeyar? The name of the Lord who belongs to those who seek him is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The passing of days brings us closer to death and fills the mind with dread. The Lord has already proven his power over mortality by rescuing the young devotee Markandeyar, defeating the God of Death to grant the boy eternal life. Trusting in the Lord's name drives away all fear of time and the grave.

translit: malaṅkum māluṭal piṇikaḷai nīkka maruntu vēṇṭiṉai vāḻi-eṉ neñcē kalaṅku ṟēlaruḷ tiruveṇṇī ṟeṉatu karatti runtatu kaṇṭilai pōlum vilaṅku ṟāpperum kāmanōy tavirkka virumpi ēṅkiṉai vempuṟēl aḻiyā nalaṅkoḷ ceñcaṭai nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: May you prosper, my heart. You sought a medicine to cure the diseases of this bewildering physical body. Do not be troubled. It seems you did not notice the sacred white ash of grace resting in my hand. You yearned eagerly to dispel the inescapable great disease of desire. Do not grieve. The name of the Lord with beautiful red matted hair is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The cure for physical illness and the inner torment of desire is already within reach. The sacred white ash of grace resting in Vallalar's hand, given to devotees of Siva, acts as a divine medicine. The companion through all struggles is the five-syllable mantra Namasivaya, meaning 'adoration to Siva.'

translit: mālum tuñcuvāṉ malaravaṉ iṟappāṉ maṟṟai vāṉavar muṟṟilum aḻivār ēlum naṟṟuṇai yārnamak keṉṟē eṇṇi niṟṟiyō ēḻainī neñcē kōlum āyiram kōṭi-aṇ ṭaṅkaḷ kulaiya nīkkiyum ākkiyum aḷikkum nālu māmaṟaip paramporuḷ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: Vishnu will perish. Brahma will die. The other celestial beings will be utterly destroyed. My poor heart, do you stand wondering who will be a fitting and good companion for us? He destroys, creates, and sustains thousands of crores of universes. The name of the supreme reality proclaimed by the four great Vedas is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: Even the greatest celestial gods are bound by time and will eventually pass away. The only eternal reality is the supreme Lord who creates and sustains countless universes. Our companion in a temporary world is the divine name Namasivaya.

translit: kanta vaṇṇamām kamalaṉmāl mutalōr kaṇṭi lāreṉil kailaiyam patiyai enta vaṇṇamnām kāṇkuva teṉṟē eṇṇi eṇṇinī ēṅkiṉai neñcē anta vaṇṇaveḷ āṉaimēl nampi amarntu ceṉṟatai aṟintilai pōlum nantam vaṇṇamām nātaṉtaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: O heart, you thought over and over and yearned, wondering how we could possibly see the city of Kailash if Brahma and Vishnu have not seen it. It seems you do not know how the great devotee sat upon that beautiful white elephant and journeyed there. The name of our beautiful Lord is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The highest spiritual realm is open to devotion, even if powerful gods cannot find it. Vallalar recalls the story of a great saint who journeyed straight to the divine city of Kailash riding a white elephant. That same path is open to anyone who holds fast to the name Namasivaya.

translit: vīra māntarum muṉivarum curarum mēvu taṟkoṇā veḷḷiyaṅ kiriyaic cēra nāmceṉṟu vaṇaṅkumvā ṟetuvō ceppeṉ ṟē-eṉai nacciya neñcē ūra ṉāruṭaṉ cēraṉār turaṅkam ūrntu ceṉṟa-av uḷavaṟin tilaiyō nāra mārmatic caṭaiyavaṉ nāmam namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: O heart, you begged me to tell you how we can go and worship at the silver mountain of Kailash, which is inaccessible even to heroic humans, sages, and celestials. Do you not know the secret of how the Chera king rode a horse and journeyed there alongside Uranar? The name of the Lord who wears the river and the moon in His matted hair is Namasivaya. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: Sincere devotion grants access to heights that exclude even powerful sages and celestial beings. Vallalar points to a famous story where a Chera king rode his horse to Kailash alongside his saintly friend. Chanting Namasivaya unlocks these same impossible doors.

translit: talaṅkaḷ tōṟumceṉ ṟavviṭai amarnta tampi rāṉtirut tāḷiṉai vaṇaṅki valaṅko ḷumpaṭi eṉṉaiyum kūṭa vā-eṉ kiṉṟaṉai vāḻi-eṉ neñcē ilaṅkaḷ tōṟumceṉ ṟirantiṭum avaṉē eṉṉai uṉṉaiyum īrkkuvaṉ ataṟku nalaṅko ḷumtuṇai yāteṉil kēṭṭi namacci vāyamkāṇ nāmpeṟum tuṇaiyē.
translation: May you prosper, my heart. You ask me to come with you to visit every sacred shrine, to worship the holy feet of the Lord residing there, and to walk around them in reverence. The Lord who begs from house to house will Himself draw you and me. If you ask what good companion we have for this journey, listen. Namasivaya is the companion we have obtained.
commentary: The desire to visit physical temples and walk around sacred shrines is natural, but God takes the initiative to draw the soul inward. Vallalar tells his heart that the Lord will pull them close. For this inner spiritual path, the only necessary guide and companion is the divine name Namasivaya.

translit: tōṭuṭai yārpulit tōluṭai yārkaṭal tūṅkumoru māṭuṭai yārmaḻu māṉuṭai yārpira maṉtalaiyām ōṭuṭai yāroṟṟi yūruṭai yārpukaḻ ōṅkiyaveṇ kāṭuṭai yārneṟṟik kaṇuṭai yārem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Our God wears a woman's earring and a tiger skin. He rides a matchless bull resting by the sea. He holds a battle-axe and a deer. He carries Brahma's skull as an alms bowl. He is the Lord of Otriyur and the highly praised Thiruvenkadu. He bears an eye on his forehead.
commentary: God appears in his traditional form as Siva, marked by a striking mix of wild and divine symbols. Vallalar grounds his devotion in these familiar images of the Lord worshipped at the local temple in Otriyur.

translit: vaṇṇappal māmalar māṟṟum paṭikku makiḻntematu tiṇṇappar cāttum ceruppaṭi mēṟkoṇṭu tīñcuvaittāy uṇṇap parintunal ūṉtara uṇṭukaṇ ottakkaṇṭē kaṇṇappa niṟka eṉakkaitoṭ ṭārem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Rejoicing to replace the many colorful great flowers, our God accepted the sandal marks placed on him by our Tinnappar. He affectionately ate the fine, sweet-tasting meat offered to him. Seeing him gauge and pluck out his matching eye, our God touched his hand and said, 'Stop, Kannappa!'
commentary: Deep devotion matters more to God than ritual purity. Vallalar recalls the famous story of Kannappa, a hunter who offered Siva chewed meat and placed his sandaled foot on the deity. When Siva tested him by making the statue's eye bleed, Kannappa gouged out his own eye to replace it, prompting God to appear directly to stop him.

translit: celiṭik kumkural kārmata vēḻac ciṉa-uriyār valaṭuk kumkoṅkai mātoru pākar vaṭappoṉveṟpām vileṭuk kumkaiyar cākkiyar aṉṟu virainteṟinta kallaṭik kumkati kāṭṭiṉar kāṇem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Our God wears the skin of a furious, dark elephant in musth whose roar strikes like thunder. He shares half his body with the goddess of firm breasts. His hands lift the northern golden mountain as a bow. See how our God showed the supreme path to Sakkiyar who swiftly hurled stones at him that day.
commentary: God accepts any act as worship if the heart is focused on him. Sakkiyar was a devotee who expressed his love by throwing stones at the deity every day because he had no other offering. The divine received those stones as perfect worship and granted him the highest spiritual state.

translit: ēḻiyal paṇpeṟ ṟamutō ṭaḷāvi ilaṅkutamiḻk kēḻiyal campantar antaṇar vēṇṭak kiḷarntanaṟcīr vīḻiyil tampatik kēviṭai kēṭkaveṟ pāḷuṭaṉē kāḻiyil taṉṉuruk kāṭṭiṉa rālem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Sambandar sang radiant Tamil infused with ambrosia and the seven musical notes. When he asked for leave to return to his own town from highly renowned Thiruveezhimizhalai, our God appeared with the Daughter of the Mountain and showed him his Sirkazhi form.
commentary: The divine meets devotees where their hearts feel most at home. When the child saint Sambandar wanted to return to his hometown of Sirkazhi, God instantly transformed the local shrine to look like his home temple. The bond between God and the devotee is so intimate that the divine alters physical reality to comfort them.

translit: nāṭṭil pukaḻpeṟṟa nāvuk karacarmuṉ nāḷpatikap pāṭṭiṟ kirakkamil līrem pirāṉeṉap pāṭa-aṉṟē āṭṭiṟ kicainta malarvāḻtti vētam amaittamaṟaik kāṭṭil katavam tiṟantaṉa rālem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: The world-renowned Navukkarasar sang a decad asking, 'My Lord, do you have no pity for my song?' That very day, our God opened the doors in Maraikkadu, where the Vedas had previously worshipped him with fitting flowers and shut the gates.
commentary: Devotion can move physical barriers that ancient traditions have locked shut. The doors of the temple at Maraikkadu had been sealed long ago by the Vedas (the oldest sacred scriptures of India). The saint Navukkarasar sang with longing, and God opened the doors for him, proving a single heart's cry is more powerful than scriptural authority.

translit: paiccūr aravap paṭanaṭat tāṉayaṉ paṟpalanāḷ eyccūr tavañcey yiṉumkiṭai yāppatam ēyntumaṇmēl vaiccūraṉ vaṉtoṇṭaṉ cuntaraṉ eṉṉunam vaḷḷalukkuk kaccūril cōṟiran tūṭṭiṉa rālem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Our God begged for food in Kacchur and fed our benefactor called Sundarar, the steadfast devotee on earth. Yet His state remains unattainable even if Brahma and Vishnu, who dances upon the hooded serpent, perform exhausting penance for many days.
commentary: God is beyond the reach of cosmic deities, yet close to His devotees. The creator god Brahma and the preserver god Vishnu cannot reach Him even through penance. Yet for the sake of Sundarar, a hungry saint on earth, God Himself went begging for food in the town of Kacchur.

translit: ēṇap pariceñ caṭaimuta lāṉa-el lāmmaṟaittuc cēṇap parikaḷ naṭattiṭu kiṉṟanal cēvakaṉpōl māṇap paripavam nīkkiya māṇikka vācakarkkāyk kāṇap parimicai vantaṉa rālem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Our God hid all His divine signs like the red matted hair and came visibly mounted on a horse. He appeared like a noble warrior guiding magnificent steeds to remove the great distress of Manikkavasagar.
commentary: To save a devotee in trouble, God is willing to hide His majesty. The saint Manikkavasagar faced punishment from his king over a failure to deliver horses. To rescue him, God concealed His divine signs and appeared as an ordinary cavalry commander.

translit: ellām ceyavalla cittariṉ mēvi eḻilmaturai vallāriṉ vallavar eṉṟaṟi yāmuṭi maṉṉaṉmuṉṉē pallā yira-aṇṭa mumpayam eytap parākkiramittuk kallāṉai tiṉṉak karumpaḷit tārem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: Our God took the form of the all-powerful Siddha in beautiful Madurai. Standing before the crowned king who did not realize He is the mightiest of the mighty, He performed wonders that struck awe across thousands of universes and fed sugarcane to a stone elephant.
commentary: A Siddha is a mystic possessing special powers. In this story from Madurai, an arrogant king doubted God's power. To humble the king, God appeared as a wandering Siddha and performed a miracle, bringing a stone elephant to life and feeding it sugarcane.

translit: māleṭut tōṅkiya mālayaṉ ātiya vāṉavarum ālaṭut tōṅkiya antaṇa ṉē-eṉ ṟaṭaintiraṇṭu pāleṭut tēttanam pārppati kāṇap pakarceymaṉṟil kāleṭut tāṭum karuttarkaṇ ṭīrem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: The exalted Vishnu, Brahma, and the other celestial beings approached Him and praised Him from both sides as the supreme sage seated beneath the banyan tree. Behold, our God is the Lord who lifts His foot and dances in the celebrated hall for our Parvati to witness.
commentary: God manifests in two contrasting forms. First, He sits in stillness under a banyan tree as the supreme sage, receiving the praise of all celestial gods. Second, He becomes the active cosmic dancer, lifting His foot in the hall of creation to perform the dance of existence for His consort Parvati.

translit: māṟpatam ceṉṟapiṉ intirar nāṉmukar vāmaṉarmāṉ mēṟpatam koṇṭa uruttirar viṇṇavar mēlmaṟṟuḷḷōr āṟpatam koṇṭapal āyiram kōṭi-aṇ ṭaṅkaḷellām kāṟpatam oṉṟil oṭukkiniṟ pārem kaṭavuḷarē.
translation: When the realm of Vishnu passes away, our God will absorb into a single foot Indra, the four-faced Brahma, Rudra who mounts the deer, the celestial beings, all those above them, and many thousands of millions of universes. He alone will stand supreme.
commentary: At the end of time, the cosmos will undergo dissolution. All celestial rulers, millions of universes, and the realms of the gods themselves will come to an end. God alone will remain standing, gathering all of creation back into a single point within Himself.

translit: kaṭavuḷ nīṟiṭāk kaṭaiyaraik kaṇkāḷ kaṉavi lēṉumnīr kāṇutal oḻika aṭavuḷ mācutīrt taruḷtiru nīṟṟai aṇiyum toṇṭarai aṉpuṭaṉ kāṇka taṭavum iṉṉicai vīṇaikēṭ ṭarakkaṉ taṉakku vāḷoṭu nāḷkoṭut tavaṉai naṭavum mālviṭai oṟṟiyūr uṭaiya nātaṉ taṉṉainām naṇṇutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O eyes, do not look upon those degraded people who refuse to wear the divine ash even in your dreams. Look with love upon the devotees who wear the sacred ash that graciously removes inner impurities. Do this so we may reach our Lord of Otriyur. He rides the great bull, and He granted a sword and a long life to the demon Ravana when he played sweet music on the lute.
commentary: The senses must be strictly trained to focus on God. The sacred ash is the traditional mark of purity and the burning away of worldly attachments. Vallalar recalls the story of King Ravana, who received a long life and a sword from God by playing music, showing how quickly divine grace responds to devotion.

translit: pōṟṟi nīṟiṭāp pulaiyaraik kaṇṭāl pōka pōkanīr pulamiḻan tavamē nīṟṟiṉ mēṉiyar taṅkaḷaik kaṇṭāl niṟka niṟka-an nimalaraik kāṇka cāṟṟiṉ naṉṉeṟi ītukāṇ kaṇkāḷ tamaṉi yapperum taṉu-eṭut teyilaik kāṟṟi niṉṟanam kaṇnutaṟ karumpaik kailai āḷaṉaik kāṇutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O eyes, if you see base people who do not revere and wear the ash, turn away immediately. It is futile to waste your sight on them. If you see those whose bodies are adorned with ash, stay right there and gaze upon those pure ones. This is the true path. Do this so we may see the ruler of Kailash, our sweet Lord with an eye on his forehead, who lifted the great golden mountain as a bow to destroy the three forts.
commentary: The sight of people living without spiritual discipline is treated as a waste of time. Vallalar remembers God as the mighty destroyer of the three flying forts of the demons, a cosmic feat performed using a golden mountain as a bow.

translit: teyva nīṟiṭāc ciṟiyaraik kaṇṭāl cīṟu pāmpukaṇ ṭeṉa-oḷit tēka caiva nīṟiṭum talaivaraik kaṇkāḷ cārntu niṉṟunīr taṉivirun tuṇka ceypa vaṉceya lumavai uṭaṉē ceyvip pāṉumāyt tillai-am palattuḷ uyva tētarak kūttukan tāṭum oruvaṉ nammuḷam uṟṟiṭaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O eyes, if you see petty people who do not wear the divine ash, flee and hide from them just as you would from a hissing snake. When you see the noble devotees who wear the Saiva ash, stand close to them and feast your sight on them. Do this so that the One Lord may reside in our hearts. He is the doer, the deed, and the instigator of the deed. He dances joyously in the hall of Thillai to grant us salvation.
commentary: The spiritual danger of worldly company is compared to a venomous snake. The purpose of this discipline is to hold God in the heart, recognizing him as the divine dancer of Thillai (the temple town of Chidambaram) who is the doer behind every action in the universe.

translit: tūya nīṟiṭāp pēyarkaḷ oṉṟu collu vāreṉil pulleṉa aṭaikka tāya nīṟiṭum nēyaroṉ ṟuraittāl taḻuvi yē-atai muḻuvatum kēṭka cēya naṉṉeṟi aṇittatu cevikāḷ cēra māṉiṭait tirumukam koṭuttu āya pāṇaṟkup poṉpeṟa aruḷum aiyar cēvaṭi aṭaikutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O ears, if demonic people who do not wear the pure ash say anything, shut yourselves tightly against their worthless words. If loving devotees who wear the sacred ash speak, embrace their words and listen to them fully. This will bring the distant good path near to you. Do this so we may reach the sacred feet of our Lord, who sent a divine letter to the Chera king to help the devoted bard receive gold.
commentary: Vallalar commands the ears to close against the empty talk of those lacking devotion. This path of listening only to the sacred is supported by a famous legend where God wrote a personal letter to a king to help a poor musician get gold, proving his active care for his followers.

translit: nalla nīṟiṭā nāykaḷiṉ tēkam nāṟṟam nērntiṭil naṇuyirp paṭakka valla nīṟiṭum vallavar eḻiṉmey vācam nēriṭil makiḻvuṭaṉ mukarka colla rumpari maḷantarum mūkkē collum vaṇṇamit tūyneṟi oṉṟām allal nīkkinal aruṭkaṭal āṭi aiyar cēvaṭi aṭaikutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O nose that perceives rare fragrances, if the scent of the bodies of wretched people who do not wear the good ash reaches you, hold your breath. If the fragrance of the beautiful bodies of the steadfast devotees who wear the potent ash reaches you, inhale it with joy. This is the one pure path you must follow. Do this so we may dispel all sorrow, bathe in the great ocean of grace, and reach the sacred feet of our Lord.
commentary: This discipline of the physical senses is presented as the single pure path to God. By guarding what enters through the eyes, ears, and nose, the mind remains free from sorrow and stays bathed in the ocean of grace.

translit: aruḷcey nīṟiṭār amutuṉak kiṭiṉum amma lattiṉai aruntutal oḻika teruḷkoḷ nīṟiṭum celvarkūḻ iṭiṉum cērntu vāḻtti-at tiru-amu tuṇka iruḷcey tuṉpanīt teṉṉuṭai nāvē iṉpa nalamu tiṉitirun tarunti maruḷcey yāṉaiyiṉ tōluṭut teṉṉuḷ vatiyum īcaṉpāl vāḻutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O my tongue, even if those who do not wear the grace-bestowing ash offer you ambrosia, refuse to consume that filth. If the blessed ones who wear the clear ash offer you mere gruel, approach them, praise them, and eat it as sacred ambrosia. Banish the sorrow that creates darkness. Sit happily and consume the good ambrosia of joy, so that we may live with the Lord who wears the hide of the wild elephant and resides within me.
commentary: Vallalar instructs his tongue to value the spiritual state of the giver over the quality of the food. The "grace-bestowing ash" is vibhuti, worn by worshippers of Siva. A humble bowl of gruel given by a devoted person is true nourishment, while a feast offered by someone without devotion is worthless.

translit: mutti nīṟiṭār muṉkaiyāl toṭiṉum muḷḷu ṟuttalpōl muṉivuṭaṉ naṭuṅka patti nīṟiṭum pattarkaḷ kālāl pāyntu taikkiṉum parintatai makiḻka putti ītukāṇ eṉṉuṭai uṭampē pōṟṟa lārpuram poṭipaṭa nakaittōṉ catti vēṟkarat taṉayaṉai makiḻvōṉ taṉṉai nāmeṉṟum cārntiṭaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O my body, heed this instruction. If those who do not wear the liberating ash touch you even with their forearms, tremble with anger as if pierced by a thorn. If devotees who wear the devotional ash kick and strike you with their feet, accept it with affection and rejoice. Do this so that we may forever unite with the Lord who laughed and reduced the cities of His enemies to ashes and who rejoices in His son wielding the powerful spear.
commentary: Recoiling from the gentle touch of the worldly while joyfully accepting harsh treatment from devotees illustrates a state of surrender. Here, connection to God's devotees matters far more than physical comfort or personal pride.

translit: iṉiya nīṟiṭā īṉanāyp pulaiyark keḷḷil pātiyum īkutal oḻika iṉiya nīṟiṭum civaṉaṭi yavarkaḷ emmaik kēṭkiṉum eṭuttavark kīka iṉiya naṉṉeṟi ītukāṇ karaṅkāḷ īcaṉ nammuṭai iṟaiyavaṉ tutippōrk kiṉiya mālviṭai ēṟivan taruḷvōṉ iṭaṅkoṇ ṭemmuḷē icaikutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O my hands, understand this sweet and noble path. Do not give even half a sesame seed to the base, dog-like people who do not wear the sweet ash. If devotees of Siva who wear the sweet ash ask us for anything, gladly take it and offer it to them. Act in this way so that the Lord, our Master, who gracefully arrives on His great bull for those who praise Him, may take His seat and reside within us.
commentary: Vallalar sets a strict rule for giving based on devotion to Siva. This fierce loyalty—withholding from the worldly while giving freely to devotees—is the way to invite the Lord to reside within.

translit: nāṭa nīṟiṭā mūṭarkaḷ kiṭakkum naraka illiṭai naṭappatai oḻika ūṭal nīkkumveṇ nīṟiṭum avarkaḷ ulavum vīṭṭiṭai ōṭiyum naṭakka kūṭa naṉṉeṟi ītukāṇ kālkāḷ kumaraṉ tantai-em kuṭimuḻu tāḷvōṉ āṭa ampalat tamarntavaṉ avaṉtaṉ aruṭka ṭalpaṭin tāṭutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O my feet, know that this is the noble path you must join. Stop walking into the hellish homes of fools who do not wear the sacred ash. Run and walk instead in the homes of those who wear the white ash that dispels discord. Do this so that we may plunge and bathe in the ocean of grace of the Lord who is the father of Kumaran, who rules our entire lineage, and who resides in the hall of dance.
commentary: Comparing the homes of those without devotion to hell, Vallalar tells his feet to seek out the homes of those who wear the white ash. The company of devotees is the path to bathe in God's grace.

translit: nilaikoḷ nīṟiṭāp pulaiyarai maṟantum niṉaippa teṉpatai neñcamē oḻika kalaikoḷ nīṟiṭum karuttarai nāḷum karuti niṉṟuḷē kaṉintunek kuruka malaikoḷ villiṉāṉ mālviṭai uṭaiyāṉ malara yaṉtalai maṉṉiya karattāṉ alaikoḷ nañcamu tākkiya miṭaṟṟāṉ avaṉai nāmmakiḻn taṭaikutaṟ poruṭṭē.
translation: O my heart, cease thinking even in forgetfulness about the base people who do not wear the enduring ash. Meditate daily upon the wise ones who wear the radiant ash, and let yourself tenderly melt within. Act in this way so that we may joyfully reach the Lord who wields a mountain as a bow, who mounts the great bull, who holds the skull of lotus-born Brahma in His hand, and whose throat turned the swirling ocean poison into ambrosia.
commentary: Finally, Vallalar speaks to his own heart. He tells his inner self to completely forget those who do not wear the sacred ash, and to constantly meditate on the wise who do. By melting in love for the community of devotees, he says, the heart prepares itself to reach the Lord.

translit: oṟṟi ūraṉaip paṟṟi neñcamē niṟṟi nī-aruḷ peṟṟi cēravē.
translation: O heart, hold onto the Lord of Otriyur and stand firm so that you may attain the state of grace.
commentary: The mind must focus on the Lord of Otriyur (a temple town near Chennai) to reach a state of divine grace. Steadfastness is the foundation of spiritual attainment.

translit: cēra neñcamē tūram aṉṟukāṇ vāram vaittiyēl cārum muttiyē.
translation: O heart, it is not far away. If you hold true devotion, liberation will reach you.
commentary: Liberation is often thought to be a distant or impossible goal. Vallalar reassures his heart that it is close at hand. Devotion is the only requirement for freedom.

translit: mutti vēṇṭumēl patti vēṇṭumāl catti yamitu putti neñcamē.
translation: If you desire liberation, you need devotion. This is the truth. Understand this well, O heart.
commentary: Spiritual freedom requires love for the divine. Without devotion (patti), liberation (mutti) is impossible. The wandering mind must accept this truth.

translit: neñca mē-itu vañca mē-ala piñca kaṉpatam tañcam eṉpatē.
translation: O heart, this is no deception. The feet of the supreme Lord are the only refuge.
commentary: The mind can be skeptical of spiritual promises. Vallalar reassures his heart that relying on the divine is trustworthy. Surrendering to the feet of the Lord is the surest protection.

translit: eṉpa tēṟṟavaṉ aṉpa tēṟṟunī vaṉpu māṟṟuti iṉpam ūṟṟavē.
translation: The Lord wears a garland of bones. Embrace love for Him and cast away your hardness, so that bliss may spring forth within you.
commentary: In Hindu tradition, Siva wears a garland of bones to show that he remains after all things die. Loving this eternal divine presence melts the hardness of the human ego. Once the heart softens, joy begins to flow.

translit: ūṟṟam uṟṟuveṇ nīṟṟaṉ oṟṟiyūr pōṟṟa nīṅkumāl āṟṟa nōykaḷē.
translation: With firm devotion, praise Otriyur of the Lord adorned in white ash. Severe afflictions will depart.
commentary: Praising the divine presence at Otriyur cures suffering and illness. Vallalar worshipped here as a young man. The Lord wears white ash, a traditional symbol of purity and the eternal divine. Devotion in this place heals body and mind.

translit: nōykaḷ koṇṭiṭum pēykaḷ paṟpalar tūytaṉ oṟṟiyūrk kēytal illaiyē.
translation: The many demons that bring diseases do not approach pure Otriyur.
commentary: Otriyur is a pure sanctuary. Negative forces and the diseases they bring cannot cross into its sacred space. The town's divine purity keeps physical and spiritual harm away from those taking shelter there.

translit: illai illaikāṇ ollai oṟṟiyūr ellai cēravē allal eṉpatē.
translation: See, there is absolutely no such thing as suffering upon swiftly reaching the borders of Otriyur.
commentary: Merely stepping into the borders of Otriyur ends all suffering. The Tamil verse repeats the word for 'no' to stress that sorrow ceases to exist in this holy place. Reaching this sacred destination guarantees peace.

translit: allal eṉpatēṉ tollai neñcamē mallal oṟṟiyūr ellai ceṉṟumē.
translation: O troubled heart, why speak of suffering even after reaching the borders of abundant Otriyur?
commentary: Once a person reaches the grace of Otriyur, they must let go of past worries. Vallalar asks his troubled mind why it still holds on to old fears when surrounded by divine abundance.

translit: ceṉṟu vāḻttuti naṉṟu neñcamē eṉṟum nalvaḷam oṉṟum oṟṟiyē.
translation: Go and praise Otriyur, O heart. This is good. Otriyur forever abounds in fine prosperity.
commentary: The mind finds well-being by praising the grace of Otriyur. This sacred town offers unending spiritual wealth. Directing the heart toward this divine presence guarantees lasting goodness and peace.

translit: ūti yam peṟā otayiṉēṉ matipōy uḻalum pāviyēṉ uṇmai-oṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ vāti yampuṟum vañcakar uṭaṉē vāyi ḻukkuṟa vaṉmaikaḷ pēci āti emperu māṉuṉai maṟantēṉ aṉpi lāta-eṉ vaṉpiṉai niṉaikkil tīti yampiya nañcamum kalaṅkum tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I am a useless fool who gains nothing. A wandering sinner who has lost his mind, I know not a single truth. Joining deceivers who endlessly argue, I spoke harsh words until my mouth hurt, and I forgot you, our Primal Lord. When I think of my loveless, hard heart, even deadly poison trembles. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur.
commentary: Vallalar regrets the time he wasted in harsh, useless debates. His heart has grown so cold and hard from these arguments that even deadly poison would fear it.

translit: kali kantavaṉ neñcakak koṭiyēṉ kayavar taṅkaḷuḷ kalantunāḷ tōṟum mali kantavāy vātamiṭ ṭulaṟi varuntu kiṉṟatuṉ mārkkattai niṉaikkil ili kanta-eṉ mīteṉak kētāṉ ikalum kōpamum irukkiṉṟa tāṉāl tillai yāyuṉtaṉ uḷattukkeṉ ṉāmō tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I am a cruel man with a heart harder than stone. Every day I mix with vile men, babble in stubborn arguments, and suffer. When I think of your path and look at my destitute self, I feel intense disgust and anger toward my own being. If I feel this way, O Lord of Thillai, what must your heart feel? O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur.
commentary: Clear sight of our own flaws brings self-disgust. Vallalar feels such anger at his own stubbornness that he wonders how God can bear to look at him. He addresses the divine as the Lord of Thillai, the sacred temple town of Chidambaram.

translit: kaita vattartam kaḷippiṉil kaḷittē kālam pōkkiṉēṉ kaḷaikaṇmaṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ ceyta vattartam tiṟamciṟi tuṇarēṉ ceyva teṉṉainiṉ tiruvaruḷ peṟavē eyta vattiru aruḷeṉak kiraṅki īyil uṇṭumaṟ ṟiṉṟeṉil iṉṟē ceyta vattiru maṭantaiyar naṭaṉam tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I wasted my time rejoicing in the revelry of deceitful men. I know no other refuge. I do not understand even a little of the greatness of those who perform true penance. What can I do to attain your divine grace? If you take pity and bestow your grace upon me, I will have it. If not, I am left with nothing today. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur, where holy women dance.
commentary: Spiritual practices and true penance are foreign to him. He admits he has no merits of his own to offer and relies on God taking pity on his empty hands.

translit: aḻuta piḷḷaikkē pāluṇa vaḷippāḷ aṉṉai eṉparkaḷ aḻavali illāk koḻutu nērciṟu kuḻavikkum koṭuppāḷ kuṟṟam aṉṟatu maṟṟavaḷ ceyalē toḻutu niṉṉaṭi tutikkiṉṟōrk keṉavē tuṭṭa ṉēṉukkum cūḻntaruḷ ceyalām ceḻutu mātavi malarticai maṇakkat tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: They say a mother feeds milk only to the child who cries. Yet she also feeds the tender infant who lacks the strength to cry. That is not a fault, for it is simply her nature. Just as you grant grace to those who worship and praise your feet, you can surely surround me, a wicked man, with your grace. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur, where lush madhavi flowers spread their fragrance in every direction.
commentary: People say a mother only feeds the child who cries for milk. Yet a caring mother also feeds the infant too weak to make a sound. Vallalar asks God to show this same maternal grace, feeding him spiritually even though he lacks the strength or merit to ask.

translit: uḷḷi yō-eṉa alaṟiniṉ ṟētti uruki nekkilā uḷattaṉyāṉ eṉiṉum vaḷḷi yōyuṉai maṟakkavum māṭṭēṉ maṟṟait tēvarai matikkavum māṭṭēṉ veḷḷi yōveṉap poṉmakiḻ ciṟakka viraintu mummatil vilvaḷait terittōy teḷḷi yōrpukaḻn tarakara eṉṉat tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: Though my heart does not melt and cry out in praise, searching for you within, I will never forget you, O generous Lord. I will never revere other gods. With a radiant golden smile, you swiftly bent the bow and burned the three walled cities. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur, whom the wise praise, chanting Hara Hara.
commentary: Though his heart feels dry and unable to melt in devotion, Vallalar promises absolute loyalty. Vallalar recalls the story of Siva destroying three flying demonic cities just by smiling, proving divine power is swift and effortless. Relying on this generous Lord, Vallalar vows never to seek other gods.

translit: viruppi lēṉtiru mālayaṉ patavi vēṇṭik koḷkeṉa viḷampiṉum koḷḷēṉ maruppiṉ mā-uri yāyuṉtaṉ aṭiyār matikkum vāḻvaiyē maṉaṅkoṭu niṉṟēṉ oruppa ṭāta-iv veṉṉaḷa viṉi-uṉ uḷḷam eppaṭi appaṭi aṟiyēṉ tiruppu yācala maṉṉarmā tavattōr tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I have no desire for the status of Tirumal or Ayan. Even if they offer it and tell me to take it, I will not accept. Oh Lord wearing the skin of the great tusked elephant! I stand with my mind set only on the life esteemed by Your devotees. Given my unsteady nature, I do not know what Your heart thinks of me now. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur with great ascetics and kings who have shoulders like sacred mountains!
commentary: The highest cosmic ranks mean nothing to a devotee. Vallalar would refuse the power of the creator god Ayan (Brahma) and the preserving god Tirumal (Vishnu), even if offered directly. He wants only the simple life of those who love God. Knowing his unsteady nature, he worries if God will accept him.

translit: nilaiyi lā-ula kiyalpaṭum maṉattai niṟutti lēṉoru niyamamum aṟiyēṉ vilaiyi lāmaṇi yē-uṉai vāḻtti vīṭṭu naṉṉeṟik kūṭṭeṉa viḷampēṉ alaiyil ārnteḻum turumpeṉa alaintēṉ aṟpa ṉēṉtiru aruḷaṭai vēṉē cilaiyil āraḻal kaṇaitoṭut tavaṉē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I have not steadied my mind, which suffers in transient worldly ways. I know no discipline. Oh priceless gem! I do not praise You and ask You to unite me with the good path of liberation. I wandered like a piece of straw tossing on swelling waves. Will I, a base one, ever attain Your holy grace? Oh Lord who shot the fiery arrow from the mountain bow! O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur!
