commentary: A mind caught in worldly life is like a piece of straw thrown about by ocean waves. Vallalar confesses he lacks all spiritual discipline and has not even asked God for the way to liberation. Tossed by transient distractions, he wonders how he can hope to receive divine grace.

translit: kāyam eṉpatā kāyameṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ kalaṅki ṉēṉoru kaḷaikaṇum illēṉ cēya naṉṉeṟi aṇitteṉak kāṭṭum teyva niṉaruḷ tiṟamciṟi taṭaiyēṉ tūya niṉaṭi yavaruṭaṉ kūṭit toḻumpu ceyvatē cukameṉat tuṇiyēṉ tīya ṉēṉtaṉai āḷvatev vāṟō tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: I do not realize that the body is an illusion of empty space. I am confused. I have no refuge. I have not attained even a little of Your divine grace, which shows the distant good path as very near. I do not resolve that joining Your pure devotees and serving them is true happiness. How will You rule over me, a wicked one? O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur!
commentary: The physical body is temporary and will pass into empty space, but Vallalar laments that he is trapped in its illusion. Without divine grace, the spiritual path feels distant. He grieves that he is confused, lacks a safe refuge, and has not yet found happiness in the simple act of serving other devotees.

translit: puṉṉu ṉippaṭum tuḷiyiṉum ciṟiya pōkam vēṭṭuniṉ poṉaṭi maṟantēṉ eṉṉi ṉippaṭum vaṇṇamaḵ taṟiyēṉ eṉcey kēṉeṉai eṉceyap pukukēṉ miṉṉi ṉilpoli vēṇiyam perumāṉ vēṟa lēṉeṉai virumpaluṉ kaṭaṉē teṉṉa ṉippaṭum cōlaicūḻn tōṅkit tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: Desiring worldly pleasure smaller than a dewdrop on the tip of a blade of grass, I forgot Your golden feet. I do not know what will happen to me now. What will I do? What state will I enter? Oh Lord with matted hair shining like lightning! I am not apart from You. It is Your duty to accept me. O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur, where lofty groves sway in the southern breeze!
commentary: Worldly pleasures are smaller than a single dewdrop on a blade of grass, yet they easily distract the mind from God. After admitting he chased these tiny pleasures and lost his way, Vallalar makes a bold claim on divine grace. He tells God, "I am not apart from You," insisting it is God's duty to take him back.

translit: aṭiya ṉēṉalaṉ eṉṉiṉum aṭiyēṉ āka niṉṟaṉaṉ ammai-im maiyiṉum kaṭiya ṉēṉpiḻai yāvaiyum poṟukkak kaṭaṉu ṉakkalāl kaṇṭilaṉ aiyā poṭikoḷ mēṉi-em puṇṇiya mutalē puṉṉai yañcaṭaip puṅkavar ēṟē ceṭiyar tēṭuṟāt tivviya oḷiyē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākamā maṇiyē.
translation: Even if I say I am not Your devotee, I stand as Your devotee in the next life and this life. It is Your duty alone to forgive all the faults of this cruel one. I see no one else to do this, Oh Lord. Oh our righteous source whose body is smeared with ash! Oh supreme among the gods with beautiful matted hair! Oh divine light unsought by the wicked! O great gem Thyagar of shining Otriyur!
commentary: The bond between the soul and God is permanent across lifetimes. Vallalar declares that even if he denies being a devotee, he still belongs to the divine in this life and the next. Because this tie cannot be broken, God is the only one who can, and must, forgive his flaws.

translit: vāṉai nōkkimaṇ vaḻinaṭap pavaṉpōl vayaṅkum niṉaruḷ vaḻiyiṭai naṭappāṉ ūṉai nōkkiṉēṉ āyiṉum aṭiyēṉ uyyum vaṇṇamnī uvantaruḷ purivāy māṉai nōkkiya nōkkuṭai malaiyāḷ makiḻa maṉṟiṭai mānaṭam purivōy tēṉai nōkkiya koṉṟaiyañ caṭaiyōy tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man walking the earthly path while gazing up at the sky, I sought to walk the path of your radiant grace but looked only toward worldly flesh. Even so, you must joyfully bestow your grace so that I, your servant, may be saved. You perform the great dance in the hall so the mountain goddess with glances like a deer rejoices. O Lord with matted hair adorned with honey-laden konrai flowers! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur!
commentary: Seeking grace while distracted by worldly desires is like tripping on the ground while staring at the sky. Human attention is easily captured by the physical body. Therefore, Vallalar asks God to grant grace out of pure generosity rather than waiting for perfect focus.

translit: vāyi lāṉperu vaḻakkuraip patupōl vaḷḷal uṉṉaṭi malarkaḷuk kaṉpām tuyi lātuniṉ aruḷpeṟa viḻaintēṉ tuṭṭa ṉēṉaruḷ cukampeṟa niṉaivāy kōyi lākanal aṉpartam uḷattaik koṇṭa marntiṭum kuṇapperuṅ kuṉṟē tēyi lātapal vaḷañceṟin tōṅkit tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a mute man attempting to argue a great lawsuit, I desired to obtain your grace without possessing love for your lotus feet, O benevolent Lord. You must resolve to bestow the bliss of your grace on me, a wicked person. O great mountain of virtue who takes the hearts of good devotees as your temple and resides there! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, rising and shining with abundant and undiminishing wealth!
commentary: Wishing for spiritual bliss without cultivating love for the divine is like a mute person trying to win a complex court case. God naturally makes a home in the hearts of those who love him, yet Vallalar pleads for grace even for those who struggle to find that love.

translit: vittai iṉṟiyē viḷaittiṭu pavaṉpōl meyya niṉiru meṉmalarp patattil patti iṉṟiyē muttiyai viḻaintēṉ pāvi yēṉaruḷ paṇpuṟa niṉaivāy mittai iṉṟiyē viḷaṅkiya aṭiyār viḻainta yāvaiyum taḻaintiṭa aruḷvōy citti vēṇṭiya muṉivarar paravit tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man trying to harvest a crop without planting seeds, I desired liberation without having devotion for your two soft lotus feet. O Lord of Truth, please resolve to bestow the virtue of your grace upon me, a sinner. You graciously cause all the desires of your flawless devotees to flourish. O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, praised by sages seeking spiritual attainments!
commentary: A farmer cannot harvest a field he never planted. Expecting spiritual freedom without first planting the seeds of devotion is just as impossible. Acknowledging this fault, Vallalar appeals directly to divine compassion to make up for human spiritual poverty.

translit: kalami lātuvāṉ kaṭalkaṭap pavaṉpōl kaṭavuḷ niṉaṭik kamalaṅkaḷ vaḻuttum nalami lātuniṉ aruḷpeṟa viḻainta nāyi ṉēṉceyum navaipoṟut taruḷvāy malami lātanal vaḻiyiṭai naṭappōr maṉattuḷ mēviya māmaṇic cuṭarē cilami lāñcamā tiyatarup poḻilkaḷ tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man attempting to cross the vast ocean without a ship, I desired to obtain your grace without the virtue of praising your lotus feet, O God. Please forgive the faults committed by this lowly one and grant your grace. O great light of the jewel dwelling in the hearts of those who walk the good and flawless path! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, filled with groves of beautiful shade trees!
commentary: Trying to cross the sea of worldly life without the boat of worship is bound to fail. The divine light dwells naturally in those who walk a flawless path, but grace is still asked to forgive the mistakes of those who stumble while longing for the farther shore.

translit: pōrkkum veḷḷattil poṉputaip pavaṉpōl pulaiya neñciṭaip puṉitaniṉ aṭiyaic cērkkum vaṇṇamē niṉaikkiṉṟēṉ eṉiṉum ciṟiya ṉēṉukkuṉ tiruvaruḷ purivāy kūrkkum neṭṭilai vēṟpaṭaik karaṅkoḷ kumaraṉ tantaiyē koṭiyatī viṉaiyait tīrkkum teyvamē caivavai tikaṅkaḷ tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man trying to bury gold in a raging flood, I attempt to establish your pure feet in my base heart. Even so, please grant your divine grace to this lowly one. O father of Kumaran whose hand holds the sharp and long spear! O God who eradicates cruel karma! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, where Saiva and Vedic traditions flourish!
commentary: Attempting to hold onto God in an impure and restless heart is like trying to bury treasure in a raging flood. The chaos of the mind washes everything away. Yet the divine destroys the heavy burdens of past actions (karma) and can secure that treasure even in a troubled mind.

translit: ōṭa uṉṉiyē uṟaṅkukiṉ ṟavaṉpōl ōṅkum uttama uṉaruṭ kaṭalil āṭa uṉṉiyē maṅkaiyar mayalil aḻuntu kiṉṟa-eṟ karuḷceya niṉaivāy nāṭa uṉṉiyē mālayaṉ ēṅka nāyi ṉēṉuḷam naṇṇiya poruḷē tēṭa uṉṉiya mātava muṉivar tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man who intends to run but falls asleep, I intended to bathe in your supreme, rising ocean of grace, yet I sink in the delusion of women. Please resolve to grant me your grace. Vishnu and Brahma yearned as they sought you, yet you are the supreme reality who approached the heart of this dog. O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, where sages of great penance gather to seek you!
commentary: Good intentions are easily derailed by worldly distractions. Vallalar planned to bathe in divine grace but fell asleep in desire, much like a runner who falls asleep at the starting line. Yet he finds hope in a paradox: the supreme reality that great gods struggle to find has willingly come to his own humble heart.

translit: mutali lāmalū tiyampeṟa viḻaiyum mūṭaṉ eṉṉaniṉ moykaḻal patamēt tutali lātuniṉ aruḷpeṟa viḻaintēṉ tuṭṭa ṉēṉaruṭ cukampeṟu vēṉō nutalil āraḻal kaṇṇuṭai yavaṉē nōkkum aṉparkaḷ tēkkumiṉ amutē citali lāvaḷam ōṅki-en nāḷum tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a fool who desires profit without capital, I desired to attain your grace without praising your strong, ankleted feet. Will I, a wicked man, ever attain the bliss of your grace? O Lord with a fiercely burning eye on your forehead! O sweet nectar welling up in the devotees who gaze at you! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, shining forever with rising, imperishable fertility!
commentary: Spiritual progress requires active devotion. Vallalar admits the foolishness of wanting the bliss of grace without first making the effort to worship, comparing it to a merchant who expects a profit without investing any capital.

translit: kallai untivāṉ natikaṭap pavarpōl kāmam untiya nāmaneñ cakattāl ellai untiya pavakkaṭal kaṭappāṉ eṇṇu kiṉṟaṉaṉ eṉakkaruḷ vāyō allai untiya oṇcuṭark kuṉṟē akila kōṭikaṭ karuḷceyum oṉṟē tillai niṉṟoḷir maṉṟiṭai amutē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a person who tries to use a stone as a float to cross a great river, I think of crossing the boundless ocean of birth with a treacherous heart pushed by lust. Will you grant me your grace? O brilliant mountain of light that drives away darkness! O One who grants grace to all the millions of worlds! O nectar in the shining hall of Thillai! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur!
commentary: Relying on worldly attachments to reach spiritual freedom guarantees failure. Trying to escape the endless cycle of birth and death using a heart heavy with desire is like trying to use a heavy stone as a life raft. Only the divine light can pull the drowning soul to safety.

translit: neyyi ṉālcuṭu neruppavip pavaṉpōl neṭiya tuṉpamām koṭiyavai niṟainta poyyi ṉālpavam pōkkiṭa niṉaittēṉ pulla ṉēṉukkuṉ nalaruḷ varumō kaiyi ṉāltoḻum aṉpartam uḷḷak kamalam mēviya vimalavit takaṉē ceyyi ṉālpolin tōṅkinal vaḷaṅkaḷ tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man who tries to extinguish a blazing fire by pouring ghee on it, I thought I could dispel worldly birth through falsehood filled with cruel, endless sorrow. Will your good grace ever come to me, a lowly person? O pure and wise one who dwells in the heart-lotus of devotees who worship you with their hands! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, rising and shining with the rich fertility of its fields!
commentary: Worldly illusions feed human suffering instead of curing it. Relying on falsehood to escape the sorrows of life is like pouring ghee (clarified butter) onto a blazing fire: the false remedy only makes the flames burn higher. True relief comes only from the pure divine presence dwelling in the hearts of devotees.

translit: nīrco rintoḷi viḷakkerip pavaṉpōl nittam niṉṉiṭai nēcamvait tiṭuvāṉ pārco rintiṭum pavaneṟi muyaṉṟēṉ pāvi yēṉtaṉaik kūviniṉ ṟāḷvāy kārco rinteṉak karuṇai-īn taṉpar kaḷitta neñciṭai oḷittirup pavaṉē tērco rintamā maṇittiru vītit tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrt tiyākanā yakaṉē.
translation: Like a man who pours water to keep a bright lamp burning, I pursued the worldly path of earthly existence in order to place my daily love upon you. Please call out and rule over me, a sinner. O Lord who grants grace like pouring rain and hides within the joyous hearts of devotees! O Lord Thyagar of radiant Otriyur, where the holy streets are scattered with great gems fallen from chariots!
commentary: You cannot sustain spiritual love using the habits of ordinary worldly life. This is as foolish as trying to keep a lamp burning by pouring water into it instead of oil. The soul must abandon these backward attempts and rely on God, whose grace pours down freely like rain.

translit: tuccilai virumpit tuyarkoḷum koṭiyēṉ tuṭṭaṉēṉ tūymai-oṉ ṟillā eccilai aṉaiyēṉ pāviyēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ paccilai iṭuvār pakkamē maruvum paramaṉē-em pacu patiyē accilai virumpum avaruḷat tamutē aiyaṉē oṟṟiyūr araicē.
translation: Desiring a wretched life and gathering sorrow, I am cruel. I am wicked and lack all purity. I am like discarded food. I am a sinner. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O Supreme One who stands by those who offer even a fresh green leaf! O Lord of souls! O nectar in the hearts of those who desire that sacred form! O Sire, King of Otriyur!
commentary: The feeling of impurity and unworthiness is a heavy burden for the soul. Vallalar feels like discarded food, yet the Divine does not require grand rituals or perfect purity. God stands by anyone who offers even a fresh green leaf with a sincere heart.

translit: tūṅkiṉēṉ cōmpaṟ kuṟaiviṭa māṉēṉ tōkaiyar mayakkiṭai aḻunti ēṅkiṉēṉ avamē iruntaṉaṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ vāṅkimē ruviṉai vaḷaittiṭum pavaḷa māmaṇik kuṉṟamē maruntē oṅkivāṉ aḷavum poḻilceṟi oṟṟi yūrvarum eṉṉuṭai uyirē.
translation: I slept. I became a dwelling place for laziness. Sinking into the delusion of women, I languished. I lived in vain. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O great hill of coral gems who bent Mount Meru into a bow! O Medicine! O my Life who comes to Otriyur, rich with groves soaring to the sky!
commentary: Spiritual laziness and physical desires pull the mind away from the truth. Vallalar finds his cure by calling God the medicine. The image of the Lord bending Mount Meru into a bow shows that divine grace is powerful enough to conquer any human weakness.

translit: karappavark kellām muṟpaṭum koṭiya kaṭaiyaṉēṉ viṭaiyamē uṭaiyēṉ irappavark kaṇuvum īntilēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ tirappaṭum karuṇaic celvamē civamē teyvamē teyvanā yakamē urappaṭum aṉpar uḷoḷi viḷakkē oṟṟiyūr vāḻumeṉ uvappē.
translation: I am the foremost among all hoarders, a cruel and base person. I possess only sensory desires. I have not given even an atom to those who beg. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O wealth of enduring grace! O Sivam! O God! O Lord of gods! O inner lamp of light for devotees of strong love! O my Joy residing in Otriyur!
commentary: Refusing to share with those in need is a severe spiritual failing. For Vallalar, turning away beggars is a failure of Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings). The cure for this cruelty is God, who shines as a guiding inner lamp in loving hearts.

translit: illai-eṉ pataṉuk kañciṭēṉ nāykkum iṇaiyilēṉ iḻiviṉēṉ tuyarkkōr ellaimaṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ otiyaṉēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ kallaivil ākkum karuṇaivā ritiyē kaṇṇutal uṭaiyaceṅ kaṉiyē tillaivāḻ aracē teyvamā maṇiyē tiruvoṟṟi yūrvarum tēvē.
translation: I do not fear refusing beggars. I am not even equal to a dog. I am despicable. I know no bounds to my sorrow. I am utterly useless. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O ocean of grace who turned a stone mountain into a bow! O sweet red fruit with an eye on your forehead! O King residing in Thillai! O great divine gem! O God who comes to Otriyur!
commentary: The hardest heart is one that turns away a beggar without a second thought. Vallalar views this total lack of compassion as making a person lower than a street dog. Against this deep human failure, he praises the Divine as a vast ocean of grace. The Lord who can bend a mountain of stone into a bow can surely soften the hardest and most useless human heart.

translit: maṇṇilē mayaṅkum maṉattiṉai mīṭṭuṉ malaraṭi vaḻuttiṭac ciṟitum eṇṇilēṉ koṭiya ēḻaiyēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ viṇṇilē viḷaṅkum oḷiyiṉuḷ oḷiyē viṭaiyilvan taruḷviḻi viruntē kaṇṇilē viḷaṅkum arumpeṟal maṇiyē kāṭciyē oṟṟiyaṅ karumpē.
translation: I have not thought even a little of withdrawing my mind from worldly delusion and praising your lotus feet. I am a cruel wretch. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O light within the light that shines in the sky! O feast for the eyes who comes on a bull to bestow grace! O precious gem shining in the eye! O Vision! O sweet sugarcane of Otriyur!
commentary: The human mind naturally clings to the material world, requiring conscious effort to withdraw from these delusions and turn toward the divine. Vallalar confesses his failure to make this effort. He seeks rescue from the Lord, the light hidden within all light, who arrives to offer grace as a feast for the eyes.

translit: muṭṭiyē maṭavār mulaittalai uḻakkum mūṭaṉēṉ muḻuppulai muṟiyēṉ eṭṭiyē aṉaiyēṉ pāviyēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ oṭṭiyē aṉpar uḷatteḻum kaḷippē oḷikkuḷām cōtiyē karumpiṉ kaṭṭiyē tēṉē caṭaiyuṭaik kaṉiyē kālamum kaṭantavar karuttē.
translation: I am a fool who wallows at the breasts of women. I am completely wretched and do not break free from my baseness. I am a sinner as bitter as the Etti tree. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O joy that rises in the hearts of devotees who cleave to you! O Jothi within the light! O block of raw sugar! O honey! O sweet fruit bearing matted hair! O truth realized by those who have transcended time!
commentary: Vallalar laments being trapped by lust and base desires, comparing his bitterness to the poisonous Etti tree. He contrasts this worldly state with the sweetness of the divine, calling God the light (Jothi) and the pure joy known to devotees. He asks how such an affliction can ever be cured.

translit: karuteṉa aṭiyār kāṭṭiyum tēṟāk kaṉmaṉak kuraṅkaṉēṉ utavā eruteṉa niṉṟēṉ pāviyēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ marutiṭai niṉṟa māṇikka maṇiyē vaṉpavam tīrttiṭum maruntē orutiṟam uṭaiyōr uḷḷattuḷ oḷiyē oṟṟiyūr mēvumeṉ uṟavē.
translation: Even when your devotees point the way and tell me to meditate, my stony heart does not understand. I am a monkey. I stand like a useless ox. I am a sinner. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O ruby gem standing amidst the Marutha trees! O medicine that cures cruel karma! O light within the hearts of those with singular focus! O my kin dwelling in Otriyur!
commentary: Spiritual guidance falls on deaf ears when the human heart is hardened. Vallalar compares his restless mind to a monkey and his stubbornness to a useless ox. He looks to God as the only medicine capable of curing the consequences of past actions (karma), an inner light available to those with steady focus.

translit: vaitilēṉ vaṇaṅkā tikaḻpavar tammai vañcaṉēṉ niṉṉaṭi yavarpāl eytilēṉ pēyēṉ ēḻaiyēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ koytumā malariṭ ṭaruccaṉai purivōr kōlaneñ coḷir kuṇak kuṉṟē uytiṟam uṭaiyōr paravunal oṟṟi yūrakat tamarntaruḷ oṉṟē.
translation: I did not rebuke those who refuse to bow and mock you instead. I am deceitful. I did not seek the company of your devotees. I am a demon and a poor wretch. I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O mountain of virtues shining in the beautiful hearts of those who pluck great flowers and perform worship! O Supreme One gracefully seated in good Otriyur, praised by those who possess the means to salvation!
commentary: It is a spiritual regret to remain silent when the sacred is mocked and to avoid the company of devotees. Feeling deceitful for these failures, Vallalar recognizes that God stands as a mountain of virtue inside the hearts of those who offer worship.

translit: tevvaṇa maṭavār cīkkuḻi viḻuntēṉ tīyaṉēṉ pēyaṉēṉ ciṟiyēṉ evvaṇam uyvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ evvaṇap poruppē eṉṉiru kaṇṇē iṭaiyiṭarp paciyacem poṉṉē cevvaṇa maṇiyē tikaḻkuṇak kaṭalē tiruvoṟṟi yūrcceḻun tēṉē.
translation: I fell into the foul pit of deceitful women. I am evil, a demon, a lowly wretch. How will I be saved? What will I do? I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O mountain of all colors! O my two eyes! O pure red gold that removes troubles! O red gem! O radiant ocean of virtues! O rich honey of Otriyur!
commentary: Sensual entanglement pulls the mind downward into a foul pit, leaving the seeker feeling lost and unworthy. In this despair, Vallalar turns to the divine as his very eyes and only source of rescue, trusting that this pure gold and radiant ocean of virtues can wash away human troubles.

translit: vātamē purivēṉ koṭumpuli aṉaiyēṉ vañcaka maṉattiṉēṉ pollā ētamē uṭaiyēṉ eṉceyvēṉ eṉṉai eṉceytāl tīrumō aṟiyēṉ pōtamē aintām pūtamē oḻiyāp puṉitamē putumaṇap pūvē pātamē caraṇam caraṇameṉ taṉṉaip pātukāt taḷippatuṉ paramē.
translation: I only argue. I am like a cruel tiger. I have a deceitful mind and possess terrible flaws. What will I do? I do not know what must be done to me to cure this. O supreme awareness! O fifth element of space! O undiminishing purity! O freshly fragrant flower! Your feet are my refuge, my refuge. It is your supreme responsibility to protect and save me.
commentary: The habit of constant arguing reveals a cruel and deceitful mind. Recognizing these flaws in himself, Vallalar abandons all self-reliance and surrenders to the divine, declaring that it is now God's responsibility to protect and save him.

sections.title: Inquiring About the Nature of Grace

note: Editor's note: sung at Thirumullaivayil (tirumullaivāyil, திருமுல்லைவாயில்), a Siva temple west of Chennai.
translit: tēṉeṉa iṉikkum tiruvaruṭ kaṭalē teḷḷiya amutamē civamē vāṉeṉa niṟkum teyvamē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē ūṉeṉa niṉṟa uṇarvilēṉ eṉiṉum uṉtiruk kōyilvan taṭaintāl ēṉeṉak kēḷā tiruntaṉai aiyā ītuniṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: O ocean of divine grace sweet as honey! O clear nectar! O Sivam! O Deity standing as the sky! O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil! Even if I lack awareness and stand as mere flesh, when I come and reach your holy temple, you remain there without asking me "Why?", O Lord. Is this the nature of your divine grace?
commentary: Vallalar stands before the shrine, wondering at the divine silence. Admitting his spiritual dullness, he feels like mere flesh. He asks if it is the nature of grace to watch a seeker arrive and not even ask what brought them.

translit: pūṅkoṭi iṭaiyaip puṇarntacen tēṉē puttamu tēmaṟaip poruḷē vāṅkoṭi viṭaikoḷ aṇṇalē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē tīṅkoṭi yāta viṉaiyaṉēṉ eṉiṉum celvaniṉ kōyilvan taṭaintāl īṅkoṭi yāta aruṭkaṇāl nōkki ēṉeṉā tiruppatum iyalpō.
translation: O pure honey united with the goddess whose waist is like a flowering vine! O fresh nectar! O meaning of the scriptures! O Lord holding the banner of the bull! O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil! Even if I am a person of cruel and unyielding karma, when I come and reach your majestic temple, is it your nature to look upon me with steady eyes of grace and yet remain without asking me "Why?"
commentary: The silence feels heavy because the Lord is looking directly at him. Even if burdened by a history of harsh actions (karma), Vallalar asks how the divine can gaze with steady eyes of grace but refuse to speak a single word.

translit: tuppunēr itaḻi makiḻntakal yāṇa cuntarā cuntaraṉ tūtā maippoti miṭaṟṟāy vaḷartiru mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē appaṉē uṉṉai viṭuvaṉō aṭiyēṉ aṟivilēṉ eṉiṉuniṉ kōyiṟ keyppuṭaṉ vantāl vā-eṉa uraiyā tiruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: O beautiful Lord who rejoices in the kondrai flowers! O messenger for Sundarar! O Lord with a dark throat! O flawless gem dwelling in prosperous Thirumullaivayil! O Father, will I ever leave you? Even if I, your servant, lack wisdom, when I come to your temple in weariness, is it the nature of your divine grace to remain without saying "Come!"?
commentary: Traditional stories say this Lord once acted as a personal messenger for the saint Sundarar, showing an active closeness to his devotees. Remembering this intimacy, Vallalar asks why a weary servant arriving at the temple doors is not at least greeted with the word "Come."

translit: kaṅkai-añ caṭaikoṇ ṭōṅkuceṅ kaṉiyē kaṇkaḷmūṉ ṟōṅkuceṅ karumpē maṅkalil lāta vaṇmaiyē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē tuṅkaniṉ aṭiyait tutittiṭēṉ eṉiṉum toṇṭaṉēṉ kōyilvan taṭaintāl eṅkuvan tāynī yāreṉa vēṉum iyampiṭā tiruppatum iyalpō.
translation: O ripe red fruit standing exalted with the river Ganga in your beautiful matted hair! O tall red sugarcane with three eyes! O unfading bounty! O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil! Even if I do not praise your pure feet, when I, your servant, come and reach your temple, is it your nature to remain without asking even, "Where have you come from? Who are you?"
commentary: A host usually asks a stranger for their name and origins. Vallalar confesses he has failed to properly praise the divine feet. Even so, he wonders how the Lord of unfading bounty can let a servant arrive and not even ask who they are.

translit: naṉṟuvan taruḷum nampaṉē yārkkum nallava ṉētirut tillai maṉṟuvan tāṭum vaḷḷalē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē tuṉṟuniṉ aṭiyait tutittiṭēṉ eṉiṉum toṇṭaṉēṉ kōyilvan taṭaintāl eṉṟuvan tāyeṉ ṟorucolum collā tiruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: O trusted Lord who graciously grants goodness! O Lord who is good to everyone! O benevolent one who comes to dance in the holy hall of Thillai! O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil! Even if I do not praise your feet, when I, your servant, come and reach your temple, is it the nature of your divine grace to remain without saying a single word like, "When did you come?"
commentary: Vallalar calls upon the dancing Lord of Thillai (the sacred temple at Chidambaram), known for being good to everyone. He presses his question: is it the nature of grace to see a servant arrive and withhold even the most basic greeting, like asking when they got there?

translit: paṇṇiṉuḷ icaiyē pāliṉuḷ cuvaiyē pattarkaṭ karuḷceyum paramē maṇṇiṉuḷ ōṅki vaḷampeṟum mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē peṇṇiṉum pētai matiyiṉēṉ eṉiṉum perumaniṉ aruḷpeṟa lāmeṉ ṟeṇṇivan taṭaintāl kēḷviyil lāmal iruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: You are the melody within the tune, the sweetness within milk, the Supreme who grants grace to devotees, O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil that rises and flourishes on earth. Even though my mind is more foolish than a naive girl, if I come to you thinking I can obtain your great grace, is it the nature of your divine grace to remain silent without asking me anything?
commentary: God's presence is hidden but essential, like the sweetness inside milk or the melody within a tune. A seeker approaching God for grace expects to be welcomed. Vallalar asks if it is the nature of divine grace to stay silent and ignore someone who comes seeking help.

translit: muṉṉiya maṟaiyiṉ muṭiviṉuṭ poruḷē mukkaṇā mūvarkkum mutalvā maṉṉiya karuṇai vāriyē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē aṉṉiyaṉ allēṉ toṇṭaṉēṉ uṉtaṉ aruṭperum kōyilvan taṭaintāl eṉitu civaṉē pakaivaraip pōlpārt tiruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: You are the inner truth at the end of the esteemed Vedas, the three-eyed Lord, the source of the primal three, the enduring ocean of compassion, O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil. I am no stranger. I am your servant. If I come and reach your great temple of grace, what is this, Siva? Is it the nature of your divine grace to look at me as if I were an enemy?
commentary: God is the ultimate truth of the ancient scriptures (the Vedas) and an ocean of compassion. A devotee belongs to God. Vallalar asks how a supreme being defined by mercy could look at a devoted servant as if they were an enemy.

translit: nallavar peṟumnaṟ celvamē maṉṟuḷ ñāṉanā ṭakampuri nalamē vallavar matikkum teyvamē mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē pullavaṉ eṉiṉum aṭiyaṉēṉ aiyā poyyala ulakaṟin tatunī illaiyeṉ ṟālum viṭuvaṉō cummā iruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: You are the excellent wealth obtained by good people, the goodness that performs the dance of wisdom in the hall, the deity revered by the capable, O flawless gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil. Even if I am a lowly person, I am your servant, Lord. This is not a lie. The world knows it. Even if you say no, will I let you go? Is it the nature of your divine grace to remain completely silent?
commentary: A sincere seeker refuses to take no for an answer. Vallalar admits his flaws but promises never to let go, even if God tries to turn him away. He challenges this divine silence by insisting the whole world knows he is a true servant.

translit: potuviṉiṉ ṟaruḷum mutaltaṉip poruḷē puṇṇiyam viḷaikiṉṟa pulamē matuviṉiṉ ṟōṅkum poḻiltiru mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē putumaiyaṉ allēṉ toṉṟutoṭ ṭuṉatu pūṅkaḻaṟ kaṉpupūṇ ṭavaṉkāṇ etuniṉain taṭaintāy eṉṟukē ḷāmal iruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: You are the first unique reality that grants grace from the common hall, the field where merit flourishes, O flawless gem dwelling in sacred Thirumullaivayil surrounded by tall groves dripping with nectar. I am no newcomer. Look at me, I am one who has loved your flower-like feet since ancient times. Is it the nature of your divine grace to remain silent without asking, "What did you seek in coming here?"
commentary: True love for the divine is an ancient, enduring bond. Vallalar reminds God that his devotion is not a passing phase. He questions how the supreme giver of grace could refuse to even ask a lifelong devotee what brings them to the temple.

translit: poṉṉaiyuṟ ṟavaṉum ayaṉumniṉ ṟaṟiyāp puṇṇiyā kaṇṇutal karumpē maṉṉaṉē maruntē vaḷartiru mullai vāyilvāḻ mācilā maṇiyē uṉṉaināṉ kaṉaviṉ iṭattumviṭ ṭoḻiyēṉ uṉtiru aṭittuṇai aṟiya eṉṉai-īṉ ṟavaṉē mukamaṟi yārpōl iruppatuṉ tiruvaruṭ kiyalpō.
translation: You are the holy one who remained unknowable to Vishnu and Brahma, the sweet sugarcane with an eye on the forehead, the king, the medicine, O flawless gem dwelling in flourishing sacred Thirumullaivayil. I will never let go of you even in my dreams. Your twin sacred feet are my witness. You who gave birth to me, is it the nature of your divine grace to act like a stranger who does not recognize my face?
commentary: God is the supreme parent of the soul, standing far above deities like Vishnu (the preserver) and Brahma (the creator) who could not comprehend him. Vallalar promises to hold onto this divine parent even in his dreams, asking how a parent could look at their child and pretend not to recognize their face.

translit: tāyiṉ mēviya taṟpara mēmullai vāyiṉ mēviya māmaṇi yē-uṉtaṉ kōyiṉ mēviniṉ kōmalart tāḷtoḻā tēyiṉ mēvi iruntaṉaṉ eṉṉaiyē.
translation: Supreme Lord, more loving than a mother. Great gem dwelling in Thirumullaivayil. I stayed away and faded in ignorance, without coming to your temple to worship your beautiful lotus feet.
commentary: God's love is greater than a mother's love, and failing to seek it is a life wasted in ignorance. Vallalar regrets staying away from this grace for so long.

translit: tillai vāynta ceḻuṅkaṉi yē tiru mullai vāyil mutalciva mūrttiyē tollai yēṉuṉtaṉ tūytiruk kōyiliṉ ellai cēra-iṉ ṟettavam ceytatē.
translation: Rich fruit found in Thillai. Primal form of Siva in sacred Thirumullaivayil. What penance did I, a person burdened by ancient karma, perform to reach the boundary of your pure and sacred temple today?
commentary: Reaching a sacred place is a rare gift that feels unearned. Weighed down by ancient karma (the accumulated effects of past actions), Vallalar wonders what good deeds brought him here. He links the local deity at Thirumullaivayil to the famous dancing Siva of Thillai (Chidambaram), seeing them as the same divine fruit.

translit: vaḷaṅko ḷummullai vāyilil mēviya kuḷaṅko ḷumkaṇ kurumaṇi yē-uṉai uḷamko ḷumpaṭi uṉtiruk kōyilik kaḷaṅkoḷ neñciṉaṉ kaṇṭatum kaṇṭatē.
translation: Precious pupil of the eye, dwelling in fertile Thirumullaivayil. This person with a blemished heart has indeed seen your sacred temple, so as to hold you firmly within the heart.
commentary: Seeing the physical temple installs the divine into the heart. Calling God the pupil of the eye shows how intimate this presence is to his vision. Despite feeling blemished, standing before the sanctuary allows Vallalar to internalize that pure light.

translit: malaivi lāmullai vāyilil mēviya vilaiyi lāmaṇi yēviḷak kēcaṟṟum kulaivi lātavar kūṭumniṉ kōyilil talaini lāvatta vameṉkol ceytatē.
translation: Priceless gem and shining lamp dwelling in doubtless Thirumullaivayil. What penance did I perform to stand steadfast in your temple, where devotees entirely free of agitation gather?
commentary: The divine sanctuary gathers those who have found inner peace. Vallalar marvels at his fortune to stand among devotees free of mental agitation. The divine presence acts as a gem and shining lamp that makes this stillness possible.

translit: cīrci ṟakkum tirumullai vāyilil ērci ṟakkum iyaṉmaṇi yēkoṉṟait tārci ṟakkum caṭaikkaṉi yē-uṉtaṉ ūrci ṟakka uṟuvatev vaṇṇamē.
translation: Beautiful, natural gem dwelling in exceptionally glorious, sacred Thirumullaivayil. Sweet fruit whose matted hair is adorned with a splendid garland of kondrai flowers. How will I ever attain the glory of reaching your city?
commentary: Visiting the earthly temple sparks a longing to reach the spiritual realm. Vallalar praises the divine form adorned with golden kondrai flowers. Overwhelmed by this beauty, he asks how he will ever be ready to enter the eternal city of divine grace.

translit: cēlkoḷ poykait tirumullai vāyilil pālkoḷ vaṇṇap parañcuṭa rēviṭai mēlkoḷ caṅkara ṉēvima lā-uṉtaṉ kālkoḷ aṉpar kalaṅkutal naṉṟatō.
translation: O Supreme Flame of milk-white hue in Thirumullaivayil of carp-filled ponds! O Sankara mounted on the bull! O pure one! Is it right that devotees who cling to Your feet suffer in distress?
commentary: True devotees often face distress, raising a direct, painful question. How can a compassionate God allow those who cling to Him to suffer? The stark contrast between God's purity, seen as a milk-white flame, and the devotee's pain makes this silence confusing.

translit: vaṇṇa māmullai vāyiliṉ mēviya aṇṇa lē-amu tē-arai cēnutal kaṇṇa ṉē-uṉaik kāṇavan tōrkkelām naṇṇa runtuyar nalkutal naṉṟatō.
translation: O Lord abiding in beautiful, great Thirumullaivayil! O divine nectar! O king! O Lord with the eye on Your forehead! Is it right to inflict insurmountable sorrow on all who have come to behold You?
commentary: It seems wrong for pure devotion to be rewarded with sorrow. Is it fitting for God to inflict grief on those who travel to see Him? Vallalar speaks to the divine like a close friend, demanding that love be met with mercy rather than hardship.

translit: maṇṇiṉ ōṅki vaḷarmullai vāyilvāḻ kaṇṇuṉ māmaṇi yēkarum pē-uṉai eṇṇum aṉpar iḻivaṭain tālatu paṇṇum niṉaruḷ pāriṭai vāḻkavē.
translation: O great gem of the eye dwelling in Thirumullaivayil that rises high upon the earth! O sweet sugarcane! If devotees who constantly fix their thoughts on You meet with disgrace, may Your grace that causes this flourish on earth!
commentary: Vallalar uses bold irony to demand God's attention. If true devotees face public disgrace, the divine grace responsible for this must be something to behold. This loving sarcasm reveals a relationship secure enough to shame the Lord into acting compassionately.

translit: tīti lātati rumullai vāyilvāḻ kōti lātaku ṇapperum kuṉṟamē vāti lātuṉai vāḻttavan tōrtamai ēti lāreṉṟi ruppatum eṉkolō.
translation: O great mountain of faultless virtues dwelling in flawless Thirumullaivayil! Why do You treat those who come to praise You with unquestioning devotion as if they are strangers?
commentary: A perfect being should not treat loving devotees like strangers. Praising God as a mountain of flawless virtues makes His distant behavior toward loyal followers puzzling. Vallalar asks the divine to recognize this devotion and respond with warmth.

translit: tēcu lāviya cīrmullai vāyilvāḻ māci lāmaṇi yēmarun tēcaṟṟum kūci ṭāmalniṉ kōyilvan tuṉpukaḻ pēci ṭāta piḻaipoṟut tāḷvaiyē.
translation: O flawless gem dwelling in glorious, radiant Thirumullaivayil! O divine medicine! Forgive my fault of failing to come boldly to Your temple to sing Your praises, and take me under Your rule.
commentary: Human hesitation and frailty require divine forgiveness. Vallalar admits his fault in failing to step forward boldly to sing praises. Calling God a divine medicine, he seeks the cure: to be pardoned and taken under divine protection.

note: Editor's note: sung at Thiruvalithayam (tiruvalitāyam, திருவலிதாயம்), the Siva temple at Padi in Chennai.
translit: tiraipa ṭātace ḻuṅkaṭa lēcaṟṟum uraipa ṭāmalo ḷiceypoṉ ṉēpukaḻ varaipa ṭātuva ḷarvalli kēcanī taraipa ṭākkantai cāttiya teṉkolō.
translation: O rich ocean without waves! O shining gold beyond the reach of words! O Vallikesa whose fame grows without limits! Why have you worn this short rag that does not even reach the ground?
commentary: Addressing God as an ocean without waves, Vallalar pictures the divine as perfect, undisturbed stillness. Yet this being of endless majesty chooses to wear a short, ragged cloth.

translit: cintai niṉṟaci vānantac celvamē entai yē-emai āṭkoṇṭa teyvamē tantai yēvali tāyatta laivanī kantai cuṟṟumka ṇakkatu eṉkolō.
translation: O wealth of supreme bliss residing in the mind! O my father! O deity who claimed us! O father, Lord of Validayam! What is the reason you wrap yourself in a rag?
commentary: God is experienced internally as supreme bliss, yet appears externally in the poorest of clothes. Vallalar approaches the divine with the familiar affection of a child.

translit: vēlai koṇṭa viṭamuṇṭa kaṇṭaṉē mālai koṇṭa vaḷarvalli kēcaṉē pālai koṇṭa parāpara nīpaḻañ cēlai koṇṭa tiṟamitu eṉkolō.
translation: O Lord with the throat that consumed the ocean's poison! O Vallikesa who wears a garland! O Supreme Lord sharing half your form! What is the reason for you wearing this old cloth?
commentary: Traditional stories say God drank the ocean's poison to save the world, showing his power and mercy. Vallalar contrasts this mighty protector with his worn-out garments.

translit: paṉṉu vārkkaru ḷumpara mēṭṭiyē maṉṉum māmaṇi yēvalli kēcaṉē uṉṉa nī-iṅku ṭuttiya kantaiyait tuṉṉu vārillai yōparañ cōtiyē.
translation: O Supreme Lord who bestows grace on those who praise you! O eternal great gem! O Vallikesa! O Supreme Jothi! Is there no one here to stitch the rag you wear?
commentary: The questions become tender and practical. Seeing the supreme light of grace (Jothi) dressed in torn fabric, Vallalar wonders where the devotees are to stitch the Lord's clothes.

translit: kaṭutta tumpiya kaṇṭa-a kaṇṭaṉē maṭutta naṟpukaḻ vāḻvalli kēcanī toṭutta kantaiyai nīkkittu ṇintoṉṟai uṭuttu vārilai yō-ivvu lakilē.
translation: O infinite Lord with a throat filled with dark poison! O Vallikesa of abundant true fame! Is there no one in this world to remove your patched rag and dress you in a proper cloth?
commentary: Vallalar feels a personal concern for the deity's appearance. He wonders if no one in the world can offer the infinite Lord a proper set of clothes.

translit: āla ṭutta-a rumporu ḷētiru māla ṭuttuma kiḻvalli kēcanī pālu ṭuttapa ḻaṅkantai yaiviṭat tōlu ṭuppatu vēmikat tūymaiyē.
translation: O rare reality seated beneath the banyan tree, O Vallikesar who delights when Vishnu approaches you, rather than wearing these torn old rags, wearing animal skin is much purer.
commentary: The image of the Lord seated beneath a banyan tree is a classic depiction of the divine teacher. Vallalar contrasts this majesty with the chosen beggar clothes, playfully suggesting that even a raw animal skin—the traditional garment of a forest ascetic—would be cleaner than these torn rags.

translit: tuṉṉum māmarun tēcuṭa rē-aruḷ maṉṉum māṇikka mēvalli kēcarē tuṉṉu kantaiyaic cuṟṟiniṟ pīreṉil eṉṉa nīremak kīyumpa ricatē.
translation: O great medicine that draws near, O flame, O ruby filled with grace, O Vallikesar, if you stand wrapped in stitched old rags, what reward will you give us?
commentary: Vallalar uses a tone of loving banter common in Tamil devotional poetry. The playful logic is simple: if the master of the universe, a supreme treasure and healing medicine, dresses in patched scraps, what kind of reward can his followers expect?

translit: mācil cōtima ṇiviḷak kēmaṟai vāci mēviva rumvalli kēcanīr tūcil kantaiyaic cuṟṟi-ai yōpara tēci pōlirun tīreṉkol ceyvaṉē.
translation: O flawless luminous jeweled lamp, O Vallikesar who comes riding the horse of the Vedas, alas, wrapping yourself in dusty rags you look like a destitute wanderer. What shall I do?
commentary: The contrast between God's true glory and physical appearance causes Vallalar sorrow. The Vedas are ancient sacred scriptures. The Lord rides upon them as his royal horse, yet he wanders the earth looking like a beggar covered in dust.

translit: tērum naṟṟavar cintai-e ṉuntalam cārum naṟporu ḷāmvali tāyanīr pārum maṟṟippa ḻaṅkantai cāttiṉīr yārum aṟṟava rōcolum aiyarē.
translation: O good reality dwelling in the minds of analyzing ascetics, O Lord of Valithayam, look, you wear these old rags. Tell me, O Lord, are you someone who has no one?
commentary: The intimacy between Vallalar and the divine reaches a point of protective love. The Lord dwells in the minds of the greatest sages and rules the universe. Seeing him in old rags makes Vallalar ask tenderly if the Creator is alone, with no family to look after his needs.

translit: melli tāyavi raimalarp pātaṉē valli tāyama ruviya nātaṉē pulli tāya-ik kantaiyaip pōrttiṉāl kalli tāyaneñ camkarai kiṉṟatē.
translation: O Lord with soft and fragrant flower-like feet, O Lord who dwells in Valithayam, if you cover yourself with these lowly rags, my stony heart melts.
commentary: The Lord takes on this impoverished form to stir the human soul. Seeing the divine being with soft, flower-like feet wrapped in harsh rags breaks through Vallalar's defenses. It melts a heart that was otherwise as hard as stone, transforming it through love.

translit: tirappa ṭumtiru mālayaṉ vāḻttat tiyākar eṉṉumōr tiruppeyar aṭaintīr varappa ṭuntiṟat tīrumai aṭaintāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr irappa varkkoṉṟum īkilīr āṉāl yātuk kaiyanīr ippeyar eṭuttīr urappa ṭumtavat tōrtutit tōṅka ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭaiyīrē.
translation: Praised by Tirumal and Ayan, you took the holy name Thyagar. O Lord capable of granting boons, when I approach you, you do not open your mouth to speak even a single word. If you give nothing to those who beg, why did you take this name? You possess Otriyur of supreme renown, praised highly by those of intense penance.
commentary: Vallalar playfully challenges God's famous title, Thyagar (the Great Giver). He asks why the creator, Ayan (Brahma), and the preserver, Tirumal (Vishnu), praise God's generosity when God refuses to speak a single word to a devotee asking for grace.

translit: veḷḷi māmalai vīṭeṉa uṭaiyīr viḷaṅkum poṉmalai vileṉak koṇṭīr vaḷḷi yīreṉa nummaivan taṭaintāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr eḷḷil eṇṇeypōl eṅkaṇum niṉṟīr ēḻai yēṉkuṟai ēṉaṟi yīrō oḷḷi yīrumai aṉṟi-oṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: You have the great silver mountain as your home and the shining golden mountain as your bow. When I approach you calling you a generous giver, you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. You stand everywhere like oil in a sesame seed. Why do you not know the grievance of this poor devotee? O brilliant Lord, I know nothing but you. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Having a silver mountain for a home and a golden mountain for a bow shows God lacks no wealth. Though present everywhere, hidden but pervasive like oil in a sesame seed, God still refuses to acknowledge a poor devotee's plea.

translit: kaḷḷa maṟṟavāk karacumput tirarum kaḷikka vēpaṭik kācaḷit taruḷum vaḷḷal eṉṟumai vantaṭain tēṟṟāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr eḷḷa rumpukaḻt tiyākareṉ ṟorupēr ēṉkoṇ ṭīrirap pōrkkiṭa aṉṟō uḷḷam iṅkaṟi vīreṉai āḷvīr ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: To bring joy to the deceit-free King of Words and the Son, you graciously gave them coins. When I approach and beg you as a generous giver, you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. Why did you take the peerless name Thyagar if not to give to those who beg? You know my heart and you rule me. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: The King of Words is the saint Appar, and the Son is the saint Sambandar, two great devotees to whom God miraculously gave gold coins during a famine. Vallalar wonders why God was so generous to them in the past but will not grant him a single word today.

translit: aṇmai yākumcun tararkkaṉṟu kaccūr ālak kōyilil cōṟiran taḷitta vaṇmai kēṭṭiṅku vantaṭain tēṟṟāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr tiṇmai cērtiru mālviṭai ūrvīr tēva rīrukkuc ciṟumaiyum uṇṭō uṇmai yāṉumai aṉṟimaṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: Hearing of your generosity long ago when you begged for food at the temple in Kacchur and gave it to your close friend Sundarar, I approach you here and beg. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. You ride the strong bull of Tirumal. Do you suffer any scarcity? In truth, I know no one but you. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: God once walked through a town begging for food just to feed his exhausted friend, the saint Sundarar. Vallalar points to this legendary kindness and asks why that same generous Lord remains silent now.

translit: cintai nontula kilpiṟar tammaic cērnti ṭātunum tiruppeyar kēṭṭu vanta ṭainta-eṟ kuṇṭilai eṉavē vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr inta vaṇṇamnīr iruntiṭu vīrēl eṉco lārumai ivvula kattār unti vantava ṉōṭari ētta ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: My heart aching, I did not approach others in this world but heard your holy name and came to you. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word to tell me yes or no. If you remain like this, what will the people of this world say of you? Praised by Hari and the one who emerged from his navel, you possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Vallalar uses an intimate tactic of devotion, worrying aloud about God's reputation. He warns God that if He ignores someone who relies on Him and asks no one else for help, the world will question His kindness. Hari is Vishnu, and the one who emerged from his navel is Brahma.

translit: kallai yumpacum poṉeṉap purinta karuṇai kēṭṭumaik kātalit tiṅku vallai vantuniṉ ṟēṟṟiṭil ciṟitum vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr illai nīrpiccai eṭukkiṉṟī rēṉum irakkiṉ ṟōrkaḷum iṭṭuṇpar kaṇṭīr ollai iṅkeṉa tuḷaṅkoṇṭa taṟivīr ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: Hearing of the grace that turns even stone into pure gold, I longed for you, came swiftly, stood here and praised you. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. You may have nothing and wander begging for alms, but know that even beggars share what they are given before they eat. You know how swiftly you captured my heart here. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Vallalar gently scolds God for accepting his devotion without a single word in return. He notes that even destitute beggars share their alms. Since God has already captured his heart, it is only fair to receive a word of grace in exchange.

translit: tuḷikkum kaṇṇuṭaṉ cōrvuṟa neñcam tōṉṟa lē-umait tuṇai-eṉa nampi vaḷikkuḷ pañcaṉai yēṉaṭain tēṟṟāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr aḷikkum taṉmaiyīr vāḻntivaṇ irukka aṭiya ṉēṉalai kiṉṟatum aḻakō oḷikkum taṉmaitāṉ umakkumuṇ ṭēyō ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: With tears welling in my eyes and my heart growing weary, O noble Lord, I trusted you as my companion. Tossed like cotton in the wind, I reached you and praised you. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. You possess the nature of a benefactor and live here in prosperity. Is it fair that your servant wanders like this? Do you too possess the nature of hiding yourself? You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Vallalar highlights the painful gap between the Lord's vast spiritual wealth and his own vulnerability. Tossed about like cotton in the wind, he asks how a generous God can sit comfortably in prosperity while a devoted servant wanders in pain. He wonders if the divine is hiding from him.

translit: kuṟṟam ettaṉai attaṉai ellām kuṇame ṉakkoḷum kuṇakkaṭal eṉṟē maṟṟum nāṉnampi īṅkuvan tēṟṟāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr kaṟṟa naṟṟavark kē-aruḷ vīrēl kaṭaiya ṉēṉentak kaṭaittalaic celkēṉ uṟṟa naṟṟuṇai umai-aṉṟi aṟiyēṉ ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: Knowing you as the ocean of virtue who accepts whatever flaws one has as good qualities, I trusted you completely. I came here and praised you. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. If you bestow your grace only upon the learned and the virtuous, to whose doorstep shall I, the lowest of the low, go? I know no true companion other than you. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: God's true nature is an ocean of virtue that transforms human flaws into good qualities. If divine grace were reserved for the learned and the righteous, ordinary people would have nowhere to turn. Vallalar brings his imperfection to the Lord, trusting that God is the only refuge for those who fall short.

translit: poyyi lārkkumuṉ poṟkiḻi aḷitta pulavar ēṟeṉap pukaḻntiṭak kēṭṭu maiyal koṇṭiṭum maṉattoṭum vantāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr aiya numaṭi aṉṟi-ōr tuṇaiyum aṟinti lēṉiḵta ṟintaru ḷīrēl uyyum vaṇṇamev vaṇṇameṉ ceykēṉ ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: Hearing you praised as the chief of poets who gave a purse of gold in the past to the truthful one, I came to you with a heart full of infatuation. Yet you do not open your mouth to speak a single word. O Lord, I know no companion other than your feet. If you know this and still do not grant your grace, how will I find salvation and what will I do? You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Stories tell of the Lord giving a purse of gold to a truthful poet, proving his generosity. Drawn by this history of grace, Vallalar brings a heart full of love but meets only silence. He states that he has no backup plan or other refuge if this plea fails.

translit: tāyi lāreṉa neñcakam taḷarntēṉ tantai umtiruc canniti aṭaintēṉ vāyi lāreṉa irukkiṉṟīr allāl vāyti ṟantoru vārttaiyum collīr kōyi lāka-eṉ neñcakat tamarnta kuṇatti ṉīreṉtaṉ kuṟai-aṟi yīrō ōyi lātunal toṇṭaruk karuḷvāṉ ōṅku cīroṟṟi yūruṭai yīrē.
translation: My heart grew weary like one without a mother, and I reached the sacred presence of you, my father. You remain as if you have no mouth. You do not open your mouth to speak a single word. You have the nature of dwelling in my heart as your temple. Do you not know my distress? You bestow grace endlessly upon your good devotees. You possess Otriyur of supreme renown.
commentary: Vallalar approaches God with the desperation of a motherless child running to its father. Though the Lord dwells inside Vallalar's heart as a temple, God remains silent. This makes the silence feel personal, since God lives within the very aching heart and must already know its distress.

translit: maṉamutām uṉtāḷ vaḻuttukiṉṟa nallōrkkē iṉamutam ōrpoḻutum iṭṭaṟiyēṉ āyiṭiṉum muṉamutā uṇṭakaḷam muṉṉimuṉṉi vāṭukiṉṟēṉ eṉamutē iṉṉum irakkantāṉ tōṉṟātō.
translation: Even if I have never once served sweet food to the good people who praise your feet that are enduring nectar, I languish, thinking over and over of your throat that long ago drank poison as nectar. My sweet nectar, has your pity still not arisen?
commentary: Vallalar admits to a failure of generosity, having never fed those who sing God's praises. Yet he begs for mercy by recalling how Siva swallowed deadly poison to save the universe. He hopes a God capable of such vast compassion will take pity on his current despair.

translit: tōṉṟāt tuṇaiyākum cōtiyē niṉaṭikkē āṉṟārtta aṉpō ṭakaṅkuḻaiyēṉ āyiṭiṉum ūṉṟārt tarittataṉai uṉṉi-uṉṉi vāṭukiṉṟēṉ tēṉṟārc caṭaiyāyuṉ cittam iraṅkātō.
translation: O Jothi who is the unseen companion, even if my heart does not melt with abundant love at your feet, I languish, thinking over and over of how you wore the garland of bones. O Lord with honey-dripping flowers in your matted hair, will your heart not show pity?
commentary: The divine light (Jothi) acts as an invisible companion to the soul. Vallalar confesses his heart lacks melting devotion, yet he dwells on the image of the Lord wearing a garland of bones. This stark image of death and eternity contrasts with his plea for living warmth and pity.

translit: kātār kaṭuviḻiyār kāmavalaik kuḷḷāki ātāram iṉṟi alaitantēṉ āyiṭiṉum pōtār niṉatukaḻal poṉaṭiyē pōṟṟukiṉṟēṉ nītāvō uṉṉuṭaiya neñcam iraṅkātō.
translation: Caught in the net of lust set by women with fierce eyes reaching their ears, even if I wander aimlessly without any support, I praise your golden feet adorned with flower-like anklets. O Lord of justice, will your heart not show pity?
commentary: Lust has left Vallalar wandering without an anchor. In spite of his personal failings, he continues to praise the divine presence, asking if this persistent devotion is enough to awaken the Lord's mercy.

translit: ilaivēṭṭa mātartama tīṉanala mēviḻaintu kolaivēṭ ṭuḻalum koṭiyaṉēṉ āyiṭiṉum nilaivēṭṭa niṉaruṭkē niṉṟuniṉṟu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ kalaivēṭṭa vēṇiyaṉē karuṇaicaṟṟum koṇṭilaiyē.
translation: Lusting after the base pleasures of women and wandering as a cruel person with murderous intent, even so, I stand and languish, seeking your eternal grace. O Lord with matted hair wearing the crescent moon, you have not shown even a little compassion.
commentary: Vallalar admits to a cruel, destructive life driven by base desires. Despite this heavy burden, he remains fixed on the hope of eternal grace, expressing anguish that the divine remains silent and withholding.

translit: koṇṭalniṟat tōṉum kuṇikkariya niṉaṭikkē toṇṭaṟintu ceyyāta tuṭṭaṉēṉ āyiṭiṉum eṇṭakaniṉ poṉaruḷai eṇṇi-eṇṇi vāṭukiṉṟēṉ taṇṭalaicūḻ oṟṟiyuḷāy tayavucaṟṟum cārntilaiyē.
translation: At your feet, which even the cloud-colored Vishnu finds hard to comprehend, even if I am a wicked person who knows not how to perform service, I think over and over of your esteemed golden grace and languish. O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by cool groves, you have not shown even a little mercy.
commentary: The divine is so vast that even Vishnu cannot understand it. Vallalar acknowledges his wickedness and ignorance of spiritual service. Still, he spends his days agonizing over the promise of golden grace, pleading for a fraction of mercy from the Lord of Otriyur.

translit: cārā vaṟuñcārpil cārntaraicē uṉṉuṭaiya tārār malaraṭiyait tāḻntēttēṉ āyiṭiṉum nērāyniṉ cannitikkaṇ niṉṟuniṉṟu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ ōrāyō caṟṟēṉum oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē.
translation: O King, I have clung to barren attachments. Even if I do not bow and praise your garlanded flower-feet, I stand continually in your direct presence and wither away. Will you not consider this even a little, O Supreme Lord of Otriyur?
commentary: Distracted by useless worldly attachments and lacking proper worship, Vallalar offers only his physical presence and suffering. He hopes standing broken before God is enough to earn a little grace.

translit: ūrmatikka vīṇil uḷaṟukiṉṟa tallatuniṉ cīrmatikka niṉaṭiyait tērntēttēṉ āyiṭiṉum kārmatikkum nañcamuṇṭa kaṇṭaniṉain tuḷkukiṉṟēṉ ērmatikkum oṟṟiyūr entai-aḷi eytāyō.
translation: I babble in vain just to gain the town's respect. Even if I do not thoughtfully praise your feet to revere your glory, I melt within as I think of your throat that swallowed the dark poison. Will you not grant me your grace, my Father of beautiful Otriyur?
commentary: Public vanity is a trap that keeps people talking to impress others. Vallalar admits falling into this habit instead of singing God's praises. Yet he finds hope in recalling the swallowed poison, trusting that such immense compassion will save him too.

translit: tāykkumiṉi tākumuṉtaṉ tāḷmalarai ēttātu nāykkum kaṭaiyāy nalikiṉṟēṉ āyiṭiṉum vāykkumuṉtaṉ cantitikkaṇ vantuvantu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ tūykkumaraṉ tantāyeṉ cōrvaṟintu tīrāyō.
translation: I do not praise your flower-feet that are sweeter than a mother. Even if I languish as a being lower than a dog, I come repeatedly to your holy presence and wither away. O Father who gave us the pure Kumaran, will you not recognize my exhaustion and dispel it?
commentary: Divine grace is sweeter and more nurturing than a mother's love. Vallalar feels unworthy, comparing his state to an animal. He returns endlessly to the temple in exhaustion, trusting that the father of Kumaran (Murugan) cannot ignore a tired child forever.

translit: aṟiyāp paruvat taṭiyēṉai āṭkoṇṭa neṟiyām karuṇai niṉainturukēṉ āyiṭiṉum kuṟiyāp poruḷē-uṉ kōyiliṭai vantuniṉṟum paṟiyāp piṇiyēṉ paratavippaip pārttilaiyē.
translation: You claimed me as your own during my age of ignorance. Even if I do not melt at the thought of that righteous grace, O Inconceivable Reality, I come and stand in your temple. Yet you have not looked upon the anguish of this devotee afflicted by a relentless disease.
commentary: Divine compassion can act early, claiming a soul before it understands. Vallalar regrets his lack of gratitude for this intervention, bringing his pain directly to the temple and pleading with the divine to cure his persistent inner sickness.

translit: pārnaṭaiyām kāṉil parintuḻalva tallatuniṉ cīrnaṭaiyām naṉṉeṟiyil cērntilēṉ āyiṭiṉum nērnaṭaiyām niṉkōyil niṉṟuniṉṟu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ vārnaṭaiyār kāṇā vaḷaroṟṟi maṉamutē.
translation: I wander sorrowfully in the forest of worldly ways. Even if I have not joined the good path of your glorious nature, I stand repeatedly in your righteous temple and wither away. O eternal Nectar of flourishing Otriyur, unseen by the lofty ones!
commentary: Worldly life is a confusing forest where a person easily loses their way. Vallalar confesses he has strayed from the spiritual path. He relies on his stubborn return to the temple, knowing that lofty people overlook the divine presence right in front of them.

tamil: தேவியல் அறியாச் சிறியனேன் பிழையைத் திருவுளத் தெண்ணிநீ கோபம்
மேவிஇங் கையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
மூவிரு முகம்சேர் முத்தினை அளித்த முழுச்சுவை முதிர்ந்தசெங் கரும்பே
சேவின்மேல் ஓங்கும் செழுமணிக் குன்றே திருவொற்றி யூர்மகிழ் தேவே.
translit: tēviyal aṟiyāc ciṟiyaṉēṉ piḻaiyait tiruvuḷat teṇṇinī kōpam mēvi-iṅ kaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē mūviru mukamcēr muttiṉai aḷitta muḻuccuvai mutirntaceṅ karumpē cēviṉmēl ōṅkum ceḻumaṇik kuṉṟē tiruvoṟṟi yūrmakiḻ tēvē.
translation: O Siva! I am a lowly one who does not know the divine way. If you keep my faults in your divine mind, grow angry, and alas, abandon me here, what else can I do? You gave us the six-faced pearl. You are the fully ripened red sugarcane of perfect sweetness. You are the rich mountain of gems rising high upon the bull. O God who rejoices in Otriyur!
commentary: Vallalar comes before God with a plea of helplessness. He praises Siva as the father of the six-faced god Murugan, calling Murugan a precious pearl, and pictures Siva in his traditional form, riding a bull.

tamil: உய்யஒன் றறியா ஓதியனேன் பிழையை உன்திரு உள்ளத்தில் கொண்டே
வெய்யன்என் றையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
செய்யநெட் டிலைவேல் சேய்தனை அளித்த தெய்வமே ஆநந்தத் திரட்டே
மையலற் றவர்தம் மனத்தொளிர் விளக்கே வளம்பெறும் ஒற்றியூர் மணியே.
translit: uyya-oṉ ṟaṟiyā ōtiyaṉēṉ piḻaiyai uṉtiru uḷḷattil koṇṭē veyyaṉeṉ ṟaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē ceyyaneṭ ṭilaivēl cēytaṉai aḷitta teyvamē ānantat tiraṭṭē maiyalaṟ ṟavartam maṉattoḷir viḷakkē vaḷampeṟum oṟṟiyūr maṇiyē.
translation: O Siva! I am an ignorant one who knows no way to salvation. If you hold my faults in your divine mind, judge me as wicked, and alas, abandon me, what else can I do? O God who gave us the child holding the long red leaf-spear! O solid mass of bliss! O lamp shining in the minds of those freed from delusion! O gem of flourishing Otriyur!
commentary: Absolute dependence on divine mercy shapes these verses. Vallalar again addresses Siva as the father of Murugan, identifying the son by his sacred weapon, the vel (spear). To those who clear their minds of worldly delusion, God becomes a shining inner lamp.

tamil: கழல்கொள்உன் அருமைத் திருவடி மலரைக் கருதிடாப் பிழைதனைக் குறித்தே
விழலன்என் றையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
அழல்அயில் கரத்தெம் ஐயனை ஈன்ற அப்பனே அயனுமால் அறியாத்
தழல்நிறப் பவளக் குன்றமே ஒற்றித் தனிநகர் அமர்ந்தருள் தகையே.
translit: kaḻalkoḷuṉ arumait tiruvaṭi malaraik karutiṭāp piḻaitaṉaik kuṟittē viḻalaṉeṉ ṟaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē aḻalayil karattem aiyaṉai īṉṟa appaṉē ayaṉumāl aṟiyāt taḻalniṟap pavaḷak kuṉṟamē oṟṟit taṉinakar amarntaruḷ takaiyē.
translation: O Siva! I failed to meditate on your precious lotus feet adorned with anklets. If you note this fault, judge me as worthless, and alas, abandon me, what else can I do? O Father who bore our Lord wielding the fiery spear! O mountain of flame-colored coral unknown to Brahma and Vishnu! O gracious one seated in the unparalleled city of Otriyur!
commentary: Vallalar confesses forgetting to meditate on the divine presence. He compares God to a mountain of fiery red coral. This refers to an ancient story where the creator god Brahma and the preserver god Vishnu try to find the top and bottom of a massive pillar of divine fire, failing to measure its vastness.

tamil: வாடனக் குறழும் வடுக்கணார்க் குருகும் வஞ்சனேன் பிழைதனைக் குறித்தே
வேடன்என் றையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
நீடயில் படைசேர் கரத்தனை அளித்த நிருத்தனே நித்தனே நிமலா
ஏடகத் தமர்ந்த ஈசனே தில்லை எந்தையே ஒற்றியூர் இறையே.
translit: vāṭaṉak kuṟaḻum vaṭukkaṇārk kurukum vañcaṉēṉ piḻaitaṉaik kuṟittē vēṭaṉeṉ ṟaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē nīṭayil paṭaicēr karattaṉai aḷitta niruttaṉē nittaṉē nimalā ēṭakat tamarnta īcaṉē tillai entaiyē oṟṟiyūr iṟaiyē.
translation: O Siva! I am a deceitful one who melts for women with eyes shaped like tender mango slits. If you note my faults, judge me as a savage, and alas, abandon me, what else can I do? O Dancer who gave us the Lord holding the long spear! O eternal one! O immaculate one! O Lord seated upon the bull! O my Father of Thillai! O sovereign of Otriyur!
commentary: Vallalar admits to being easily distracted by worldly desires and physical attraction. He asks forgiveness from the Lord of Thillai (the temple town of Chidambaram), where God is worshipped as the cosmic dancer. Despite feeling driven by basic urges, he trusts in God's eternal purity.

tamil: நாணம்ஒன் றில்லா நாயினேன் பிழையை நாடிநின் திருவுளத் தடைத்தே
வீணன்என் றையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
காணநின் றடியார்க் கருள்தரும் பொருளே கடிமதில் ஒற்றியூர்க் கரசே
பூணயில் கரத்தோர் புத்தமு தெழுந்த புண்ணியப் புனிதவா ரிதியே.
translit: nāṇamoṉ ṟillā nāyiṉēṉ piḻaiyai nāṭiniṉ tiruvuḷat taṭaittē vīṇaṉeṉ ṟaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē kāṇaniṉ ṟaṭiyārk karuḷtarum poruḷē kaṭimatil oṟṟiyūrk karacē pūṇayil karattōr puttamu teḻunta puṇṇiyap puṉitavā ritiyē.
translation: O Siva! I am a dog possessing no shame whatsoever. If you examine my faults, hold them in your divine mind, judge me as a useless person, and alas, abandon me, what else can I do? O supreme reality who stands visible to grant grace to your devotees! O king of Otriyur with its well-guarded walls! O holy and pure ocean from which arose the fresh nectar holding the adorned spear!
commentary: Calling oneself a dog is a traditional way for Tamil poets to express humility and unworthiness. Vallalar pictures God as a holy ocean, and Murugan as the fresh nectar of immortality that rose from those divine waters.

tamil: அஞ்செழுத் தோதி உய்ந்திடாப் பிழையை ஐயநின் திருவுளத் தெண்ணி
வெஞ்சன்என் றையோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
கஞ்சன்மால் முதலோர் உயிர்பெற விடத்தைக் களத்திருத் தியஅருட்கடலே
சஞ்சித மறுக்கும் சண்முகம் உடையோன் தந்தையே ஒற்றிஎம் தவமே.
translit: añceḻut tōti uyntiṭāp piḻaiyai aiyaniṉ tiruvuḷat teṇṇi veñcaṉeṉ ṟaiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē kañcaṉmāl mutalōr uyirpeṟa viṭattaik kaḷattirut tiya-aruṭkaṭalē cañcita maṟukkum caṇmukam uṭaiyōṉ tantaiyē oṟṟi-em tavamē.
translation: Lord, if you hold in your divine heart my fault of failing to chant the five letters to attain salvation, and if you abandon me as a cruel person, alas, O Siva, what else will I do? O ocean of grace who held the poison in your throat so that Brahma, Vishnu, and others could survive! O father of the six-faced Lord who destroys accumulated karma! O our very penance in Otriyur!
commentary: The soul fears abandonment for failing basic spiritual practices, like chanting the five-letter sacred phrase of Siva. Pleading for mercy, Vallalar points to the ancient story where Siva swallowed deadly poison to save all living beings. A God with such compassion will surely not abandon a flawed soul.

tamil: நம்பினேன் நின்றன் திருவடி மலரை நாயினேன் பிழைதனைக் குறியேல்
வெம்பினேன் ஐயோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
தும்பிமா முகனை வேலனை ஈன்ற தோன்றலே வச்சிரத் தூணே
அம்பிகா பதியே அண்ணலே முக்கண் அத்தனே ஒற்றியூர் அமுதே.
translit: nampiṉēṉ niṉṟaṉ tiruvaṭi malarai nāyiṉēṉ piḻaitaṉaik kuṟiyēl vempiṉēṉ aiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē tumpimā mukaṉai vēlaṉai īṉṟa tōṉṟalē vaccirat tūṇē ampikā patiyē aṇṇalē mukkaṇ attaṉē oṟṟiyūr amutē.
translation: I placed my trust in your lotus feet. Do not mark the faults of this dog. I have suffered greatly. Alas, if you abandon me, O Siva, what else will I do? O Lord who fathered the elephant-faced god and the spear-wielding god! O diamond pillar! O husband of Ambika! O supreme master! O three-eyed father! O nectar of Otriyur!
commentary: Surrender requires recognizing our own smallness. Despite feeling unworthy, Vallalar trusts in God's protection. He calls out to the divine father of Vinayakar (the elephant-faced god) and Murugan (the spear-wielding god), trusting that a father's protective love will save him.

tamil: சூழ்ந்தவஞ் சகனேன் பிழைதனைக் குறியேல் துன்பசா கரந்தனில் அழுந்தி
வீழ்ந்தனன் ஐயோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
வாழ்ந்தமா தவர்கள் மனத்தொளிர் ஒளியே வள்ளலே மழவிடை யவனே
போழ்ந்தவேல் படைகொள் புனிதனை அளித்த பூரணாஒற்றியூர்ப் பொருளே.
translit: cūḻntavañ cakaṉēṉ piḻaitaṉaik kuṟiyēl tuṉpacā karantaṉil aḻunti vīḻntaṉaṉ aiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē vāḻntamā tavarkaḷ maṉattoḷir oḷiyē vaḷḷalē maḻaviṭai yavaṉē pōḻntavēl paṭaikoḷ puṉitaṉai aḷitta pūraṇā-oṟṟiyūrp poruḷē.
translation: Do not mark the faults of this deceitful person. I have sunk and fallen into the ocean of sorrow. Alas, if you abandon me, O Siva, what else will I do? O light shining in the minds of the exalted ascetics! O bountiful Lord! O rider of the young bull! O perfect one who gave us the pure Lord holding the piercing spear! O true wealth of Otriyur!
commentary: The pain of feeling separated from the divine is like drowning in an ocean of sorrow. Vallalar praises God as the radiant light that shines within the minds of great sages. By calling on this inner light, he hopes to draw that same divine clarity into his own troubled mind.

tamil: துரும்பினேன் பிழையைத் திருவுளத் தடையேல் துய்யநின் அருட்கடல் ஆட
விரும்பினேன் ஐயோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
கரும்பின்நேர் மொழியார் இருவரை மணக்கும் கனிதனை அளித்தகற் பகமே
இரும்பின்நேர் நெஞ்சர் எனினும்என் போல்வார்க் கின்அருள் தரும்ஒற்றி இறையே.
translit: turumpiṉēṉ piḻaiyait tiruvuḷat taṭaiyēl tuyyaniṉ aruṭkaṭal āṭa virumpiṉēṉ aiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē karumpiṉnēr moḻiyār iruvarai maṇakkum kaṉitaṉai aḷittakaṟ pakamē irumpiṉnēr neñcar eṉiṉumeṉ pōlvārk kiṉaruḷ tarumoṟṟi iṟaiyē.
translation: Do not hold in your divine heart the faults of this worthless one. I yearned to bathe in your pure ocean of grace. Alas, if you abandon me, O Siva, what else will I do? O wish-fulfilling tree who gave us the sweet fruit who marries the two brides with words sweet as sugarcane! O Lord of Otriyur who grants sweet grace to people like me even if our hearts are made of iron!
commentary: A sincere desire for grace is enough to invite God's mercy. Vallalar confesses his heart has grown as hard and unfeeling as iron, yet he longs to bathe in the pure ocean of divine compassion. He trusts the Lord of Otriyur will freely grant this grace to soften even the hardest of hearts.

tamil: கட்டினேன் பாபக் கொடுஞ்சுமை எடுப்பேன் கடும்பிழை கருதிடேல் நின்னை
விட்டிலேன் ஐயோ கைவிடில் சிவனே வேறுநான் யாதுசெய் வேனே
சுட்டிலாப் பொருளே சுகப்பெருங் கடலே தூய்த்திரு ஒற்றியூர்த் துணையே
தட்டிலாக் குணத்தோர் புகழ்செயும் குகனைத் தந்தருள் தருந்தயா நிதியே.
translit: kaṭṭiṉēṉ pāpak koṭuñcumai eṭuppēṉ kaṭumpiḻai karutiṭēl niṉṉai viṭṭilēṉ aiyō kaiviṭil civaṉē vēṟunāṉ yātucey vēṉē cuṭṭilāp poruḷē cukapperuṅ kaṭalē tūyttiru oṟṟiyūrt tuṇaiyē taṭṭilāk kuṇattōr pukaḻceyum kukaṉait tantaruḷ taruntayā nitiyē.
translation: I bound up and carry a cruel burden of sins. Do not consider my severe faults. I have never let you go. Alas, if you abandon me, O Siva, what else will I do? O reality beyond all designation! O vast ocean of bliss! O companion of pure and holy Otriyur! O treasure of compassion who grants us grace and gave us Lord Guha praised by those of flawless character!
commentary: Holding tightly to God is the only way to carry the heavy weight of past mistakes. Vallalar addresses God as a reality beyond all human names and categories. Even though humans try to define the divine, it remains an ocean of bliss that washes away all severe faults.

tamil: நாயினும் கடையேன் என்செய்வேன் பிணியால் நலிகின்ற நலிவினை அறிந்தும்
தாயினும் இனியாய் இன்னும்நீ வரவு தாழ்த்தனை என்கொலென் றறியேன்
மாயினும் அல்லால் வாழினும் நினது மலரடி அன்றிஒன் றேத்தேன்
காயினும் என்னைக் கனியினும் நின்னைக் கனவினும் விட்டிடேன் காணே.
translit: nāyiṉum kaṭaiyēṉ eṉceyvēṉ piṇiyāl nalikiṉṟa naliviṉai aṟintum tāyiṉum iṉiyāy iṉṉumnī varavu tāḻttaṉai eṉkoleṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ māyiṉum allāl vāḻiṉum niṉatu malaraṭi aṉṟi-oṉ ṟēttēṉ kāyiṉum eṉṉaik kaṉiyiṉum niṉṉaik kaṉaviṉum viṭṭiṭēṉ kāṇē.
translation: I am lower than a dog. What shall I do? Even knowing the suffering I endure from this affliction, you who are sweeter than a mother still delay your coming. I do not know why. Whether I die or live, I will praise nothing but your lotus feet. Whether you are harsh to me or gentle with me, I will not leave you even in a dream. See this to be true.
commentary: True devotion remains unbroken in hardship or comfort. Vallalar wonders why the divine delays ending his suffering, declaring his absolute loyalty will not fail even in a dream.

tamil: காண்பது கருதி மாலொடு மலர்வாழ் கடவுளர் இருவரும் தங்கள்
மாண்பது மாறி வேறுரு எடுத்தும் வள்ளல்நின் உருஅறிந் திலரே
கோண்பதர் நெஞ்சக் கொடியனேன் எந்தக் கொள்கைகொண் டறிகுவதையா
பூண்பது பணியாய் பொதுவில்நின் றாடும் புனிதநின் அருளலா தின்றே.
translit: kāṇpatu karuti māloṭu malarvāḻ kaṭavuḷar iruvarum taṅkaḷ māṇpatu māṟi vēṟuru eṭuttum vaḷḷalniṉ uru-aṟin tilarē kōṇpatar neñcak koṭiyaṉēṉ entak koḷkaikoṇ ṭaṟikuvataiyā pūṇpatu paṇiyāy potuvilniṉ ṟāṭum puṉitaniṉ aruḷalā tiṉṟē.
translation: Intending to see you, the two gods Vishnu and Brahma shed their majestic forms and took different shapes. Yet they could not comprehend your form, O generous Lord. How will I, a cruel person with a crooked and empty heart, comprehend you by any doctrine, O Lord? I can know you only through your grace today, O pure one who wears a serpent as an ornament and dances in the common hall.
commentary: Human effort cannot grasp divine truth. Vallalar recalls the ancient story of Vishnu and Brahma transforming themselves to search for the supreme Lord, yet failing. If these mighty beings failed, a flawed human cannot succeed through intellect or will. God is known only when revealing himself through grace.

tamil: இன்றுவந் தெனைநீ அடிமைகொள் ளாயேல் எவ்வுல கத்தரும் தூற்ற
நன்றுநின் றன்மேல் பழிவரும் என்மேல் பழியிலை நவின்றனன் ஐயா
அன்றுவந் தொருசேய்க் கருள்புரிந் தாண்ட அண்ணலே ஒற்றியூர் அரசே
நின்றுசிற் சபைக்குள் நடம்செயும் கருணா நிலயமே நின்மலச் சுடரே.
translit: iṉṟuvan teṉainī aṭimaikoḷ ḷāyēl evvula kattarum tūṟṟa naṉṟuniṉ ṟaṉmēl paḻivarum eṉmēl paḻiyilai naviṉṟaṉaṉ aiyā aṉṟuvan torucēyk karuḷpurin tāṇṭa aṇṇalē oṟṟiyūr aracē niṉṟuciṟ capaikkuḷ naṭamceyum karuṇā nilayamē niṉmalac cuṭarē.
translation: If you do not come today and take me as your servant, the people of all worlds will slander you. Blame will rightfully fall upon you. There will be no blame on me. I have spoken this clearly, O Lord. O great one who came that day to bestow grace upon a child and rule him! O King of Otriyur! O abode of compassion who stands and dances within the small hall! O pure flame!
commentary: Intimate devotion allows one to demand salvation with bold threats. Vallalar warns that abandoning a helpless soul brings rightful worldly blame upon the divine. His own conscience is clear because he cried out for help. This warning shows a trusting relationship where the devotee holds God accountable.

tamil: சுடர்கொளும் மணிப்பூண் முலைமட வியர்தம் தொடக்கினில் பட்டுழன் றோயா
இடர்கொளும் எனைநீ ஆட்கொளும் நாள்தான் எந்தநாள் அந்தநாள் உரையாய்
படர்கொளும் வானோர் அமுதுண நஞ்சைப் பரிந்துண்ட கருணைஅம் பரமே
குடர்கொளும் சூலப் படைஉடை யவனே கோதையோர் கூறுடையவனே.
translit: cuṭarkoḷum maṇippūṇ mulaimaṭa viyartam toṭakkiṉil paṭṭuḻaṉ ṟōyā iṭarkoḷum eṉainī āṭkoḷum nāḷtāṉ entanāḷ antanāḷ uraiyāy paṭarkoḷum vāṉōr amutuṇa nañcaip parintuṇṭa karuṇai-am paramē kuṭarkoḷum cūlap paṭai-uṭai yavaṉē kōtaiyōr kūṟuṭaiyavaṉē.
translation: Caught in the ties of young women wearing radiant jeweled ornaments on their breasts, I wander without rest and endure suffering. What day will you take me as your own? Tell me that day. O supreme heaven of compassion who willingly consumed poison so the suffering celestials could eat ambrosia! O Lord wielding the trident weapon that pierces intestines! O Lord who shares half his body with the lady wearing a flower garland!
commentary: Physical desire and worldly attachments are an exhausting trap. Vallalar asks when he will finally be rescued from these torments and given lasting peace. He appeals directly to God's ultimate compassion. He recalls how the Lord drank deadly poison to save the celestial beings, hoping that same boundless mercy will now save him from his own toxic worldly ties.

tamil: உடைமைவைத் தெனக்கின் றருள்செயா விடினும் ஒப்பிலாய் நின்னடிக் கெனையே
அடைமைவைத் தேனும் நின்அருட் பொருள்இங் களித்திட வேண்டும் இன்றெவைக்கும்
கடைமையேன் வேறோர் தேவரை அறியேன் கடவுள்நின் திருவடி அறிக
படைமைசேர் கரத்தெம் பசுபதி நீயே என்உளம் பார்த்துநின் றாயே.
translit: uṭaimaivait teṉakkiṉ ṟaruḷceyā viṭiṉum oppilāy niṉṉaṭik keṉaiyē aṭaimaivait tēṉum niṉaruṭ poruḷiṅ kaḷittiṭa vēṇṭum iṉṟevaikkum kaṭaimaiyēṉ vēṟōr tēvarai aṟiyēṉ kaṭavuḷniṉ tiruvaṭi aṟika paṭaimaicēr karattem pacupati nīyē eṉuḷam pārttuniṉ ṟāyē.
translation: Even if you do not grant me grace today by claiming me as your outright possession, O peerless one, you must at least keep me as a pledge at your feet and grant me the wealth of your grace here. I am the lowest of the low. I know no other gods. Let your divine feet know this, O God. You are our Lord of souls holding a weapon in your hand. You stand there looking deep into my heart.
commentary: The soul begs to belong to God in any capacity. If unworthy to be an outright possession, Vallalar asks God to at least hold him as a pledge or collateral. Stripping away all allegiances, he invites the Lord to look into his heart and verify this total surrender.

tamil: பார்த்துநிற் கின்றாய் யாவையும் எளியேன் பரதவித் துறுகணால் நெஞ்சம்
ஆர்த்துநிற் கின்றார் ஐம்புல வேடர் அவர்க்கிலக் காவனோ தமியேன்
ஓர்த்துநிற் கின்றார் பரவுநல் ஒற்றி யூரில்வாழ் என்உற வினனே.
translit: pārttuniṟ kiṉṟāy yāvaiyum eḷiyēṉ paratavit tuṟukaṇāl neñcam vērttuniṟ kiṉṟēṉ kaṇṭilaikollō viṭamuṇṭakaṇṭaṉnī-aṉṟō ārttuniṟ kiṉṟār aimpula vēṭar avarkkilak kāvaṉō tamiyēṉ ōrttuniṟ kiṉṟār paravunal oṟṟi yūrilvāḻ eṉuṟa viṉaṉē.
translation: You stand watching everything. I, a helpless one, languish and stand with a sweating heart due to great sorrow. Do you not see this? Are you not the one whose throat swallowed the poison? The hunters of the five senses stand roaring. Will I, a lonely soul, become their target? O my relative living in good Otriyur, praised by those who stand in reflection!
commentary: God sees all things, yet seems to stand by while the soul suffers in terror of the five senses. Vallalar asks why the Lord will not intervene to save a lonely soul from these relentless sensory hunters.

tamil: உறவனே உன்னை உள்கிநெஞ் சழலின் உறும்இழு தெனக்கசிந் துருகா
மறவனேன் தன்னை ஆட்கொளா விடில்யான் வருந்துவ தன்றிஎன் செய்கேன்
நிறவனே வெள்ளை நீறணி பவனே நெற்றிமேல் கண்ணுடை யவனே
அறவனே தில்லை அம்பலத் தாடும் அப்பனே ஒற்றியூர்க் கரைசே.
translit: uṟavaṉē uṉṉai uḷkineñ caḻaliṉ uṟumiḻu teṉakkacin turukā maṟavaṉēṉ taṉṉai āṭkoḷā viṭilyāṉ varuntuva taṉṟi-eṉ ceykēṉ niṟavaṉē veḷḷai nīṟaṇi pavaṉē neṟṟimēl kaṇṇuṭai yavaṉē aṟavaṉē tillai ampalat tāṭum appaṉē oṟṟiyūrk karaicē.
translation: O relative! Thinking of you, my heart does not melt and flow like butter placed in fire. I am a cruel-hearted person. If you do not claim me, what can I do except suffer? O radiant one! O wearer of the white ash! O one who has an eye on the forehead! O embodiment of dharma! O Father who dances in the hall of Thillai! O King of Otriyur!
commentary: True devotion melts the heart like butter in a fire. Lamenting his unfeeling nature, Vallalar pleads with the dancing Lord of Thillai (the sacred temple town of Chidambaram) to claim him anyway, having no other refuge from suffering.

tamil: கரைபடா வஞ்சப் பவக்கடல் உழக்கும் கடையனேன் நின்திரு வடிக்கு
திரைபடாக் கருணைச் செல்வவா ரிதியே திருவொற்றி யூர்வளர் தேனே
உரைபடாப் பொன்னே புரைபடா மணியே உண்ணுதற் கினியநல் அமுதே.
translit: karaipaṭā vañcap pavakkaṭal uḻakkum kaṭaiyaṉēṉ niṉtiru vaṭikku viraipaṭā malarpōl iruntuḻalkiṉṟēṉveṟṟaṉēṉ eṉceya viraikēṉ tiraipaṭāk karuṇaic celvavā ritiyē tiruvoṟṟi yūrvaḷar tēṉē uraipaṭāp poṉṉē puraipaṭā maṇiyē uṇṇutaṟ kiṉiyanal amutē.
translation: I am the lowest one, struggling in the shoreless deceptive ocean of birth. I wander like a scentless flower meant for your holy feet. I am empty. What shall I rush to do? O waveless ocean of the wealth of grace! O honey flourishing in Otriyur! O gold beyond words! O flawless gem! O good nectar sweet to consume!
commentary: Caught in the endless cycle of physical birth, the soul feels as useless as a scentless flower. Against this emptiness, the divine stands as an immense, still ocean of pure grace.

tamil: நல்அமு தனையார் நின்திரு வடிக்கே நண்புவைத் துருகுகின் றனரால்
புல்அமு தனையேன் என்செய்வான் பிறந்தேன் புண்ணியம் என்பதொன் றறியேன்
சொல்அமு தனைய தோகைஓர் பாகம் துன்னிய தோன்றலே கனியாக்
கல்அமு தாக்கும் கடன்உனக் கன்றோ கடையனேன் கழறுவ தென்னே.
translit: nalamu taṉaiyār niṉtiru vaṭikkē naṇpuvait turukukiṉ ṟaṉarāl pulamu taṉaiyēṉ eṉceyvāṉ piṟantēṉ puṇṇiyam eṉpatoṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ colamu taṉaiya tōkai-ōr pākam tuṉṉiya tōṉṟalē kaṉiyāk kalamu tākkum kaṭaṉuṉak kaṉṟō kaṭaiyaṉēṉ kaḻaṟuva teṉṉē.
translation: Those who resemble good nectar place their friendship on your holy feet and melt. I resemble worthless grass. Why was I born? I do not know a single meritorious deed. O Lord who keeps closely on one side the peacock-like Goddess whose words are like nectar! Is it not your duty to turn an unripening stone into nectar? What is there for this lowest one to say?
commentary: Divine grace can turn a lifeless stone into sweet nectar. Contrasting the pure love of true saints with his own worthlessness, Vallalar reminds God that transforming an unyielding heart is the duty of the divine.

tamil: என்னைநின் னவனாக் கொண்டுநின் கருணை என்னும்நன் னீரினால் ஆட்டி
அன்னைஅப் பனுமாய்ப் பரிவுகொண் டாண்ட அண்ணலே நண்ணரும் பொருளே
