உன்னருந் தெய்வ நாயக மணியே ஒற்றியூர் மேவும்என் உறவே
நன்னர்செய் கின்றோய் என்செய்வேன் இதற்கு நன்குகைம் மாறுநா யேனே.
translit: eṉṉainiṉ ṉavaṉāk koṇṭuniṉ karuṇai eṉṉumnaṉ ṉīriṉāl āṭṭi aṉṉai-ap paṉumāyp parivukoṇ ṭāṇṭa aṇṇalē naṇṇarum poruḷē uṉṉarun teyva nāyaka maṇiyē oṟṟiyūr mēvumeṉ uṟavē naṉṉarcey kiṉṟōy eṉceyvēṉ itaṟku naṉkukaim māṟunā yēṉē.
translation: You took me as your own and bathed me with the good water called your grace. You acted as mother and father and ruled me with affection. O Lord! O reality hard to attain! O gem of a divine Lord hard to comprehend! O my relative dwelling in Otriyur! You perform good deeds. What proper return can I, a dog, offer for this?
commentary: Divine grace cares for the soul with the affection of a mother and father. Washed in this sustaining love, Vallalar realizes a human being can offer nothing in return for such a gift.

translit: pōkam koṇṭa puṇarmulai mātoru pākam koṇṭa paṭampakka nātarē mākam koṇṭa vaḷampoḻil oṟṟiyiṉ mōkam koṇṭa-em muṉniṉ ṟaruḷirō.
translation: O Lord Padambakkanathar, you hold on one side the lady with alluring breasts who shares your bliss. Will you not stand before us who are utterly enamored of you here in Otriyur, a place of rich groves that touch the sky, and bestow your grace?
commentary: Vallalar addresses God by his local name at the Otriyur temple, Padambakkanathar. He appeals to Siva's form sharing half his body with the goddess. Since God keeps his consort so intimately close, Vallalar asks why he will not show the same closeness to devotees desperately in love with him.

translit: tavaḷa nīṟṟumeyc cāntavi ṉōtarē pavaḷa mēṉip paṭampakka nātarē kavaḷa vīṟṟuk kari-uri pōrttanīr ivaḷai oṟṟiviṭ ṭeṅṅaṉam ceṉṟirō.
translation: O wondrous one who applies bright white ash as a paste upon your body! O Lord Padambakkanathar with a coral-hued form! You draped yourself in the skin of a majestic elephant that fed on great mouthfuls. How did you abandon this woman in Otriyur and depart?
commentary: In Tamil poetry, a lovelorn woman's friend often speaks on her behalf to scold the lover. The friend points out the Lord's wild, fierce appearance, smearing himself with cremation ash and wearing the skin of a demonic elephant he defeated. She wonders how someone with a beautiful coral-red form could be coldhearted enough to abandon a devoted woman.

translit: cīla mēvit tikaḻaṉal kaṇoṉṟu pāla mēvum paṭampakka nātarē ñāla mēvum navaiyai-a kaṟṟamuṉ ālam uṇṭavar allirkol aiyarē.
translation: O Lord Padambakkanathar, you bear a radiant, fiery eye of pure virtue upon your forehead. O Master, are you not the one who drank the deadly poison long ago to dispel the affliction covering the world?
commentary: Vallalar reminds the Lord of his greatest act of compassion. When a deadly poison threatened to destroy the universe, Siva swallowed it to save all living beings. How can the same God who showed such vast mercy to the world refuse to show mercy to Vallalar now?

translit: uṭaikoḷ kōvaṇat tuṟṟa-a ḻakarē paṭaikoḷ cūlap paṭampakka nātarē kaṭaikoḷ nañcuṇṭu kaṇṭamka ṟuttanīr iṭaiyil oṟṟiviṭ ṭeṅṅaṉam ceṉṟirō.
translation: O beautiful Lord who wears a mere loincloth! O Lord Padambakkanathar wielding a trident weapon! You drank the ultimate poison and your throat turned black. How did you abandon her midway and depart?
commentary: The black mark on the Lord's throat is the permanent scar of his sacrifice, left where the poison stopped. Vallalar is baffled that a deity so willing to sacrifice himself for others would leave a devotee stranded halfway along the spiritual path.

translit: niṟaiya vāḻtoṇṭar nīṭuṟa vaṉpavam paṟaiya niṉṟapa ṭampakka nātarē uṟaiya māṇikku yir aḷit tiṭṭanīr kuṟaiyi lā-oṟṟik kōyiṟkaṇ uḷḷirō.
translation: O Lord Padambakkanathar, you stand ready to destroy the lingering cruel karma of your devoted servants who live fully in your grace. You restored the life of the young celibate boy so he could endure forever. Are you now residing within the flawless temple of Otriyur?
commentary: Vallalar recalls an ancient story where the Lord saved a young boy from the God of Death, granting him eternal life. God is a protector who wipes out the heavy burdens of past actions (karma) for his true servants. Knowing he possesses this power to save, Vallalar wonders if he is hiding away inside the local temple instead of coming out to rescue him.

translit: vaṇaṅkoḷ nākama ṇittalai aintuṭaip paṇaṅkoḷ celvappa ṭampakka nātarē kaṇaṅkoḷ kāmaṉaik kāyntuyir īntanīr vaṇaṅku vārkkeṉkol vāytiṟa vātatē.
translation: O wealthy Lord Patampakka Nathar who wears the gem-bearing, five-headed, hooded serpent. You burned the god of love and his army and then restored his life. Why do You not open Your mouth to speak to those who bow before You?
commentary: Vallalar recalls the story of Siva burning the god of love to ashes and then mercifully restoring him to life. This creates a painful contrast: if God holds the sweeping power of life and death, it is confusing when he stays silently frozen before a seeker asking for a single word.

translit: nāṭa nalicai nalkiya mūvartam pāṭal kēṭkumpa ṭampakka nātarē vāṭal eṉṟoru māṇik kaḷittanīr īṭil eṉṉaḷa veṅkoḷit tiṭṭirō.
translation: O Lord Patampakka Nathar who listens to the songs of the three saints who graced the world with beautiful music. You saved a young student and told him not to wither away. Where have You hidden Yourself from worthless me?
commentary: The three saints are the famous ancient poets whose hymns form the heart of traditional temple worship. The Lord also once saved a young boy from death in a classic story of divine rescue. The poem asks why a God so ready to save others in the past is now hiding from this one voice.

translit: culavu kāṟṟaṉal tūyamaṇ viṇpuṉal palavu mākumpa ṭampakka nātarē nilavu taṇmati nīḷmuṭi vaittanīr kulavum eṉṟaṉku ṟaitavirk kīrkolō.
translation: O Lord Patampakka Nathar who becomes the swirling wind, fire, pure earth, sky, water, and all manifold things. You placed the cool, shining moon in Your long hair. Will You not remove my lingering flaws?
commentary: God is not a distant figure in the heavens. The divine presence becomes the five physical elements that make up our world: earth, water, fire, wind, and sky. Since God is woven into everything around us, Vallalar asks him to use that encompassing power to heal human flaws.

translit: aṭiyar neñcatta ruṭperuñ cōti-ōr paṭiva mākumpa ṭampakka nātarē neṭiya mālukku nēmi aḷittanīr miṭiya ṉēṉaruḷ mēva virumpirō.
translation: O Lord Patampakka Nathar who takes the form of the great Jothi of grace in the hearts of devotees. You gave the discus weapon to the tall Lord Vishnu. Do You not wish for destitute me to attain Your grace?
commentary: God appears to true seekers as ArutPerunJothi, the vast light of supreme grace shining inside their hearts. The Lord is powerful enough to grant mighty weapons to other great gods like Vishnu. Why can this same immense power not grant grace to someone poor and needy?

translit: matikoḷ aṉparma ṉameṉum tivviyap patikoḷ celvappa ṭampakka nātarē vitikoḷ tuṉpattai vīṭṭi aḷittanīr tutikoḷ vīreṉtu yaraittu rattumē.
translation: O wealthy Lord Patampakka Nathar who resides in the divine abode of the minds of wise and loving devotees. You destroyed the sorrows dictated by fate and granted Your grace. You who accept our praises, please drive away my sorrow.
commentary: The true temple of God is the mind of a loving person. People usually think of fate as an unbreakable chain of past actions, but divine grace has the power to shatter it. Vallalar pleads for that same grace to step in and drive all present sorrow away forever.

translit: cintai mayaṅkit tiyaṅkukiṉṟa nāyēṉai muntai viṉaitolaittuṉ moykaḻaṟkāḷ ākkātē nintai-uṟum nōyāl nikaḻavaittal nītiyatō entainī oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am like a dog, my mind confused and bewildered. Without destroying my past karma and making me a servant to your strong feet, is it just to keep me suffering from this blameworthy disease? You are my father, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman of Otriyur!
commentary: Vallalar boldly asks why God allows him to struggle with confusion and past actions (karma) when the divine has the power to erase that burden and take him into service.

translit: mattaṉaivaṉ neñcakaṉai vañcakaṉai vaṉpiṇikoḷ pittaṉaivīṇ nāḷpōkkum pēyēṉai nāyēṉai muttaṉaiyāy uṉṟaṉ muḷarittāṭ kāḷākka ettaṉaināḷ cellum eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am arrogant, hard-hearted, and deceitful. I am a madman gripped by severe disease. I waste my days like a demon and a dog. O Lord who is like a pearl, how many days will it take to make me a servant to your lotus feet, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Vallalar piles up harsh insults against himself. Taking on the persona of a flawed person is a common way in Tamil devotional poetry to highlight the purity of God's grace.

translit: naṉṉeṟicēr aṉpartamai nāṭiṭavum niṉpukaḻiṉ ceṉṉeṟiyaic cērntiṭavum ceytāy eṉakkuṉakku muṉaṟiyēṉ piṉaṟiyēṉ mūṭaṉēṉ kaimmāṟiṅ keṉaṟivēṉ aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: You made me seek out the devotees who walk the good path and join the righteous path of your glory. I know nothing before and I know nothing after. I am a fool. What return can I possibly offer you here, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Faced with God's freely given grace, Vallalar admits his ignorance and realizes he has nothing of value to offer in return.

translit: maippaṭiyum kaṇṇār mayaluḻakkac ceyvāyō kaippaṭiya uṉṟaṉ kaḻalkarutac ceyvāyō ippaṭi-eṉ ṟappaṭi-eṉ ṟeṉṉaṟivēṉ uṉcittam eppaṭiyō aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Will you make me suffer the delusion of women with kohl-lined eyes? Or will you make me contemplate your feet and attain them? How can I know if it will be this way or that way? Whatever your will may be, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: Human vulnerability to worldly distractions is placed in God's hands. Vallalar wonders if he will fall back into physical desires or remain focused on the divine, surrendering his future to whatever God decides.

translit: nillā uṭampai nilai-eṉṟē nēcikkum pollāta neñcap pulaiyaṉēṉ ivvulakil collā maṉanōyāl cōrvuṟ ṟalaiyumallal ellām aṟivāy eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I love this impermanent body as if it were permanent. I am a base one with an evil heart in this world. You know all the suffering I endure as I wander exhausted by an unspeakable disease of the mind, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: People naturally cling to the physical body as if it will last forever. Vallalar confesses that this false attachment causes him an exhausting mental anguish that only God understands.

translit: tītaṟivēṉ naṉkaṇuvum ceyyēṉvīṇ nāḷpōkkum vātaṟivēṉ vañcakaṉēṉ valviṉaiyēṉ vāymaiyilēṉ cūtaṟivēṉ mālayaṉum collaṟiya niṉperumai yātaṟivēṉ aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I know evil. I do not do even an atom of good. I know the arguments that waste days. I am deceitful. I am bound by harsh karma. I lack truth. I know cunning trickery. What can I know of your greatness, which even Thirumal and Brahma cannot adequately describe, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: Vallalar strips away spiritual pride, confessing to human faults like deceit, empty arguments, and a lack of goodness. He contrasts his smallness with the vastness of the divine. Even the creator god Brahma and the preserver god Thirumal cannot grasp God's scale. If the highest deities fall short, a flawed human can only approach the Lord with humility.

translit: māṟāta vaṉpiṇiyāl māḻāntu neñcayarntē kūṟāta tuṉpak koṭuṅkaṭaṟkuḷ vīḻntaṭiyēṉ āṟā taraṟṟi aḻukiṉṟēṉ niṉceviyil ēṟātō aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Suffering from unrelenting severe disease, fainting and weary in heart, I fall into a cruel sea of untold sorrow. I wail and cry inconsolably. Will my cries not reach your ears, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Physical illness and mental exhaustion have pushed Vallalar to the breaking point. In his despair, he cries out with the raw fear that God might not be listening.

translit: uṇṇāṭum valviṉaiyāl ōyāp piṇi-uḻantu puṇṇāka neñcam puḻuṅkukiṉṟēṉ puṇṇiyaṉē kaṇṇāḷā uṉṟaṉ karuṇai eṉakkaḷikka eṇṇāyō aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Tormented by harsh karma churning within, I suffer ceaseless afflictions. I agonize, my heart turning into a raw wound. O embodiment of virtue, O Lord of compassionate eyes, will you not consider granting me your grace, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: The consequences of karma churn inside the mind and body. The resulting pain is so constant that the heart feels like an open wound. In this agony, the only hope left is that the Lord might choose to grant grace out of compassion.

translit: puṉceykai māṟāp pulaiyamaṭa maṅkaiyartam vaṉceykai yālē mayaṅkukiṉṟa vañcakaṉēṉ koṉceykai māṟāta kūṟṟaṉ varuvāṉēl eṉceyvēṉ aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am a deceitful person, deluded by the forceful acts of ignorant, base women engaged in relentless petty deeds. If the god of death arrives with his unchanging murderous intent, what will I do, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Worldly distractions and physical desires have kept the mind trapped in delusion. A sudden clarity cuts through this fog: time is running out. Vallalar asks how he will face the god of death when his life has been wasted on petty illusions instead of enduring truth.

translit: caṅkuṭaiyāṉ tāmaraiyāṉ tāḷmuṭiyum kāṇparitām koṅkuṭaiya koṉṟaik kuḷircaṭaiyāy kōtai-oru paṅkuṭaiyāy ēḻaimukam pārātu taḷḷiviṭṭāl eṅkaṭaivēṉ aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: The god holding the conch and the god seated on the lotus found it impossible to see your feet and crown. O Lord with cool matted hair adorned with fragrant konrai flowers, O Lord who shares half your form with the goddess. If you push me away without looking upon the face of this poor soul, where will I find refuge, O Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Vallalar recalls the ancient story in which the great gods Vishnu (holding the conch) and Brahma (seated on the lotus) searched the universe but could not find the top or bottom of the supreme divine light. The Lord is pictured here in a traditional form, wearing fragrant konrai flowers and sharing half his body with the Goddess. Facing this boundless, awe-inspiring presence, Vallalar makes a final plea. If the ultimate refuge of the universe pushes a poor soul away, there is simply nowhere else to go.

translit: maṉṟi ṉiṭainaṭañcey māṇikka māmalaiyē veṉṟimaḻuk kaiyuṭaiya vittakaṉē eṉṟeṉṟu kaṉṟiṉ ayarntaḻumeṉ kaṇṇīr tuṭaittaruḷa eṉṟu varuvāy eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O great ruby mountain dancing in the hall! O wise one holding the victorious battle-axe in your hand! Calling out to you again and again, I weep and languish like a separated calf. When will you come to wipe my tears and bestow your grace, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: The soul longs for God with the helpless sorrow of a separated calf calling for its mother, seeking the direct comfort of divine grace.

translit: maṉṉaḷavil cōti maṇipōlvāy mātavattōr teṉṉaḷavum vēṇic civamē eṉa-orukāl coṉṉaḷavil coṉṉavartam tuṉpoḻippāy eṉparatu eṉṉaḷavil kāṇēṉ eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: You are like a gem of boundless light. They say that if great ascetics call out even once, "O Siva with matted hair stretching to the south," you instantly destroy the sorrow of those who spoke. I do not see that happening in my case, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: Tradition holds that God instantly removes the sorrow of great ascetics the first time they call out his name. Vallalar wonders why this swift response does not happen for him, expressing a feeling of spiritual delay.

translit: miṉpōlvār iccaiyiṉāl vempukiṉṟēṉ āṉālum taṉpōlvāy eṉīṉṟa tāypōlvāy cārnturaiyāp poṉpōlvāy niṉaruḷip pōtaṭiyēṉ peṟṟēṉēl eṉpōlvār illai eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I burn with desire for women who flash like lightning. Even so, you have no equal but yourself, and you are like the mother who bore me. You are like pure gold beyond the reach of words. If I receive your grace right now, there will be no one as blessed as me, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: A child trusts its mother even when it has done wrong. Vallalar confesses his daily struggles with worldly desires, yet he tells God that receiving divine grace would make him the most blessed person alive.

translit: pūmāntum vaṇṭeṉaniṉ poṉṉaruḷaip puṇṇiyarkaḷ tāmānti niṉṉaṭikkīḻc cārntuniṉṟār aiyōnāṉ kāmānta kārameṉum kaḷḷuṇṭu kaṇmūṭi ēmāntēṉ oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Like bees drinking nectar from a flower, the virtuous drink your golden grace and stand sheltered beneath your feet. Alas, I drank the intoxicating liquor of blinding lust, closed my eyes, and was utterly deceived, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman in Otri.
commentary: The virtuous soul draws spiritual nourishment directly from God, like a bee taking nectar from a flower. Vallalar contrasts this focus with his past, saying he was blinded by the intoxicating pull of worldly lust.

translit: paṉṉarumip pārnaṭaiyil pāṭuḻaṉṟa pātakaṉēṉ tuṉṉiyaniṉ poṉṉaṭiyaic cūḻātēṉ āyiṭiṉum puṉṉikarēṉ kuṟṟam poṟukkap poṟuppuṉakkē eṉṉarumait tāynī eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am a sinner who wandered and suffered in the unspeakable ways of this world. Even if I fail to draw near and worship your golden feet, it is your responsibility to forgive the faults of someone as worthless as grass. You are my precious mother, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: A mother is responsible for her child, no matter how the child has failed. Vallalar tells God that even though he feels worthless and has wandered into worldly suffering, it is God's duty as a mother to forgive him.

translit: vīṭṭuk kaṭaṅkā viḷaiyāṭṭup piḷḷai-eṉat tēṭṭuk kaṭaṅkāta tīmaṉattāl āntuyaram pāṭṭuk kaṭaṅkāniṉ pattar aṭippukaḻpōl ēṭṭuk kaṭaṅkā teḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman! Like an uncontrollable playful child who does not stay at home, my evil mind defies all restraint. The sorrow it causes me cannot be contained in written leaves, just as the praise of your devotees' feet cannot be contained in songs.
commentary: The mind is like an unruly child that refuses to stay at home. Vallalar says the sorrow this restless mind causes is so vast it cannot be written down. He compares this endless grief to the boundless praise owed to devotees.

translit: paṉṉu maṉattāl pariciḻanta pātakaṉēṉ tuṉṉumala veṅkatirōṉ cūḻkiṉṟa cōṭaiyiṉāl niṉṉaruḷnīr vēṭṭu nilaikalaṅki vāṭukiṉṟēṉ iṉṉumaṟi yāyō eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman! I am a sinner who lost his true state because of a wandering mind. Exhausted by the scorching sun of dense impurities, I wither and lose my balance. I yearn for the water of your grace. Do you still not know this?
commentary: Spiritual exhaustion feels like a physical thirst. Vallalar describes his selfish attachments as a scorching sun that dries up his true nature, calling God's grace the only water that can save him from withering away.

translit: kallai nikarām kaṭaimaṉampōm kāṉneṟiyil pullai matit taiyōpaim pū-iḻanta poyyaṭiyēṉ ollaipaṭu kiṉṟa oṟuvē taṉaitaṉakkōr ellai aṟiyēṉ eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman! My lowly mind is like a stone. Wandering in its forest path, alas, I valued mere grass and lost the fresh flower. I am a false devotee. I know no bounds to the torment I suffer.
commentary: Worldly distractions cause us to trade what is precious for what is worthless. Vallalar regrets walking through the forest of his mind and choosing grass over a fresh flower. This illustrates the pain of chasing worldly pleasures and missing out on the lasting beauty of the divine.

translit: poṉṉaimatit taiyāniṉ poṉṉaṭiyaip pōṟṟāta kaṉṉikarum neñcāl kalaṅkukiṉṟa kaitavaṉēṉ iṉṉal uḻakkiṉṟa ēḻaikaṭkum ēḻaikaṇṭāy eṉṉai viṭātē eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman! I valued worldly gold and failed to praise your golden feet. I am a deceitful man bewildered by a heart as hard as stone. See me as the poorest among the poor who endure such affliction. Do not abandon me.
commentary: Valuing material wealth over spiritual devotion hardens the heart into stone. True poverty is a state of the soul. Vallalar calls himself the poorest of the poor because he chased worldly gold instead of the divine presence, begging God to save him from this destitution.

translit: mācuvarē eṉṉum malakkaṭalil vīḻntulakōr ācuvarē eṉṉa alaivēṉai āḷāyēl kūcuvarē kaikoṭṭik kūṭic cirittaṭiyār ēcuvarē oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman of Otriyur! I have fallen into the ocean of impurities that stains the soul. Worldly people declare me ruined. If you do not claim me as I wander like this, your devotees will shrink back in shame. They will gather, clap their hands, laugh, and mock.
commentary: If God abandons a struggling soul, the community of the faithful might lose heart. Vallalar argues that his ruin would bring shame to other believers. He asks to be rescued from his spiritual stains, warning that leaving him to wander would invite mockery.

translit: ūrcolvēṉ pērcolvēṉ uttamaṉē niṉtiruttāḷ cīrcolvēṉ eṉṟaṉainī cērkkā takaṟṟuvaiyēl nērcolvāy uṉṟaṉakku nītiyī talla-eṉṟē yārcolvār aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I will speak your town's name. I will speak your name. O supreme one, I will sing the glory of your holy feet. If you do not gather me to yourself but push me away, tell me directly, who is there to tell you that this is not justice? O master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: Vallalar promises to praise the Lord's name and glory, but he fears being rejected. He asks a simple question: if God pushes him away, who has the authority to tell God that this is unjust? Since God is supreme, there is no higher court of appeal. The devotee relies entirely on divine mercy.

translit: nīkkamilā meyyaṭiyar nēcamilāp poyyaṭiyēṉ ūkkamilā neñcattiṉ ōṭṭakalac ceyvāyēl tūkkamilā āṉantat tūkkamaṉṟi maṟṟumiṅkōr ēkkamilēṉ oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am a false devotee without love for your inseparable true devotees. If you stop the wandering of my unmotivated heart, I will have no other longing in this world except for the sleepless sleep of bliss, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman of Otriyur.
commentary: The "sleepless sleep of bliss" is a state of spiritual awakening where the soul rests in divine joy while remaining conscious. Vallalar calls himself false for lacking love toward true devotees, showing that loving others is essential to finding this peace.

translit: pōkiṉṟa vañcakaraip pōkki-uṉṟaṉ poṉaṭikkāḷ ākiṉṟa mēlōr aṭivaḻuttā nāyēṟkup pākiṉ taṉiccuvaiyiṟ pāṅkākum niṉaruḷai īkiṉṟa teṉṟō eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: You drive away the deceitful ones who go astray. I am a dog who does not praise the feet of the exalted ones who serve your golden feet. When will you grant me your grace, which is sweet like the matchless taste of syrup? O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: Fearing his own flaws will keep him from the sweetness of grace, Vallalar throws himself on the Lord's compassion. He knows God turns away the deceitful, making divine mercy his only hope.

translit: ūḻai akaṟṟa uḷavaṟiyāp poyyaṉivaṉ pīḻaimaṉam nammaip peṟātam maṉaṅkoṭiya tāḻai-eṉa eṇṇi-eṉṉait taḷḷiviṭṭāl eṉceyvēṉ ēḻaināṉ oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: You might think: "This liar does not know the secret to remove his past karma. His troubled mind cannot attain us. His mind is cruel like the thorny screw pine." If you think this way and push me aside, what will I, a poor wretch, do? O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman of Otriyur.
commentary: Vallalar imagines God judging his unworthiness and inability to shed the weight of past actions, known as karma. If God rejects him based on these faults, he is helpless. Spiritual freedom relies on God's forgiveness, not on human perfection.

translit: maṭukka muṭiyā mala-iruṭṭil ceṉṟumaṉam kaṭukkamuṭi yāppulaṉāl kaṭṭic cumakkavaitta toṭukka muṭiyāta tuṉpac cumaiyai-iṉi eṭukkamuṭi yātē eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: My mind plunged into the impenetrable darkness of impurity and suffered intensely. Bound by the invincible senses, I was forced to carry an unending burden of sorrow. I can no longer lift this weight, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman.
commentary: Vallalar describes the exhaustion of worldly life. His mind is trapped in the darkness of spiritual impurity (mala) and tied down by the unstoppable pull of the physical senses. He pleads with the Lord to finally lift this heavy burden of sorrow.

translit: muḷḷaḷavu neñca muḻuppulaiya mātarkaḷām kaḷḷaḷavu nāyil kaṭaippaṭṭa eṉṟaṉakku uḷḷaḷavum aṉpark kutavumuṉtāṭ kaṉporuciṟ ṟeḷḷaḷavum uṇṭō eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am worse than a deceitful dog. I associate with entirely base women who possess thorn-like hearts. Is there even a sesame seed's worth of love in me for your feet, which help your devotees as long as they live? O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: Vallalar strips away all self-worth to stand bare before the divine, highlighting the vast gap between human flaws and divine perfection. God's grace remains constant and helpful for those who love him, even when the seeker feels unworthy.

translit: paṇṇa muṭiyāp paripavaṅkoṇ ṭivvulakil naṇṇa muṭiyā nalaṅkaruti vāṭukiṉṟēṉ uṇṇamuṭi yā-amutām uṉṉai-aṉṟi evvaurkkum eṇṇamuṭi yātē eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Enduring unbearable humiliation in this world, I wither away seeking an unattainable good. No one can comprehend anything except you, the inexhaustible nectar. O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: The pursuit of worldly life brings humiliation and exhaustion. True goodness feels impossible to reach on one's own. God is an endless nectar, serving as the only real source of spiritual nourishment when the world drains the soul.

translit: veṅkoḷittēḷ pōṉṟa viṉaiyāl vetumpimaṉam aṅkoḷikkā tuṉṉai aḻaittaḻutu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ iṅkoḷikkā nañcamuṇṭa eṉarumai appānī eṅkoḷittāy oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Scorched by karma that stings like a cruel scorpion, my mind suffers. Without hiding anything, I call out to you, weeping and withering. You drank the manifest poison, my precious father. Where have you hidden yourself in Otriyur, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman?
commentary: Vallalar appeals to God's compassion by recalling a central story of Lord Siva, who drank a deadly poison to save the universe from destruction. If the Lord is a father willing to consume poison to protect all beings, Vallalar asks why he stays hidden from a weeping child stung by karma.

translit: pittaḷaikkum kāmap perumpēy mayakkumayal vittaṉaittām āṇavampoy vīṟumaḻuk kāṟuciṉam kottaṉaittām vañcam kolaimutalām pāvaṅkaḷ ittaṉaikkum nāṉkāṇ eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: I am the very abode of all these things: the maddening great demon of lust, confusing delusion, the seed of ego, lies, swelling envy, anger, deceit, and clusters of sins beginning with murder. O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: True spiritual honesty requires facing the darkest parts of the human mind. Confessing such wickedness is a traditional way to beg for grace, showing that only divine mercy can save a lost soul.

translit: ollaiyē nañcaṉaittum uṇṭa tayānitinī allaiyō niṉṟiṅ kayarvēṉmuṉ vantorucol collaiyō oṟṟiyūrt tūyatiruk kōyiluḷnī illaiyō aiyā eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: Are you not the treasure of compassion who swiftly consumed all the poison? Will you not come before me as I stand here exhausted and speak a single word? Are you not inside the pure holy temple of Otriyur, O Master? O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman!
commentary: The plea becomes urgent and personal. God's reputation as a treasure of compassion is put to the test. If the divine presence is alive inside the holy temple, it must answer the desperate cry of a suffering devotee.

translit: niṉaiyuṭaiyāy nī-aṉṟi nēṭileṅkum illātāy maṉaiyuṭaiyār makkaḷeṉum vāḻkkaiyiṭaip paṭṭavamē iṉaiyuṭaiyāṉ eṉṟiṅ keṉaiyāḷva tuṉkaṭaṉē eṉaiyuṭaiyāy oṟṟi eḻuttaṟiyum perumāṉē.
translation: You belong only to yourself. If one searches, there is nothing anywhere without you. I am caught in vain in the domestic life of wife and children. It is your duty to declare that I bear this affliction and to take charge of me here. You are my Master, O Lord Ezhuthariyum Peruman of Otriyur.
commentary: God is everywhere and is the only reality. Yet human beings get trapped in the distractions of worldly life, like family attachments. Feeling lost in these domestic illusions, Vallalar appeals to Ezhuthariyum Peruman (the presiding deity of Otriyur), telling the Lord it is his duty to step in and rescue him.

translit: okka neñcamē oṟṟi yūrppaṭam pakka nātaṉaip paṇintu vāḻttiṉāl mikka kāmattiṉ vemmai yālvarum tukka miyāvaiyum tūra ōṭumē.
translation: O agreeable heart, if we bow to and praise the Lord Padambakkanathar of Otriyur, all the sorrows born of the heat of intense lust will run far away.
commentary: Devotion cures worldly suffering. Vallalar guides his heart to focus on Padambakkanathar, a name for Lord Siva at Otriyur, to drive away the burning distress of physical lust.

translit: ōṭum neñcamē oṉṟu kēṭṭinī nīṭum oṟṟiyūr nimalaṉ mūvarkaḷ pāṭum empaṭam pakka nātaṉtāḷ nāṭu nāṭiṭil nāṭu nammatē.
translation: O wandering heart, listen to one thing. The pure Lord of enduring Otriyur, sung by the three great saints, is our Lord Padambakkanathar. Seek his feet. If you seek them, the supreme realm is ours.
commentary: The restless mind is easily distracted. To steady it, Vallalar recalls the Lord praised by the three great saints of Tamil Shaivism. Seeking the divine feet wins the supreme spiritual realm.

translit: nampu neñcamē naṉmai eytumāl ampu yaṉpukaḻ aṇṇal oṟṟiyūrp pampu cīrppaṭam pakkaṉ oṉṉalār tampu rañcuṭum tampi rāṉaiyē.
translation: O heart, trust the Supreme Lord who burned the cities of his foes. He is the Lord Patampakkan of abundant glory in Otriyur, the master praised by Brahma born of the lotus. Goodness will surely come to us.
commentary: Trusting the divine brings lasting goodness. Vallalar reminds his heart of the Lord who burned the three flying cities of the demons, a story symbolizing the total destruction of ego and spiritual ignorance. Even Brahma, the creator god born from a lotus, praises this master.

translit: tampa lampeṟum taiya lārkaṇāl vempa lantarum veyya neñcamē ampa lattiṉil amutai oṟṟiyūrc cempa lattainī cintai ceyvaiyē.
translation: O cruel heart, you suffer great distress caused by the eyes of beautiful women. Instead, meditate upon the nectar of the Hall, the perfect fruit of Otriyur.
commentary: Physical beauty and romantic attraction leave the mind in distress. Vallalar tells his heart to abandon passing desires and meditate on the divine nectar in the Hall, representing the inner space of pure spiritual awareness.

translit: ceyyum vaṇṇamnī tēṟi neñcamē uyyum vaṇṇamām oṟṟi yūrkkuḷē meyyum vaṇṇamā ṇikka veṟparuḷ peyyum vaṇṇamē peṟutal vēṇṭumē.
translation: O heart, understand clearly what must be done. To attain salvation in Otriyur, we must receive the showering grace of the Lord who stands as the true and beautiful ruby mountain.
commentary: True salvation comes through receiving the showering grace of the divine. Vallalar pictures the Lord of Otriyur as a brilliant ruby mountain, asking his heart to understand this path and prepare to receive the light.

translit: vēṇṭum neñcamē mēvi oṟṟiyūr āṇṭu niṉṟaruḷ araciṉ poṟpatam pūṇṭu koṇṭuḷē pōṟṟi niṟpaiyēl yāṇṭum tuṉpamnī aṭaital illaiyē.
translation: O yearning heart, reach Otriyur. If you embrace the golden feet of the King of Grace who rules there and stand praising Him within, you will never experience sorrow anywhere.
commentary: Holding firmly to divine grace ends all suffering. By inwardly embracing the King of Grace at Otriyur, the yearning heart secures lasting peace.

translit: illai uṇṭeṉa eyti aiyuṟum kallai yotta-eṉ kaṉma neñcamē ollai oṟṟiyūr uṟṟu vāḻtiyēl nallai nallainī naṭpiṉ mēlaiyē.
translation: O my stony karmic heart plagued by doubts over whether He exists or not, if you quickly reach Otriyur and live there, you are good, you are truly good, and you will become greater than a friend.
commentary: Doubt makes the human heart heavy and hard like a stone. Letting go of the endless question of whether God exists and turning to Otriyur will transform this stubborn, karma-bound mind into a supportive friend.

translit: mēlai antakaṉ veyya tūtuvar ōlai kāṭṭumuṉ oṟṟi yūrilvāḻ pālai cērpaṭam pakka nātartam kālai nāṭinaṟ katiyiṉ niṟpaiyē.
translation: Before the cruel messengers of the god of death show you their summons, seek the feet of Lord Padambakkanathar who dwells in Otriyur alongside Goddess Balai, and stand in the good state of liberation.
commentary: Time in a human body is limited. Liberation must be sought before the final summons of death arrives. The path offered here is devotion to the divine presence at Otriyur: Lord Padambakkanathar and Goddess Balai.

translit: niṟpa teṉṟunī nīla neñcamē aṟpa mātartam avalam nīṅkiyē ciṟpa raṉtirut tillai ampalap poṟpaṉ oṟṟiyil pukuntu pōṟṟiyē.
translation: O dark heart, when will you stand firm? Leave the misery of petty women. Enter Otriyur and praise the Golden One, the Lord of supreme consciousness in the holy hall of Thillai.
commentary: Worldly desires pull the mind away from its true center. Abandoning the fleeting miseries of physical attraction allows the dark, unsettled heart to find stability. Focus belongs to the Lord of supreme consciousness, whose cosmic presence is available in Otriyur.

translit: pōṟṟi oṟṟiyūrp puṇṇi yaṉtiru nīṟṟi ṉāṉtaṉai niṉaintu niṟpaiyēl tōṟṟa rumparañ cōti nalaruḷ ūṟṟe ḻumkaṭal okka neñcamē.
translation: O heart, if you praise and stand remembering the pure Lord of Otriyur adorned with holy ash, the good grace of the supreme Jothi will surge up like a swelling ocean.
commentary: Sincere remembrance of the divine brings a flood of grace. Focusing on the Lord adorned with holy ash causes the supreme Jothi (the ultimate light of grace) to rise up within like a swelling ocean.

translit: tuṅka veṇpoṭi aṇintuniṉ kōyil toḻumpu ceytuniṉ tuṇaippatam ēttic ceṅkaṇ mālayaṉ tēṭiyum kāṇāc celva niṉaruḷ cērkuva teṉṟō eṅkaḷ uḷḷuvan tūṟiya amutē iṉpa mē-imai yāṉmakaṭ karacē tiṅkaḷ taṅkiya caṭaiyuṭai maruntē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O nectar welling up in our hearts! O Bliss! O King of the daughter of the mountain! O Medicine with matted hair where the moon rests! O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur! When will I wear pure white ash, do service in your temple, praise your twin feet, and attain your wealth of grace that even red-eyed Vishnu and Brahma searched for and could not see?
commentary: Vallalar longs for a life of simple devotion. He recalls an ancient story where the gods Brahma and Vishnu searched for the top and bottom of Siva's cosmic pillar of light but could not find them. This shows the divine cannot be measured by ego or intellect, but only reached through pure grace.

translit: kaṇṇa ṉōṭayaṉ kāṇparum cuṭarē kantaṉ eṉṉumōr kaṉitarum taruvē eṇṇa mētakum aṉpartam tuṇaiyē ilaṅkum tivviya eṇkuṇap poruppē aṇṇa lētiru ālaṅkāṭ ṭuṟaiyum ammai appaṉē aṭiyaṉēṉ taṉṉait tiṇṇa mē-aṭit toḻumpaṉāyc ceyvāy tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O flame difficult for Krishna and Brahma to see! O tree that yields the matchless fruit called Kandan! O companion of devotees with exalted thoughts! O mountain of eight shining divine attributes! O Lord! O Mother and Father residing in holy Alangadu! O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur! You will surely make me, your servant, a bonded slave at your feet.
commentary: God is a blazing light beyond the reach of other gods, and a fruitful tree yielding Kandan, the warrior-god Murugan. The divine is both Mother and Father, showing a relationship of unconditional care. Vallalar asks only to serve at God's feet.

translit: viṭaṅka lantaruḷ miṭaṟuṭai yavaṉē vētaṉ mālpukaḻ viṭaiyuṭai yavaṉē kaṭaṅka lantamā uriyuṭai yavaṉē kanta ṉaittarum kaṉivuṭai yavaṉē iṭaṅka lantapeṇ kūṟuṭai yavaṉē eḻilkoḷ cāmattiṉ icaiyuṭai yavaṉē tiṭaṅka lantakūr maḻuvuṭai yavaṉē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O One with a throat graced by poison! O One with the bull praised by Brahma and Vishnu! O One wearing the hide of the great elephant flowing with rut! O tender One who gave us Kandan! O One sharing your left side with a woman! O One holding the beautiful music of the Sama Veda! O One wielding the firm and sharp battle-axe! O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur!
commentary: Classic images of Siva show a perfect balance of terrifying power and compassion. He swallowed cosmic poison to save the world, holding it safely in his throat, and shares exactly half his body with the Goddess to show the unity of male and female energies. Even while wielding a sharp battle-axe and wearing the rough hide of a wild elephant, he remains the source of music and tender grace.

translit: kañca ṉōrtalai nakattaṭart tavaṉē kāmaṉ ventiṭak kaṇviḻit tavaṉē tañca māṉavark karuḷceyum paraṉē cāmik kōrtirut tantaiyā ṉavaṉē nañcam ārmaṇi kaṇṭaṉē evaikkum nāta ṉēciva ñāṉikaṭ karacē ceñcol māmaṟai ēttuṟum pataṉē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O One who pinched off a head of Brahma with a fingernail! O One who opened an eye to burn Kama to ashes! O Supreme Being who grants grace to those who seek refuge! O One who became the holy father of Swami! O One with a beautiful throat filled with poison! O Lord of all things! O King of the sages of Siva! O One whose feet are praised by the great Vedas of perfect words! O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur!
commentary: God destroys ego and worldly desire. In traditional stories, Siva pinched off one of Brahma's heads to curb his arrogance and opened his blazing third eye to burn Kama, the god of desire, to ashes. Yet this same fierce Lord is the loving father and refuge for anyone who seeks his protection.

translit: ēla vārkuḻa lāḷ iṭat tavaṉē eṉṉai āṇṭava ṉē-eṉa taracē kōla mākamāl urukkoṇṭum kāṇāk kuraika ḻaṟpatak kōmaḷak koḻuntē ñāla mītilem pōlpavar piḻaiyai nāṭi ṭātaruḷ naṟkuṇak kuṉṟē cīla mēviya tavattiṉar pōṟṟat tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O One with the lady of long fragrant hair on your left side! O One who rules me! O my King! O tender shoot whose feet wearing ringing anklets remained unseen even by Vishnu when he took the form of a great boar! O hill of good qualities who grants grace without scrutinizing the faults of people like us on this earth! O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur, you are praised by ascetics of virtuous conduct.
commentary: God's absolute majesty contrasts with his unending forgiveness. Taking the form of a giant boar to dig into the earth, Vishnu could not find the bottom of Siva's feet. Still, this supreme, unreachable Lord acts as a mountain of kindness, freely giving grace without counting the everyday faults of ordinary people.

translit: āṟu vāṇmukat tamuteḻum kaṭalē ayaṉum mālumniṉ ṟaṟivarum poruḷē ēṟu mītuvan tēṟumem aracē entai yē-emai ēṉṟukoḷ iṟaiyē vīṟu koṉṟaiyam caṭaiyuṭaik kaṉiyē vētam nāṟiya meṉmalarp pataṉē tēṟu neñciṉar nāḷtoṟum vāḻttat tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O ocean of nectar welling up with six radiant faces, O Reality difficult for Brahma and Vishnu to comprehend, our King who arrives mounting the bull, my Father, the Lord who accepts us, O sweet fruit with matted hair adorned with majestic konrai flowers, the one whose soft flower-like feet carry the fragrance of the Vedas, O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur, praised daily by those with clear hearts.
commentary: The ultimate reality is too vast for even powerful gods to comprehend, yet the divine is also a sweet, intimate father who guides us. The truth that escapes the might of gods reveals itself gently to clear, devoted human hearts.

translit: māṟu pūtta-eṉ neñciṉait tirutti mayakkam nīkkiṭa varukuva teṉṟō ēṟu pūtta-eṉ iṉṉuyirk kuyirē yāvu mākiniṉ ṟilaṅkiya poruḷē nīṟu pūttoḷi niṟaintaveṇ neruppē nitti yāṉantark kuṟṟanal uṟavē cēṟu pūttacen tāmarai muttam tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: When will you come to reform my conflicted heart and remove my delusion? O life of my sweet life blooming with greatness, O Reality shining as all things, O bright white fire smeared with ash, the good kin to those established in eternal bliss, O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur, where pearls shine on red lotuses blooming in the mud.
commentary: God is the very spark of life hidden within the soul. The divine acts as a bright, purifying fire that shines through all things to bring peace to a confused mind, clearing away conflicted feelings and mental fog.

translit: māliṉ kaṇmalar malartirup pataṉē mayiliṉ mēlvaru makavuṭai yavaṉē āliṉ kīḻaṟam aruḷpurin tavaṉē ara-eṉ pōrkaḷai aṭimaikoḷ pavaṉē kālil kūṟṟutait taruḷceyum civaṉē kaṭavu ḷēneṟṟik kaṇṇuṭai yavaṉē cēliṉ nīḷvayal ceṟinteḻil ōṅkit tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O one whose sacred feet bloomed with Vishnu's flower-like eye, the one whose son arrives upon a peacock, the one who graciously taught dharma beneath the banyan tree, the one who takes as slaves those who chant "Hara", O Siva who kicked Death with your foot and granted grace, O God who has an eye on your forehead, O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur, rising in beauty with vast fields leaping with carp.
commentary: Grace actively protects the world through ancient stories: Vishnu offers his own eye as a lotus flower in worship, the divine teacher shares wisdom beneath a banyan tree, and God kicks away the lord of death to save a devoted child. The supreme reality steps in directly to rescue those who cry out for help.

translit: nāṭṭum muppuram nakaitterit tavaṉē naṇṇi ampalam naṭañceyum pataṉē vēṭṭu veṇtalait tārpuṉain tavaṉē vēṭaṉ eccilai virumpi-uṇ ṭavaṉē kōṭṭu mēruvaik kōṭṭiya puyaṉē kuṟṟa muṅkuṇa mākkuṟip pavaṉē tīṭṭum meyppukaḻt ticaiparan tōṅkat tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O one who laughed and burned down the three fortified cities, the one whose feet reach the Hall to perform the dance, the one who gladly wore a garland of white skulls, the one who eagerly ate the hunter's tasted food, the one whose shoulders bent the peaked Mount Meru, the one who treats even faults as virtues, O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur, whose recorded true glory spreads and towers in every direction.
commentary: The divine is an overwhelming force that can burn down cosmic cities with a simple laugh, yet it melts for genuine love. Stories tell of a simple hunter who lovingly offered meat from his own mouth, an unconventional gift God eagerly accepted. The supreme reality completely ignores ritual purity and chooses to treat the messy actions of true devotion as perfect virtues.

translit: ampa lattuḷniṉ ṟāṭaval lāṉē āṉi varntuvan taruḷpuri pavaṉē campu caṅkara civaciva eṉpōr taṅkaḷ uḷḷakam cārntirup pavaṉē tumpai vaṉṉiyam caṭaimuṭi yavaṉē tūya ṉēparañ cōtiyē eṅkaḷ cempo ṉēceḻum pavaḷamā malaiyē tikaḻum oṟṟiyūrc civaperu māṉē.
translation: O one capable of dancing in the Hall, the one who mounts the bull and comes to bestow grace, the one who dwells within the hearts of those who chant "Sambu, Sankara, Siva, Siva", the one with a matted crown adorned with tumbai flowers and vanni leaves, O pure one, O supreme Jothi, our pure gold, O great mountain of rich coral, O Lord Siva of radiant Otriyur.
commentary: The supreme light (Jothi) is a living energy that dances through the universe and makes its home inside us. This pure golden presence does not wait in a distant heaven. It lives directly in the hearts of anyone who remembers it with love.

sections.title: The Divine Qualities of the Sacred Emblems

note: Editor's note: a general poem (potu, பொது), not tied to one temple.
translit: uṭaiyāyuṉ aṭiyavarkkum avarmēl pūṇṭa oṇmaṇiyām kaṇmaṇikkum ōṅku caiva aṭaiyāḷam eṉṉa-oḷir veṇṇīṟ ṟukkum aṉpilēṉ añcāmal antō antō naṭaiyāya uṭal muḻutum nāvāy niṉṟu navilkiṉṟēṉ eṉpāvi nāvaic caṟṟum iṭaiyāta koṭuntīyāl kaṭiṉum aṉṟi eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O Master! I have no love for your devotees, for the bright rudraksha beads worn on them, or for the shining white holy ash that stands as the exalted Saiva emblem. Without fear, alas, alas, turning my whole walking body into a tongue, I speak endlessly. Even if you punish my sinful tongue with unceasing fierce fire, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: Paralyzed by hypocrisy, Vallalar confesses he talks endlessly about spirituality but feels no actual love for God's devotees or sacred emblems like holy ash and rudraksha (prayer beads). The image of his entire body turning into a babbling tongue shows how empty words replace genuine devotion.

translit: kaṇṇutalē niṉaṭiyār tamaiyum nōkkēṉ kaṇmaṇimā laikkeṉiṉum kaṉintu nillēṉ paṇṇutalcēr tirunīṟṟuk kōlam taṉṉaip pārttēṉum añcukilēṉ payaṉi lāmē naṇṇutalcēr uṭampellām nāvāy niṉṟu navilkiṉṟēṉ eṉkoṭiya nāvai antō eṇṇutalcēr koṭuntīyāl cuṭiṉum aṉṟi eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O Lord with an eye on your forehead! I do not look upon your devotees. I do not melt with reverence even for a garland of rudraksha beads. I do not feel awe even when looking upon a form adorned with sacred ash. Uselessly, turning my whole body into a tongue, I speak endlessly. Even if you burn my cruel tongue with fierce fire, alas, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: True reverence softens the heart, but Vallalar laments that his remains unmoved by holy sights. His endless, empty chatter is such a severe spiritual failure that even the harshest physical punishment could not atone for it.

translit: vañcamilār neñcakattē maruvum mukkaṇ māmaṇiyē uṉainiṉaiyēṉ vāḷā nāḷaik kañcamalar mukattiyarkkum vātil tōṉṟum kaḷippiṉukkum kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ kaṭaiya ṉēṉai nañcamuṇak koṭuttumaṭit tiṭiṉum vāḷāl nacippuṟavē tuṇittiṭiṉum naliyat tīyāl eñcaluṟac cuṭiṉumaṉṟi antō iṉṉum eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O great gem with three eyes who abides in the hearts of those without deceit! I do not think of you. I waste my days uselessly on lotus-faced women and on the joy of arguments. For me, the lowest one, even if you feed me poison and kill me, even if you chop me to pieces with a sword, even if you burn me to cinders with tormenting fire, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: The Divine lives in honest, open hearts, but Vallalar's mind is scattered by worldly attractions and the shallow thrill of winning debates. Alienated from this inner purity, he invites absolute destruction, convinced his deceitful life deserves nothing less.

translit: aruḷpaḻukkum kaṟpakamē aracē mukkaṇ āramutē niṉaippukaḻēṉ antō vañca maruḷpaḻukkum neñcakattēṉ vāḷā nāḷai vātamiṭṭuk kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ matiyi lēṉai veruḷpaḻukkum kaṭuṅkāṭṭil viṭiṉum āṟṟu veḷḷattil aṭittēka viṭiṉum pollā iruḷpaḻukkum pilañcēra viṭiṉum aṉṟi eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O wish-fulfilling tree ripening with grace! O King! O rare nectar with three eyes! I do not praise you. Alas, possessing a heart ripening with deceit and delusion, I waste my days uselessly in arguments. For me, the mindless one, even if you abandon me in a fierce forest ripening with terror, even if you let me be swept away by a river flood, even if you cast me into a cavern ripening with evil darkness, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: Wasting life on trivial arguments creates inner darkness. Vallalar contrasts God's boundless grace with his own delusion. Being lost in a terrifying forest or swept away in a flood would merely match the spiritual wasteland he has already built inside himself.

translit: peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭalē-eṉ kuruvē mukkaṇ perumāṉē niṉaippukaḻēṉ pēyēṉ antō karuṅkalmaṉak kuraṅkāṭṭi vāḷā nāḷaik kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ payaṉaṟiyāk kaṭaiya ṉēṉai oruṅkuruḷa uṭalpataippa uṟuṅkuṉ ṟēṟṟi uruṭṭukiṉum uyirnaṭuṅka uḷḷam ēṅka iruṅkaḻuvil ēṟṟukiṉum aṉṟi iṉṉum eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O ocean of great compassion! O my Guru! O Lord with three eyes! I am a demon and I do not praise you. Alas, making my black-stone mind dance like a monkey, I waste my days uselessly. For me, the lowest one who knows no purpose, even if you take me up a steep mountain and roll me down so my body shudders and tumbles all at once, even if you impale me on a large stake so my life trembles and my heart despairs, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: God is an ocean of mercy, yet Vallalar's mind remains hard as stone and restless as a wild monkey. The violent physical punishments he imagines express the inner agony caused by knowing life's highest purpose but failing to live it.

translit: toḻukiṉṟōr uḷattamarnta cuṭarē mukkaṇ cuṭarkkoḻuntē niṉpatattait tutiyēṉ vātil viḻukiṉṟēṉ nallōrkaḷ veṟuppap pēci veṟittuḻalum nāyaṉaiyēṉ viḻala ṉēṉai uḻukiṉṟa nukappaṭaikoṇ ṭulaiyat taḷḷi uḻakkiṉumneṭ ṭuṭalnaṭuṅka uṟukki mēṉmēl eḻukiṉṟa kaṭaliṭaivīḻt tiṭiṉum aṉṟi eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O Flame seated in the hearts of those who worship! O three-eyed blazing shoot of light! I do not praise your feet. I fall into arguments. I speak words that good people detest. I wander madly like a dog. I am utterly worthless. Even if you push me under a heavy ploughing yoke and crush me, or terrify me until my tall body trembles and hurl me into the ever-rising sea, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: Vallalar feels intense remorse for wasting his life on bitter arguments and unkind words instead of devotion. This failure of love is so deep that even the most terrifying physical punishments could never atone for it.

translit: viruppākum maticcaṭaiyāy viṭaiyāy eṉṟē meyyaṉpō ṭuṉaittutiyēṉ viraintu vañcak karuppāyum vilaṅkeṉavē vaḷarntē nāḷaik kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ karuneñcak kaḷva ṉēṉaip poruppāya yāṉaiyiṉ kāl iṭiṉum pollāp puḻuttalaiyil cōripuṟam poḻiya nīṇṭa iruppāṇi ēṟṟukiṉum aṉṟi iṉṉum eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O Lord wearing the beloved crescent moon in your matted hair! O Rider of the bull! I do not praise you with true love. Growing rapidly like a deceitful wild beast, I waste my days. I am a dark-hearted thief. Even if you crush me under the feet of mountain-like elephants, or drive a long iron nail into my wicked, worm-infested head so that blood pours out, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: A life without true love for God is no better than that of a wild, deceitful beast. Vallalar sees his lack of devotion as a dark theft of the soul. The most brutal executions imaginable are insufficient penalties for a heart that refuses to love.

translit: akkanutal piṟaiccaṭaiyāy niṉtāḷ ēttēṉ āṇpaṉaipōl mikanīṇṭēṉ aṟivoṉ ṟillēṉ mikka-oti pōlparuttēṉ karuṅka ṭāppōl vīṇkarumat tuḻalkiṉṟēṉ viḻala ṉēṉaic cekkiṭaivait tuṭalkuḻampic citaiya antō tiruppiṭiṉum iruppaṟaimuṭ cērac cērttu ekkariṭai uruṭṭukiṉum aṉṟi iṉṉum eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O Lord with a forehead eye and a crescent moon in your matted hair! I do not praise your feet. I have grown very tall like a male palmyra tree. I possess no wisdom at all. I have grown stout like an Odi tree. Like a black he-goat, I wander around doing worthless deeds. I am completely useless. Alas, even if you place me in an oil press and grind me until my body is crushed to a pulp, or bind me with iron spikes and roll me across sandy dunes, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: Physical growth means nothing without spiritual wisdom. Vallalar compares himself to a male palmyra palm and an Odi tree (a species known for soft, useless wood), which grow large but yield no real benefit. Wandering through life doing empty deeds leaves him so hollow that no punishment is enough.

translit: aṉpuṭaṉniṉ patampukaḻāp pāvi nāvai aṟattuṇiyēṉ niṉaḻakai amarntu kāṇāt tuṉpuṟukaṇ iraṇṭiṉaiyum cūṉṟēṉ niṉṉait toḻākkaiyai vāḷataṉāl tuṇṭa mākkēṉ vaṉpaṟaniṉ taṉaivaṇaṅkāt talaiyai antō maṭittilēṉ otiyēpōl vaḷarntēṉ eṉṉai iṉpaṟuval eriyiṭaivīḻt tiṭiṉum aṉṟi eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: I do not sever this sinner's tongue that fails to praise your feet with love. I do not pluck out these two miserable eyes that fail to sit and gaze upon your beauty. I do not chop into pieces with a sword these hands that fail to worship you. Alas, to rid myself of arrogance, I do not destroy this head that fails to bow to you. I have merely grown like a useless Odi tree. Even if you cast me into a fierce fire that consumes all joy, or whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: The physical body only has value if its organs and senses are used to experience the divine. Vallalar expresses violent frustration with his own anatomy, wishing to sever the sensory organs that fail to seek God. Arrogance is a sickness that renders the entire body useless, making it fit only for the fire.

translit: tēvēniṉ aṭiniṉaiyā vañca neñcait tīmūṭṭic citaikkaṟiyēṉ cetukku killēṉ kōvēniṉ aṭiyartamaik kūṭāp poymaik kuṭikoṇṭēṉ pulaikoṇṭa koṭiyēṉ antō nāvēṟa niṉaittutiyēṉ nalamoṉ ṟillēṉ nāykkaṭaikkum kaṭaippaṭṭēṉ naṇṇu kiṉṟōrk kīvētum aṟiyēṉiṅ keṉṉai yantō eṉceyiṉum pōtātē entāy entāy.
translation: O God! I do not know how to set fire to and destroy this deceitful heart that never thinks of your feet, nor do I carve it out. O King! I harbor falsehood and fail to associate with your devotees. Alas, I am a cruel and base person. I do not praise you aloud with my tongue. I possess no goodness at all. I am lower than the lowest dog. I do not know how to give anything to those who approach me. Alas, whatever else you do to me, it is not enough, my Father, my Father!
commentary: The ultimate spiritual failure is a closed heart that neither remembers God nor helps others. Vallalar connects his lack of devotion directly to a lack of Jeevakarunyam (compassion for all living beings), confessing he cannot give to those in need. Placing himself lower than a stray dog, he feels a life without charity and truth is worthless.

sections.title: The Decad on the Beauty of Lord Thyagar

tamil: காரார் குழலாள் உமையோ டயில்வேல் காளையொ டுந்தான் அமர்கின்ற
ஏரார் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் எண்ணும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
நீரார் சடைமேல் பிறையொன் றுடையான் நிதிக்கோன் தோழன் எனநின்றான்
பேரார் ஒற்றி யூரான் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: kārār kuḻalāḷ umaiyō ṭayilvēl kāḷaiyo ṭuntāṉ amarkiṉṟa ērār kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ eṇṇum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl nīrār caṭaimēl piṟaiyoṉ ṟuṭaiyāṉ nitikkōṉ tōḻaṉ eṉaniṉṟāṉ pērār oṟṟi yūrāṉ tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: If He does not grant a single boon to us who long to rejoice at the sight of His beautiful form seated with Uma whose hair is like dark clouds and the youth wielding the sharp spear, then He who wears the crescent moon on His water-drenched matted hair, He who stands known as the friend of the lord of wealth, the Lord of renowned Otriyur, Lord Thyagar, is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Vallalar playfully scolds Siva, demanding a vision of his divine family. He points out an irony: the Lord is the close friend of the god of wealth, yet if he refuses to grant a single wish to a longing devotee, he is just a wandering beggar. This loving reproach shows a fearless intimacy with the divine.

tamil: தண்ணார் நீபத் தாரா னொடும்எம் தாயோ டும்தான் அமர்கின்ற
கண்ணார் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் கருதும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
பண்ணார் இன்சொல் பதிகம் கொண்டு படிக்கா சளித்த பரமன்ஓர்
பெண்ணார் பாகன் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: taṇṇār nīpat tārā ṉoṭumem tāyō ṭumtāṉ amarkiṉṟa kaṇṇār kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ karutum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl paṇṇār iṉcol patikam koṇṭu paṭikkā caḷitta paramaṉōr peṇṇār pākaṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: If He does not grant a single boon to us who yearn to rejoice at the sight of His enchanting form seated with our Mother and the youth wearing a garland of cool kadamba flowers, then the Supreme Lord who gave daily gold coins for decads of sweet musical words, He who shares half His form with a woman, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Vallalar references a legend where Siva gave daily gold coins to saints who sang hymns to him. If a God so generous in the past will not grant a vision to a yearning soul today, his grand titles mean nothing and he is merely a lord of alms.

tamil: பத்தர்க் கருளும் பாவையொ டும்வேல் பாலனொ டும்தான் அமர்கின்ற
நித்தக் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் நினைக்கும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
சித்தப் பெருமான் தில்லைப் பெருமான் தெய்வப் பெருமான் சிவபெருமான்
பித்தப் பெருமான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: pattark karuḷum pāvaiyo ṭumvēl pālaṉo ṭumtāṉ amarkiṉṟa nittak kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ niṉaikkum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl cittap perumāṉ tillaip perumāṉ teyvap perumāṉ civaperumāṉ pittap perumāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: If He does not grant a single boon to us who long to rejoice at the sight of His eternal form seated with the Goddess who bestows grace upon devotees and the boy holding the spear, then the Lord of the mind, the Lord of Thillai, the divine Lord, Lord Siva, the mad Lord, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: A vision of God includes his boundless grace and protective power, represented by the Mother goddess and her spear-wielding son. Vallalar contrasts the grandest titles of the divine—the ruler of the mind and the cosmos—with the lowly title of a mad beggar. Piling up glorious names highlights the absurdity of such a supreme being refusing a prayer.

tamil: மன்னும் கதிர்வேல் மகனா ரோடும் மலையா ளொடும்தான் வதிகின்ற
துன்னும் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் துதிக்கும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
மின்னும் சூலப் படையான் விடையான் வெள்ளிமலையொன் றதுஉடையான்
பின்னும் சடையான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: maṉṉum katirvēl makaṉā rōṭum malaiyā ḷoṭumtāṉ vatikiṉṟa tuṉṉum kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ tutikkum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl miṉṉum cūlap paṭaiyāṉ viṭaiyāṉ veḷḷimalaiyoṉ ṟatu-uṭaiyāṉ piṉṉum caṭaiyāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: If He does not grant a single boon to us who praise Him, longing to rejoice at the sight of His intimately seated form with the Daughter of the Mountain and His son holding the enduring radiant spear, then He who wields the gleaming trident, He who rides the bull, He who owns the peerless silver mountain, He who has braided matted hair, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Siva owns an entire mountain of silver and rides a mighty bull, but Vallalar suggests this vast cosmic wealth is useless if kept to himself. A God who hoards his grace instead of sharing it with those who praise him is no better than a beggar.

tamil: அணிவேல் படைகொள் மகனா ரொடும்எம் அம்மை யொடுந்தான் அமர்கின்ற
தணியாக் கோலம்கண்டு களிக்கத் தகையா தெமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
மணிசேர் கண்டன் எண்தோள் உடையான் வடபால் கனக மலைவில்லான்
பிணிபோக் கிடுவான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: aṇivēl paṭaikoḷ makaṉā roṭumem ammai yoṭuntāṉ amarkiṉṟa taṇiyāk kōlamkaṇṭu kaḷikkat takaiyā temakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl maṇicēr kaṇṭaṉ eṇtōḷ uṭaiyāṉ vaṭapāl kaṉaka malaivillāṉ piṇipōk kiṭuvāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: If He does not freely grant a single boon to us who long to rejoice at the sight of His endlessly beautiful form seated with our Mother and His son wielding the beautiful spear, then He who has a jewel-hued throat, He who has eight shoulders, He who holds the northern golden mountain as a bow, He who dispels all disease, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Vallalar praises the Lord as the healer who removes the diseases of worldly life. Yet holding the northern golden mountain as a mighty bow means little if that immense power does not translate into freely given grace. The relentless repetition of the beggar insult is a classic technique of Tamil devotion, transforming apparent disrespect into the highest expression of intimacy.

tamil: சூத மெறிவேல் தோன்ற லொடும்தன் துணைவி யொடும்தான் அமர்கின்ற
காதல் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் கருதும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
ஈதல் வல்லான் எல்லாம் உடையான் இமையோர் அயன்மாற் கிறையானான்
பேதம் இல்லான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: cūta meṟivēl tōṉṟa loṭumtaṉ tuṇaivi yoṭumtāṉ amarkiṉṟa kātal kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ karutum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl ītal vallāṉ ellām uṭaiyāṉ imaiyōr ayaṉmāṟ kiṟaiyāṉāṉ pētam illāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: He sits with His consort and His son who hurled the spear at the mango tree. We long to see this loving form and rejoice. If He does not grant us a boon, then He who is capable of giving, who possesses everything, the Lord of the celestials, Brahma, and Vishnu, who is free from partiality, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Vallalar longs to see the divine family together: the Lord, his consort, and their son who destroyed a demon disguised as a mango tree. If the ruler of all things refuses to grant this wish, he might as well be called a beggar.

tamil: வெற்றிப் படைவேல் பிள்ளை யோடும் வெற்பா ளொடும்தான் அமர்கின்ற
மற்றிக் கோலம் கண்டு களிப்பான் வருந்தும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
கற்றைச் சடையான் கண்மூன் றுடையான் கரியோன் அயனும் காணாதான்
பெற்றத் திவர்வான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: veṟṟip paṭaivēl piḷḷai yōṭum veṟpā ḷoṭumtāṉ amarkiṉṟa maṟṟik kōlam kaṇṭu kaḷippāṉ varuntum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl kaṟṟaic caṭaiyāṉ kaṇmūṉ ṟuṭaiyāṉ kariyōṉ ayaṉum kāṇātāṉ peṟṟat tivarvāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: He sits with the daughter of the mountain and His son wielding the victorious weapon, the spear. We ache to see this form and rejoice. If He does not grant us a boon, then He with the thick matted hair, the one with three eyes, whom the dark Vishnu and Brahma could not see, who mounts the bull, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Siva has three eyes and thick matted hair, remaining unseen even by the creator gods. Yet if he withholds the joy of letting a devotee see his loving family form, all his greatness amounts to nothing more than a beggar's poverty.

tamil: வரமன் றலினார் குழலா ளொடும்வேல் மகனா ரொடும்தான் அமர்கின்ற
திரமன் றவுநின் றெழில்கண் டிடுவான் சிறக்க எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
பரமன் தனிமால் விடைஒன் றுடையான் பணியே பணியாப் பரிவுற்றான்
பிரமன் தலையான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: varamaṉ ṟaliṉār kuḻalā ḷoṭumvēl makaṉā roṭumtāṉ amarkiṉṟa tiramaṉ ṟavuniṉ ṟeḻilkaṇ ṭiṭuvāṉ ciṟakka emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl paramaṉ taṉimāl viṭai-oṉ ṟuṭaiyāṉ paṇiyē paṇiyāp parivuṟṟāṉ piramaṉ talaiyāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: He sits with His son holding the spear and the lady with tresses filled with exceptional fragrance. We stand firmly hoping to see this beautiful form. If He does not grant us an excellent boon, then the Supreme Being, the incomparable one who owns a single bull, who affectionately wears a snake as an ornament, who holds Brahma's skull, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: Vallalar waits with steady hope to see the Lord seated beside his fragrant goddess and warrior son. This is an affectionate challenge: a supreme being who wears a serpent and holds a skull must prove his wealth by granting grace, or else he is just a destitute wanderer.

tamil: அறங்கொள் உமையோ டயிலேந் தியஎம் ஐய னொடுந்தான் அமர்கின்ற
திறங்கொள் கோலம் கண்டுக ளிப்பான் சிறக்க எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
மறங்கொள் எயில்மூன் றெரித்தான் கனக மலையான் அடியார் மயல்தீர்ப்பான்
பிறங்கும் சடையான்ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: aṟaṅkoḷ umaiyō ṭayilēn tiya-em aiya ṉoṭuntāṉ amarkiṉṟa tiṟaṅkoḷ kōlam kaṇṭuka ḷippāṉ ciṟakka emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl maṟaṅkoḷ eyilmūṉ ṟerittāṉ kaṉaka malaiyāṉ aṭiyār mayaltīrppāṉ piṟaṅkum caṭaiyāṉoṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: He sits with Uma who embodies dharma, and our lord holding the sharp spear. We wish to see this majestic form and rejoice. If He does not grant us an excellent boon, then He who burned the three fierce fortresses, whose bow is the golden mountain, who clears the delusions of His devotees, who possesses radiant matted hair, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: The Lord's consort embodies dharma (righteous duty), and Siva himself is fierce enough to burn down three demonic fortresses. Despite this power to destroy evil and clear the mind's delusions, he is playfully scolded as a beggar if he will not share a glimpse of his majestic form.

tamil: தேசார் அயில்வேல் மகனா ரொடும்தன் தேவி யொடும்தான் அமர்கோலம்
ஈசா எனநின் றேத்திக் காண எண்ணும் எமக்கொன் றருளானேல்
காசார் அரவக் கச்சேர் இடையான் கண்ணார் நுதலான் கனிவுற்றுப்
பேசார்க்கருளான் ஒற்றித் தியாகப் பெருமான் பிச்சைப் பெருமானே.
translit: tēcār ayilvēl makaṉā roṭumtaṉ tēvi yoṭumtāṉ amarkōlam īcā eṉaniṉ ṟēttik kāṇa eṇṇum emakkoṉ ṟaruḷāṉēl kācār aravak kaccēr iṭaiyāṉ kaṇṇār nutalāṉ kaṉivuṟṟup pēcārkkaruḷāṉ oṟṟit tiyākap perumāṉ piccaip perumāṉē.
translation: He sits in form with His goddess and His son holding the radiant sharp spear. We stand praising Him, crying out to the Lord, hoping to see this. If He does not grant us a boon, then He who has a dark serpent bound around His waist, who has a beautiful eye on His forehead, who denies His grace to those who do not speak with a melting heart, Lord Thyagar of Otriyur is indeed a Lord of alms.
commentary: The Lord demands devotion and denies his grace to anyone whose heart does not melt with love. Vallalar stands crying out in praise, arguing that if such heartfelt longing goes unanswered, the mighty Lord is no better than a common beggar.

sections.title: Ten Verses on the Nectar of the Dance

note: Editor's note: sung at Otriyur and at Thillai (Chidambaram) (tiruvoṟṟiyūrum tiruttillaiyum, திருவொற்றியூரும் திருத்தில்லையும்).
translit: cintai nontunon tayarkiṉṟēṉ civaṉē ceyva tōrntilēṉ tīkkuṇa muṭaiyēṉ vantu niṉṉaṭik kāṭceya eṉṟāl vañca neñcameṉ vacamniṉṟa tilaiyē entai niṉṉaruḷ uṇṭeṉil uyvēṉ illai eṉṉilnāṉ illai-uyn tiṭalē anti vāṉniṟat toṟṟiyūr aracē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: My mind aches and aches. I languish, O Siva. I do not know what to do. I possess an evil nature. When I tell my deceitful heart to come and serve your feet, it does not remain under my control. O my Father, if I have your grace, I will be saved. Without it, there is no salvation for me. O King of Otriyur, radiant with the color of the evening sky! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: The mind has a will of its own, resisting every effort to turn toward the divine. Vallalar confesses that his own heart is deceitful and out of his control. Personal effort is useless without grace, which alone makes spiritual survival possible.

translit: māya neñcamō niṉṉaṭi vaḻuttā vaṇṇa meṉtaṉai valikkiṉṟa tataṉāl tīyaṉ āyiṉēṉ eṉceyvēṉ civaṉē tiruva ruṭkunāṉ cēyaṉum āṉēṉ kāya vāḻkkaiyil kāmamuṇ ṭuḷḷam kalaṅku kiṉṟaṉaṉ kaḷaikaṇmaṟ ṟaṟiyēṉ āya oṟṟiyūr aṇṇalē tillai ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: My illusory heart forcefully pulls me away from praising your feet. Because of this, I have become wicked. What shall I do, O Siva? I have become distant from your divine grace. Entangled in lust during this bodily life, my heart is troubled. I know no other refuge. O Lord of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall of Thillai!
commentary: The physical senses drag attention away from spiritual practice. Caught in the urges of bodily life, the distracted mind feels cut off from grace. With personal willpower failing, the divine becomes the only refuge.

translit: uṉṉai uṉṉinek kurukiniṉ ṟētta uḷḷam eṉvacam uṟṟatiṉ ṟēṉum eṉṉai āḷutal uṉkaṭaṉ aṉṟēl irakkam eṉpatuṉ ṉiṭattilai aṉṟō muṉṉai valviṉai muṭittiṭil civaṉē mūṭa ṉēṉukku muṉṉiṟpa tevaṉō aṉṉai appaṉē oṟṟiyūr aracē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: I try to think of you, to melt and praise you, but my mind does not remain under my control today. Even so, if ruling me is not your duty, does that not mean you lack compassion? If you let my ancient strong karma destroy me, O Siva, who will stand before this fool to help? O Mother and Father! O King of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: Vallalar boldly questions divine compassion. If God is merciful, saving a struggling soul is a matter of duty. When past actions, known as karma, threaten to destroy a person, they cannot save themselves. The divine must step in and take responsibility.

translit: eṉṉa nāṉcoli niṟuttiṉum nillā tēku kiṉṟativ ēḻaiyēṉ maṉantāṉ uṉṉa tiṉṉaruḷ oruciṟi tuṇṭēl oṭukki niṟpaṉāl uṇmaimaṟ ṟiṉṟēl iṉṉa teṉṟaṟi yāmala iruḷil iṭarkoḷ vēṉaṉṟi eṉceyvēṉ civaṉē aṉṉa tuṉceyal oṟṟiyūr aracē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: Whatever I say to stop it, the mind of this poor wretch does not remain still but wanders away. If even a little of your sweet grace falls upon me, I will subdue it and stand firm. Truly, if I lack your grace, I will only suffer in the darkness of ignorance without understanding anything. What else can I do, O Siva? That outcome rests in your hands, O King of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: Words and logic are powerless against a wandering mind. Only a small drop of grace is needed to quiet thoughts and anchor attention. Without that direct help, a person remains trapped in the dark, at the mercy of their own confusion.

translit: pāvi neñcameṉ pālirā tōṭip pāvai yārmayal paṭintuḻaip pataṉāl cēvi yāta-eṉ piḻaipoṟut tāḷum ceykai niṉṉatē ceppaleṉ civaṉē kāvi nērviḻi malaimakaḷ kāṇak kaṭaliṉ nañcuṇṭu kaṇṇaṉā tiyarkaḷ āvi īntaruḷ oṟṟi-em iṟaiyē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: My sinful heart does not stay with me. It runs away and struggles, steeped in the delusion of women. Forgiving my failure to serve you and taking me into your rule is your duty alone. What more can I say, O Siva? As the Mountain's Daughter with lily-dark eyes watched, you consumed the ocean's poison and graciously saved the lives of Vishnu and the other gods, O my Lord of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: The mind naturally prefers delusion over devotion, so asking for help requires forgiveness. An ancient story tells how Siva drank the ocean's poison to save the other gods. Just as the Lord absorbed that fatal poison to protect the world, he must now absorb Vallalar's flaws and save him from his own mind.

translit: mūṭa neñcameṉ moḻivaḻi nillā mōka vāriyiṉ muḻukukiṉ ṟatukāṇ tēṭa eṉvacam aṉṟatu civaṉē tiruva ruṭkaṭal tivalai-oṉ ṟuṟumēl nāṭa nāṭiya nalampeṟum ataṉāl nāṉum uykuvēṉ nalkiṭal vēṇṭum āṭal oṟṟiyāy perumpaṟṟap puliyūr ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: My foolish heart does not heed my words. Look, it drowns in the ocean of delusion. Restraining it is beyond my control, O Siva. If a single drop from the ocean of your divine grace reaches it, it will attain the true good it seeks. Through that, I too will be saved. You must grant this. O Lord of dancing Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall of Perumbatrappuliyur!
commentary: The human mind is stubborn and easily lost in worldly illusions. Vallalar admits he cannot rein in his wandering thoughts by willpower alone. Yet divine grace is so powerful that even a single drop can calm his mind and save him.

translit: kalaṅku kiṉṟa-eṉ kaṇuṉa taruḷōr kaṭukiṉ ellaitāṉ kalantiṭu māṉāl vilaṅku kiṉṟa-eṉ neñcamniṉ ṟiṭumāl vēṟu nāṉpeṟum vēṭkaiyum iṉṟāl malaṅku kiṉṟatai māṟṟuvaṉ uṉatu malarppoṉ tāḷalāl maṟṟilaṉ civaṉē alaṅku kiṉṟacīr oṟṟiyūr iṟaiyē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: If your grace mixes with my troubled eyes even to the measure of a mustard seed, my straying heart will stand still. I have no other desire to achieve. I will dispel this confusion. I have no refuge other than your golden lotus feet, O Siva. O Lord of radiant and glorious Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: A mustard seed is a traditional measure for something very small. This tiny speck of grace is enough to make a wandering heart stand still. Vallalar asks for nothing else, knowing this small touch of the divine will clear away all worldly confusion.

translit: maṟaiva teṉṉaiyum maṟaippatu pollā vañca neñcameṉ vacappaṭal ilaikāṇ iṟaiva niṉṉaruṭ keṉceyvōm eṉavē eṇṇi eṇṇināṉ ēṅkukiṉ ṟaṉaṉāl uṟaiva tuṉṉaṭi malaraṉṟi maṟṟoṉ ṟuṇarnti lēṉiḵ tuṇmainī aṟiti aṟaiva teṉṉanāṉ oṟṟiyūr aracē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: Look, this evil and deceitful heart conceals everything, it conceals me, and it refuses to come under my control. I yearn, constantly wondering what I can do to earn your grace, O Lord. I know no dwelling place other than your lotus feet. This is the truth, and you know it. What more can I say? O King of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: The deceitful mind acts as a veil, hiding the truth and making a person forget their true nature. Unable to tame his thoughts, Vallalar feels helpless and worries about how to earn God's grace. He brings this anxiety directly to the divine, a reminder that he has nowhere else to turn.

translit: oruka ṇappoḻu tēṉuniṉ aṭiyai uḷki ṭātuḷam ōṭukiṉ ṟataṉāl tiruka ṇappeṟum tīyaṉēṉ ceyyum tiṟama ṟintilēṉ ceppaleṉ civaṉē varuka ṇattuṭal niṟkumō viḻumō māyu mō-eṉa mayaṅkuvēṉ taṉṉai aruka ṇaittaruḷ oṟṟiyūr iṟaiyē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: My heart runs astray without contemplating your feet even for a split second. Because of this, I am wicked and cursed with twisted vision. I do not know what to do. What can I say, O Siva? I am bewildered, wondering whether my body will stand, fall, or perish in the very next second. Draw me near and bestow your grace. O Lord of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: A scattered mind creates a distorted view of the world. Vallalar is struck by the fragile nature of life, realizing his physical body could fail at any moment. This acute awareness of mortality makes the need for divine shelter urgent.

translit: yātu niṉkarut taṟintilēṉ maṉamō eṉva cappaṭā tiruttalai uraittēṉ tītu ceyyiṉum poṟutteṉaic civaṉē tīya valviṉaic cērntiṭā vaṇṇam pātu kāppatuṉ paramiṉṟēl palavāyp pakartal eṉṉakāṇ paḻivarum uṉakkē ātu kāṇṭi-em oṟṟiyūr aracē ampa lattiṉiṉ ṟāṭalcey amutē.
translation: I do not know your intention. I have already told you that my mind remains utterly beyond my control. Bear with me even if I commit evil, O Siva. It is your burden to protect me so that cruel karma does not attach to me. If you do not do this, why should I speak at length? The blame will fall entirely on you. See to this, our King of Otriyur! O Nectar who dances in the Hall!
commentary: This is a moment of absolute surrender. Vallalar places the responsibility for his spiritual safety squarely on God. He states boldly that if God allows him to fall into the consequences of bad actions, the blame will rest on the divine.

sections.title: Taking Refuge at the Holy Feet

translit: ōṭal eṅkaṇum namakkeṉṉa kuṟaikāṇ uṟṟa naṟṟuṇai oṉṟumil lārpōl vāṭal neñcamē varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē makiḻntu nāmiru varumceṉṟu makiḻvāyk kūṭal nērtiru oṟṟiyūr akattuk kōyil mēvinam kuṭimuḻu tāḷat tāḷta lantarum namataruḷ celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: Stop running everywhere. What do we lack? O heart, do not wither like those who have no good companion. Come with me joyfully. The two of us will gladly go to the temple in beautiful Otriyur. He grants the refuge of His feet to rule our entire lineage. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father.
commentary: Vallalar speaks directly to his own heart, treating it as a close friend who has lost its way. He promises that peace and spiritual wealth wait for them at the divine feet, offering a permanent home away from wandering.

translit: ēṅki nōkiṉṟa teṟṟiṉuk kōnī eṇṇi vēṇṭiya tiyāvaiyum uṉakku vāṅki īkuvaṉ oṉṟukkum añcēl makiḻntu neñcamē varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē ōṅki vāḻoṟṟi yūriṭai aravum oḷikoḷ tiṅkaḷum kaṅkaiyum caṭaimēl tāṅki vāḻumnam tāṇuvām celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: Why do you yearn and ache? I will get you everything you think of and desire. Do not fear anything. O heart, come with me joyfully. He bears a snake, the luminous moon, and the River Ganga on His matted hair. He lives as the eternal pillar in highly prosperous Otriyur. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father.
commentary: The anxious mind is assured it has nothing to fear and nothing to lack. The imagery of Siva, bearing a snake, the moon, and the river Ganga, presents God as the eternal, immovable pillar who grants everything the heart needs.

translit: kayavar illiṭaik kalaṅkalai neñcē kāma aimpulak kaḷvarai vīṭṭi vayama ḷikkuvaṉ kāṇṭi-eṉ moḻiyai maṟutti ṭēliṉṟu varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē uyava ḷikkunal oṟṟiyūr amarntaṅ kuṟṟu vāḻttiniṉ ṟuṉṉukiṉ ṟavarkkut tayava ḷikkunam taṉimutal celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: O heart, do not suffer in the houses of base men. I will destroy the thieves of the five senses driven by lust and grant you victory. See this truth. Do not reject my words. Come with me today. He resides in good Otriyur that grants salvation. He bestows mercy on those who gather, praise, and meditate upon Him. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father, the supreme primal Lord.
commentary: Seeking favors from base people only brings suffering. The five physical senses are thieves because they steal the mind's peace through constant craving. The cure is to turn toward the supreme Lord, who offers mercy and victory over these distractions.

translit: caṇṭa vempavap piṇiyiṉāl tantai tāyi lāreṉat tayaṅkukiṉ ṟāyē maṇṭa lattuḻal neñcamē cukamā vāḻa vēṇṭiṭil varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē oṇta lattiru oṟṟiyūr iṭattum uṉṉu kiṉṟavar uḷḷakam eṉumōr taṇta lattiṉum cārntanam celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: You hesitate and suffer like someone without a father or mother, afflicted by the fierce and cruel disease of worldly birth. O heart wandering in this world, if you wish to live happily, come with me. He dwells in the bright realm of Otriyur and in the cool realm of the inner heart of those who meditate upon Him. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father.
commentary: The endless cycle of birth makes the soul feel like an orphan afflicted by the disease of worldly life. Yet God is never far away. He dwells equally in the physical temple of Otriyur and in the quiet, cool space of the meditating heart.

translit: viṭaṅkoḷ kaṇṇiṉār aṭiviḻun taiyō veṭki ṉāyinta viti-uṉak kēṉō maṭaṅkoḷ neñcamē niṉakkiṉṟu nalla vāḻvu vantatu varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē iṭaṅkoḷ pāriṭai namakkiṉi oppā riyārkaṇ ṭāyoṉṟum eṇṇalai kamalat taṭaṅkoḷ oṟṟiyūr amarntanam celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: Alas, you fell at the feet of women with poison-like eyes and suffered shame. Why do you have this fate? O ignorant heart, a good life has come to you today. Come with me. Who in this vast world is equal to us now? Understand this truth. Do not worry about anything. He resides in Otriyur, a place filled with broad lotus ponds. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father.
commentary: The heart is reminded of the pain and shame that come from chasing lust and transient pleasures. Once the mind decides to seek divine refuge, a new and dignified life begins. Freed from old desires, the soul gains a spiritual wealth that makes it unmatched in the world.

translit: porunti īṉaruḷ pukuntuvīṇ kālam pōkki niṉṟaṉai pōṉatu pōka varunti iṉṉumiṅ kuḻaṉṟiṭēl neñcē vāḻka vāḻkanī varuti-eṉ ṉuṭaṉē tirunti niṉṟanam mūvartam patikac ceyya tīntamiḻt tēṟaluṇ ṭaruḷait tarunteṉ oṟṟiyūr vāḻunam celvat tantai yāraṭic caraṇpuka lāmē.
translation: You mingled with the base and wasted your time. Let the past be past. Do not suffer and wander here any longer, O heart. May you prosper, may you prosper. Come with me. Let us take refuge at the feet of our wealthy Father who dwells in beautiful southern Otriyur.
