commentary: The approach of death brings terrifying clarity. Vallalar realizes that when death's messengers arrive, without the saving grace of Shambu (a name for Siva), he will have no refuge.

tamil: நீரின்மேல் எழுதும் எழுத்தினும் விரைந்து நிலைபடா உடம்பினை ஓம்பிப்
பாரின்மேல் அலையும் பாவியேன் தனக்குப் பரிந்தருள் பாலியாய் என்னில்
காரின்மேல் வரல்போல் கடாமிசை வரும்அக் காலன்வந் திடில்எது செய்வேன்
வாரின்மேல் வளரும் திருமுலை மலையாள் மணாளனே ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: nīriṉmēl eḻutum eḻuttiṉum viraintu nilaipaṭā uṭampiṉai ōmpip pāriṉmēl alaiyum pāviyēṉ taṉakkup parintaruḷ pāliyāy eṉṉil kāriṉmēl varalpōl kaṭāmicai varumak kālaṉvan tiṭiletu ceyvēṉ vāriṉmēl vaḷarum tirumulai malaiyāḷ maṇāḷaṉē oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: I cherish this unstable body that fades faster than writing on water. If you do not compassionately grant your grace to me, a sinner wandering upon the earth, what will I do when the God of Death arrives riding a buffalo like a dark thundercloud? O husband of the Mountain Goddess whose divine breasts swell above her corset! O life of Otriyur!
commentary: In Hindu tradition, Yama, the God of Death, rides a dark buffalo. Vallalar asks how he will face that terrifying arrival if he has not secured divine protection.

tamil: கருங்கணம் சூழக் கசியும்இவ் வுடலம் கருதும்இக் கணமிருந் ததுதான்
வருங்கணம் ஏதாய் முடியுமோ ஐயோ வஞ்சனேன் என்செய வல்லேன்
பெருங்கணம் சூழ வடவனத் தாடும் பித்தனே உத்தம தவத்தோர்
மருங்கண வுறநின் றரகர எனுஞ்சொல் வான்புகும் ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: karuṅkaṇam cūḻak kaciyumiv vuṭalam karutumik kaṇamirun tatutāṉ varuṅkaṇam ētāy muṭiyumō aiyō vañcaṉēṉ eṉceya vallēṉ peruṅkaṇam cūḻa vaṭavaṉat tāṭum pittaṉē uttama tavattōr maruṅkaṇa vuṟaniṉ ṟarakara eṉuñcol vāṉpukum oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: This oozing body surrounded by swarms of black flies exists in this conscious moment. But how will it end in the very next moment? Alas, what can I, a deceitful wretch, do? O Madman who dances in the banyan forest surrounded by great hordes of ghouls! Sages of supreme penance draw near and chant "Hara Hara," their voices reaching the heavens, O life of Otriyur!
commentary: The physical body is decaying matter whose survival into the next moment is never guaranteed. Sages chant "Hara" (a name for the divine as the remover of illusions) to secure freedom, while Vallalar feels lost to the suddenness of death.

tamil: கன்னியர் அளகக் காட்டிடை உழன்ற கல்மனக் குரங்கினேன் தனைநீ
அன்னியன் என்றே கழித்திடில் உனக்கிங் கார்சொல வல்லவர் ஐயா
என்னியல் அறியேன் நமன்தமர் வருநாள் என்செய்வேன் என்செய்வேன் அந்தோ
மன்னிய வன்னி மலர்ச்சடை மருந்தே வளங்கொளும் ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: kaṉṉiyar aḷakak kāṭṭiṭai uḻaṉṟa kalmaṉak kuraṅkiṉēṉ taṉainī aṉṉiyaṉ eṉṟē kaḻittiṭil uṉakkiṅ kārcola vallavar aiyā eṉṉiyal aṟiyēṉ namaṉtamar varunāḷ eṉceyvēṉ eṉceyvēṉ antō maṉṉiya vaṉṉi malarccaṭai maruntē vaḷaṅkoḷum oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: I possess the stony mind of a monkey roaming in the dark forest of young women's tresses. If you cast me aside as a stranger, who here has the power to question you, O Lord? I do not know my own nature. When the messengers of death arrive, what will I do? What will I do, alas? O healing medicine wearing enduring vanni flowers in your matted hair! O fertile one! O life of Otriyur!
commentary: A distracted, lustful mind is a restless monkey wandering in a dark forest. Vallalar confesses his lack of self-mastery and begs the healing Lord, who wears sacred vanni flowers, not to abandon him when death comes.

tamil: பசிக்குண வுழன்றுன் பாததா மரையைப் பாடுதல் ஒழிந்துநீர்ப் பொறிபோல்
விசிக்கும்நல் அரவக்கச்சினோய் நினது மெய்அருள் அலதொன்றும் விரும்பேன்
வசிக்கும்நல் தவத்தோர்க் கருள்செயஓங்கி வளம்பெறும் ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: pacikkuṇa vuḻaṉṟuṉ pātatā maraiyaip pāṭutal oḻintunīrp poṟipōl nacikkumivvuṭalai nampiṉēṉ eṉṉai namaṉtamar varuttileṉceykēṉ vicikkumnal aravakkacciṉōy niṉatu meyaruḷ alatoṉṟum virumpēṉ vacikkumnal tavattōrk karuḷceya-ōṅki vaḷampeṟum oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: Wandering for food to satisfy my hunger, I stopped singing of your lotus feet. I placed my trust in this body that perishes like a water bubble. When the messengers of death torment me, what will I do? O Lord who wears a tight serpent belt! I desire nothing other than your true grace. O life of Otriyur, flourishing supremely to grant grace to the good ascetics dwelling there!
commentary: Spending a lifetime feeding the physical body is a tragic distraction. People trust this fragile vessel while ignoring their spiritual life. Vallalar warns that when death approaches, obsession with physical survival leaves a person terrified and empty-handed. Security comes only from divine grace.

tamil: கான்றசோ றருந்தும் சுணங்கனின் பலநாள் கண்டபுன் சுகத்தையே விரும்பும்
நான்றநெஞ் சகனேன் நமன்தமர் வருநாள் நாணுவ தன்றிஎன் செய்கேன்
சான்றவர் மதிக்கும் நின்திரு வருள்தான் சார்ந்திடில் தருக்குவன் ஐயா
மான்தனிக் கரத்தெம் வள்ளலே என்னை வாழ்விக்கும் ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: kāṉṟacō ṟaruntum cuṇaṅkaṉiṉ palanāḷ kaṇṭapuṉ cukattaiyē virumpum nāṉṟaneñ cakaṉēṉ namaṉtamar varunāḷ nāṇuva taṉṟi-eṉ ceykēṉ cāṉṟavar matikkum niṉtiru varuḷtāṉ cārntiṭil tarukkuvaṉ aiyā māṉtaṉik karattem vaḷḷalē eṉṉai vāḻvikkum oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: Like a dog eating vomited food, I desire the petty pleasures I have seen over many days with a degraded heart. When the messengers of death arrive, what will I do but feel ashamed? If your holy grace esteemed by the wise reaches me, I will stand proud, O Lord! O our benefactor holding a peerless deer in your hand! O life of Otriyur who makes me live!
commentary: Chasing temporary worldly pleasures degrades the human spirit. Returning to the same petty desires is like a dog returning to its own vomit. When death comes, a life spent on base appetites yields nothing but shame. By contrast, receiving God's grace gives the soul dignity and pride.

tamil: மடிக்குறும் நீர்மேல் எழுத்தினுக் கிடவே மைவடித் தெடுக்குநர் போல
நொடிக்குளே மறையும் உடம்பினை வளர்க்க நொந்தனன் நொந்ததும் அல்லால்
படிக்குளே மனத்தால் பரிவுறு கின்றேன் பாவியேன் தனக்கருள் புரியாய்
வடிக்குறும் தமிழ்கொண் டன்பருக் கருளும் வள்ளலே ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: maṭikkuṟum nīrmēl eḻuttiṉuk kiṭavē maivaṭit teṭukkunar pōla noṭikkuḷē maṟaiyum uṭampiṉai vaḷarkka nontaṉaṉ nontatum allāl paṭikkuḷē maṉattāl parivuṟu kiṉṟēṉ pāviyēṉ taṉakkaruḷ puriyāy vaṭikkuṟum tamiḻkoṇ ṭaṉparuk karuḷum vaḷḷalē oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: Like someone extracting ink to write letters on vanishing water, I suffered to nourish this body that disappears in an instant. Beyond this suffering, I agonize in my mind in this world. Please grant your grace to this sinner. O benefactor who grants grace to devotees through refined Tamil! O life of Otriyur!
commentary: Trying to secure permanent happiness through the physical body is futile. All the agonizing effort spent on worldly survival vanishes in an instant when life ends. Vallalar asks for divine grace to rescue the mind from this useless suffering.

tamil: அங்கையில் புண்போல் உலகவாழ் வனைத்தும் அழிதரக் கண்டுநெஞ் சயர்ந்தே
பங்கமுற் றலைவ தன்றிநின் கமல பாதத்தைப் பற்றிலேன் அந்தோ
இங்கெனை நிகரும் ஏழையார் எனக்குன் இன்னருள் எவ்வணம் அருள்வாய்
மங்கையோர் புடைகொள் வள்ளலே அழியா வளங்கொளும் ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: aṅkaiyil puṇpōl ulakavāḻ vaṉaittum aḻitarak kaṇṭuneñ cayarntē paṅkamuṟ ṟalaiva taṉṟiniṉ kamala pātattaip paṟṟilēṉ antō iṅkeṉai nikarum ēḻaiyār eṉakkuṉ iṉṉaruḷ evvaṇam aruḷvāy maṅkaiyōr puṭaikoḷ vaḷḷalē aḻiyā vaḷaṅkoḷum oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: Seeing all worldly life perishing as plainly as a wound on the palm of the hand, my heart grows weary. I wander in disgrace and alas, I do not grasp your lotus feet. Who here is as destitute as me? How will you grant your sweet grace to me? O benefactor who keeps the Goddess on one side! O life of Otriyur possessing imperishable wealth!
commentary: The fragility of worldly life is not a hidden mystery. It is as obvious as an open wound on the palm of the hand, yet people fail to seek the divine. Realizing this stubborn blindness fills the heart with weariness and a sense of poverty. Wealth is found in the imperishable grace of God, untouched by the world's decay.

tamil: கணத்தினில் உலகம் அழிதரக் கண்டும் கண்ணிலார் போல்கிடந் துழைக்கும்
குணத்தினில் கொடியேன் தனக்குநின் அருள்தான் கூடுவ தெவ்வணம் அறியேன்
பணத்தினில் பொலியும் பாம்பரை ஆர்த்த பரமனே பிரமன்மால் அறியா
வணத்தினால் நின்ற மாணிக்கச் சுடரே வள்ளலே ஒற்றியூர் வாழ்வே.
translit: kaṇattiṉil ulakam aḻitarak kaṇṭum kaṇṇilār pōlkiṭan tuḻaikkum kuṇattiṉil koṭiyēṉ taṉakkuniṉ aruḷtāṉ kūṭuva tevvaṇam aṟiyēṉ paṇattiṉil poliyum pāmparai ārtta paramaṉē piramaṉmāl aṟiyā vaṇattiṉāl niṉṟa māṇikkac cuṭarē vaḷḷalē oṟṟiyūr vāḻvē.
translation: Even seeing the world perishing in an instant, I toil on like the blind. I do not know how your grace will ever reach me, a person of cruel character. O Supreme Lord who ties a snake with a glowing hood around your waist! O ruby flame standing in a form unknown to Brahma and Vishnu! O benefactor! O life of Otriyur!
commentary: Humans witness death and destruction daily, yet chase worldly goals as if blind to reality. This willful ignorance is a cruel flaw in human character. Vallalar wonders how divine grace can reach a mind so stubborn. Only God, appearing here as a flame beyond the grasp of traditional deities, has the power to save such a lost soul.

tamil: மண்ணை மனத்துப் பாவியன்யான் மடவார் உள்ளே வதிந்தளிந்த
புண்ணை மதித்துப் புகுகின்றேன் போதம் இழந்தேன் புண்ணியனே
எண்ண இனிய நின்புகழை ஏத்தேன் ஒதிபோல் இருக்கின்றேன்
தண்நல் அமுதே நீஎன்னைத் தடுத்திங் காளத் தக்கதுவே.
translit: maṇṇai maṉattup pāviyaṉyāṉ maṭavār uḷḷē vatintaḷinta puṇṇai matittup pukukiṉṟēṉ pōtam iḻantēṉ puṇṇiyaṉē eṇṇa iṉiya niṉpukaḻai ēttēṉ otipōl irukkiṉṟēṉ taṇnal amutē nī-eṉṉait taṭuttiṅ kāḷat takkatuvē.
translation: I am a sinner with an ignorant mind. O Holy One, I have lost my wisdom. Valuing the festering wound residing inside women, I enter it. I do not praise your glory, which is so sweet to contemplate. I sit like a useless tree. O cool and pure nectar, it is right for you to stop me and rule me here.
commentary: Vallalar admits he is blinded by physical desire, reducing human intimacy to a festering wound. Like a numb, useless tree unable to sing God's praises, he begs the divine to step in, block his downward path, and take control of his life.

tamil: தக்க தறியேன் வெறியேன்நான் சண்ட மடவார் தம்முலைதோய்
துக்கம் அதனைச் சுகம் என்றே துணிந்தேன் என்னைத் தொழும்பன்எனில்
மிக்க அடியார் என்சொல்லார் விண்ணோர் மண்ணோர் என்புகலார்
செக்கர் நிறத்துப் பொன்மேனித் திருநீற் றொளிசேர் செங்கரும்பே.
translit: takka taṟiyēṉ veṟiyēṉnāṉ caṇṭa maṭavār tammulaitōy tukkam ataṉaic cukam eṉṟē tuṇintēṉ eṉṉait toḻumpaṉeṉil mikka aṭiyār eṉcollār viṇṇōr maṇṇōr eṉpukalār cekkar niṟattup poṉmēṉit tirunīṟ ṟoḷicēr ceṅkarumpē.
translation: I do not know what is proper. I am a madman. I resolved that the sorrow of sinking into the breasts of fierce women is actually pleasure. If you call me your servant, what will the great devotees say? What will the celestials and earthly beings declare? O red sugarcane, shining with sacred ash upon your crimson-hued golden body!
commentary: Human ignorance mistakes the sorrow of lust for actual happiness. Vallalar feels unworthy to be called a servant of God; if pure devotees and heavenly beings heard him claim that title, they would be shocked. He addresses God in the traditional form of Siva at Otriyur, wearing white sacred ash over a crimson-lit golden body.

tamil: கரும்பே ஒற்றி யூர்அமர்ந்த கனியே உன்தன் கழல்அடியை
விரும்பேன் அடியார் அடித்தொண்டில் மேவேன் பொல்லா விடமனைய
பெரும்பேய் மாதர் பிணக்குழியில் பேதை மனம்போந் திடச்சூறைத்
துரும்பே என்னச் சுழல்கின்றேன் துணையொன் றறியேன் துனியேனே.
translit: karumpē oṟṟi yūramarnta kaṉiyē uṉtaṉ kaḻalaṭiyai virumpēṉ aṭiyār aṭittoṇṭil mēvēṉ pollā viṭamaṉaiya perumpēy mātar piṇakkuḻiyil pētai maṉampōn tiṭaccūṟait turumpē eṉṉac cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ tuṇaiyoṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ tuṉiyēṉē.
translation: O sugarcane, O fruit seated in Otriyur! I do not desire your anklet-adorned feet. I do not engage in serving your devotees. As my foolish mind enters the corpse-pit of great demon-like women who act as evil poison, I spin like a straw caught in a whirlwind. I know no companion. I am engulfed in sorrow.
commentary: Instead of finding joy in God or serving other devotees, the mind becomes consumed by physical obsession. Vallalar describes lust as a deadly poison and a dark pit that traps the foolish. Tossed about by intense cravings, he feels like a helpless piece of straw caught in a whirlwind, alone and overwhelmed by grief.

tamil: துனியே பிறத்தற் கேதுஎனும் துட்ட மடவார் உள்ததும்பும்
பனிஏய் மலம்சூழ் முடைநாற்றப் பாழும் குழிக்கே வீழ்ந்திளைத்தேன்
இனிஏ துறுமோ என்செய்கேன் எளியேன் தனைநீ ஏன்றுகொளாய்
கனியே கருணைக் கடலேஎன் கண்ணே ஒற்றிக் காவலனே.
translit: tuṉiyē piṟattaṟ kētu-eṉum tuṭṭa maṭavār uḷtatumpum paṉi-ēy malamcūḻ muṭaināṟṟap pāḻum kuḻikkē vīḻntiḷaittēṉ iṉi-ē tuṟumō eṉceykēṉ eḷiyēṉ taṉainī ēṉṟukoḷāy kaṉiyē karuṇaik kaṭalē-eṉ kaṇṇē oṟṟik kāvalaṉē.
translation: I fell into the desolate, foul-smelling pit of wicked women who cause sorrowful rebirth. I tumbled into that pit welling with fluid and surrounded by filth, and I grew utterly exhausted. What will happen now? What shall I do? You must accept this poor wretch. O fruit, O ocean of mercy, O my eye, O protector of Otriyur!
commentary: Worldly attachment and lust bind the soul to an endless cycle of painful rebirths. Vallalar expresses disgust for the physical body, seeing it as a vessel of fluid and filth. Exhausted by relentless cravings, he cries out for rescue, appealing directly to the Lord of Otriyur as an ocean of mercy and the only true protector.

tamil: வலமே உடையார் நின்கருணை வாய்ந்து வாழ்ந்தார் வஞ்சகனேன்
மலமே உடையேன் ஆதலினால் மாதர் எனும்பேய் வாக்கும் உவர்ச்
சலமே ஒழுக்குப் பொத்தரிடைச் சாய்ந்து தளர்ந்தேன் சார்பறியேன்
நலமே ஒற்றி நாடுடையாய் நாயேன் உய்யும் நாள்என்றோ.
translit: valamē uṭaiyār niṉkaruṇai vāyntu vāḻntār vañcakaṉēṉ malamē uṭaiyēṉ ātaliṉāl mātar eṉumpēy vākkum uvarc calamē oḻukkup pottariṭaic cāyntu taḷarntēṉ cārpaṟiyēṉ nalamē oṟṟi nāṭuṭaiyāy nāyēṉ uyyum nāḷeṉṟō.
translation: Those who possess merit have received your grace and flourished. I am a deceiver possessing only impurity. Therefore, I leaned into the leaking hole pouring out salty fluid belonging to the demons called women, and I grew weary. I know no refuge. O embodiment of goodness who rules the land of Otriyur! When will the day come for this dog to find salvation?
commentary: Spiritual success comes to those who carry merit and receive divine grace. Vallalar contrasts their flourishing lives with his own exhausting obsession with physical bodies. Stripped of dignity, he compares himself to a stray dog crying for help, asking the Lord of goodness when his day of true salvation will finally arrive.

tamil: நாளை வருவ தறியேன்நான் நஞ்சம் அனைய நங்கையர்தம்
ஆளை அழுத்தும் நீர்க்குழியில் அழுந்தி அழுந்தி எழுந்தலைந்தேன்
கோளை அகற்றி நின்அடிக்கே கூடும் வண்ணம் குறிப்பாயோ
வேளை எரித்த மெய்ஞ்ஞான விளக்கே முத்தி வித்தகமே.
translit: nāḷai varuva taṟiyēṉnāṉ nañcam aṉaiya naṅkaiyartam āḷai aḻuttum nīrkkuḻiyil aḻunti aḻunti eḻuntalaintēṉ kōḷai akaṟṟi niṉaṭikkē kūṭum vaṇṇam kuṟippāyō vēḷai eritta meyññāṉa viḷakkē mutti vittakamē.
translation: I do not know what tomorrow brings. I sank deep into the watery pit of women who are like poison, a pit that drowns a man. I sank, rose, and wandered aimlessly. Will you remove my afflictions and decree that I may unite at your very feet? O lamp of true wisdom who burnt the god of lust! O marvel of liberation!
commentary: Human life is fragile, and sensory desires drown the soul. Vallalar pleads for rescue from the pull of lust. He addresses God as the light of wisdom who burned the god of lust, referencing the traditional story of Siva destroying Kama (the deity of desire).

tamil: முத்தி முதலே முக்கணுடை மூரிக் கரும்பே நின்பதத்தில்
பத்தி முதலே இல்லாதேன் பரம சுகத்தில் படிவேனோ
எத்தி அழைக்கும் கருங்கண்ணார் இடைக்குள் பிளந்த வெடிப்பதனில்
தத்தி விழுந்தேன் எழுவேனேல் தள்ளா நின்ற தென்மனமே.
translit: mutti mutalē mukkaṇuṭai mūrik karumpē niṉpatattil patti mutalē illātēṉ parama cukattil paṭivēṉō etti aḻaikkum karuṅkaṇṇār iṭaikkuḷ piḷanta veṭippataṉil tatti viḻuntēṉ eḻuvēṉēl taḷḷā niṉṟa teṉmaṉamē.
translation: O source of liberation! O grand sugarcane with three eyes! I have no basic devotion for your feet. Will I ever immerse myself in supreme bliss? I leaped and fell into the cleft split beneath the waists of women with dark eyes who deceive and beckon. If I try to rise, my mind keeps pushing me back down.
commentary: The mind itself acts as the enemy, pulling a person back into physical craving just when they try to rise above it. Vallalar admits a total lack of devotion, addressing God as a sweet sugarcane with three eyes (Siva). The struggle is internal, with the mind actively trapping the soul in worldly lust.

tamil: மனமே முன்னர் வழிகாட்டப் பின்னே சென்று மங்கையர்தம்
தனமே என்னும் மலைஏறிப் பார்த்தேன் இருண்ட சலதிஒன்று
முனமே தோன்ற மதிமயங்கி விழுந்தேன் எழுவான் முயலுகின்றேன்
இனமே என்னை நீஅன்றி எடுப்பார் இல்லை என்அரசே.
translit: maṉamē muṉṉar vaḻikāṭṭap piṉṉē ceṉṟu maṅkaiyartam taṉamē eṉṉum malai-ēṟip pārttēṉ iruṇṭa calati-oṉṟu muṉamē tōṉṟa matimayaṅki viḻuntēṉ eḻuvāṉ muyalukiṉṟēṉ iṉamē eṉṉai nī-aṉṟi eṭuppār illai eṉaracē.
translation: With my mind showing the way, I followed behind and climbed the mountain of women's breasts. When I looked, a dark ocean appeared right before me. My mind grew dizzy and I fell. I am trying to rise. My King, my true kin, there is no one but you to lift me up.
commentary: Following the mind leads straight to spiritual ruin. Sensual attraction looks appealing from a distance, but up close it reveals itself as a dark, dizzying ocean where the soul falls. Once trapped, human effort alone cannot pull a person back up; only divine grace can lift them to safety.

tamil: என்னைக் கொடுத்தேன் பெண்பேய்கட் கின்பம் எனவே எனக்கவர்நோய்
தன்னைக் கொடுத்தார் நான்அந்தோ தளர்ந்து நின்றேன் அல்லதுசெம்
பொன்னைக் கொடுத்தும் பெறஅரிய பொருளே உன்னைப் போற்றுகிலேன்
இன்னல் கொடுத்த பவமுடையேன் எற்றுக் கிவண்நிற் கின்றேனே.
translit: eṉṉaik koṭuttēṉ peṇpēykaṭ kiṉpam eṉavē eṉakkavarnōy taṉṉaik koṭuttār nāṉantō taḷarntu niṉṟēṉ allatucem poṉṉaik koṭuttum peṟa-ariya poruḷē uṉṉaip pōṟṟukilēṉ iṉṉal koṭutta pavamuṭaiyēṉ eṟṟuk kivaṇniṟ kiṉṟēṉē.
translation: I gave myself to demonic women thinking it was pleasure. They gave me disease in return. Alas, I stood exhausted. I do not praise you, O treasure rare to obtain even by giving pure gold. I bear a birth that yields only suffering. Why do I still stand here?
commentary: Chasing physical pleasure is a terrible trade that brings only suffering and disease. Vallalar regrets wasting life on temporary bodily urges instead of seeking God, a rare and pure treasure. The result of this trade is sheer exhaustion and a painful questioning of why life is worth living under such conditions.

tamil: எற்றுக் கடியர் நின்றதுநின் இணைத்தாள் மலரை ஏத்தஅன்றோ
மற்றிக் கொடியேன் அஃதின்றி மடவார் இடைவாய் மணிப்பாம்பின்
புற்றுக் குழன்றேன் என்னேஎன் புந்தி எவர்க்குப் புகல்வேனே
கற்றுத் தெளிந்தோர் புகழ் ஒற்றிக் கண்ணார்ந் தோங்கும் கற்பகமே.
translit: eṟṟuk kaṭiyar niṉṟatuniṉ iṇaittāḷ malarai ētta-aṉṟō maṟṟik koṭiyēṉ aḵtiṉṟi maṭavār iṭaivāy maṇippāmpiṉ puṟṟuk kuḻaṉṟēṉ eṉṉē-eṉ punti evarkkup pukalvēṉē kaṟṟut teḷintōr pukaḻ oṟṟik kaṇṇārn tōṅkum kaṟpakamē.
translation: Why do devotees exist? Is it not to praise your twin lotus feet? But I am a cruel man. Instead of praising you, I writhed in the cobra's anthill beneath the waists of foolish women. What is this mind of mine? To whom will I confess this? O wish-fulfilling tree rising gracefully in Otriyur, praised by those who have learned and gained clarity!
commentary: The true purpose of human life is to praise the divine, but people squander it on dangerous bodily desires. Lust is compared to a cobra's anthill, showing how an attractive physical form hides lethal spiritual danger. In total despair at his own mind's choices, Vallalar looks to the divine at Otriyur as a wish-fulfilling tree that grants clarity.

tamil: ஓங்கும் பொருளே திருஒற்றி யூர்வாழ் அரசே உனைத்துதியேன்
தீங்கும் புழுவும் சிலைநீரும் சீழும் வழும்பும் சேர்ந்தலைக்கத்
தூங்கும் மடவார் புலைநாற்றத் தூம்பில் நுழையும் சூதகனேன்
வாங்கும் பவம்தீர்த் தருள்வதுநின் கடன்காண் இந்த மண்ணிடத்தே.
translit: ōṅkum poruḷē tiru-oṟṟi yūrvāḻ aracē uṉaittutiyēṉ tīṅkum puḻuvum cilainīrum cīḻum vaḻumpum cērntalaikkat tūṅkum maṭavār pulaināṟṟat tūmpil nuḻaiyum cūtakaṉēṉ vāṅkum pavamtīrt taruḷvatuniṉ kaṭaṉkāṇ inta maṇṇiṭattē.
translation: O exalted Reality! O King who dwells in sacred Otriyur! I do not praise You. I am a deceitful wretch who enters the foul-smelling, fleshly passage of women of sagging flesh, where impurities, worms, phlegm, pus, and slime gather and churn. It is Your duty to end the worldly bondage that grips me and bestow Your grace upon me on this earth.
commentary: Worldly lust pulls the mind away from divine reality. To shatter the illusion of physical attraction, Vallalar describes the human body with harsh honesty, exposing it as a decaying vessel of flesh, fluids, and worms. Confessing his failure to praise God, he admits he is caught in these base desires. Yet he makes a bold demand to the Lord of Otriyur, declaring it is God's own duty to reach down into this earthly mess, cut away the chains of worldly bondage (pavam), and grant true grace.

tamil: துள்ளிவாய் மடுக்கும் காளையர் ஆட்டத் துடுக்கினை ஒடுக்குறும் காமக்
கொள்ளிவாய்ப் பேய்கள் எனுமட வியர்தம் கூட்டத்துள் நாட்டம்வைத் துழன்றேன்
உள்ளிவாய் மடுத்துள் உருகிஆ னந்த உததிபோல் கண்கள்நீர் உகுப்பார்
அள்ளிவாய் மடுக்கும் அமுதே எங்கள் அண்ணலே ஒற்றியூர் அரசே.
translit: tuḷḷivāy maṭukkum kāḷaiyar āṭṭat tuṭukkiṉai oṭukkuṟum kāmak koḷḷivāyp pēykaḷ eṉumaṭa viyartam kūṭṭattuḷ nāṭṭamvait tuḻaṉṟēṉ uḷḷivāy maṭuttuḷ uruki-ā ṉanta utatipōl kaṇkaḷnīr ukuppār aḷḷivāy maṭukkum amutē eṅkaḷ aṇṇalē oṟṟiyūr aracē.
translation: Our Lord! King of Otriyur! You are the nectar scooped up and drunk by those who think of you, who melt within, and who shed tears like a sea of bliss. I wandered about, setting my gaze upon the company of women who act as fire-mouthed demons of lust to subdue the arrogant prancing of leaping youths.
commentary: Divine grace is a sweet nectar that brings tears of joy. Yet instead of seeking this bliss, the mind falls into physical desire. Vallalar confesses to wasting his youth chasing lust, a fire-mouthed demon that consumes vital energy.

tamil: ஒற்றியூர் அமரும் ஒளிகெழு மணியே உன்அடி உள்கிநின் றேத்தேன்
முற்றியூர் மலினக் குழிஇருள் மடவார் முலைஎனும் மலநிறைக் குவையைச்
சுற்றிஊர் நாயின் சுழன்றனன் வறிதே சுகம்எனச் சூழ்ந்தழி உடலைப்
பற்றியூர் நகைக்கத் திரிதரு கின்றேன் பாவியேன் உய்திறம் அரிதே.
translit: oṟṟiyūr amarum oḷikeḻu maṇiyē uṉaṭi uḷkiniṉ ṟēttēṉ muṟṟiyūr maliṉak kuḻi-iruḷ maṭavār mulai-eṉum malaniṟaik kuvaiyaic cuṟṟi-ūr nāyiṉ cuḻaṉṟaṉaṉ vaṟitē cukameṉac cūḻntaḻi uṭalaip paṟṟiyūr nakaikkat tiritaru kiṉṟēṉ pāviyēṉ uytiṟam aritē.
translation: Radiant gem seated in Otriyur! I did not meditate on your feet and praise them. Instead, I circled like a stray village dog around women's breasts, those heaps of filth and dark pits of fully formed impurity. Vainly grasping this decaying body and believing it brings pleasure, I wander about while the town mocks me. Salvation is difficult for a sinner like me.
commentary: The physical body is temporary and constantly breaks down, yet humans chase it as if it holds lasting happiness. To break the illusion of sexual attraction, Vallalar compares his lustful behavior to a stray dog circling filth, ignoring God's radiant presence to run after bodily desires that only bring shame.

tamil: அரியது நினது திருவருள் ஒன்றே அவ்வருள் அடைதலே எவைக்கும்
பெரியதோர் பேறென் றுணர்ந்திலேன் முருட்டுப் பேய்களை ஆயிரம்கூட்டிச்
சரிஎனச் சொலினும் போதுறா மடமைத் தையலார் மையலில் அழுந்திப்
பிரியமுற் றலைந்தேன் ஏழைநான் ஒற்றிப் பெருமநின் அருளெனக் குண்டே.
translit: ariyatu niṉatu tiruvaruḷ oṉṟē avvaruḷ aṭaitalē evaikkum periyatōr pēṟeṉ ṟuṇarntilēṉ muruṭṭup pēykaḷai āyiramkūṭṭic cari-eṉac coliṉum pōtuṟā maṭamait taiyalār maiyalil aḻuntip piriyamuṟ ṟalaintēṉ ēḻaināṉ oṟṟip perumaniṉ aruḷeṉak kuṇṭē.
translation: Your sacred grace alone is rare. I failed to realize that attaining that grace is the greatest boon of all. I plunged into infatuation with ignorant women whose fierceness cannot be matched even if you gather a thousand savage demons to equal them. I wandered about with fondness for them. I am a wretched man. Lord of Otriyur, will I ever receive your grace?
commentary: Receiving divine grace is the greatest achievement a soul can reach. Vallalar mourns his ignorance, having spent his life infatuated with worldly attachments rather than seeking this rare spiritual gift. Lust overpowers the mind with the fierce, destructive grip of a thousand savage demons.

tamil: பெருமநின் அருளே அன்றிஇவ் வுலகில் பேதையர் புழுமலப் பிலமாம்
கருமவாழ் வெனைத்தும் வேண்டிலேன் மற்றைக் கடவுளர் வாழ்வையும் விரும்பேன்
தருமவா ரிதியே தடம்பணை ஒற்றித் தலத்தமர் தனிமுதல் பொருளே
துருமவான் அமுதே அடியனேன் தன்னைச் சோதியா தருள்வதுன் பரமே.
translit: perumaniṉ aruḷē aṉṟi-iv vulakil pētaiyar puḻumalap pilamām karumavāḻ veṉaittum vēṇṭilēṉ maṟṟaik kaṭavuḷar vāḻvaiyum virumpēṉ tarumavā ritiyē taṭampaṇai oṟṟit talattamar taṉimutal poruḷē turumavāṉ amutē aṭiyaṉēṉ taṉṉaic cōtiyā taruḷvatuṉ paramē.
translation: Lord! Except for your grace, I do not want any part of this karmic worldly life with ignorant women who are mere pits of worms and filth. I do not desire the life of other gods. Ocean of virtue! Peerless original reality seated in the shrine of Otriyur surrounded by vast fields! Pure heavenly nectar! It is your burden to bless me, your servant, without testing me.
commentary: True spiritual liberation requires rejecting all lesser goals, including the heavenly realms of other gods. Vallalar declares that nothing matters except the grace of the one supreme reality. Recognizing his weakness, he asks the Lord to grant this grace freely, without testing him through further worldly trials.

tamil: அருள்வதுன் இயற்கை உலகெலாம் அறியும் ஐயவோ நான்அதை அறிந்தும்
மருள்வதென் இயற்கை என்செய்வேன் இதனை மனங்கொளா தருள்அரு ளாயேல்
தெருள்வதொன் றின்றி மங்கையர் கொங்கைத் திடர்மலைச் சிகரத்தில் ஏறி
உருள்வதும் அல்குல் படுகுழி விழுந்தங் குலைவதும் அன்றிஒன் றுண்டோ.
translit: aruḷvatuṉ iyaṟkai ulakelām aṟiyum aiyavō nāṉatai aṟintum maruḷvateṉ iyaṟkai eṉceyvēṉ itaṉai maṉaṅkoḷā taruḷaru ḷāyēl teruḷvatoṉ ṟiṉṟi maṅkaiyar koṅkait tiṭarmalaic cikarattil ēṟi uruḷvatum alkul paṭukuḻi viḻuntaṅ kulaivatum aṉṟi-oṉ ṟuṇṭō.
translation: O Lord, the whole world knows that granting grace is your nature. Even knowing this, falling into delusion remains my nature. What can I do? If you do not overlook my flaws and grant me your grace, what else awaits me? Devoid of all clarity, I will only climb the steep mountain peaks of women's breasts to roll back down, and fall into the deep pit of their loins to perish.
commentary: Human nature is prone to delusion, climbing the heights of physical desire only to fall into despair. God's nature is pure compassion. Vallalar pleads with the divine to act according to its forgiving nature, knowing that without grace, he is powerless to escape the cycle of lust and ruin.

tamil: உண்டுநஞ் சமரர் உயிர்பெறக் காத்த ஒற்றியூர் அண்ணலே நின்னைக்
கண்டுநெஞ் சுருகிக் கண்கள்நீர் சோரக் கைகுவித் திணையடி இறைஞ்சேன்
வண்டுநின் றலைக்கும் குழல்பிறை நுதலார் வஞ்சக விழியினால் மயங்கிக்
குண்டுநீர் ஞாலத் திடைஅலை கின்றேன்கொடியனேன் அடியனேன் அன்றே.
translit: uṇṭunañ camarar uyirpeṟak kātta oṟṟiyūr aṇṇalē niṉṉaik kaṇṭuneñ curukik kaṇkaḷnīr cōrak kaikuvit tiṇaiyaṭi iṟaiñcēṉ vaṇṭuniṉ ṟalaikkum kuḻalpiṟai nutalār vañcaka viḻiyiṉāl mayaṅkik kuṇṭunīr ñālat tiṭai-alai kiṉṟēṉkoṭiyaṉēṉ aṭiyaṉēṉ aṉṟē.
translation: O Lord of Otriyur who consumed poison to protect the lives of the celestials! Seeing you, my heart does not melt, my eyes do not pour tears, and I do not fold my hands and worship your twin feet. Bewitched by the deceitful eyes of women with crescent-like foreheads and hair swarming with bees, I wander aimlessly across this world surrounded by deep waters. I am cruel. I am truly not your devotee.
commentary: Vallalar contrasts the supreme compassion of God with his own shallow distractions. He recalls the story of Siva drinking a deadly ocean of poison to save the celestials from death. Instead of melting with gratitude for a God who sacrifices so much, Vallalar laments wasting his life chasing physical beauty and worldly desires.

tamil: அன்றுநீ அடிமைச் சாதனம் காட்டி ஆண்டஆ ரூரனார் உன்னைச்
சென்றுதூ தருள்என் றிரங்குதல் நோக்கிச் சென்றநின் கருணையைக் கருதி
ஒன்றுதோ றுள்ளம் உருகுகின் றனன்காண் ஒற்றியூர் அண்ணலே உலகத்
தென்றுமால் உழந்தேன் எனினும்நின் அடியேன் என்தனைக் கைவிடேல் இனியே.
translit: aṉṟunī aṭimaic cātaṉam kāṭṭi āṇṭa-ā rūraṉār uṉṉaic ceṉṟutū taruḷeṉ ṟiraṅkutal nōkkic ceṉṟaniṉ karuṇaiyaik karuti oṉṟutō ṟuḷḷam urukukiṉ ṟaṉaṉkāṇ oṟṟiyūr aṇṇalē ulakat teṉṟumāl uḻantēṉ eṉiṉumniṉ aṭiyēṉ eṉtaṉaik kaiviṭēl iṉiyē.
translation: O Lord of Otriyur! That day, you showed the deed of slavery and claimed Aruranar as your own. Later, when he pleaded with you to go as a messenger, you went. Thinking of your great compassion in doing so, my heart melts every time I recall it. Though I have forever suffered delusion in this world, I am your devotee. Do not abandon me now.
commentary: God's compassion is so vast that he will lower himself to serve his devotees. Vallalar recalls the story of the Tamil saint Aruranar, whom God claimed as a servant but who later asked God to act as a midnight messenger to settle a lover's quarrel. Remembering a God who acts with such intimate, forgiving love gives Vallalar hope that he will not be abandoned despite his flaws.

tamil: இனியநின் திருத்தாள் இணைமலர் ஏத்தேன் இளமுலை மங்கையர்க் குள்ளம்
கனியஅக் கொடியார்க் கேவல்செய் துழன்றேன் கடையனேன் விடயவாழ் வுடையேன்
துனியஇவ் வுடற்கண் உயிர்பிரிந் திடுங்கால்துணைநினை அன்றி ஒன் றறியேன்
தனியமெய்ப் போத வேதநா யகனே தடம்பொழில் ஒற்றியூர் இறையே.
translit: iṉiyaniṉ tiruttāḷ iṇaimalar ēttēṉ iḷamulai maṅkaiyark kuḷḷam kaṉiya-ak koṭiyārk kēvalcey tuḻaṉṟēṉ kaṭaiyaṉēṉ viṭayavāḻ vuṭaiyēṉ tuṉiya-iv vuṭaṟkaṇ uyirpirin tiṭuṅkāltuṇainiṉai aṉṟi oṉ ṟaṟiyēṉ taṉiyameyp pōta vētanā yakaṉē taṭampoḻil oṟṟiyūr iṟaiyē.
translation: O Lord of the Vedas who is the singular true wisdom! O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by vast groves! I do not praise your sweet twin lotus feet. I wander around serving cruel women to win their hearts. I am the lowest of the low, living a life addicted to worldly pleasures. When life finally departs from this miserable body, I know no companion other than you.
commentary: Worldly attachments offer no real security when life ends. Vallalar confesses he has spent his time flattering others and chasing temporary pleasures instead of seeking divine wisdom. He realizes that when the body fails, all human companions fall away, leaving God as his only support.

tamil: இறையும்நின் திருத்தாள் கமலங்கள் ஏத்தேன் எழில்பெற உடம்பினை ஓம்பிக்
குறையும்வெண் மதிபோல் காலங்கள் ஒழித்துக் கோதையர் குறுங்குழி அளற்றில்
பொறையும் நல் நிறையும் நீத்துழன் றலைந்தேன் பொய்யனேன் தனக்குவெண் சோதி
நிறையும்வெள் நீற்றுக் கோலனே ஒற்றி நிமலனே அருளுதல் நெறியே.
translit: iṟaiyumniṉ tiruttāḷ kamalaṅkaḷ ēttēṉ eḻilpeṟa uṭampiṉai ōmpik kuṟaiyumveṇ matipōl kālaṅkaḷ oḻittuk kōtaiyar kuṟuṅkuḻi aḷaṟṟil poṟaiyum nal niṟaiyum nīttuḻaṉ ṟalaintēṉ poyyaṉēṉ taṉakkuveṇ cōti niṟaiyumveḷ nīṟṟuk kōlaṉē oṟṟi nimalaṉē aruḷutal neṟiyē.
translation: O Lord adorned with bright white ash radiating pure light! O flawless Lord of Otriyur! I do not praise your lotus feet even for a moment. Instead, I cherish this body to keep it beautiful, wasting my days like the waning white moon. Losing my patience and good composure, I wander astray in the narrow muddy pit of lust for women. Granting grace to a liar like me is the true path of righteousness.
commentary: Wasting time on physical vanity is like watching the moon disappear. Vallalar admits he has focused on preserving his body's beauty while losing his dignity to lust. He appeals to a higher spiritual law: the nature of divine grace is to rescue the flawed, and saving a liar like him is the proof of God's righteousness.

tamil: நெறியிலேன் கொடிய மங்கையர் மையல் நெறியிலே நின்றனன் எனினும்
பொறியிலேன் பிழையைப் பொறுப்பதுன் கடனே பொறுப்பதும் அன்றிஇவ் வுலக
வெறியிலே இன்னும் மயங்கிடா துன்தன் விரைமலர் அடித்துணை ஏத்தும்
அறிவுளே அருள்வாய் ஒற்றியூர் அரசே அன்றினார் துள்ளறுத் தவனே.
translit: neṟiyilēṉ koṭiya maṅkaiyar maiyal neṟiyilē niṉṟaṉaṉ eṉiṉum poṟiyilēṉ piḻaiyaip poṟuppatuṉ kaṭaṉē poṟuppatum aṉṟi-iv vulaka veṟiyilē iṉṉum mayaṅkiṭā tuṉtaṉ viraimalar aṭittuṇai ēttum aṟivuḷē aruḷvāy oṟṟiyūr aracē aṉṟiṉār tuḷḷaṟut tavaṉē.
translation: O King of Otriyur! O Lord who destroyed the arrogance of your foes! I follow no righteous path. Even though I remained on the path of infatuation for cruel women, it is your duty to forgive the mistakes of this senseless fool. Along with forgiving me, grant me the inner wisdom to stop being confused by the madness of this world and to instead praise your fragrant floral twin feet.
commentary: Vallalar approaches God not with a list of virtues, but by claiming his foolishness as the reason he deserves help. He argues that a compassionate God has a duty to forgive those who do not know better. He asks for the inner clarity to cut through the madness of worldly life and turn his attention to the divine.

translit: naṟaimaṇakkum koṉṟai naticcaṭila nāyakaṉē kaṟaimaṇakkum tirunīla kaṇṭap perumāṉē uṟaimaṇakkum pūmpoḻilcūḻ oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya maṟaimaṇakkum tiru-aṭiyai vāynirampa vāḻttēṉō.
translation: O Lord with matted hair bearing the river and the fragrant konrai flowers. O Lord of the holy blue throat bearing the dark stain. O Father of Otriyur surrounded by flower groves fragrant with falling dew. Will I not praise your holy feet fragrant with the Vedas until my mouth is full?
commentary: Vallalar yearns to praise God enough to satisfy his spiritual hunger. He recalls familiar images of Siva wearing fragrant konrai blossoms, carrying the holy river in his hair, and bearing a blue throat from swallowing poison to save the world. He longs to use his speech in devotion.

translit: alaivaḷaikkum pāṟkaṭalāṉ ampuyattāṉ vāḻttinitam talaivaḷaikkum ceṅkamalat tāḷuṭaiyāy āḷuṭaiyāy ulaivaḷaikkā muttalaivēl oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya malaivaḷaikkum kaimmalariṉ vaṇmaitaṉai vāḻttēṉō.
translation: The lord of the wave-filled milky ocean and the lord on the lotus daily praise and bow their heads to your red lotus feet. O Master who rules me. O Father of Otriyur holding the trident that never bends in the forge. Will I not praise the greatness of your lotus hands that bent the mountain into a bow?
commentary: Vallalar points out that even the creator and preserver deities, Brahma and Vishnu, bow daily to the supreme Lord. He marvels at the divine strength that once bent a massive mountain into a bow, asking when he will celebrate that greatness as it deserves.

translit: āṟaṭuttuc ceṉṟa-eṅkaḷ apparukkā aṉṟukaṭṭuc cōṟeṭuttuc ceṉṟa tuṇaiyē cuyañcuṭarē ūṟeṭuttōr kāṇariya oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya nīṟaṭutta eṇtōḷ nilaimaitaṉaip pārēṉō.
translation: On that day when our Appar journeyed along the road, you walked with him as a companion carrying packed rice. O self-luminous light. O Father of Otriyur rarely seen by those mired in affliction. Will I not see the state of your eight shoulders smeared with holy ash?
commentary: Vallalar remembers a famous story of Appar, an ancient Tamil saint. Appar's devotion was so dear to God that the Lord disguised himself as a traveler to carry food for him on a long journey. Vallalar yearns to witness that same compassionate, radiant presence for himself.

translit: caivat talaivar tavattōrkaḷ tamperumāṉ meyvaitta uḷḷam viraviniṉṟa vittakaṉē uyvaitta uttamaṉē oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya teyvap pukaḻeṉ ceviniṟaiyak kēḷēṉō.
translation: O Leader of the Saivas. O Lord of the ascetics. O wise one who mingles in hearts established in truth. O Supreme one who bestows salvation. O Father of Otriyur. Will I not listen to your divine fame until my ears are full?
commentary: True spiritual fulfillment requires every sense to be absorbed in the divine. Vallalar asks when his ears will overflow with hearing God's glory. He describes this presence as a wisdom that naturally gathers and lives inside hearts grounded in truth.

translit: pāṭukiṉṟōr pāṭap paricaḷikkum puṇṇiyaṉē tēṭukiṉṟōr tēṭaniṟkum tiyākap perumāṉē ūṭukiṉṟōr illāta oṟṟiyappā ampalattuḷ āṭukiṉṟa cēvaṭikaṇ ṭallalelām tīrēṉō.
translation: O holy one who grants gifts to those who sing. O great Lord Thyagar who stands ready for those who seek you. O Father of Otriyur where no one holds a grievance. Will I not see your red feet dancing in the hall and end all my sorrows?
commentary: The goal is the ending of worldly suffering. God is a generous giver who stands waiting for those who actively seek him. Vallalar believes that witnessing the divine dance of grace will be enough to erase every sorrow he carries.

translit: pūṇāka māṭap potunaṭikkum puṇṇiyaṉē cēṇākam vāṅkum civaṉē kaṭalviṭattai ūṇāka uḷḷuvanta oṟṟiyappā mālayaṉum kāṇāta niṉuruvaik kaṇṭu kaḷiyēṉō.
translation: O virtuous one who dances in the public hall wearing a snake as an ornament! O Siva who bends the tall mountain as a bow! O Father of Otri who gladly consumed the ocean's poison as food! Will I not rejoice upon seeing your form, which even Vishnu and Brahma cannot see?
commentary: Returning to stories of Siva's mercy and power, Vallalar notes that the traditional creator and preserver gods cannot even catch a glimpse of this reality. He contrasts their blindness with his own longing, asking when he will be allowed to see and rejoice in the form hidden from the highest celestial beings.

translit: koḷḷuvār koḷḷum kulamaṇiyē mālayaṉum tuḷḷuvār tuḷaṭakkum tōṉṟalē cūḻntunitam uḷḷuvār uḷuṟaiyum oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya teḷḷuvār pūṅkaḻaṟkeṉ cintaivaittu nillēṉō.
translation: O supreme gem obtained by those fit to receive it! O Lord who subdues the arrogance of Vishnu and Brahma when they leap with pride! O Father of Otri who dwells within those who gather and constantly think of you! Will I not stand with my mind fixed upon your pure, flower-like feet wearing anklets?
commentary: The divine presence is a rare treasure given to those who prepare their hearts to receive it. While the highest traditional gods are brought low by their arrogance, the supreme Lord makes a home within people who gather in quiet, constant devotion. Vallalar longs to keep his mind anchored to this pure presence.

translit: cevvaṇṇa mēṉit tirunīṟṟup pēraḻakā evvaṇṇam niṉvaṇṇam eṉṟaṟitaṟ koṇṇātāy uvvaṇṇaṉ ēttukiṉṟa oṟṟiyappā uṉvaṭivam ivvaṇṇam eṉṟeṉ itayat teḻutēṉō.
translation: O great beauty wearing holy ash on your red-hued body! You whose nature cannot be grasped! O Father of Otri praised by the dark-hued Vishnu! Will I not draw your form in my heart, realizing it looks like this?
commentary: The absolute divine defies all ordinary descriptions and categories. Even though its nature cannot be grasped by the mind or the other gods, love makes it intimate and personal. Vallalar seeks to capture this uncontainable beauty by drawing its image within the quiet space of his own heart.

translit: maṉṟuṭaiyāy mālayaṉum maṟṟumuḷa vāṉavarum kuṉṟuṭaiyāy eṉṉak kuṟaitavirtta kōmāṉē oṉṟuṭaiyāy ūrviṭaiyāy oṟṟiyappā eṉṉuṭaiya vaṉṟuṭaiyāy eṉṟuṉ malaraṭiyaip pōṟṟēṉō.
translation: O Lord of the hall! O King who removed the distress of Vishnu, Brahma, and the other celestials when they called out to you as the Lord of the mountain! O unparalleled One! O rider of the crawling bull! O Father of Otri! Will I not praise your flower-like feet, calling you my strong support?
commentary: The divine is the refuge when all other powers fail. When celestial beings face distress they cannot overcome, they turn to this supreme source for protection. Vallalar claims this boundless power as his own personal, unfailing support. He longs to offer his praise with a feeling of reliance and trust.

translit: kuṟṟam ceyiṉum kuṇamākak koṇṭaruḷum naṟṟavartam uḷḷam naṭuniṉṟa namparaṉē uṟṟavartam naṟṟuṇaivā oṟṟiyappā eṉkaruttu muṟṟiṭaniṉ cannitiyiṉ muṉniṉṟu vāḻttēṉō.
translation: O supreme Lord who stands in the center of the hearts of great ascetics, accepting even faults as virtues and bestowing grace! O good companion to those who reach you! O Father of Otri! Will I not stand before your presence and praise you so my intention is fulfilled?
commentary: Divine grace means the Lord looks past human flaws, choosing to accept even our mistakes as virtues. He stands at the center of the devoted heart as a faithful companion rather than a distant judge. Vallalar asks to stand directly in this forgiving presence so his spiritual intentions can be fulfilled.

translit: vañca maṭavār mayakkum mayakkoḻiya nañcamaṇi kaṇṭattu nātaṉē eṉṟeṉṟu uñcavarkaḷ vāḻttukiṉṟa oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya kañca malaraṭikkē kātaluṟṟup pōṟṟēṉō.
translation: O Father of Otriyur. Those who have been saved praise you, crying out again and again, "O Lord with the poison-adorned neck!" to rid themselves of the delusion caused by deceitful women. Will I not fall in love with your lotus feet and praise them?
commentary: The distractions of worldly life pull the mind away from spiritual focus. By remembering Siva's compassion in swallowing the poison, the saved overcome their worldly delusions. Vallalar longs to share in that same devotion to God's feet.

translit: iṉṉal ulaka iruḷnaṭaiyil nāḷtōṟum tuṉṉavarum neñcat tuṭukkaḻiya nallōrkaḷ uṉṉaluṟum teḷḷamutē oṟṟiyappā eṉvāyuṉ taṉaṭaivē pāṭit taḻumpēṟak kāṇēṉō.
translation: O clear nectar meditated upon by good people to destroy the heart's arrogance that arises daily in the dark ways of this sorrowful world. O Father of Otriyur. Will I not see my mouth grow callused from singing endlessly of your refuge?
commentary: Daily life in a sorrowful world can breed arrogance and confusion in the human heart. To cure this darkness, good people meditate on God as a clear, purifying nectar. Vallalar asks for a devotion so continuous and intense that his mouth would grow callused from singing of God's protection.

translit: peṇmaṇiyē eṉṟulakil pētaiyaraip pēcāteṉ kaṇmaṇiyē kaṟpakamē kaṇṇutalil koḷkarumpē oṇmaṇiyē tēṉē-eṉ ṟoṟṟiyappā uṉtaṉaināṉ paṇmaṇañcey pāṭṭil paravit tutiyēṉō.
translation: Instead of calling foolish women in this world "jewels among women," I will call you "apple of my eye, wish-fulfilling tree, sweet sugarcane with an eye on your forehead, bright gem, honey!" O Father of Otriyur, will I not extol and praise you in songs fragrant with melody?
commentary: People often waste their beautiful words flattering ordinary, flawed human beings. Instead of spending his poetry on worldly praise, Vallalar redirects all his endearments to God. He calls the divine his vision, his wish-fulfilling tree, and his sweet honey, pouring his love into fragrant melodies.

translit: māṉamilār niṉtāḷ vaḻuttāta vaṉmaṉattār īṉaravar pālpōy iḷaittēṉ iḷaippāṟa ūṉamilār pōṟṟukiṉṟa oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya ñāṉa aṭiyiṉniḻal naṇṇi makiḻēṉō.
translation: I grew exhausted seeking out base people without honor and hard-hearted ones who do not praise your feet. To rest from this weariness, O Father of Otriyur praised by the flawless, will I not reach the shade of your feet of wisdom and rejoice?
commentary: Seeking help from hard-hearted people who care nothing for the divine leaves the soul exhausted. Vallalar has tired himself out trying to find support among such worldly individuals. To heal from this weariness, he longs to rest in the shade of God's wisdom, where the flawless find their joy.

translit: kallārk kitaṅkūṟik kaṟpaḻintu nillāmal ellārkkum nallavaṉē eṉaracē naltarumam ollār purameritta oṟṟiyappā uṉaṭikkē collāl malartoṭuttuc cūḻntaṇintu vāḻēṉō.
translation: Instead of losing my integrity by speaking pleasing words to the ignorant, O one who is good to all! My King! O Father of Otriyur who burned the cities of foes who rejected good virtue. Will I not weave a garland of words for your feet, adorn you with it, and live?
commentary: Flattering the ignorant just to get by destroys a person's inner integrity. Rather than compromising his truth for worldly gain, Vallalar chooses to offer his words to God. He envisions his poetry as a flower garland, woven and placed at the feet of the divine King who destroys all evil.

translit: kaṟpavaṟṟaik kallāk kaṭaiyariṭam ceṉṟavarmuṉ aṟpa-aṟṟaik kūlik kalaiyum alaippoḻiya uṟpavattai nīkkukiṉṟa oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya naṟpatattai ētti-aruḷ nalnalantāṉ naṇṇēṉō.
translation: O Father of Otri who ends the cycle of birth! To escape the distress of wandering for a meager daily wage before the lowest of men who have learned nothing of worth, will I not attain the great good of praising your noble feet?
commentary: The struggle for survival often forces people to serve ignorant and ungracious masters. Vallalar begs to be freed from this degrading pursuit of a daily wage. He asks instead for the grace to seek the divine, which alone can put an end to the cycle of birth and suffering.

translit: tantaitāy makkaḷmaṉai tārameṉum caṅkaṭattil cintaitāṉ ceṉṟu tiyaṅki mayaṅkāmē untai-eṉpōr illāta oṟṟiyappā uṉaṭikkīḻ muntaiyōr pōṉṟu muyaṅki makiḻēṉō.
translation: O Father of Otri who has no father! Instead of letting my mind wander and become bewildered by the entanglements of father, mother, children, house, and wife, will I not unite and rejoice beneath your feet like the sages of old?
commentary: Family life brings entanglements. The everyday ties to parents, spouses, and children can bewilder the mind and pull it away from spiritual clarity. Vallalar asks the Father of Otri, who is himself unborn and without a father, for the strength to stand clear of these worldly webs. His goal is to find the same joyful union with the divine that the ancient sages knew.

translit: poyoṉṟē aṉṟip puṟampoṉṟum pēcāta vaiyoṉṟum tīnāṟṟa vāyārkku mēlāṉēṉ uyeṉ ṟaruḷīyum oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya meyoṉṟu nīṟṟiṉ viḷakkamatu pārēṉō.
translation: O Father of Otri who grants grace and commands me to live! I have become worse than those with foul-smelling mouths who speak lies and nothing else. Will I not behold the radiance of the sacred ash adorning your body?
commentary: Vallalar feels lower than habitual liars whose words only bring corruption. To cleanse this impurity, he longs to see the sacred ash shining on the divine form. In the Tamil Saiva tradition, this ash represents the truth and purity that remains when all worldly illusions are burned away.

translit: tūkkamummuṉ tūṅkiyapiṉ cōṟilaiyē eṉṉumanta ēkkamumē aṉṟimaṟṟōr ēkkamilā ēḻaiyaṉēṉ ūkkamuḷōr pōṟṟukiṉṟa oṟṟiyappā niṉaṭikkīḻ nīkkamilā āṉanta nittiraitāṉ koḷḷēṉō.
translation: I am a poor wretch who knows only sleep and the anxiety of lacking food when I wake. I have no other longing. O Father of Otri praised by the diligent! Will I not find the uninterrupted sleep of bliss beneath your feet?
commentary: Many people live trapped in the mechanics of survival. The mind becomes consumed by the hollow routine of waking up only to worry about the next meal. Vallalar longs to trade this anxious physical exhaustion for a different kind of rest. He asks for the unbroken sleep of bliss, a state of spiritual peace and absorption in the divine presence.

translit: vātupurin tīṉa maṭavār matittiṭuvāṉ pōtunitam pōkkip pulampum pulaināyēṉ ōtumaṟai yōrkulavum oṟṟiyappā ūraṉukkāt tūtuceṉṟa niṉtāḷ tuṇaippukaḻaip pāṭēṉō.
translation: I am a base dog who argues to win the esteem of foolish women. I waste my days and lament. O Father of Otri celebrated by those who chant the scriptures! Will I not sing the protective glory of your feet that went as a messenger for Sundarar?
commentary: Wasting time on frivolous arguments to impress others is a common human failing. Vallalar regrets spending his days chasing worldly validation. He contrasts his own foolishness with the grace of God by recalling a famous Tamil story where Siva acted as a humble midnight messenger to help the saint Sundarar resolve a domestic quarrel. Seeing how far the divine will go to serve a devotee, Vallalar wishes only to sing his praises.

translit: poṉṉācai yōṭum pulaicciyartam pērācai maṉṉācai maṉṉukiṉṟa maṇṇācaip paṟṟaṟuttē uṉṉācai koṇṭē-eṉ oṟṟiyappā nāṉmakiḻntuṉ miṉṉārum poṉmēṉi veṇṇīṟṟaip pārēṉō.
translation: Severing the attachment to the desire for gold, the immense desire for base women, the desire to rule, and the enduring desire for land, I have taken up the desire for You alone. O my Father of Otriyur! Will I not rejoice and behold the white ash upon your golden body that flashes like lightning?
commentary: Desire for wealth, physical pleasure, and power consumes the mind. Vallalar replaces these worldly attachments with a single desire for the divine. He longs to turn away from earthly ambitions to look upon God's ash-smeared, golden form.

translit: kaḷuṇṭa nāypōl kaṭuṅkāma veḷḷamuṇṭu tuḷuṇṭa neñcat tuṭukkaṭakki aṉparkaḷtam uḷuṇṭa teḷamutē oṟṟiyappā uṉtaṉaināṉ veḷuṇṭa nanti viṭaimītil kāṇēṉō.
translation: Subduing the arrogance of my leaping heart, which drank the flood of fierce lust like a dog drinking toddy, I look to You. O clear ambrosia partaken within by devotees! O my Father of Otriyur! Will I not see You mounted upon the white bull Nandi?
commentary: Worldly lust degrades the mind, making a person erratic and foolish like an animal that has drunk alcohol. Vallalar seeks to tame this restless mind to receive the nectar of grace that devotees experience. He prays to see God riding upon the white bull Nandi, a traditional image of divine majesty.

translit: pērāta kāmap piṇikoṇṭa neñcakaṉēṉ vārāta āṉanta vāḻvuvantu vāḻntiṭavē ōrātārk keṭṭāta oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya nīrār caṭaimēl nilavoḷiyaik kāṇēṉō.
translation: My heart holds the unyielding disease of lust. So that the elusive life of bliss may come and I may truly live, O Father of Otriyur who is unreachable to those who do not meditate on You! Will I not see the moonlight upon your matted hair that holds the river waters?
commentary: Lust is a stubborn disease that prevents a person from experiencing spiritual bliss. To cure this sickness of the heart, Vallalar longs for a vision of divine grace. He visualizes this grace as the gentle moonlight resting on God's matted hair, a peaceful sight revealed only to those who reflect on the truth.

translit: vaṉṉeñcap pētai maṭavārk kaḻintalaiyum kaṉṉeñcap pāviyaṉyāṉ kātalittu nekkuruki uṉṉeñcat tuḷuṟaiyum oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya veṉṉañ caṇimiṭaṟṟai mikkuvantu vāḻttēṉō.
translation: I am a stone-hearted sinner who wanders in ruin after ignorant women with hard hearts. Loving You and melting within, O Father of Otriyur who resides within the meditating heart! Will I not come near and abundantly praise your throat adorned with fierce poison?
commentary: Pursuing shallow earthly romances hardens the heart and leads to ruin. Vallalar repents for this wasted time, asking for his stone-like heart to melt with love for the divine. He wishes to praise God, whose throat holds the deadly poison swallowed to save the universe, showing that love is found in divine compassion rather than worldly attachment.

translit: puṇṇiyamōr pōtum purintaṟiyāp poyyavaṉēṉ eṇṇiyatōr eṇṇam iṭariṉṟi muṟṟiyiṭa uṇṇilavu naloḷiyē oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya taṇṇilavu tāmaraippoṉ tāḷmuṭiyil koḷḷēṉō.
translation: I am a false man who has never performed a virtuous deed at any time. So that my cherished thought may be fulfilled without obstacle, O good Light shining within! O my Father of Otriyur! Will I not hold your cool, lotus-like golden feet upon my head?
commentary: Vallalar admits he has lived a false life lacking in virtue. Despite his past wrongs, he trusts the good light shining within to guide him toward his spiritual goal. He asks to receive God's golden feet upon his head, a gesture of surrender and blessing.

translit: naṉṟitu-eṉ ṟōrntumatai nāṭātu nalneṟiyaik koṉṟitunaṉ ṟeṉṉak kuṟikkum koṭiyavaṉyāṉ oṉṟumaṉat tuḷoḷiyē oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya veṉṟi maḻuppaṭaiyiṉ mēṉmaitaṉaip pāṭēṉō.
translation: Even knowing what is good, I do not seek it. I destroy the path of virtue and point to evil, calling it good. I am a cruel person. O light within the unified mind! O Father of Otriyur! Will I ever sing the greatness of your victorious battle-axe?
commentary: Vallalar openly confesses the human flaw of knowing the right path but actively destroying it. He turns to the divine light within the quiet mind, longing to praise the Lord's battle-axe, a symbol of the power to cut through such ignorance.

translit: maṇkiṭanta vāḻviṉ matimayakkum maṅkaiyarāl puṇkiṭanta neñcap pulaiyēṉ puḻukkamaṟa oṇkiṭanta muttalaivēl oṟṟiyappā nāraṇaṉtaṉ kaṇkiṭanta cēvaṭiyiṉ kāṭcitaṉaik kāṇēṉō.
translation: My heart lies wounded by women who bewilder the mind in this earthly life. I am a base person. For my torment to cease, O Father of Otriyur who holds the bright trident! Will I ever see the vision of your red feet where Narayana offered his eye?
commentary: Worldly attachments and desires leave the mind bewildered and the heart wounded. To end this torment, Vallalar longs to see the Lord's feet. He recalls an ancient story where Narayana (the god Vishnu) plucked out his own eye to offer it as a lotus in worship at those very feet.

translit: kūṭṭuvikkuḷ mēleḻavē kūṟṟuvaṉvan tāvitaṉai vāṭṭuvikkum kālam varumuṉṉē evvuyirkkum ūṭṭuvikkum tāyākum oṟṟiyappā nī-ulakai āṭṭuvikkum ampalattuṉ āṭṭamataip pārēṉō.
translation: Before the time comes when the God of Death arrives to extract the breath rising within the cage of this body and torments my soul, O Father of Otriyur! You are the mother who feeds every living being. Will I ever see your dance in the open hall that makes the whole world dance?
commentary: Time in the physical body is limited, and death will eventually arrive to extract the breath. Before that moment comes, Vallalar begs to witness the Lord's cosmic dance. He describes the divine as a mother who feeds all life, whose step in the open hall keeps the universe in motion.

translit: miṉoppām vāḻvai viyantiṭaruḷ vīḻntalaintēṉ poṉoppāy teyvamaṇap pū-oppāy eṉṉiṉumē uṉoppār illāta oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya taṉoppām vēṇiyiṉmēl cārpiṟaiyaip pārēṉō.
translation: I marvelled at this life that flashes like lightning, fell into sorrow, and wandered aimlessly. Even if you are compared to gold and to a divinely fragrant flower, you have no equal, O Father of Otriyur! Will I ever see the crescent moon resting upon your peerless matted hair?
commentary: Human life flashes and vanishes as quickly as lightning. Realizing he has wandered through this fleeting existence in sorrow, Vallalar looks to the divine, which has no equal. He asks for a vision of the crescent moon resting in the Lord's matted hair.

translit: cīlamaṟa niṟkum ciṟiyār uṟaviṭainal kālamaṟap pēcik kaḻikkiṉṟēṉ vāṉavartam ōlamaṟa nañcaruntum oṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya nīla maṇimiṭaṟṟiṉ nērmaitaṉaip pārēṉō.
translation: In the company of petty people who stand devoid of virtue, I waste my good time in endless talk. To end the wailing of the celestials, you drank the poison, O Father of Otriyur! Will I ever see the beauty of your sapphire-blue throat?
commentary: It is easy to waste precious time in empty talk with people who lack virtue. Vallalar contrasts this petty human behavior with an act of divine compassion. He asks to see the Lord's sapphire-blue throat, stained by the poison.

translit: cīrpukaḻum mālpukaḻum tēvarayaṉ taṉpukaḻum yārpukaḻum vēṇṭēṉ aṭiyēṉ aṭināyēṉ ūrpukaḻum nalvaḷaṅkoḷ oṟṟiyappā uṉitaḻit tārpukaḻum naltoḻumpu cārntuṉpāl naṇṇēṉō.
translation: I do not want the exalted praise of Thirumal, the praise of the Devas and Brahma, or the praise of anyone else. I am your devotee, worse than a lowly dog. O Father of Otriyur, possessing fine wealth praised by the whole town! Will I not approach you and perform good service that praises your laburnum garland?
commentary: Devotion leaves no room for the desire to be praised by others, even by the highest gods like Brahma or Vishnu (Thirumal). The only reward worth seeking is the chance to serve God directly.

translit: ātavaṉtaṉ paliṟutta aiyaṟ karuḷpurinta nāta-ara ṉē-eṉṟu nāttaḻumpu koṇṭētti ōtavaḷa mikka-eḻil oṟṟiyappā maṇṇiṭantum mātavaṉmuṉ kāṇā malaraṭikkaṇ vaikēṉō.
translation: Praising you until my tongue grows calluses, I cry out to you as Lord Hara who bestowed grace upon the heroic lord who shattered the sun's teeth. O Father of beautiful Otriyur, rich with the roaring sea! Will I not abide at your lotus feet, which great Vishnu could not see even after digging through the earth?
commentary: Unceasing praise is the mark of longing for the divine. The reference to Vishnu digging through the earth recalls an ancient story where the greatest gods tried to find the limits of Siva's form and failed. Where power and effort fall short, devoted praise opens the way to his feet.

translit: kallaip puṟaṅkaṇṭa kāymaṉattuk kaitavaṉēṉ tollaip paḻaviṉaiyiṉ tōyvakaṉṟu vāyntiṭavē ollait tiruvaruḷkoṇ ṭoṟṟiyappā uṉṉuṭaiya tillaip potuvil tirunaṭaṉam kāṇēṉō.
translation: I am a deceiver with a harsh heart that surpasses stone in hardness. To be freed completely from the taint of ancient karma, O Father of Otriyur, will I not swiftly receive your divine grace and witness your sacred dance in the public hall of Thillai?
commentary: The weight of past actions (karma) hardens the heart like stone. Only the swift arrival of divine grace can break through this hardness and free the soul. Witnessing the sacred dance at Thillai represents experiencing the bliss of God's presence.

translit: kaṭaiyavaṉēṉ kaṉmaṉattēṉ kaitavaṉēṉ vañca naṭaiyavaṉēṉ nāṇiliyēṉ nāykkiṇaiyēṉ tuṉpoḻiya uṭaiyavaṉē ulakēttum oṟṟiyappā niṉpālvan taṭaiyaniṉṟu meykuḷirntē āṉantam kūṭēṉō.
translation: I am the lowest of the low. I have a stony heart. I am a trickster. I walk a path of deceit. I am shameless and equal to a dog. O Master, Father of Otriyur praised by the world! So that my sorrow perishes, will I not come to you, stand firm as your refuge, and unite in bliss as my body cools with joy?
commentary: Spiritual transformation begins with a painful honesty about one's own faults and deceit. Taking refuge in God melts away this sorrow. The physical sensation of the body cooling with joy is a direct sign of spiritual union.

translit: vātai mayalkāṭṭum maṭavār malakkuḻiyil pētai eṉavīḻntē piṇi-uḻanta pēyaṭiyēṉ ōtai kaṭaṟkaraivāy oṟṟiyappā vāḻttukiṉṟōr tītai akaṟṟumuṉṟaṉ cīraruḷaic cērēṉō.
translation: Falling like a fool into the foul pit of women who display agonizing delusion, I am a demonic devotee suffering from disease. O Father of Otriyur by the shore of the roaring sea! Will I not reach your glorious grace, which removes the evil from those who praise you?
commentary: Sensual delusion acts like a trap that brings physical and spiritual suffering. Constant praise is the medicine that invites God's grace. That grace has the power to wash away all evil, no matter how foolishly a person has lived.

translit: poyyark kutavukiṉṟa puṉmaiyiṉēṉ vaṉmaiceyum veyyaṟ kirimiyeṉa meycōrn tiḷaittalaintēṉ uyyaṟ karuḷceyyum oṟṟiyappā uṉaṭicēr meyyark kaṭimai ceytuṉ meṉmalarttāḷ naṇṇēṉō.
translation: I am a wretched person who helps the false. Like a worm suffering in the harsh heat, my body weakened and I wandered in exhaustion. O Father of Otriyur who grants grace for salvation, will I not serve the true devotees who have reached your feet and thereby attain your soft flower-like feet?
commentary: Supporting those who live false, worldly lives brings only exhaustion. Vallalar compares this spiritual fatigue to a worm agonizing in the blazing sun. Crying out to the Lord of Otriyur for rescue, he seeks a different way to live. He asks to serve the devotees of God, showing that the path to divine grace lies in serving those who have already found it.

translit: caḻakki runtateṉ ṉiṭattilā yiṉumnīr tantai ātaliṉ cārntanal neṟiyil paḻakki vaippatu tēvarīrk kuriya paṇpaṉ ṟō-eṉaip parintilīr āṉāl vaḻakki ruppatiṅ kumakkumeṉ ṟaṉakkum vakuttuk kūṟutal marapumaṟ ṟaṉṟāl puḻaikkai māvuri yīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Though flaws exist in me, since You are the Father, is it not Your nature to train me in the good path I have reached? If You do not show me compassion, there will be a dispute here between You and me. It is not tradition to state this in detail. O Lord who wears the skin of the elephant with a tubular trunk! O Lord of Otriyur! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: A child has a natural right to be guided by their father, regardless of their flaws. Vallalar claims this intimacy, arguing it is the divine duty to train and correct him. Otriyur is a famous temple town near Chennai. The image of the elephant's skin belongs to traditional stories of Siva conquering pride. If the ultimate refuge turns you away, there is nowhere left to turn.

translit: aḻutu neñcayarn tumainiṉaik kiṉṟēṉ aiya nīraṟi yātatum aṉṟē kaḻutu tuṉṟiya kāṭṭakat tāṭum katiyi līreṉak kaḻaṟiṉaṉ allāl paḻutu pēciṉa toṉṟilai oṟṟip patiyil vāḻpaṭam pakkanā yakarē poḻutu pōkiṉṟa teṉceykēṉ eṉainīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Weeping and with a weary heart, I think of You. O Lord, this is not unknown to You. I said You dance in the forest swarming with ghouls and have no other refuge. Other than that, I spoke no fault. O Lord of the hooded serpent who lives in the city of Otriyur! Time is passing away. What shall I do? If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: Intimacy with the divine allows for playful teasing. Vallalar reminds God that his only fault was joking about the divine dwelling in a cremation ground surrounded by ghosts. This refers to the traditional depiction of Siva dancing in the ashes of the dead, symbolizing the end of worldly attachments. Beneath the playful tone is an urgency about time running out and the need for grace.

translit: muṉṉai mātava muyaṟci-oṉ ṟillā mūṭa ṉēṉtaṉai muṉvara vaḻaittup piṉṉai oṉṟumvāyp pēccilī rāṉāl pittar eṉṟumaip pēciṭa lāmē eṉṉai nāṉpaḻit tiṭukiṉṟa tallāl ikaḻki lēṉumai eḻiloṟṟi uṭaiyīr puṉṉai añcaṭai yīreṉai uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Calling me forth, a fool with no effort of great past penance, if You do not speak a word afterwards, people can call You a madman. I only blame myself; I do not scorn You. O Lord of beautiful Otriyur! O Lord with beautiful matted hair adorned with punnai flowers! O Lord who owns me! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: The divine takes the first step by drawing the soul inward. Vallalar argues that since God initiated this connection without any prior merit, staying silent now makes no sense. He gently warns that the world might call God foolish for starting a relationship and not finishing it. Even in this bold argument, the devotee takes the blame for his own shortcomings.

translit: vaṉmai pēciya vaṉtoṇṭar poruṭṭāy vaḻakkup pēciya vaḷḷalnīr aṉṟō iṉmai yāḷarpōl valiyavan tiṭiṉum ēḻai yāmivaṉ eṉṟoḻit tiṭṭāl taṉmai aṉṟatu tarumamum aṉṟāl tamiya ṉēṉiṉṉum cāṟṟuva teṉṉē poṉmai añcaṭai yīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Are You not the generous Lord who argued a case for the sake of Vanthondar who spoke harshly? Even if I approach forcefully like a destitute person, if You abandon me saying I am poor, that is not Your nature and it is not righteous. What more can I, a lonely man, declare? O Lord with beautiful golden matted hair! O Lord of Otriyur! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: God has a long history of helping devotees in trouble. Vanthondar was a famous ancient saint who spoke harshly to God, yet God still intervened in a legal dispute on his behalf. Vallalar uses this precedent to argue that ignoring a desperate beggar goes against the nature of divine generosity. True grace means rescuing the seeker because they are helpless.

translit: uṟaṅku kiṉṟatum viḻippatum makiḻvāy uṇṇu kiṉṟatum uṭuppatum mayakkuḷ iṟaṅku kiṉṟatum ēṟukiṉ ṟatumāy eykkiṉ ṟēṉmaṉam eṉṉiṉum aṭiyēṉ aṟaṅkoḷ numaṭi araṇeṉa aṭaintēṉ ayarvu tīrtteṉai āṭkoḷa niṉaiyīr puṟaṅkoḷ kāṭṭakat tīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Sleeping, waking, eating joyfully, dressing, descending into delusion and rising out of it, my mind grows weary. Even so, as Your servant, I reached Your righteous feet as my fortress. You do not think of curing my weariness and making me Your own. O Lord of the cremation ground on the outskirts! O Lord of Otriyur! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: The daily cycles of ordinary life are exhausting and keep the mind trapped in confusion. Vallalar describes the endless loop of sleeping, waking, and eating, which slowly drains the soul's energy. Taking shelter at the divine feet is meant to be a permanent fortress against this worldly weariness. He has abandoned all worldly defenses and relies on being accepted by the divine.

translit: karumpiṉ kaṭṭiyum kaṉiyaiyum koṭuttāl kayavar āyiṉum kacakkumeṉ ṟuraiyār arumpiṉ kaṭṭiḷa mulai-umai makiḻum aiya nīruma taruḷeṉak kaḷikka irumpiṉ kaṭṭinēr neñciṉēṉ eṉiṉum ēṟṟu vāṅkiṭā tiruntatuṇ ṭēyō porumpiṉ kaṭṭuri yīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: If someone offers a block of sugarcane jaggery and a sweet fruit, even the basest of people will not say they taste bitter. Oh Lord who delights Umai of firm, bud-like young breasts! If you grant me your grace, even though I have a heart like a block of iron, have I ever refused to receive it? Oh Lord of Otriyur who wears the tied hide of a fierce beast! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: Just as no one turns down the sweetness of sugar or fruit, the soul instinctively recognizes the sweetness of divine grace. Even a person with a hardened, iron-like heart would never refuse this gift once it is offered.

translit: viruppu niṉṟatum patamalar micai-av viruppai māṟṟutal virakumaṟ ṟaṉṟāl karuppu nēriṉum vaḷḷiyōr koṭukkum kaṭamai nīṅkuṟār uṭamaiyiṉ ṟēṉum neruppu numuru āyiṉum arukil niṟka añcuṟēṉ nīlaṉum aṉṟāl poruppu villuṭai yīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: My desire stands fixed upon your lotus feet. Relinquishing that desire is no clever strategy. Even when famine strikes, generous people never abandon their duty to give, even if they lack wealth. Even though your form is fire, I do not fear to stand near you, nor am I dark-hearted. Oh Lord who wields the mountain as a bow! Oh Lord of Otriyur! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: True generosity does not stop when times are hard. Vallalar trusts that God will never withhold grace, comparing the divine nature to noble people who share what they have even during a famine. Although God appears as fierce fire, pure devotion removes all fear of approaching that intense light.

translit: koṭiya nañcamu tākkiya umakkik koṭiya ṉēṉai-āṭ koḷḷutal aritō aṭiyar tamporuṭ ṭaṭipaṭu vīrem aiya nummaṭik kāṭpaṭa viraintēṉ neṭiya mālayaṉ kāṇkila rēṉum niṉṟu kāṇkuval eṉṟuḷam tuṇintēṉ poṭiya nīṟaṇi vīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: You transformed deadly poison into sweet nectar. Is it difficult for you to take this cruel one as your devotee? You endure blows for the sake of your devotees. Oh my Lord! I hastened to become a servant at your feet. Even though tall Vishnu and Brahma could not see you, I resolved in my heart that I would stand and see you. Oh Lord of Otriyur who wears holy ash! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: If the Divine can turn deadly poison into sweet nectar, transforming a flawed soul into something pure is an easy task. In traditional lore, the great gods Brahma and Vishnu searched the universe for the Divine and failed because of their pride. Vallalar proves that ordinary souls can succeed in seeing God through humble determination.

translit: viṉaiyi ṉāluṭal eṭuttaṉa ṉēṉum mēlai nāḷumai virumpiya aṭiyēṉ eṉai-iṉ ṉāṉeṉa aṟintili rōnīr eḻumaic ceykaiyum iṟṟeṉa aṟivīr maṉaiyi ṉālvarum tuyarkeṭa umatu marapu vēṇṭiyē vantuniṟ kiṉṟēṉ puṉaiyi ṉālamarn tīroṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Even though I took this body because of my past karma, I am a devotee who loved you in days gone by. Do you not know who I am? You know my deeds across all seven births. I come and stand before you, seeking your customary grace so that the sorrows of household life may perish. Oh beautifully adorned Lord of Otriyur! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: The connection between the soul and the Divine stretches far beyond a single lifetime. While human birth is shaped by karma (the accumulated results of past actions), the soul's devotion is an ancient bond spanning countless births. Appealing to this history of love, Vallalar asks for shelter from the exhausting struggles of ordinary household life.

translit: piḻaipu rintaṉaṉ ākilum umatu perumai nōkkilap piḻaiciṟi taṉṟō maḻaipu rintiṭum vaṇkaiyai māṟṟa matikkiṉ ṟōrevar maṟṟilai atupōl uḻaipu rintaruḷ vīreṉil taṭuppār umpar imparil oruvarum ilaikāṇ puḻaipu rintakai ulavoṟṟi uṭaiyīr poyyaṉ eṉṉilyāṉ pōmvaḻi etuvō.
translation: Even if I have committed faults, when compared to your greatness, are those faults not small? Who would ever think to stop the generous hand that pours down rain? There is no one. Likewise, if you exert yourself to grant me your grace, there is no one in heaven or on earth who can stop you. Oh Lord of Otriyur where elephants with tubular trunks roam! If You call me a false one, which way will I go?
commentary: Human mistakes are tiny next to the infinite greatness of God. Grace is compared to a heavy rainstorm: just as no one on earth can stop the skies from pouring down water, nothing can block the flow of God's compassion once it begins to fall.

tamil: பசைஇலாக் கருங்கல் பாறைநேர் மனத்துப் பதகனேன் படிற்றுரு வகனேன்
வசைஇலார்க் கருளும் மாணிக்க மணியே வள்ளலே நினைத்தொழல் மறந்து
நசைஇலா மலம்உண் டோடுறும் கொடிய நாய்என உணவுகொண் டுற்றேன்
தசைஎலாம் நடுங்க ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: pacai-ilāk karuṅkal pāṟainēr maṉattup patakaṉēṉ paṭiṟṟuru vakaṉēṉ vacai-ilārk karuḷum māṇikka maṇiyē vaḷḷalē niṉaittoḻal maṟantu nacai-ilā malamuṇ ṭōṭuṟum koṭiya nāyeṉa uṇavukoṇ ṭuṟṟēṉ tacai-elām naṭuṅka oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: I am a sinner with a heart like a dry black rock. I am a hypocrite of deceitful form. O ruby gem who graces the flawless! O generous Lord! Forgetting to think of you and worship you, I took food like a cruel dog that runs around eating undesirable filth. Because of this, with all my flesh trembling, I was punished by you in Otriyur, was I not?
commentary: Eating without devotion reduces human nourishment to animal scavenging. Forgetting the divine hardens the heart and disconnects the soul from grace. The trembling flesh describes a visceral bodily shock, which Vallalar sees as a necessary correction for his thoughtlessness.

tamil: அன்னைபோன் றடியர்க் கருத்தியில் அருத்தும் அப்பநின் அடியினை காணா
தென்னையோ மலம்உண் டுழன்றிடும் பன்றி என்னஉண் டுற்றனன் அதனால்
புன்னைஅம் சடைஎம் புண்ணிய ஒளியே பூதநா யகஎன்றன் உடலம்
தன்னைநீ அமர்ந்த ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: aṉṉaipōṉ ṟaṭiyark karuttiyil aruttum appaniṉ aṭiyiṉai kāṇā teṉṉaiyō malamuṇ ṭuḻaṉṟiṭum paṉṟi eṉṉa-uṇ ṭuṟṟaṉaṉ ataṉāl puṉṉai-am caṭai-em puṇṇiya oḷiyē pūtanā yaka-eṉṟaṉ uṭalam taṉṉainī amarnta oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: O Father who feeds devotees with love like a mother! Without seeing your feet, why did I take food like a pig that wanders eating filth? Because of this, O our meritorious light with matted hair beautiful like the Punnai tree! O Lord of all beings! in my body I was punished by you in Otriyur, where you abide, was I not?
commentary: God provides nourishment with a mother's tender love, yet humans often consume it with the blind greed of wandering animals. Eating without looking to the divine source is a failure of gratitude. The physical suffering reflects the heavy toll of living only to satisfy the senses.

tamil: கண்ணினால் உனது கழற்பதம் காணும் கருத்தினை மறந்துபாழ் வயிற்றை
மண்ணினால் நிறைத்தல் எனஉண வருந்தி மலம்பெற வந்தனன் அதனால்
எண்ணினால் அடங்கா எண்குணக் குன்றே இறைவனே நீஅமர்ந் தருளும்
தண்ணினால் ஓங்கும் ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: kaṇṇiṉāl uṉatu kaḻaṟpatam kāṇum karuttiṉai maṟantupāḻ vayiṟṟai maṇṇiṉāl niṟaittal eṉa-uṇa varunti malampeṟa vantaṉaṉ ataṉāl eṇṇiṉāl aṭaṅkā eṇkuṇak kuṉṟē iṟaivaṉē nī-amarn taruḷum taṇṇiṉāl ōṅkum oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: Forgetting the intention to see your anklet-adorned feet with my eyes, I ate food as if filling this ruined stomach with dirt, and ended up only producing waste. Because of this, O mountain of eight attributes that defy counting! O God! I was punished by you in Otriyur, which thrives with coolness and where you graciously abide, was I not?
commentary: Feeding the body without feeding the soul is a hollow act. Without spiritual focus, the food we eat might as well be dirt, serving only to fill a ruined stomach and produce waste. The divine presence is described as a mountain of eight infinite qualities (the traditional attributes of the supreme Lord), standing in stark contrast to mere physical digestion.

tamil: நின்முனம் நீல கண்டம்என் றோதும் நெறிமறந் துணவுகொண் டந்தோ
பொன்முனம் நின்ற இரும்பென நின்றேன் புலையனேன் ஆதலால் இன்று
மின்முனம் இலங்கும் வேணிஅம் கனியே விரிகடல் தானைசூழ் உலகம்
தன்முனம் இலங்கும் ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: niṉmuṉam nīla kaṇṭameṉ ṟōtum neṟimaṟan tuṇavukoṇ ṭantō poṉmuṉam niṉṟa irumpeṉa niṉṟēṉ pulaiyaṉēṉ ātalāl iṉṟu miṉmuṉam ilaṅkum vēṇi-am kaṉiyē virikaṭal tāṉaicūḻ ulakam taṉmuṉam ilaṅkum oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: Alas, forgetting the rule to chant Neelakantam before you, I took food. I stood like iron before gold. Since I am a base person, today, O beautiful fruit with matted hair shining before lightning! I was punished by you in Otriyur, which shines before this world surrounded by the vast ocean's forces, was I not?
commentary: The sacred custom is to chant the name Neelakantam (the blue-throated Lord who drank deadly poison to save all beings) before taking food. Forgetting this act of compassion reduces the human to base iron standing before pure gold. Remembering the divine sacrifice transforms eating from a selfish impulse into a moment of reverence.

tamil: குழிக்குமண் அடைக்கும் கொள்கைபோல் பாழும் கும்பியை ஓம்பினன் அல்லால்
செழிக்கும்உன் திருமுன் நீலகண் டந்தான் செப்புதல் மறந்தனன் அதனால்
விழிக்குள்நின் றிலங்கும் விளங்கொளி மணியே மென்கரும் பீன்றவெண் முத்தம்
தழிக்கொளும் வயல்சூழ் ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: kuḻikkumaṇ aṭaikkum koḷkaipōl pāḻum kumpiyai ōmpiṉaṉ allāl ceḻikkumuṉ tirumuṉ nīlakaṇ ṭantāṉ cepputal maṟantaṉaṉ ataṉāl viḻikkuḷniṉ ṟilaṅkum viḷaṅkoḷi maṇiyē meṉkarum pīṉṟaveṇ muttam taḻikkoḷum vayalcūḻ oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: I nurtured this ruined stomach as if filling a pit with dirt, but I forgot to utter Neelakantam before your flourishing divine presence. Because of this, O radiant luminous gem shining within the eyes! I was punished by you in Otriyur, surrounded by fields abundant with white pearls yielded by soft sugarcane, was I not?
commentary: Treating the stomach like an empty pit is a failure to honor the body as a sacred space. God is the radiant light shining inside our own eyes, witnessing our every action. Ignoring this inner presence while shoveling food away brings a painful correction, reminding the soul to pause and remember the divine.

tamil: கமரிடை மலநீர் கவிழ்த்தல்போல் வயிற்றுக் கடன்கழித் திட்டனன் அல்லால்
அமரிடைப் புரமூன் றெரித்தருள் புரிந்த ஐயனே நினைத்தொழல் மறந்தேன்
சமரிடை மனத்தேன் ஆதலால் முனிவர் சங்கர சிவசிவ என்றே
தமரிடை ஓங்கும் ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: kamariṭai malanīr kaviḻttalpōl vayiṟṟuk kaṭaṉkaḻit tiṭṭaṉaṉ allāl amariṭaip puramūṉ ṟerittaruḷ purinta aiyaṉē niṉaittoḻal maṟantēṉ camariṭai maṉattēṉ ātalāl muṉivar caṅkara civaciva eṉṟē tamariṭai ōṅkum oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: Like pouring foul water into a fissure in the earth, I merely paid the debt of my stomach. O Lord who burned the three cities in battle and bestowed grace, I forgot to worship You. Because my mind is always in conflict, I was punished by you in Otriyur, where sages and devotees flourish chanting "Sankara, Siva Siva", was I not?
commentary: Eating merely to satisfy physical hunger is as pointless as pouring dirty water into a crack in the earth. When the mind focuses on the stomach and forgets the divine, it remains trapped in conflict. Vallalar feels this disconnection from God as a heavy punishment.

tamil: அருமருந் தனையாய் நின்திரு முன்போந் தரகர எனத்தொழல் மறந்தே
இருளுறும் மனத்தேன் மலத்தினும் இழிந்த இயல்புற உண்டனன் அதனால்
கருமருந் தனைய அஞ்செழுத் தோதும் கருத்தர்போல் திருத்தம தாகத்
தருமநின் றோங்கும் ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: arumarun taṉaiyāy niṉtiru muṉpōn tarakara eṉattoḻal maṟantē iruḷuṟum maṉattēṉ malattiṉum iḻinta iyalpuṟa uṇṭaṉaṉ ataṉāl karumarun taṉaiya añceḻut tōtum karuttarpōl tiruttama tākat tarumaniṉ ṟōṅkum oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: O rare medicine, I came before Your sacred presence and forgot to worship You chanting "Hara Hara". With a darkened mind, I ate food and took on a nature worse than filth. Because of this, I was punished by you in Otriyur, where dharma flourishes perfectly like the wise who chant the five syllables that act as a cure for birth, was I not?
commentary: Approaching food with a dark, forgetful mind turns eating into something degrading. Vallalar contrasts this spiritual numbness with the clarity of the wise who constantly remember God, chanting the five sacred syllables of Siva (Na-Ma-Si-Va-Ya) as a cure for the suffering of worldly life.

tamil: கண்நுதல் கரும்பே நின்முனம் நீல கண்டம்என் றோதுதல் மறந்தே
உண்ணுதற் கிசைந்தே உண்டுபின் ஒதிபோல் உன்முனம் நின்றனன் அதனால்
நண்ணுதல் பொருட்டோர் நான்முகன் மாயோன் நாடிட அடியர்தம்உள்ளத்
தண்ணுதல் கலந்த ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: kaṇnutal karumpē niṉmuṉam nīla kaṇṭameṉ ṟōtutal maṟantē uṇṇutaṟ kicaintē uṇṭupiṉ otipōl uṉmuṉam niṉṟaṉaṉ ataṉāl naṇṇutal poruṭṭōr nāṉmukaṉ māyōṉ nāṭiṭa aṭiyartamuḷḷat taṇṇutal kalanta oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: O sugarcane with an eye on Your forehead, I forgot to chant "Neelakantam" before You. I focused only on eating, and having eaten, I stood before You like a chameleon. Because of this, I was punished by you in Otriyur, where You abide cooling the hearts of devotees while the four-faced Brahma and Vishnu search for a way to approach You, was I not?
commentary: Focusing on food leaves a person bloated and spiritually sluggish, staring blankly like a chameleon before the very divine presence that other deities desperately seek.

tamil: கற்றவர்க் கினிதாம் கதியருள் நீல கண்டம்என் றுன்திரு முன்னர்
சொற்றிடல் மறந்தேன் சோற்றினை ஊத்தைத் துருத்தியில் அடைத்தனன் அதனால்
செற்றமற் றுயர்ந்தோர் சிவசிவ சிவமா தேவஓம் அரகர எனும்சொல்
சற்றும்விட் டகலா ஒற்றியில் உன்னால் தண்டிக்கப் பட்டனன் அன்றே.
translit: kaṟṟavark kiṉitām katiyaruḷ nīla kaṇṭameṉ ṟuṉtiru muṉṉar coṟṟiṭal maṟantēṉ cōṟṟiṉai ūttait turuttiyil aṭaittaṉaṉ ataṉāl ceṟṟamaṟ ṟuyarntōr civaciva civamā tēva-ōm arakara eṉumcol caṟṟumviṭ ṭakalā oṟṟiyil uṉṉāl taṇṭikkap paṭṭaṉaṉ aṉṟē.
translation: I forgot to chant "Neelakantam" in Your sacred presence to attain the sweet liberation granted to the learned. I stuffed food into this foul leather bag of a body. Because of this, I was punished by you in Otriyur, where the words "Siva Siva, Mahadeva, Om, Hara Hara" never leave the lips of the exalted ones free of anger, was I not?
