commentary: True generosity means feeding anyone who arrives hungry, even uninvited. Vallalar presents himself as an exhausted guest seeking the nectar of divine grace, desperate to escape worldly deceit. If God turns away a suffering soul, that reputation for generosity means nothing.

translit: poyyaṉ ākilum pōkkiṭam aṟiyāp pulaiyaṉ āṇṭavaṉ pukaḻuraip pāṉēl uyya vaippaṉī tuṇmai-iv vulakil otiya ṉēṉpukal ōriṭam aṟiyēṉ aiya nummaṭik kāṭceyal uṭaiyēṉ āṇṭa nīreṉai akaṟṟutal aḻakō naiyal aṟṟiṭa aruḷoṟṟi uṭaiyīr ñāṉa nāṭakam naviṟṟukiṉ ṟīrē.
translation: Even if someone is a liar, if a lowly person with nowhere to go praises the Lord, the Lord will save him. This is the truth. In this world, I am a useless person and I know no other refuge. O Lord, I have the duty to serve your feet. Is it fair for you who rule me to cast me away? O Lord of Otriyur who grants grace to end despair! You perform a drama of wisdom.
commentary: The divine nature is so merciful that even the most flawed person is saved the moment they call for help. Vallalar claims this universal promise. He admits his faults and declares he has no other refuge. Since he belongs to the Lord, casting him away would be unjust.

translit: tantai āyavar taṉaiyaraik keṭukkac camaivar eṉpatu caṟṟumiṉ ṟulakil entai nīreṉai vañcaka vāḻvil iruttu vīreṉil yārkkitu pukalvēṉ panta mēliṭa eṉpari tāpam pārppi rō-aruṭ paṅkaya viḻiyīr nanta voṇpaṇai oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr ñāṉa nāṭakam naviṟṟukiṉ ṟīrē.
translation: There is absolutely no talk in this world of fathers being ready to ruin their own sons. My Father, if you keep me in this deceitful life, to whom will I complain about this? Will you watch my suffering as my worldly bondage increases, O Lord with lotus eyes of grace? O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by flourishing bright fields! You perform a drama of wisdom.
commentary: No father deliberately destroys his child. Addressing God as the ultimate father, Vallalar asks how a loving parent could watch a child suffer in the trap of worldly attachments. If God allows him to remain caught in this illusion, there is no one else he can appeal to for help.

translit: kalvi vēṇṭiya makaṉtaṉaip peṟṟōr kaṭuttal ōrciṟu kataiyilum ilaikāṇ celvam vēṇṭilēṉ tiruvaruḷ viḻaintēṉ ciṟiya ṉēṉainīr tiyakkutal aḻakō palvi taṅkaḷāl paṇiceyum urimaip pāṅku nalkumap paramumak kaṉṟē nalvi tattiṉar pukaḻoṟṟi uṭaiyīr ñāṉa nāṭakam naviṟṟukiṉ ṟīrē.
translation: You will not find even in a short story that parents are angry at a son who desires education. I do not want wealth. I desire only divine grace. Is it fair for you to confuse me, a lowly person? The supreme duty to grant me the right to serve you in many ways belongs to you, does it not? O Lord of Otriyur praised by good people! You perform a drama of wisdom.
commentary: Parents are thrilled when their child wants to learn rather than chase idle things. Vallalar says he has no interest in worldly wealth and seeks only the supreme knowledge of divine grace. Since he asks for the highest possible good, it is God's duty to grant him clarity and the right to serve.

translit: maṇṇil nallavaṉ nallavar iṭattōr vaṇakkam iṉmaiyaṉ vaṇaṅkuvaṉ āṉāl eṇṇi nampuṭai iru-eṉa uraippar ēṉva ṇaṅkiṉai eṉṟuraip pārō kaṇṇiṉ nallanum kaḻaltoḻa icaintāl kalakkam kāṇpatu kaṭaṉaṉṟu kaṇṭīr naṇṇi mātavaṉ toḻumoṟṟi uṭaiyīr ñāṉa nāṭakam naviṟṟukiṉ ṟīrē.
translation: If a good person on earth, who previously lacked reverence, bows before noble people, they will thoughtfully say, "Stay by our side." Will they ever ask, "Why did you bow?" When I step forward to worship your feet, which are more precious than my own eyes, it is not proper for you to let me suffer distress. O Lord of Otri, approached and worshipped by the great Vishnu! You perform a drama of wisdom.
commentary: Just as good people welcome a respectful visitor, God should accept his devotion without leaving him in distress. If someone who usually lacks reverence bows to a kind person, they are invited to stay instead of being questioned. Vallalar asks why God lets him suffer confusion after he steps forward to worship. He concludes that the Lord of Otri, revered even by Vishnu, must be playing a deliberate game of wisdom by holding back his grace.

sections.title: The Petition to the Divine Form

translit: kaṇṇappā eṉṟaruḷum kāḷatti yappāmuṉ vaṇṇappāl vēṇṭum matalaiyaippāl vāritiyai uṇṇappā eṉṟuraitta oṟṟiyappā vantaruḷa eṇṇappā eṉṟaḻumiv ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O Father of Kalahasti who graciously called your devotee Kannappa, O Father of Otriyur who told the infant crying for sweet milk to drink from the ocean of milk, will you not look at the face of this poor one who cries and begs you to come and bestow your grace?
commentary: The Lord accepted the untutored devotion of the hunter Kannappa, and gave an ocean of milk to the crying child-sage Upamanyu. If God is so quick to answer their needs, Vallalar asks, why will he not look at his own tears?

translit: mañcupaṭum ceñcaṭila vaḷḷalē uḷḷukiṉṟōr uñcupaṭum vaṇṇamaruḷ oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē nañcupaṭum kaṇṭamuṭai namparaṉē vaṉtuyarāl pañcupaṭum pāṭupaṭum pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: O generous Lord with red matted hair touching the clouds, O supreme Lord of Otriyur who grants grace to save those who think of you, O our highest Lord with a poison-stained throat, will you not look at the face of this sinner who suffers intense agony and is beaten like cotton by harsh sorrow?
commentary: The poison in Siva's throat shows his compassion, as he swallowed deadly venom to save all living beings. Vallalar describes his sorrow as beating him down like cotton struck to separate the seeds.

translit: kaṇṇār amutē karumpē-eṉ kaṇṇē-eṉ aṇṇā-uṉ poṉṉaruḷtāṉ ārntiṭumō allateṉṟum naṇṇātō yātu naṇukumō eṉṟuruki eṇṇātum eṇṇuminta ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O nectar filling my eyes, O sweet sugarcane, O my very eye, O my Lord, will I attain your golden grace? Or will it never reach me? What will befall me? Melting with these questions and thinking unimaginable thoughts, will you not look at the face of this poor one?
commentary: The greatest pain of devotion is the agonizing uncertainty of grace. Vallalar remains tormented by the thought that this golden grace might never reach him.

translit: nāṭiyacīr oṟṟi nakaruṭaiyāy niṉkōyil nīṭiyanaṟ cannitiyil niṉṟuniṉṟu mālayaṉum tēṭi-aṟi oṇṇāt tiru-uruvaik kaṇṭurukip pāṭi-aḻu tēṅkumintap pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: O Lord of the glorious city of Otriyur sought by all, I stand again and again in the vast and holy sanctum of your temple. Seeing your sacred form which even Vishnu and Brahma could not comprehend despite their search, I melt, sing, cry, and languish. Will you not look at the face of this sinner?
commentary: Vishnu and Brahma tried and failed to find the top and bottom of Siva's infinite pillar of light. Vallalar stands in the temple before that same incomprehensible form, weeping and singing in his longing for a response.

translit: vāṅkimalai villākkum maṉṉavaṉē eṉaracē ōṅki vaḷantaḻuvum oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē tūṅkiya tuṉpac cumaicumakka māṭṭātu ēṅki-aḻu kiṉṟa-inta ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O King who bent the great mountain into a bow, O my sovereign, O highest Lord of highly prosperous Otriyur, unable to bear this heavy burden of sorrow, I languish and cry. Will you not look at the face of this poor one?
commentary: Siva used the massive Mount Meru as a bow to destroy the three flying cities. Vallalar contrasts this image of divine strength with his own exhaustion, begging the Lord to relieve him of a sorrow he can no longer carry.

translit: toṇṭark karuḷum tuṇaiyē iṇaiyilviṭam uṇṭac cutaṟkaruḷum oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē caṇṭap pavanōyāl tāyilāp piḷḷaiyeṉap paṇṭait tuyarkoḷumip pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: O companion who graces the devotees. O righteous Lord of Otriyur who drank the peerless poison and granted grace to Vishnu. Afflicted by the fierce disease of worldly existence, I suffer ancient sorrow like a motherless child. Will you not look at the face of this sinner?
commentary: God is the protector who granted grace even to deities like Vishnu. Lost in the suffering of worldly life, Vallalar begs for this divine protection, crying out like a motherless child longing for a comforting glance.

translit: uṭṭikaḻnta mēlavaṉē oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē maṭṭilaṅkum uṉṟaṉ malaraṭiyaip pōṟṟātu taṭṭilaṅku neñcattāl cañcalittuṉ cannitikkaṇ eṭṭiniṉṟu pārkkuminta ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O Supreme One shining within. O righteous Lord of Otriyur. Instead of praising your fragrant flower-like feet, I stand far away and look at your sanctum with an unsteady and agitated heart. Will you not look at the face of this poor soul?
commentary: Vallalar confesses his heart is too agitated to offer proper praise. Feeling unworthy, he stands at the edge of the sanctuary, hoping the Divine will look his way despite his flaws.

translit: naccai miṭaṟṟaṇinta nāyakaṉē ōrpākam paccainiṟam koṇṭa pavaḷat taṉimalaiyē miccai tavirkkumoṟṟi vittakaṉē niṉaruṭkē iccaikoṭu vāṭuminta ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O Lord who wears poison on your throat. O peerless coral mountain with a green hue on one half. O wise Lord of Otriyur who dispels illusion. Will you not look at the face of this poor one who yearns and languishes for your grace?
commentary: God is pictured as a red mountain of coral sharing half of his form with the green hue of the Goddess. This divine presence clears away all worldly illusions. Vallalar brings his longing to this powerful figure, asking only for the gift of grace.

translit: mālayarntum kāṇā malaraṭiyāy vañcaviṉaik kālayarntu vāṭa-aruṭ kaṇṇuṭaiyāy viṇṇuṭaiyāy cēlayarnta kaṇṇār tiyakkatti ṉāluṉaruṭ pālayarntu vāṭumintap pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: You possess the flower-like feet that Vishnu grew weary seeking and could not find. You possess the eye of grace and the heavenly realm that make the foundation of deceitful karma wither. Bewildered by women with carp-like eyes, I have forgotten the milk of your grace. Will you not look at the face of this languishing sinner?
commentary: Worldly desires easily distract the human heart from spiritual truth. Vallalar admits that physical attraction has clouded his mind and made him forget the nourishment of divine grace. He calls upon the Supreme to burn away his burden of past actions (karma) with a single look.

translit: contamuṟa eṇṇit toḻukiṉṟa meyyaṭiyar cantamuṟum neñcat talattamarnta tattuvaṉē nantavaṉañ cūḻoṟṟi nāyakaṉē vāḻkkai-eṉum pantamatil vāṭumintap pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: O Supreme Truth seated in the beautiful hearts of true devotees who claim you as their own and worship you. O Lord of Otriyur surrounded by flower gardens. Will you not look at the face of this sinner who languishes in the bondage of worldly life?
commentary: God dwells within the hearts of those who love him. Vallalar contrasts this inner peace with his own struggle, feeling tangled in the bonds of ordinary life. He pleads for the Divine to notice his suffering and offer a way out of this confinement.

translit: tillaiyiṭai mēvumeṅkaḷ celvap peruvāḻvē ollai-aṭi yārkkaruḷum oṟṟiyūr uttamaṉē allai nikarkkum aḷakattār ācaitaṉak kellai-aṟi yāta-inta ēḻaimukam pārāyō.
translation: O our great life of wealth abiding in Thillai! O supreme Lord of Otriyur who swiftly graces your devotees! Will you not look upon the face of this poor wretch who knows no bounds to his desire for women with night-dark hair?
commentary: Vallalar begs for God's attention despite being trapped by endless worldly desires. He addresses the divine presence in Thillai (Chidambaram) and Otriyur (a sacred shrine in Chennai), praising God for swiftly granting grace to true devotees. Then he makes a raw confession of his own weakness, admitting he is lost in lust. By bringing his flaws directly to the divine, he shows that sincere prayer depends on complete honesty.

translit: viti-iḻanta veṇtalaikoḷ vittakaṉē vētiyaṉē mati-iḻantōrk kēlā vaḷaroṟṟi vāṉavaṉē niti-iḻantōr pōlayarntu niṉṉuṭaiya vāḻkkaip pativirumpi vāṭumintap pāvimukam pārāyō.
translation: O wise one holding the white skull of fallen Brahma! O Lord of the Vedas! O heavenly Lord of flourishing Otriyur who remains beyond the reach of the foolish! I languish like someone who has lost all his wealth. Will you not look upon the face of this sinner who withers away in longing for your realm of divine life?
commentary: Spiritual longing feels like a devastating physical loss, leaving Vallalar in the despair of someone who has lost all their wealth. He calls out to Siva, who carries the skull of the creator deity Brahma, proving that divine power outlasts all other forces. Feeling bankrupt without this presence, he begs the Lord to look at his suffering.

translit: yātu ceykuvaṉ pōtupō kiṉṟa taṇṇa lē-uma taṉparuk kaṭiyēṉ kōtu ceyyiṉum poṟuttaruḷ puriyum koḷkai yīreṉaik kuṟukiya kuṟumpar vātu ceykiṉṟār maṉantaḷar kiṉṟēṉ valiyi lēṉceyum vakai-oṉṟum aṟiyēṉ mātar ceypoḻil oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: What shall I do? Time is passing, O Lord. I am a servant to your devotees. You have the nature of forgiving and granting grace even when I commit faults. The wicked ones who surround me are attacking me. My heart is disheartened. I have no strength. I know no way to act. O Lord of Otriyur with beautiful groves! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: As time slips away, the soul stands helpless against worldly distractions. Vallalar appeals to the divine as a master known for forgiving every fault, pleading for the strength he lacks.

translit: eṉakku nīr iṅkōr āṇṭai-al līrō eṉṉai vañcakar yāvaruṅ kūṭik kaṉakkum vaṉpavak kaṭaliṭai vīḻttak kaṇṭi ruttalō kaṭaṉumak keḷiyēṉ taṉakku maṟṟoru cārpirun tiṭumēl tayavu ceytiṭat takkataṉ ṟilaikāṇ maṉakku nallavar vāḻoṟṟi uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: Are you not my Master here? All the deceivers have gathered together to cast me into the heavy, harsh ocean of worldly existence. Is it your duty to simply watch this happen? If this poor wretch had any other refuge, it might not be fitting for you to show mercy. O Lord of Otriyur where the good-hearted live! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: A true master cannot stand by and watch a servant drown in the heavy ocean of worldly existence. Having no other refuge, Vallalar tells the divine it is their duty to step in and save him.

translit: eñcal illatōr kāmamām kaṭalāḻn tiḷaikkiṉ ṟēṉiṉi eṉceyvaṉ aṭiyēṉ tañcam eṉṟuma tiṇaimalar aṭikkē caraṇpu kuntaṉaṉ tayavucey yīrēl vañca vāḻkkaiyām timiṅkilam eṉumīṉ vārik koṇṭeṉai vāymaṭut tiṭuṅkāṇ mañca ḷāviya poḻiloṟṟi uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: I am sinking and languishing in the endless ocean of lust. What will I, your servant, do now? Crying for refuge, I surrendered at your twin lotus feet. If you do not show mercy, the whale of this deceitful life will sweep me up and swallow me in its mouth! O Lord of Otriyur with groves touched by clouds! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: The struggle against physical desire is like sinking in an endless sea. Without immediate divine mercy, the massive, predatory weight of this deceitful life will swallow the soul whole.

translit: eṉpi ṟappiṉai yārkkeṭut turaippēṉ eṉcey vēṉeṉai eṉceya niṉaikkēṉ muṉpi ṟappiṭai iruntacē ṭattāl mūṭa vāḻkkaiyām kāṭakat taṭaintē aṉpi ṟantaveṅ kāmavēṭ ṭuvaṉāl alaippuṇ ṭēṉuma taruḷpeṟa viḻaintēṉ vaṉpi ṟantavar pukaḻoṟṟi uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: To whom can I describe my birth? What will I do? What can I plan to do with myself? Due to the remnants of my past births, I have entered the forest of this foolish life and am tormented by the cruel, loveless hunter of lust. I yearned to receive your grace. O Lord of Otriyur, praised by the mighty! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: The remnants of past births force the soul into the dense, confusing forest of mortal life. Here, lust is not a passing feeling but a cruel hunter actively tormenting the mind, leaving grace as the only hope of escape.

translit: kāmam eṉṉumōr kāvalil uḻaṉṟē kaluḻkiṉ ṟēṉoru kaḷaikaṇum aṟiyēṉ cēma nallaruṭ patampeṟun toṇṭar cērnta nāṭṭakam cērvuṟa viḻaintēṉ ēmam uṟṟiṭum eṉaiviṭu vippār illai eṉceyvaṉ yāriṉum ciṟiyēṉ vāma mātarāḷ maruvoṟṟi uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: Suffering in the prison of lust, I weep. I know no refuge. I yearned to reach the land where your devotees, who have attained the secure state of good grace, gather. There is no one to free me from this darkness. What will I do, I who am the lowest of all? O Lord of Otriyur, embraced by the beautiful Goddess! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: Worldly desire is a dark prison that isolates the soul from the pure company of true devotees. Left alone in this darkness, Vallalar weeps for a freedom he cannot achieve by himself.

translit: iṉpam eṉpatu viḻaintiṭar uḻantēṉ eṉṉai otta-ōr ēḻai-iṅ kaṟiyēṉ tuṉpam eṉpatu peruñcumai ākac cumakkiṉ ṟēṉaruḷ tuṇaiciṟi tillēṉ aṉpar uḷḷakat tamarntiṭun tēvar aṭikkuṟ ṟēvaluk kāṭpaṭu vēṉō vaṉpar nāṭuṟā oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: Seeking pleasure, I suffered misery. I know no wretch here equal to me. I carry sorrow as a massive burden. I have no support of grace whatsoever. Will I ever be fit to serve at the feet of the Lord who sits in the hearts of loving devotees? Lord of Otriyur, unapproachable by the cruel! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: The pursuit of worldly pleasure leads only to a heavy burden of sorrow. Vallalar feels destitute, wondering how someone weighed down by misery could be fit to serve the divine. Yet he looks to God for grace, calling the Lord the pupil of his eye: the center of his vision and his most precious guide.

translit: ūḻvi ṉaippaṭi eppaṭi aṟiyēṉ uñaṟṟu kiṉṟaṉaṉ umataruḷ peṟavē tāḻvi ṉaittarum kāmamō eṉaikkīḻt taḷḷu kiṉṟatē uḷḷukiṉ ṟatukāṇ pāḻvi ṉaikkoḷum pāviyēṉ ceyyum pāṅka ṟintilēṉ ēṅkukiṉ ṟaṉaṉāl vāḻvi ṉaittarum oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: I do not know what my past karma dictates. I strive to attain Your grace. Yet lust, which brings degradation, pushes me down and dominates my thoughts. Look upon this. A sinner burdened with ruinous karma, I do not know what to do. I simply languish. Lord of Otriyur who grants true life! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: The struggle for spiritual purity is difficult when past actions (karma, the cycle of cause and effect) pull the mind backward. Vallalar wants divine grace, yet finds his thoughts dragged down by physical desires. Paralyzed between high spiritual goals and basic human flaws, he begs the Lord for a way forward.

translit: iṟappi lārtoḻum tēvarīr patattai evvam nīkkiyē evvitat tāṉum maṟappi lātuḷam niṉaittiṭil kāmam vaḻima ṟittatai mayakkukiṉ ṟatukāṇ kuṟippi lāteṉṉāl kūṭiya maṭṭum kuṟaittum aṅkatu kuṟaikila tantō vaṟippi lāvayal oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: When I try to rid myself of flaws and hold Your feet, worshipped by the immortals, in my mind without ever forgetting, lust blocks the way and bewilders my heart. Look upon this. Even as I try my utmost to diminish it, alas, it does not decrease. Lord of Otriyur surrounded by unfailing fertile fields! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: Even with supreme effort to keep God in mind, physical desires block the way. Vallalar admits that trying to force these desires away through sheer willpower is not working. The mind becomes confused, showing that human effort alone is rarely enough to overcome our deepest flaws.

translit: cañci tantarum kāmameṉ ṟiṭumōr calati vīḻntatil talaimayak kuṟṟē añci añcināṉ alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉṉai añcal eṉpavar yāraiyum aṟiyēṉ tuñci ṉālpiṉpu cukampalit tiṭumō tuṇaiyi lārkkoru tuṇai-eṉa iruppīr mañciṉ nīḷpoḻil oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: Plunged into the ocean of lust that breeds accumulated karma, my mind is bewildered. I wander in endless fear. I know no one who will tell me to fear not. If I die, will happiness come to me later? You stand as the sole support for those without support. Lord of Otriyur with vast groves touching the clouds! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: Trapped in worldly attachments, the mind wanders in endless anxiety. Vallalar feels alone in this struggle and wonders if death might bring relief. Realizing that no human comfort can ease this spiritual fear, he turns to the divine, trusting God to be the support for the helpless.

translit: alla ōtiyar iṭaippaṭum kamaruk kācai vaitta-eṉ aṟiviṉmai aḷavaic colla vōmuṭi yāteṉai āḷat tuṇivu koḷvirō tūyarai āḷal alla vō-uma tiyaṟkai-ā yiṉumnal aruṭkaṇīreṉai āḷalum takuṅkāṇ mallal ōṅkiya oṟṟiyūr uṭaiyīr vaṇkai yīreṉkaṇ maṇi-aṉai yīrē.
translation: My ignorance in lusting after the physical crevices of dark-haired women is beyond measure. Will You resolve to accept me as Your own? Is it not Your nature to accept only the pure? Even so, You possess the eyes of supreme grace. It is fitting that You govern me as well. Lord of Otriyur towering in prosperity! O generous Lord who is like the pupil of my eye!
commentary: Most people assume God only accepts those who are already pure. Vallalar confesses his own impurity and foolishness, wondering if he has any right to be accepted. However, he concludes that divine grace is unconditional. Because the Lord looks upon all life with compassion, it is fitting for God to take in the flawed and make them pure.

translit: niṉpōṉṟa teyvamoṉ ṟiṉṟeṉa vētam nikaḻttavumniṉ poṉpōṉṟa ñāṉap putumalart tāḷtuṇaip pōṟṟukilēṉ eṉpōṉṟa ēḻaiyar yāṇṭuḷar ampalat tēnaṭañcey miṉpōṉṟa vēṇiya ṉē-oṟṟi mēviya vētiyaṉē.
translation: Although the Vedas declare there is no god like you, I do not praise your two fresh lotus feet of golden wisdom. Where are there poor wretches like me? O Lord with lightning-like matted hair who dances in the Hall! O Vedic Lord residing in Otri!
commentary: Knowing God's greatness does not guarantee devotion. Vallalar laments his failure to offer proper praise, though the ancient scriptures (Vedas) declare the absolute supremacy of the divine. He calls himself a wretch, contrasting his spiritual poverty with the radiant, dancing Lord of Otri (Otriyur, a sacred shrine town near Chennai).

translit: vētiya ṉēveḷḷi veṟpiṭai mēviya vittakaṉē nītiya ṉēmaṉṟil niṭkaḷa āṉanta nirttamiṭum ātiya ṉē-emai āṇṭava ṉēmalai yāḷmakiḻum pātiya ṉē-em parāpara ṉēmukkaṭ paṇṇavaṉē.
translation: O Vedic Lord! O wise one residing on the silver mountain! O just one! O primal Lord who performs the formless dance of bliss in the Hall! O Lord who rules over us! O Lord who shares half his form with the joyful Daughter of the Mountain! O our supreme Lord! O three-eyed supreme being!
commentary: The divine holds both absolute, formless reality and personal forms. Vallalar praises the Lord who dances invisibly in the cosmic hall, while also residing on the silver mountain (Mount Kailash, Siva's mythological abode). He celebrates the divine as a balanced whole, sharing half its form with the divine mother.

translit: paṇṇava ṉēpacu pācattai nīkkum paramparaṉē maṇṇava ṉēṉai makiḻntava ṉēmalam māṟṟukiṉṟa viṇṇava ṉēveḷ viṭaiyava ṉēveṟṟi mēvuneṟṟik kaṇṇava ṉē-eṉaik kāttava ṉē-oṟṟik kāvalaṉē.
translation: O supreme being! O transcendent Lord who removes the bonds of the soul! O Lord who delighted in me, a mere earthly being! O heavenly Lord who removes impurities! O rider of the white bull! O Lord with the victorious eye on the forehead! O Lord who protects me! O protector of Otri!
commentary: Divine grace acts directly to free human beings from ignorance. Vallalar addresses the Lord as the power that removes pacu pācam (the worldly bonds that tie the soul down) and malam (the inner impurities of ego and illusion). He marvels that this vast, victorious heavenly power delights in protecting a mere earthly being like himself.

translit: kāvala ṉē-aṉṟu māṇikkup poṟkiḻik kaṭṭaviḻtta pāvala ṉētoḻum pāṇaṉ paricuṟap pāṭṭaḷitta nāvala ṉētillai nāyaka ṉēkaṭal nañcai-uṇṭa māvala ṉēmukkaṇ vāṉava ṉē-oṟṟi maṉṉavaṉē.
translation: O protector! O poetic Lord who untied the bundle of gold for the bachelor boy that day! O eloquent Lord who offered a song so the worshiping bard could win the prize! O Lord of Thillai! O mighty Lord who consumed the ocean poison! O three-eyed heavenly Lord! O sovereign of Otri!
commentary: God steps into the world to rescue the devoted. Vallalar recalls classical stories where the divine provided gold to a poor student, gave a winning song to a struggling musician, and swallowed deadly poison to save the universe. He sees the Lord of Thillai (Chidambaram, the holy city of the cosmic dance) as a constant protector of those in need.

translit: maṉṉava ṉēkoṉṟai mālaiya ṉētiru mālayaṟku muṉṉava ṉē-aṉṟu nālvarkkum yōka muṟai-aṟantāṉ coṉṉava ṉēciva ṉē-oṟṟi mēviya tūyavaṉē eṉṉava ṉē-aiyam ēṟpava ṉē-eṉai īṉṟavaṉē.
translation: O sovereign! O wearer of the cassia garland! O Lord who existed before Vishnu and Brahma! O Lord who taught the path of yoga and dharma to the four sages that day! O Siva! O pure Lord residing in Otri! O my Lord! O Lord who accepts alms! O Lord who gave birth to me!
commentary: The ultimate creator is also a humble teacher. Vallalar points out that this Lord existed before the great gods of preservation and creation (Vishnu and Brahma), and gave the earliest teachings of yoga to ancient sages. Yet this same supreme being wanders as a beggar accepting alms, acting simultaneously as the cosmic sovereign and an approachable parent.

translit: īṉṟava ṉē-aṉpar iṉṉuyirk kiṉpuṟum iṉṉamutam pōṉṟava ṉēciva ñāṉikaḷ uḷḷuṟum puṇṇiyaṉē āṉṟava ṉē-ema tuḷḷum puṟampum aṟintuniṉṟa cāṉṟava ṉēciva ṉē-oṟṟi mēviya caṅkaraṉē.
translation: O Creator. You are like sweet ambrosia bringing joy to the precious lives of Your devotees. O Holy One abiding in the hearts of the wise ones of Siva. O Exalted One. O Witness who stands knowing our inside and outside. O Siva. O Sankara dwelling in Otri.
commentary: God is the vast creator of the universe and the intimate witness who knows everything inside and outside of us. For those who love Him, His presence is as sweet as ambrosia, the nectar of immortality. Vallalar shows that the divine is not distant, resting in the hearts of the wise.

translit: caṅkara ṉē-ara ṉēpara ṉēnaṟ carācaraṉē kaṅkara ṉēmatik kaṇṇiya ṉēnutal kaṇṇiṉaṉē naṅkara mēviya aṅkaṉi pōṉṟaruḷ nāyakaṉē ceṅkara ṉērvaṇa ṉē-oṟṟi mēviya ciṉmayaṉē.
translation: O Sankara. O Hara. O Supreme One. O Form of the good moving and unmoving worlds. O Bearer of the Ganges. O Wearer of the crescent moon. O One with the forehead eye. O Lord of grace, sweet like a beautiful fruit resting in our hands. O One with beautiful red hands. O Embodiment of pure consciousness dwelling in Otri.
commentary: The Supreme Lord makes up everything in the world, both moving and unmoving. He wears the cosmic signs of Siva, including the crescent moon and the Ganges river. Yet this vast, pure consciousness offers His grace as easily as a sweet fruit placed into our hands.

translit: ciṉmaya ṉē-aṉal ceṅkaiyil ēntiya cēvakaṉē naṉmaiya ṉēmaṟai nāṉmukaṉ mālukku nāṭaritām taṉmaiya ṉēciva caṅkara ṉē-eñ catācivaṉē poṉmaya ṉēmup purāntaka ṉē-oṟṟip puṇṇiyaṉē.
translation: O Embodiment of pure consciousness. O Warrior holding fire in Your red hand. O Form of goodness. O One whose nature is hard to comprehend even for the Vedic four-faced Brahma and Thirumal. O Siva Sankara. O our Sadasiva. O Golden One. O Destroyer of the three cities. O Holy One of Otri.
commentary: The divine nature is beyond the grasp of even the greatest gods, like Brahma the creator and Thirumal (Vishnu) the preserver. He holds fire as the fierce warrior who destroyed the three cities of demons, yet He remains the form of goodness.

translit: puṇṇiya ṉē-emaip pōlvārkkum iṉpap poruḷaḷikkum tiṇṇiya ṉēnaṟ civañāṉa neñcil teḷinta-aruḷ aṇṇiya ṉēkaṅkai āṟamar vēṇiyil ārntamatik kaṇṇiya ṉēpaṟ palavākum aṇṭaṅkaḷ kaṇṭavaṉē.
translation: O Holy One. O Resolute One who grants the treasure of bliss even to those like us. O Lord of grace who is close to hearts clear with the true wisdom of Siva. O Wearer of the crescent moon chaplet in Your matted hair where the river Ganges abides. O Creator of the manifold universes.
commentary: God is the vast architect who creates countless universes, but He stays close to human hearts that are clear with wisdom. Speaking with humility, Vallalar marvels that the Lord grants bliss even to ordinary people like himself.

translit: kaṇṭava ṉēcaṟṟum neñcuru kākkoṭuṅ kaḷvartamai viṇṭava ṉēkaṭal vēmpaṭi poṅkum viṭamaṉaittum uṇṭava ṉēmaṟṟum oppoṉ ṟilāta uyarvutaṉaik koṇṭava ṉē-oṟṟik kōyiliṉ mēvum kuruparaṉē.
translation: O Creator. O One who parts from cruel thieves whose hearts never melt even a little. O One who swallowed all the surging, bitter poison from the ocean. O One possessing an exalted greatness without any equal. O Supreme Guru dwelling in the temple of Otri.
commentary: The Lord's compassion is boundless, yet He keeps Himself distant from those whose hearts are hard and refuse to melt with love. To connect with this supreme teacher, a person must approach with genuine feeling.

translit: paṇṇāluṉ aruṭpukaḻaip pāṭu kiṉṟār paṇikiṉṟār niṉaḻakaip pārttup pārttuk kaṇṇāra uḷaṅkuḷirak kaḷittā ṉantak kaṇṇīrkoṇ ṭāṭukiṉṟār karuṇai vāḻvai eṇṇāniṉ ṟuṉai-entāy entāy entāy eṉkiṉṟār niṉaṉpar ellām eṉṟaṉ aṇṇānāṉ orupāvi vañca neñcāl alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your devotees sing your gracious glory with melodies. They bow down. They gaze endlessly at your beauty. Their eyes fill and their hearts cool. They rejoice and dance with tears of bliss. Reflecting on your life of compassion, they call out to you, "My Father, my Father, my Father!" My Lord, I am a lone sinner wandering with a deceitful heart. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: True devotion is a state of tearful joy born from recognizing God's infinite compassion. Vallalar contrasts this bliss with his own feeling of being lost. Calling himself a deceitful sinner, he adopts the voice of anyone who feels unworthy, asking for grace because he cannot save himself.

translit: eppālum niṉaṉpar ellām kūṭi ēttukiṉṟār niṉpatattai ēḻai yēṉnāṉ veppāya maṭaviyartam kalavi vēṭṭu viḻukiṉṟēṉ kaṇkeṭṭa vilaṅkē pōla ippāril mayaṅkukiṉṟēṉ naṉmai oṉṟum eṇṇukilēṉ mukkaṇuṭai iṟaivā eṉṟaṉ appā-eṉ āruyirkkōr tuṇaivā vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: Everywhere, all your devotees gather to praise your feet. I am a poor wretch. Craving the embrace of passionate women, I fall. Like a blind beast, I wander deluded in this world. I do not think of a single good deed. O Three-eyed Lord! My Father! The peerless companion to my precious soul! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: The divine is addressed as the Three-eyed Lord, a traditional name for Siva. Physical desires and worldly confusion form a painful trap. Vallalar compares this to a blind animal wandering without direction, showing how base instincts blind us to our spiritual good.

translit: iṉpuṭaiyār niṉaṉpar ellām niṉcīr icaikkiṉṟār nāṉoruvaṉ ēḻai iṅkē vaṉpuṭaiyār tamaikkūṭi avamē naccu māmarampōl niṟkiṉṟēṉ vañca vāḻkkait tuṉpuṭaiyār aṉaivarkkum talaimai pūṇṭēṉ tūymai-eṉpa taṟintilēṉ cūḻntōrk kellām aṉpuṭaiyāy eṉai-uṭaiyāy viṭaiyāy vīṇē alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: Filled with joy, all your devotees sing your glory. I am a lonely wretch here. Joining cruel people, I stand uselessly like a great poisonous tree. I took leadership of all those suffering the sorrow of a deceitful life. I know nothing of purity. You pour love on all who surround you. You possess me. O Rider of the Bull! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: God is addressed as the Rider of the Bull. A person surrounded by cruelty is like a large poisonous tree offering no safe shade or useful fruit. Taking the blame as the leader of the deceitful, Vallalar illustrates how toxic environments poison a life.

translit: viñcuṭaiyāy niṉaṉpar ellām niṉcīr meyppuḷakam eḻattutittu viḷaṅku kiṉṟār nañcuṭaiyār vañcakartam cārpil iṅkē nāṉoruvaṉ perumpāvi naṇṇi mūṭa neñcuṭaiyār tamakkellām talaimai pūṇṭu niṟkiṉṟēṉ karuṇaimuka nimalak kañcam añcuṭaiyāy āṟuṭaiya caṭaiyāy vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: O Lord of supreme excellence! All your devotees praise your glory, their bodies thrilling with joy, and they shine brightly. I am a great sinner. Associating with deceitful, venomous people here, I stand as the leader of all those with foolish hearts. You have five immaculate lotus faces radiating compassion. You wear the river in your matted hair. I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: The physical thrill of spiritual joy is a hallmark of devotion, where the body reacts to grace. Vallalar contrasts this with his association with toxic, foolish people. He invokes classic attributes of Siva: the five lotus faces and the river Ganges caught in his matted hair.

translit: poyyāta niṉaṭiyār ellām nalla puṇṇiyamē ceytuniṉaip pōṟṟu kiṉṟār naiyāniṉ ṟulaikiṉṟa maṉattāl iṅkē nāṉoruvaṉ perumpāvi nāyēṉ tīmai ceyyāniṉ ṟuḻaikkiṉṟēṉ ciṟitum niṉṉaic cintiyēṉ vantikkum tiṟamum nāṭēṉ aiyā-eṉ appā-eṉ aracē vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your truthful devotees do good, virtuous deeds and praise you. I am a lonely, great sinner, low as a dog. With a wasting and troubled mind, I labor here doing only evil. I do not think of you even a little. I do not seek the way to worship you. O Master! My Father! My King! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: True devotion is active, rooted in good deeds. Vallalar confesses to a troubled mind that produces negative actions and forgets the divine. This extreme self-criticism is a classic poetic method expressing total surrender, stripping away personal pride to rely on God's mercy.

translit: teruḷuṭaiyār niṉaṉpar ellām niṉṟāḷ cintaiyilvait tāṉantam tēkku kiṉṟār maruḷuṭaiyēṉ nāṉoruvaṉ pāvi vañca maṉattālē iḷaittiḷaittu mayaṅku kiṉṟēṉ iruḷuṭaiyēṉ ērpūṭṭum pakaṭu pōliṅ kiluḻappil uḻaikkiṉṟēṉ ellām valla aruḷuṭaiyāy āḷuṭaiyāy uṭaiyāy vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your clear-minded lovers keep your feet in their minds and brim with bliss. I am deluded. I alone am a sinner. Driven by my deceitful mind, I waste away and stand bewildered. Bound in darkness, I labor in worldly domestic toil like a bull yoked to a plow. O all-powerful Lord of Grace! O Master who rules me! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: A mind absorbed in God is full of joy, while a worldly mind is exhausted. Vallalar compares the heavy, repetitive labor of daily life to a farm bull dragging a plow. He feels trapped in draining domestic chores while true seekers rest peacefully in grace.

translit: vāramuḷār niṉaṭiyār ellām niṉṉai vāḻttukiṉṟār talaikuḷira vaṇaṅku kiṉṟār tīramilēṉ nāṉoruvaṉ pāvi vañcac ceyalviḷakkum maṉattālē tikaittēṉ caiva cāramilēṉ ācāra millēṉ citta cāntamilēṉ irakkamilēṉ takavum illēṉ āramutē mukkaṇuṭai aracē vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your devoted servants praise you and bow their heads in cool peace. I lack resolve. I alone am a sinner. I stand bewildered by a mind that drives deceitful deeds. I lack the true essence of the Saiva path. I lack righteous conduct. I lack mental peace. I lack compassion and merit. O rare nectar! O three-eyed King! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: True spiritual life requires inner peace and compassion. Looking inward, Vallalar laments finding only a restless, deceitful mind. He names the core requirements of a pure life, such as righteous conduct and a quiet mind, by expressing sorrow over not having them.

translit: vaṇmaipeṟu niṉaṉpar ellām niṉṉai vantaṉaicey tāṉanta vayattē niṉṟār peṇmaiyuṟum maṉattālē tikaittēṉ niṉcīr pēcukilēṉ kūcukilēṉ pētai nāṉōr oṇmaiyilēṉ oḻukkamilēṉ naṉmai eṉpa toṉṟumilēṉ ōtiyēpōl uṟṟēṉ mikka aṇmaiyilvan taruḷpurivōy eṉṉē vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your bountiful lovers worship you and abide in the realm of bliss. Bewildered by a timid mind, I do not speak your glory. I feel no shame. I am a fool who lacks brilliance and discipline. I possess no trace of anything called goodness. I have become like a chameleon. O Lord who draws very near to bestow Grace! I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: Fear and hesitation keep a person from speaking the truth or living a pure life. Vallalar uses a chameleon to describe a mind that constantly shifts instead of standing firm in goodness. This lack of steady discipline leaves him wandering aimlessly.

translit: umpartamak karitāmuṉ patattai aṉṟi oṉṟumaṟi yāruṉṉai uṟṟōr ellām imparviṉai yuṭaiyēṉnāṉ oruvaṉ pāvi eṭṭuṇaiyum niṉaintaṟiyēṉ eṉṟum eṅkum vampaviḻpūṅ kuḻalmaṭavār maiyal oṉṟē maṉamuṭaiyēṉ uḻaittiḷaitta māṭu pōlvēṉ ampalattem aracē-iv vāḻkkait tuṉpil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All those who have attained you know nothing but your feet, which remain rare even for the celestials. I alone am a sinner burdened by worldly karma. I do not think of you even a tiny fraction, at any time or any place. My mind holds nothing but lust for women wearing blooming, fragrant flowers in their hair. I am like a tired, overworked ox. O our King of the Hall! I wander in the misery of this worldly life. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: Worldly desire crowds out any thought of the divine. Vallalar confesses his mind is so consumed by physical attractions it leaves no room for grace. Driven by these urges, he feels reduced to an overworked ox carrying the heavy burden of worldly life.

translit: kolai-aṟiyāk kuṇattōrniṉ aṉpar ellām kuṇamēcey tuṉṉaruḷtāṉ kūṭu kiṉṟār pulai-aṟivēṉ nāṉoruvaṉ piḻaiyē ceytu pulaṅkeṭṭa vilaṅkēpōl kalaṅku kiṉṟēṉ nilai-aṟiyēṉ neṟiyoṉṟum aṟiyēṉ eṅkum niṉai-aṉṟit tuṇaiyoṉṟum aṟiyēṉ caṟṟum alai-aṟiyā aruṭkaṭalnī āḷka vīṇil alaikiṉṟēṉ eṉceykēṉ antō antō.
translation: All your lovers possess a character that knows no murder. Performing only good deeds, they unite with your Grace. I alone know baseness. Committing only mistakes, I stand bewildered like a beast devoid of senses. I do not know my true state. I know no righteous path. I know no companion but you anywhere. You are the ocean of Grace without a single wave. Rule me. I wander in vain. What shall I do? Alas, alas!
commentary: Union with divine Grace is only possible for those who know no murder of any living being. Vallalar teaches that compassion for all living beings, known as Jeevakarunyam, is the absolute foundation of a pure life. Without this strict commitment to non-violence and good deeds, a person is simply a confused beast cut off from God's perfectly calm ocean of Grace.

tamil: இருளார் மனத்தேன் இழுக்குடையேன் எளியேன் நின்னை ஏத்தாத
மருளார் நெஞ்சப் புலையரிடம் வாய்ந்து வருந்தி மாழ்கின்றேன்
அருளார் அமுதப் பெருக்கேஎன் அரசே அதுநீ அறிந்தன்றோ
தெருளார் அன்பர் திருச்சபையில் சேர்க்கா தலைக்கும் திறம்அந்தோ.
translit: iruḷār maṉattēṉ iḻukkuṭaiyēṉ eḷiyēṉ niṉṉai ēttāta maruḷār neñcap pulaiyariṭam vāyntu varunti māḻkiṉṟēṉ aruḷār amutap perukkē-eṉ aracē atunī aṟintaṉṟō teruḷār aṉpar tiruccapaiyil cērkkā talaikkum tiṟamantō.
translation: My mind is filled with darkness. I am flawed. I am lowly. I suffer and languish, caught among base people with deluded hearts who do not praise you. O flood of graceful nectar, my King, you know this well. Yet, alas, you keep me wandering without admitting me to the holy assembly of your clear-minded devotees.
commentary: Vallalar feels trapped among people absorbed in worldly delusions and indifferent to the divine. He asks God why he is left to wander in such dark company instead of being welcomed into the assembly of true devotees.

tamil: உண்மை அறியேன் எனினும்எனை உடையாய் உனையே ஒவ்வொருகால்
எண்மை உடையேன் நினைக்கின்றேன் என்னே உன்னை ஏத்தாத
வெண்மை உடையார் சார்பாக விட்டாய் அந்தோ வினையேனை
வண்மை உடையாய் என்செய்கேன் மற்றோர் துணைஇங் கறியேனே.
translit: uṇmai aṟiyēṉ eṉiṉumeṉai uṭaiyāy uṉaiyē ovvorukāl eṇmai uṭaiyēṉ niṉaikkiṉṟēṉ eṉṉē uṉṉai ēttāta veṇmai uṭaiyār cārpāka viṭṭāy antō viṉaiyēṉai vaṇmai uṭaiyāy eṉceykēṉ maṟṟōr tuṇai-iṅ kaṟiyēṉē.
translation: Though I do not know the truth, you possess me. Even lowly as I am, I think of you from time to time. Why, alas, have you abandoned me, a vessel of karma, to the company of ignorant people who do not praise you? O generous Lord, what will I do? I know no other support here.
commentary: Even an imperfect connection to God is enough to call upon divine grace. Vallalar admits his spiritual practice is inconsistent, thinking of God only from time to time. Yet he claims God as his only refuge, trusting divine generosity to outshine human imperfection.

tamil: எளியேன் இழைத்த பெறும்பிழைகள் எல்லாம் பொறுத்திங் கின்பளித்தாய்
களியேன் தனைநீ இனிஅந்தோ கைவிட் டிடில்என் கடவேனே
ஒளியே முக்கட் செழுங்கரும்பே ஒன்றே அன்பர் உறவேநல்
அளியே பரம வெளியேஎன் ஐயா அரசே ஆரமுதே.
translit: eḷiyēṉ iḻaitta peṟumpiḻaikaḷ ellām poṟuttiṅ kiṉpaḷittāy kaḷiyēṉ taṉainī iṉi-antō kaiviṭ ṭiṭileṉ kaṭavēṉē oḷiyē mukkaṭ ceḻuṅkarumpē oṉṟē aṉpar uṟavēnal aḷiyē parama veḷiyē-eṉ aiyā aracē āramutē.
translation: You forgave all the great faults I committed in my lowliness and granted me bliss. If you abandon me now in my ignorance, alas, what will be my fate? O light, O lush three-eyed sugarcane, O peerless one, O kin of the devotees, O sweet grace, O supreme space, my Lord, my King, rare nectar.
commentary: Past grace gives the soul confidence to ask for present mercy. Vallalar reminds the Lord that he has been forgiven and granted bliss in the past, making the threat of current abandonment unbearable. The divine is addressed in intimate terms as sweet sugarcane and rare nectar, blending affection with reverence.

tamil: காமக் கடலில் படிந்தஞராம் கடலில் விழுந்தேன் கரைகாணேன்
ஏமக் கொடுங்கூற் றெனும்மகரம் யாது செயுமோ என்செய்கேன்
நாமக் கவலை ஒழித்துன்றாள் நண்ணும் அவர்பால் நண்ணுவித்தே
தாமக் கடிப்பூஞ் சடையாய்உன் தன்சீர் பாடத் தருவாயே.
translit: kāmak kaṭalil paṭintañarām kaṭalil viḻuntēṉ karaikāṇēṉ ēmak koṭuṅkūṟ ṟeṉummakaram yātu ceyumō eṉceykēṉ nāmak kavalai oḻittuṉṟāḷ naṇṇum avarpāl naṇṇuvittē tāmak kaṭippūñ caṭaiyāyuṉ taṉcīr pāṭat taruvāyē.
translation: Submerged in the sea of lust, I have fallen into the sea of sorrow and cannot see the shore. What will the shark of fierce, deadly death do to me? What will I do? Banish my dreadful anxiety and place me among those who reach your feet. O Lord with braided hair adorned with fragrant flowers, grant me the grace to sing your glory.
commentary: Worldly desire leads to a sea of sorrow where the fear of death waits like a shark. Singing God's glory in the company of true devotees is the only rescue from this terrifying ocean. Finding the right spiritual community is the cure for mortal anxiety.

tamil: எண்ணா தெளியேன் செயும்பிழைகள் எல்லாம் பொறுத்திங் கெனையாள்வ
தண்ணா நினது கடன்கண்டாய் அடியேன் பலகால் அறைவதென்னே
கண்ணார் நுதற்செங் கரும்பேமுக் கனியே கருணைக் கடலேசெவ்
வண்ணா வெள்ளை மால்விடையாய் மன்றா டியமா மணிச்சுடரே.
translit: eṇṇā teḷiyēṉ ceyumpiḻaikaḷ ellām poṟuttiṅ keṉaiyāḷva taṇṇā niṉatu kaṭaṉkaṇṭāy aṭiyēṉ palakāl aṟaivateṉṉē kaṇṇār nutaṟceṅ karumpēmuk kaṉiyē karuṇaik kaṭalēcev vaṇṇā veḷḷai mālviṭaiyāy maṉṟā ṭiyamā maṇiccuṭarē.
translation: O Lord, it is your duty to forgive all the unthinking faults committed by this lowly one and to rule me here. Why should your servant say this over and over? O red sugarcane with a beautiful eye on your forehead, O sweet triple fruit, O ocean of compassion, O red-hued Lord riding the great white bull, O great radiant gem dancing in the hall.
commentary: The plea shifts from a desperate cry to a claim of right. Vallalar boldly tells the Lord that it is His divine duty to forgive human faults and guide the soul. This intimacy allows the devotee to stop begging and remind God of His own endless compassion.

tamil: பாலே அமுதே பழமேசெம் பாகே எனும்நின் பதப்புகழை
மாலே அயனே இந்திரனே மற்றைத் தேவ ரேமறைகள்
நாலே அறியா தெனில்சிறியேன் நானோ அறிவேன் நாயகஎன்
மேலே அருள்கூர்ந் தெனைநின்தாள் மேவு வோர்பால் சேர்த்தருளே.
translit: pālē amutē paḻamēcem pākē eṉumniṉ patappukaḻai mālē ayaṉē intiraṉē maṟṟait tēva rēmaṟaikaḷ nālē aṟiyā teṉilciṟiyēṉ nāṉō aṟivēṉ nāyaka-eṉ mēlē aruḷkūrn teṉainiṉtāḷ mēvu vōrpāl cērttaruḷē.
translation: O Lord! If Mal, Ayan, Indra, the other devas, and the four Vedas do not know the glory of your feet praised as milk, nectar, fruit, and red syrup, how can I, a lowly one, know it? Bestow your grace upon me and join me with those who reach your feet.
commentary: The true glory of God cannot be grasped even by the greatest figures of traditional religion. Vallalar says that Mal (Vishnu), Ayan (Brahma), Indra (king of the celestial beings), the other devas (heavenly beings), and the four Vedas (ancient scriptures) all fail to fully know the divine. Since the highest gods and texts fall short, he asks how a lowly person like him could possibly understand it. Instead of seeking intellectual knowledge, he simply begs for grace and the company of true devotees.

tamil: கண்ணார் நுதலோய் பெருங்கருணைக் கடலோய் கங்கை மதிச்சடையோய்
பெண்ணார் இடத்தோய் யாவர்கட்கும் பெரியோய் கரியோன் பிரமனொடும்
அண்ணா எனநின் றேத்தெடுப்ப அமர்ந்தோய் நின்றன் அடிமலரை
எண்ணா துழல்வோர் சார்பாக இருக்கத் தரியேன் எளியேனே.
translit: kaṇṇār nutalōy peruṅkaruṇaik kaṭalōy kaṅkai maticcaṭaiyōy peṇṇār iṭattōy yāvarkaṭkum periyōy kariyōṉ piramaṉoṭum aṇṇā eṉaniṉ ṟētteṭuppa amarntōy niṉṟaṉ aṭimalarai eṇṇā tuḻalvōr cārpāka irukkat tariyēṉ eḷiyēṉē.
translation: O Lord with an eye on your forehead, great ocean of compassion, wearer of the Ganges and the moon on your matted hair, sharing your left side with the Goddess! You are the greatest of all. You sit in majesty while the dark Vishnu and Brahma stand and praise you as their Lord. I am a poor soul. I cannot bear to remain in the company of those who wander without thinking of your lotus feet.
commentary: Living among people who have no thought of God is agony for the true seeker. Vallalar addresses the divine using the traditional attributes of Siva, praising a Lord who wears the river Ganges and the moon in his hair and shares his body with the Goddess. He pictures the great gods Vishnu and Brahma standing in reverence before this supreme reality. Overwhelmed by this majesty, his only desire is to escape the company of those who wander through life ignoring it.

tamil: பொய்யோர் அணியா அணிந்துழலும் புலையேன் எனினும் புகல்இடந்தான்
ஐயோ நினது பதம்அன்றி அறியேன் இதுநீ அறியாயோ
கைஓர் அனல்வைத் தாடுகின்ற கருணா நிதியே கண்ணுதலே
மெய்யோர் விரும்பும் அருமருந்தே வேத முடிவின் விழுப்பொருளே.
translit: poyyōr aṇiyā aṇintuḻalum pulaiyēṉ eṉiṉum pukaliṭantāṉ aiyō niṉatu patamaṉṟi aṟiyēṉ itunī aṟiyāyō kai-ōr aṉalvait tāṭukiṉṟa karuṇā nitiyē kaṇṇutalē meyyōr virumpum arumaruntē vēta muṭiviṉ viḻupporuḷē.
translation: Though I am a base man who wanders wearing falsehood as an ornament, alas, I know no refuge other than your feet. Do you not know this? O treasure of compassion dancing with fire in your hand! O Lord with an eye on your forehead! O rare medicine desired by the truthful! O supreme reality at the crown of the Vedas!
commentary: God is the only refuge for a flawed human being. Vallalar freely admits his worldly failings, saying he wears falsehood like jewelry. Yet he appeals to God's compassion, asking if the divine is not aware that he has nowhere else to turn. He calls this presence the rare medicine that cures the disease of birth and the ultimate truth standing above all ancient scriptures.

tamil: இன்னே எளியேன் பொய்யுடையேன் எனினும் அடியன் அலவோநான்
என்னே நின்னைத் துதியாதார் இடத்தில் என்னை இருத்தினையே
அன்னே என்றன் அப்பாஎன் ஐயா என்றன் அரசேசெம்
பொன்னே முக்கட் பொருளேநின் புணர்ப்பை அறியேன் புலையேனே.
translit: iṉṉē eḷiyēṉ poyyuṭaiyēṉ eṉiṉum aṭiyaṉ alavōnāṉ eṉṉē niṉṉait tutiyātār iṭattil eṉṉai iruttiṉaiyē aṉṉē eṉṟaṉ appā-eṉ aiyā eṉṟaṉ aracēcem poṉṉē mukkaṭ poruḷēniṉ puṇarppai aṟiyēṉ pulaiyēṉē.
translation: Even now, though I am lowly and full of falsehood, am I not your devotee? Why have you placed me among those who do not praise you? O Mother, my Father, my Master, my King, pure gold, three-eyed reality! I am a base man, and I do not understand your design.
commentary: The soul feels bewildered when God leaves it among worldly and indifferent people. Vallalar questions why he has been placed in such an environment when he is, despite his flaws, a dedicated devotee. He calls out to God as his mother, father, and king, expressing helplessness. He confesses that he cannot understand why the divine has designed his life this way.

tamil: வஞ்ச மடவார் மயலொருபால் மணியே நின்னை வழுத்தாத
நஞ்சம் அனையார் சார்பொருபால் நலியும் வாழ்க்கைத் துயர்ஒருபால்
விஞ்சும் நினது திருவருளை மேவா துழலும் மிடிஒருபால்
எஞ்சல் இலவாய் அலைக்கின்ற தென்செய் கேன்இவ் எளியேனே.
translit: vañca maṭavār mayalorupāl maṇiyē niṉṉai vaḻuttāta nañcam aṉaiyār cārporupāl naliyum vāḻkkait tuyarorupāl viñcum niṉatu tiruvaruḷai mēvā tuḻalum miṭi-orupāl eñcal ilavāy alaikkiṉṟa teṉcey kēṉiv eḷiyēṉē.
translation: On one side is the delusion caused by deceitful women. On another side, O gem, is the company of poison-like people who do not praise you. On another side is the sorrow of a wasting life. On another side is the poverty of wandering without attaining your abundant holy grace. These afflictions toss me about endlessly. What shall I, a lowly one, do?
commentary: Worldly life attacks the seeker from every direction. Vallalar lists the forces that pull a person away from grace: the distraction of worldly desires, the toxic company of people who ignore the divine, the sorrow of wasting one's lifespan, and the spiritual poverty of living without God's light. These pressures toss the mind about endlessly. Feeling cornered by ordinary human existence, he asks what a poor soul can do.

translit: maṇṇēyum vāḻkkaiyiṭai māḻāntu vaṉpiṇiyāl puṇṇēyum neñcam puḻuṅkukiṉṟa poyyavaṉēṉ paṇṇēyum iṉpap parañcuṭarē eṉiraṇṭu kaṇṇē-uṉ poṉmukattaik kāṇak kiṭaittilaṉē.
translation: Distressed in this worldly life and afflicted by severe disease, I am a false one with a wounded and suffering heart. O Supreme Light of musical bliss! O my two eyes! I have not been able to see your golden face.
commentary: Vallalar confesses his weariness with worldly life and illness. Calling God the supreme light and his own two eyes shows a personal intimacy. Yet, he feels a sense of failure for not being granted a vision of the divine face.

translit: maruḷārnta valviṉaiyāl vaṉpiṇiyāl vaṉtuyarāl iruḷārnta neñcāl iṭiyuṇṭa ēḻaiyaṉēṉ teruḷārnta meyññāṉac celvac civamēniṉ aruḷārnta mukkaṇ aḻakutaṉaik kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: Struck down by delusion-filled hard karma, severe disease, terrible sorrow, and a heart full of darkness, I am a helpless wretch. O Sivam, the wealth of clear true knowledge! I have not seen the beauty of your three eyes filled with grace.
commentary: Vallalar feels crushed by his past actions and the darkness in his own heart. He contrasts this inner darkness with God, whom he addresses as pure, clear knowledge itself, longing to see the grace pouring from the Lord's three eyes.

translit: vallār mulaiyār mayaluḻanta vañcakaṉēṉ pollār purameritta puṇṇiyaṉē poymaṟutta nallār toḻuntillai nāyakaṉē naṉṟaḷitta allār kaḷattiṉ aḻakutaṉaik kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: I am a deceitful one who suffered in the infatuation for women with firm breasts. O virtuous one who burned the cities of the wicked! O Lord of Thillai worshiped by the good who have rejected falsehood! I have not seen the beauty of your dark throat that bestowed goodness on the world.
commentary: Vallalar admits to being drained by physical lust. He calls out to the Lord of Thillai (the sacred temple town of Chidambaram) and remembers an act of divine mercy. Siva drank a deadly poison to save the universe, turning his throat dark. Vallalar longs to see this mark because it represents compassion for all living beings.

translit: nōyāl melintuṉaruḷ nōkkukiṉṟa noyyavaṉēṉ tāyā ṉavaṉē-eṉ tantaiyē aṉpartamaic cēyāy vaḷarkkum civaṉē civaṉē-em tūyāniṉ poṟṟōḷiṉ cuntarattaik kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: Emaciated by disease, I am a frail one looking for your grace. You became my mother and my father. O Siva who raises devotees as your own children! O Siva, our pure one! I have not seen the beauty of your golden shoulders.
commentary: Vallalar approaches God not as a distant ruler, but as family. Worn down by illness, he asks only for the comforting sight of God's strong, golden shoulders.

translit: vaṉṉēr mulaiyār mayaluḻanta vaṉmaṉattēṉ aṉṉē-eṉ appā-eṉ aiyā-eṉ āramutē maṉṉē maṇiyē malaiyāḷ makiḻuṉatu poṉṉēr itaḻip puyaṅkāṇap peṟṟilaṉē.
translation: I have a hard heart that suffered in the infatuation for women with firm breasts. O Mother! O my Father! O my Lord! O my rare ambrosia! O King! O Jewel! I have not been blessed to see your shoulders adorned with golden konrai flowers, the shoulders in which the daughter of the mountain rejoices.
commentary: Vallalar pours out a series of affectionate names for God. He longs to see the Lord's shoulders wearing garlands of golden koṉṟai flowers, sharing the joy felt by the divine Mother, known in the tradition as the daughter of the mountain.

translit: naṇṇum viṉaiyāl nalikiṉṟa nāyaṭiyēṉ eṇṇum cukātīta iṉpamē aṉpuṭaiyōr kaṇṇum karuttum kaḷikkavarum kaṟpakamē peṇorupāl vāḻumurup peṟṟitaṉaik kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: I am a dog-like devotee suffering from the karma that afflicts me. You are the supreme bliss beyond pleasure that I meditate upon. You are the wish-granting tree that comes to delight the eyes and hearts of those who love you. I have not seen the nature of your form where the Goddess dwells on one side.
commentary: Vallalar contrasts his own suffering with the joy of the divine. He longs to witness the Lord's complete form, which includes the Goddess sharing the left half of his body. This vision is described as a heavenly tree (karpakam) that grants every wish to those who approach with love.

translit: tevvaṇṇa māyaiyiṭaic cemmānta ciṟṟaṭiyēṉ ivvaṇṇam eṉṟaṟitaṟ keṭṭāta vāṉporuḷē avvaṇṇa māṉa aracē amutēniṉ cevvaṇṇa mēṉit tiṟaṅkāṇap peṟṟilaṉē.
translation: I am a lowly devotee bewildered amidst hostile illusion. O supreme reality, you cannot be understood or described as being a certain way. O King of that transcendent nature, O nectar, I have not received the blessing to see the majesty of your red-hued form.
commentary: The divine reality cannot be captured by words or limited to a shape. Yet Vallalar, lost in the confusion of worldly illusion (maya), yearns for a tangible vision of grace and grieves that he has not yet seen the Lord's red form.

translit: alvaitta neñcāl aḻuṅkukiṉṟa nāyaṭiyēṉ colvaitta uṇmait tuṇaiyē iṇaittōḷmēl vilvat toṭai-aṇinta vittakaṉē niṉṉuṭaiya celvat tiruvaṭiyiṉ cīrkāṇap peṟṟilaṉē.
translation: I am a dog-like devotee sorrowing with a heart filled with darkness. O true companion established by the sacred words. O wise Lord wearing a garland of vilva leaves across your twin shoulders. I have not received the blessing to see the glory of your precious holy feet.
commentary: A mind filled with darkness leaves the devotee feeling miserable and unworthy. In this state of sorrow, the Lord is the only companion, known through the sacred scriptures. Vallalar describes the divine wearing a garland of sacred vilva leaves, aching to see his holy feet.

translit: pottēr mayalāl puḻuṅkukiṉṟa poyyaṭiyēṉ kottēr ceḻuṅkoṉṟaik kuṉṟamē kōvāta muttē evarkkum muḻumutalē muttikku vittēniṉ poṉṉaṭikkīḻ mēviniṟka kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: I am a false devotee suffering from flawed delusion. O mountain adorned with clusters of rich konrai flowers. O unstrung pearl. O absolute primal source for all beings. O seed of liberation. I have not seen myself standing firmly beneath your golden feet.
commentary: Vallalar calls God an unstrung pearl—a perfect treasure existing naturally without being shaped by human hands. Seeing the divine as a mountain and the seed of spiritual freedom, he feels weighed down by his flaws and longs for permanent shelter at the Lord's feet.

translit: nītiyilār vāyiliṭai niṉṟalainta neñcakaṉēṉ cōti-elām cūḻntaparañ cōtiyē ceñcaṭaimēl pātinilā ōṅkum paramēnī oṟṟinakar vīti-ulā vanta-eḻil meykuḷirak kaṇṭilaṉē.
translation: I am one whose heart wandered and lingered at the gates of unjust people. O supreme Jothi encompassing all lights. O Supreme Lord bearing a crescent moon high on your red matted hair. I have not seen the beauty of your procession through the streets of Otri city to let my body cool with joy.
commentary: Vallalar regrets wasting time seeking favors from worldly people who lack fairness. He turns instead to the supreme light (Jothi) outshining all other lights. He yearns for the relief of seeing the Lord, adorned with a crescent moon, carried through the streets of Otri city in a temple procession.

translit: oppārum illāta uttamaṉē oṟṟiyileṉ appā-uṉ poṉṉaṭikkē aṉpilēṉ āṉālum tappā takameliyac cañcalattāl ēṅkukiṉṟa ippā takattēṟ kiraṅkiṉāl ākātō.
translation: O supreme one who has no equal! My father in Otriyur! I have no love for your golden feet. Even so, I languish in sorrow, and my body grows thin. Will you not show pity on this great sinner?
commentary: Vallalar admits he has no real devotion to offer. He asks if his physical and mental suffering is enough reason for God to take pity on him. Divine grace responds to sheer human misery, regardless of spiritual achievements.

translit: eñcā iṭarāl irumpiṇiyāl ēṅkimaṉam pañcāka nontu paratavikkum nāyēṉaic ceñcāli ōṅkum tiruvoṟṟi yappānī añcātē eṉṟuṉ aruḷkoṭuttāl ākātō.
translation: I suffer unending afflictions and heavy diseases. My mind aches and softens like beaten cotton. I struggle like a dog. O father of Otriyur where red paddy grows tall! Will you not say "do not fear" and bestow your grace upon me?
commentary: Disease and sorrow beat the mind down until it is as fragile as beaten cotton. Comparing his struggles to those of a stray dog, Vallalar begs for a single word of divine comfort to dispel his fear.

translit: paṟṟum ceḻuntamiḻāl pāṭukiṉṟōr ceytaperuṅ kuṟṟam kuṇamākak koḷḷum kuṇakkaṭalē maṟṟaṅkum eṇtōḷ malaiyē marakatamē peṟṟiṅ kaṭiyēṉ piṇikeṭuttāl ākātō.
translation: You take the great faults committed by those who sing in rich Tamil as virtues. O ocean of virtues! O mountain with eight shoulders! O emerald! Will you not accept me here and destroy my afflictions?
commentary: The divine overlooks the mistakes of those who sing praises in Tamil, treating their very flaws as virtues. Vallalar asks the Lord for this same forgiveness. God is an ocean of good qualities who can wipe out all earthly afflictions.

translit: entaiyē eṉpavartam iṉṉamutē eṉurimait tantaiyē tāyē tamarē-eṉ caṟkuruvē cintaiyē ōṅkum tiruvoṟṟi aiyā-eṉ nintaiyē nīṅka niḻalaḷittāl ākātō.
translation: O sweet nectar to those who call you their father! My rightful father, mother, relation, and true Guru! O Lord of Otriyur who rises high in my mind! Will you not grant me your shade so that my shame is removed?
commentary: God acts as every intimate relationship a person can have: mother, father, close relative, and true teacher (guru). Vallalar asks for the shade of divine protection, as taking shelter there is the only way to escape the shame of worldly life.

translit: uḷḷum tiruttoṇṭar uḷḷat teḻuṅkaḷippē koḷḷum civāṉantak kūttā-uṉ cēvaṭiyai naḷḷum pukaḻuṭaiya nallōrkaḷ ellārum eḷḷum pulaiyēṉ iḻivoḻittāl ākātō.
translation: O joy rising in the hearts of holy devotees who remember you! O dancer of supreme bliss! All the famous and good people who seek your red feet despise me as a lowly wretch. Will you not remove my disgrace?
commentary: God is the supreme dancer who creates the highest bliss (śivānanda) in the hearts of true devotees. Vallalar feels alienated from this joy, stating that good and pious people look down on him. He pleads with the divine to erase this disgrace and gather him in.

translit: kōtai-ōr kūṟuṭaiya kuṉṟamē maṉṟamarnta tātaiyē oṟṟit talattamarnta caṅkaraṉē tītaiyē nāḷtōṟum ceytalaintu vāṭumintap pētaiyēṉ ceyta piḻaipoṟuttāl ākātō.
translation: O Mountain who holds the Goddess as your half! O Father seated in the Hall! O Sankara residing in Otriyur! I am an ignorant fool who wanders about doing evil every day and suffering. Will you not forgive the faults I have committed?
commentary: God is addressed in majestic terms as a towering mountain and the Father of all, while Vallalar sees himself as an exhausted, ignorant fool making endless mistakes. Acknowledging our personal flaws is the first step toward receiving grace.

translit: muttikku vittē muḻumaṇiyē muttaruḷam tittikkum tēṉē civamē ceḻuñcuṭarē cattikkum nātat talaṅkaṭanta tattuvaṉē ettikkum illēṉ iḷaippoḻittāl ākātō.
translation: O seed of liberation! O flawless gem! O honey sweetening the hearts of the liberated! O Siva! O radiant flame! O supreme truth who transcends the realms of Sakti and Nada! I have no refuge in any direction. Will you not relieve my weariness?
commentary: God is the seed of spiritual freedom and the truth beyond all cosmic realms of sound (Nada) and energy (Sakti). Exhausted and feeling alone in the world, the soul looks in every direction for a safe harbor and finds none but this divine flame.

translit: vañcamilār uḷḷam maruvukiṉṟa vāṉcuṭarē kañcamuḷāṉ pōṟṟum karuṇaip peruṅkaṭalē nañcamutāk koṇṭaruḷum nallavaṉē niṉalatōr tañcamilēṉ tuṉpac caḻakkoḻittāl ākātō.
translation: O vast flame who resides in the hearts of those without deceit! O great ocean of compassion praised by Brahma on the lotus! O good Lord who graciously consumed poison as nectar! I have no refuge other than you. Will you not eradicate my miserable afflictions?
commentary: The divine is an ocean of compassion that willingly takes on suffering to save others, just as Siva consumed deadly poison to protect the universe. Recognizing this mercy, Vallalar asks for an end to the bitter miseries of worldly life. This protective grace dwells naturally in hearts free of deceit.

translit: cēypiḻaiyait tāyaṟintum cīṟāḷ poṟuppāḷin nāypiḻaiyai nīpoṟukka ñāyamumuṇ ṭaiyāvē tēymatipōl neñcam tiyakkamuṟac cañcalattāl vāyalaṟi vāṭumeṉai vā-eṉṟāl ākātō.
translation: Even when a mother knows her child's faults, she does not rage but forgives them. O Master, it is only just for you to forgive the faults of this dog. My heart shrinks in despair like the waning moon, and I cry out loud in my sorrow and wither away. Will you not bid me to come to you?
commentary: Divine grace acts like a mother's unconditional love. A mother does not rage at her child's mistakes, and Vallalar asks God to show him that same natural, maternal forgiveness. Feeling his spirit shrinking in despair like a waning moon, he begs the Lord to call him home.

translit: kaṇṇuḷ maṇipōl karutukiṉṟa nallōrai eṇṇum kaṇamumviṭut tēkāta iṉṉamutē uṇṇum uṇavukkum uṭaikkummuyaṉ ṟōṭukiṉṟa maṇṇulakat teṉṟaṉ mayakkaṟuttāl ākātō.
translation: O sweet nectar who never parts even for a fleeting moment from the good devotees who cherish you like the pupil of their eye! Will you not sever my delusion in this earthly world where I run about endlessly striving for food to eat and clothes to wear?
commentary: Most people spend their lives running in circles to secure food, clothing, and basic survival. Vallalar asks to be cut free from this exhausting material delusion, longing instead for the unbroken sweetness of God's presence. To those who cherish the divine as dearly as their own eyesight, God is a sustaining nectar that never leaves them.

translit: eḷiyēṉniṉ tirumuṉpē eṉuraikkēṉ pollāta kaḷiyēṉ koṭuṅkāmak kaṉmaṉattēṉ naṉmaiyilā veḷiyēṉ veṟiyēṉtaṉ meyppiṇiyai oṟṟiyilvāḻ aḷiyōynī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I am a poor soul. What can I say in your holy presence? I am wicked, deluded, and possess a stone heart of cruel lust. I lack goodness. I am ignorant and mad. O gracious one residing in Otriyur, this disease of my body, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Vallalar stands before God exposed. By admitting his total lack of merit, he places his healing in the hands of divine grace.

translit: muṉṉēcey vevviṉaitāṉ mūṇṭatuvō allatunāṉ iṉṉē piḻaitāṉ iyaṟṟiyatuṇ ṭō-aṟiyēṉ poṉṉēr puricaṭai-em puṇṇiyaṉē eṉnōyai aṉṉēnī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: Did the cruel karma I accumulated in the past flare up? Or did I commit a fault just now? I do not know. O virtuous one with twisted matted hair shining like gold! O Mother, this disease of mine, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: People naturally wonder if suffering comes from past actions, known as karma, or from a recent mistake. Vallalar admits he does not know why he is sick. Instead of trying to solve the mystery of his pain, he appeals to God as a caring mother.

translit: ippā riṭai-uṉaiyē ēttukiṉṟa nāyēṉai veppār uḷattiṉarpōl vemmaiceyum vempiṇiyai eppā lavarkkum iṟaivaṉām eṉarumai appānī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: On this earth, I am a dog who praises only you. This cruel disease scorches me like the cruelty of hard-hearted people. O Lord of beings everywhere! My precious Father, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Physical pain can feel as harsh and unforgiving as a cruel person. Isolated by his suffering, Vallalar turns to God as a loving father, asking for the protection that a parent provides.

translit: ōvā mayalcey ulakanaṭaik kuḷtuyaram mēvā uḻalkiṉṟa veṇmaiyēṉ meynnōyaic cēvār koṭi-em civaṉē civaṉēyō āvānī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: Caught in the sorrow of worldly ways that cause ceaseless delusion, I wander in my ignorance. O our Siva with the bull on your banner! O Siva! Alas, this physical disease of mine, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: The daily struggle of worldly life creates exhaustion and confusion. Trapped in this cycle with a failing body, Vallalar knows human remedies are useless, trusting that divine intervention is his only cure.

translit: poyyām mala-iruṭṭup pottariṭai vīḻntuḻalum kaiyām neṟiyēṉ kalaṅkavanta vempiṇiyai maiyār miṭaṟṟem maruntē maṇiyē-eṉ aiyānī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I follow the base path, falling and wandering in the dark pit of false impurity. This cruel disease has come to torment me. O our medicine with the black throat! O gem! My Lord, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: God is addressed as medicine. Siva's black throat recalls the traditional story where God drank a deadly poison to save the universe. Vallalar asks this same savior to remove the poison of his own illness.

translit: immā nilattil iṭaruḻattal pōtātē vimmā aḻuṅka-eṉṟaṉ meyuṭaṟṟum vempiṇiyaic cemmāṉ maḻukkaraṅkoḷ celvac civamē-eṉ ammānī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: Is it not enough that I suffer affliction on this vast earth? O wealthy Sivam holding the red deer and battle-axe in Your hands! O my mother! This cruel disease that torments my body and makes me sob and weep, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Vallalar describes God using traditional images of Siva holding a deer and an axe, yet appeals to the divine as a tender mother. He feels only a mother's compassion can heal the torments of the body.

translit: puraicērum neñcap pulaiyaṉēṉ vaṉkāmat taraicērum tuṉpat taṭaṅkaṭalēṉ vempiṇiyai viraicērum koṉṟai viricaṭaiyāy viṇṇavartam araicēnī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I am a base person with a flawed heart. I am a vast ocean of sorrow resting on the hard ground of lust. O Lord with matted hair spread wide with fragrant konrai flowers! O King of the celestials! This cruel disease of mine, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Internal flaws can feel like a heavy physical weight. Vallalar asks the divine King, adorned with fragrant flowers, to wash away this inner sickness.

translit: ittā raṇiyil eḷiyōraik kaṇṭumi vittāram pēcum veṟiyēṉtaṉ meyppiṇiyaik kottār kuḻali-oru kūṟuṭaiya kōvē-eṉ attānī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I am a madman who speaks pompous words upon seeing the poor on this earth. O King who shares half Your form with the Goddess whose tresses bear clusters of flowers! O my father! This physical disease of mine, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Arrogance toward the poor is a spiritual disease. For Vallalar, compassion for all living beings (Jeevakarunyam) is the foundation of spiritual life. He asks his divine Father to cure him of his worldly pride.

translit: maṟiyēr viḻiyār mayakkiṉiṭai māḻānta ciṟiyēṉ aṭiyēṉ tiyaṅkavanta valnōyaic ceṟivē peṟuntoṇṭar cintai taṉilōṅkum aṟivēnī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I am a lowly servant languishing in the delusion of women with deer-like eyes. O Supreme Knowledge rising high in the minds of devoted servants! This severe disease that has come to bewilder me, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: Worldly attractions distract the mind and cause spiritual confusion. Caught in these delusions, Vallalar looks to God for clarity. He describes the divine as the knowledge that lights up the minds of servants.

translit: tuṉpē cumaiyāc cumakkiṉṟa nāyēṉai vaṉpēcey tuḷḷa mayakkiniṉṟa vaṉnōyai iṉpē aruḷkiṉṟa eṉā ruyirē-eṉ aṉpēnī nīkkāyēl ārnīkka vallārē.
translation: I am a dog carrying sorrow as my heavy burden. O my precious life who grants pure bliss! O my love! This harsh disease that deals cruelly with me and deludes my mind, if you do not cure it, who else can cure it?
commentary: The spiritual plea becomes intimate. Shedding traditional imagery, Vallalar addresses God as his own precious life and his love, finding hope only in the divine presence that grants joy.

sections.title: Lamenting the State of the Heart

translit: āḷāka niṉpoṉ aṭikkaṉpu ceytiṭa aiyaneṭu nāḷāka iccai-uṇ ṭeṉṉaicey kēṉkoṭu naṅkaiyartam māḷā mayalcaṇṭa mārutat tālmaṉa vāci-eṉcol kēḷā talaikiṉṟa tāloṟṟi mēvum kiḷaroḷiyē.
translation: O rising Light abiding in Otriyur! O Lord! For a long time I have desired to serve and love your golden feet. What can I do? Struck by the fierce storm of endless infatuation for cruel women, the horse of my mind refuses to listen to my words and wanders astray.
commentary: The desire to love God is real, but human willpower is weak. Like a runaway horse panicked by physical infatuation, the mind refuses to listen and wanders out of control, despite every intention to serve the divine.

translit: oḷiyāy oḷikkuḷ oḷiroḷi yē-oṟṟi uttamanī aḷiyā viṭilitaṟ keṉṉaicey kēṉaṇaṅ kaṉṉavartam kaḷiyāl kaḷittut talaiteri yātu kayaṉṟulavā vaḷiyāyc cuḻaṉṟivaṇ māyā maṉameṉai vātippatē.
translation: O Light shining within the light! O Supreme Lord of Otriyur! If you do not grant your grace, what can I do? Reveling in the intoxicating charm of beautiful women, losing its reason and spinning relentlessly like a whirlwind, this illusive mind torments me here.
commentary: God is the true light shining behind all visible light. Caught in the intoxication of physical attraction, the mind loses its reason and spins like a whirlwind. Vallalar confesses that human effort alone cannot quiet this chaos without grace.

tamil: மாயா மனம்எவ் வகைஉரைத் தாலும் மடந்தையர் பால்
நாயாகி னும்கை விடார்உல கோர்உனை நான் அடுத்தேன்
translit: māyā maṉamev vakai-urait tālum maṭantaiyar pāl ōyātu celkiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉtamai uṟṟatoru nāyāki ṉumkai viṭārula kōruṉai nāṉ aṭuttēṉ nīyāki luñcaṟ ṟiraṅkukaṇ ṭāyoṟṟi niṉmalaṉē.
translation: O pure Lord of Otriyur! No matter how I instruct it, this illusive mind ceaselessly runs after women. What can I do? People of the world will not abandon even a dog that seeks refuge with them. I have sought refuge in you. You must show me at least a little pity.
commentary: Ordinary people will care for a stray dog seeking safety. Vallalar asks God for this same basic mercy. Bringing his uncontrollable mind to God for refuge, he asks to be treated with at least the pity shown to a helpless animal.

translit: malañcāṉṟa maṅkaiyar koṅkaiyi lēnacai vāyttumaṉam calañcāṉṟa tālitaṟ keṉṉaicey kēṉniṉ caraṇaṉṟiyē valañcāṉṟa naṟṟuṇai maṟṟaṟi yēṉoṟṟi vāṉavaṉē nalañcāṉṟa ñāṉat taṉimuta lēteyva nāyakaṉē.
translation: O heavenly Lord of Otriyur! O peerless source of auspicious wisdom! O Lord of gods! Developing lust for the breasts of impure women, my mind has become wholly unsteady. What can I do about this? Other than your feet, I know of no powerful and true companion.
commentary: Physical lust creates instability in the mind. Recognizing his inability to steady his own thoughts, Vallalar turns to God. He sees the divine presence as his only companion in the struggle against his untamed nature.

translit: nāyiṉum kīḻppaṭṭa eṉneñcam naṉkaṟṟa naṅkaiyarpāl ēyiṉum celkiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉuṉai ēttiyiṭēṉ āyiṉum iṅkeṉai āṭkoḷal vēṇṭumai yā-uvanta tāyiṉum nallava ṉē-oṟṟi mēvum tayānitiyē.
translation: O Lord! O one kinder than a loving mother! O treasure of compassion abiding in Otriyur! My heart is lower than a dog. It eagerly runs toward beguiling women. What can I do? I do not praise you. Even so, you must accept me into your grace here.
commentary: True grace does not depend on human perfection. Vallalar admits he is unworthy, easily distracted by desire, and failing to offer proper praise. He relies on the nature of the divine—more forgiving and affectionate than a loving mother—to save him.

translit: nitiyēniṉ poṉṉaṭi ēttātu neñcam niṟaimayalām catiyē purikiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉuṉait tāḻalartam vitiyē eṉakkum vitittataṉ ṟō-av vitiyumiḷa matiyēr caṭai-aṇṇa lē-oṟṟi yūroḷi māṇikkamē.
translation: O Treasure, my heart does not praise your golden feet and engages in the deceit of complete delusion. What can I do? Have you ordained for me the same fate as those who do not bow to you? O Lord with the young moon on your matted hair, O radiant ruby of Otriyur.
commentary: Vallalar fears his distracted mind is trapping him in delusion. He wonders if his failure to praise the divine means he must suffer the same fate as those who reject God.

translit: māṇāta eṉneñcam valnañ caṉaiya maṭantaiyarpāl nāṇātu celkiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉciva ñāṉiyartam kōṇāta uḷḷat tirukkōyil mēvik kulavumoṟṟi vāṇā-eṉ kaṇṇiṉuṇ māmaṇi yē-eṉṟaṉ vāḻmutalē.
translation: My unrefined heart goes without shame to women who are like deadly poison. What can I do? You dwell and rejoice in the holy temple of the upright hearts of realized sages. O resident of Otriyur, O great gem within my eyes, O source of my life.
commentary: Vallalar contrasts his restless mind with the steady hearts of realized sages. While his desires draw him shamelessly toward toxic worldly attachments, he knows God dwells naturally in the pure awareness of the wise.

translit: vāḻāta neñcam eṉai-alait tōṭi maṭantaiyarpāl vīḻāta nāḷillai eṉṉaicey kēṉuṉ viraimalarttāḷ tāḻāta kuṟṟam poṟuttaṭi yēṉtaṉait tāṅkikkoḷvāy cūḻā tavariṭam cūḻāta oṟṟic cuṭarkkuṉṟamē.
translation: This ruinous heart harasses me. There is no day it does not run and fall for women. What can I do? Forgive my fault of not bowing to your fragrant flower-feet and support this devotee. You keep away from those who do not approach you, O hill of flame in Otriyur.
commentary: Vallalar feels helpless against the daily pull of physical desire. He begs the divine flame to forgive his lack of focus and support him through his weakness.

translit: kuṉṟēr mulaicciyar vaṉmala ūttaik kuḻiyilmaṉam ceṉṟē viḻukiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉem civakkoḻuntē naṉṟē catāṉanta nāyaka mēmaṟai nāṉkiṉukkum oṉṟē uyaroḷi yē-oṟṟi yūrem uyirttuṇaiyē.
translation: My mind wanders and falls into the foul pit of impurities of women with hill-like breasts. What can I do? O our tender shoot of Siva, O perfectly good Lord of eternal bliss. You are the one truth of all four Vedas, O supreme light, O companion of our lives in Otriyur.
commentary: Sensual attachment is a trap of physical impurity, pulling the mind down into the flesh. In contrast, the divine is the pure, supreme light and the single truth underlying the Vedas (ancient Hindu scriptures).

translit: tuṇaiyāmuṉ poṉṉaṭi ēttā maṉamatu tōkaiyarkaṇ kaṇaiyāl iḷaikkiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉeṉṟaṉ kaṇiraṇṭiṉ iṇaiyām parañcuṭa rē-aḻi yānala mē-iṉpamē paṇaiyār tiruvoṟṟi yūrara cē-em paramporuḷē.
translation: This mind does not praise your golden feet that are my true companion. It grows weak from the arrows shot by the eyes of peacock-like women. What can I do? O supreme flame who is like my own two eyes, O imperishable goodness, O bliss. O King of holy Otriyur surrounded by fertile fields, O our supreme reality.
commentary: The distractions of physical beauty act like arrows, weakening the mind and pulling it away from its only companion. Vallalar calls out to the supreme flame, seeing God as his own vision and lasting joy.

translit: poruḷēniṉ poṉṉaṭi uṉṉāteṉ vaṉmaṉam pūvaiyartam iruḷē purikiṉṟa teṉṉaicey kēṉaṭi yēṉmayaṅkum maruḷē tavirntuṉai vāḻtti vaṇaṅki makiḻntiṭanī aruḷē aruṭkaṭa lē-oṟṟi mānakar āḷpavaṉē.
translation: O Ultimate Reality! Without thinking of your golden feet, my hard heart seeks only the darkness of women. What shall I, your servant, do? O ruler of the great city of Otri, O ocean of grace! Bestow your grace so that I may dispel this confusing delusion, praise you, bow to you, and rejoice.
commentary: Vallalar confesses his mind is trapped by sensual desires instead of focusing on God. He calls these worldly distractions a confusing delusion that hardens the heart. He begs the divine ocean of grace to clear this confusion and replace darkness with the lasting joy of devotion.

translit: ākkal ātiya aintoḻil naṭatta ayaṉmuṉ ākiya aivarai aḷittu nīkkam iṉṟi-ev viṭattiṉum niṟainta nitta nī-eṉum niccayam ataṉait tākka eṇṇiyē tāmatap pāvi talaippaṭ ṭāṉavaṉ taṉai-akaṟ ṟutaṟkē ūkkam uṟṟaniṉ tiruvaruḷ vēṇṭum oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur! You manifested the five lords starting with Brahma to perform the five cosmic functions beginning with creation. You are the eternal one, pervading all places without separation. Desiring to destroy this certainty in me, the sinner of darkness has taken hold. I need your powerful divine grace to banish him.
commentary: God is the absolute power that creates the cosmic deities and directs the universe. Vallalar feels an inner darkness trying to erase his certainty in this truth. He cries out for grace, knowing only divine power can drive it away.

translit: kaṇattil eṉṉaiviṭ ṭēkukiṉ ṟavaṉpōl kāṭṭu kiṉṟaṉaṉ mīṭṭumvan taṭuttup paṇattum maṇṇiṉum pāvaiya riṭattum parava neñciṉai viravukiṉ ṟaṉaṉkāṇ kuṇatti ṉilkoṭun tāmataṉ eṉumik koṭiya vañcakaṉ oṭiyameyp pōtam uṇarttu vārilai eṉceykēṉ eḷiyēṉ oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur! He pretends to leave me for a moment, but he returns and presses close, mixing with my heart to scatter my desires toward wealth, land, and women. See how this cruel deceiver known as the dark quality operates. There is no one to impart true wisdom to destroy him. What can I, a poor wretch, do?
commentary: The darkness in the mind is a cunning deceiver. It pretends to vanish for a moment, only to rush back and fill the heart with cravings. Vallalar feels helpless against these sudden waves of worldly desire, pleading for the wisdom to break them.

translit: imaikkum avvaḷa vēṉumneñ coṭuṅki irukkak kaṇṭilēṉ iḻivukoḷ malattiṉ cumaikku nontunon taiyavō nāḷum tuyarkiṉ ṟēṉayar kiṉṟa-eṉ tuyaraik kumaikkum vaṇṇamniṉ tiruvaruḷ iṉṉum kūṭap peṟṟilēṉ kūṟuva teṉṉē umaikku nalvaram utaviya tēvē oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur! O God who granted a great boon to Uma! I have not seen my heart stay still even for the time it takes to blink.
