Aching repeatedly under the burden of degrading impurities, alas, I suffer every day. I have not yet received your divine grace to crush this exhausting sorrow. What can I say?
commentary: The hardest spiritual struggle is a restless mind. Vallalar confesses his heart cannot sit still even for a blink. Crushed by the daily weight of his mental impurities, he waits in exhaustion for the grace to quiet his sorrow.

translit: ceṉṟa nāḷilōr iṟaippoḻu tēṉum cintai ōrvakai teḷintataṉ ṟatupōy niṉṟa nāḷiṉum niṟkiṉṟa tilaikāṇ neṭiya pāviyēṉ nikaḻttuva teṉṉē eṉṟaṉ āruyirk koruperun tuṇaiyām entai yē-eṉai eḻumaiyum kātta uṉṟa ṉāliṉṉum uvakaikoḷ kiṉṟēṉ oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur! In days past, my mind did not find clarity even for a fraction of a second. See how it refuses to stand still in the days remaining. What can I, a terrible sinner, say? O my Father, the one great companion to my precious life! You protected me through seven births. I still find joy only through you.
commentary: Vallalar sees a mind that has never known a single moment of clarity. Looking ahead, he anticipates only the same restless wandering. His only hope is the divine, the companion who has protected him across multiple lifetimes and remains his sole source of joy.

translit: kōṭi nāviṉum kūṟiṭa aṭaṅkāk koṭiya māyaiyiṉ neṭiyavāḻk kaiyiṉai nāṭi neñcakam nalikiṉṟēṉ uṉaiyōr nāḷum eṇṇilēṉ naṉkaṭai vēṉē vāṭi ṉēṉpiḻai maṉaṅkoḷal aḻiyā vāḻvai ēḻaiyēṉ vacañceyal vēṇṭum ūṭi ṉālummey aṭiyarai ikavā oṟṟi mēviya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: O Supreme Reality dwelling in Otriyur! You never abandon true devotees even if they quarrel with you. Chasing after this endless life of cruel illusion, which ten million tongues could never fully describe, I suffer in my heart. I do not think of you for a single day. Will I ever attain anything good? I have withered away. Do not hold my faults against me. You must grant imperishable life to this poor soul.
commentary: The world is an endless illusion that drains the spirit. Vallalar feels he has withered away chasing worldly life while forgetting the divine. Trusting that God never abandons a devotee, he asks him to overlook his mistakes and grant him an imperishable life.

translit: aṉpa teṉpataik kaṉaviṉum kāṇēṉ āṭu kiṉṟaṉaṉ aṉparaip pōla vaṉpa vattaiyum māyttiṭa niṉaittēṉ vañca neñciṉai vacappaṭuk killēṉ tuṉpa vāḻkkaiyil cuḻalkiṉṟēṉ niṉṉait toḻutu vāḻttinal cukampeṟu vēṉē oṉpa tākiya uruvuṭaip periyōy oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: I do not see true love even in my dreams. I merely act like a devotee. I desired to destroy this harsh worldly bondage, yet I cannot bring my deceitful heart under control. I spin in this sorrowful life. Will I ever worship and praise you and attain supreme joy? O great one possessing the ninefold form! O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur!
commentary: Spiritual longing often clashes with an unruly mind. Vallalar confesses his devotion is just an act, devoid of love. He wants to break free from worldly suffering, but his deceitful heart refuses to be controlled. He wonders if he will ever feel real devotion and the joy it brings.

translit: muṉṉai nāṉceyta valviṉai iraṇṭiṉ muṭivu tērntilaṉ vaṭiveṭut tulakil eṉṉai nāṉkaṇṭa tantanāḷ toṭaṅki inta nāḷmaṭṭum iruḷ eṉpa tallāl piṉṉai yātoṉṟum peṟṟilēṉ itaṉaip pēca eṉṉuḷam kūcukiṉ ṟatukāṇ uṉṉai nampiṉēṉ niṉkuṟip puṇarēṉ oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: I have not seen the end of the two strong deeds I committed in the past. From the day I took a form in this world and recognized myself until this very day, I have received nothing but darkness. My heart shrinks to speak of this. I placed my trust in you, yet I do not know your intention. O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur!
commentary: The soul carries the heavy burden of past karma, the accumulated results of good and bad actions. Vallalar has known only spiritual darkness since birth. The shame of this prolonged ignorance makes his heart shrink. He has placed his trust in the divine, yet he waits helplessly, unable to understand God's intention.

translit: kaṇṇi lāṉcuṭar kāṇiya viḻainta karuttai otta-eṉ karuttiṉai muṭippat teṇṇi lāmuṭic civaparam poruḷniṉ cittam eppaṭi terintilaṉ eḷiyēṉ paṇṇi lāviya pāṭalan toṭainiṉ pāta paṅkayam pativuṟap puṉaivōr uṇṇi lāviya āṉantap perukkē oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: My desire is like the wish of a blind man longing to see a flame. I am a poor soul and I do not know your will to fulfill my wish, O supreme reality of Siva wearing the clear crescent moon on your crown. You are the flood of bliss resting in the hearts of those who weave garlands of musical songs and place them firmly at your lotus feet. O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur!
commentary: Longing for divine light in ignorance is like a blind person wishing to see a flame. Unequipped to reach his spiritual goals alone, Vallalar contrasts his helpless state with the joy of devotees who offer songs of praise. Unable to cure his own blindness, he relies on divine grace.

translit: uṇmai niṉaruṭ cukampiṟa ellām uṇmai aṉṟeṉa uṇarttiyum eṉatu peṇmai neñcakam veṇmaikoṇ ṭulakap pitti lē-iṉṉum tottukiṉ ṟatukāṇ vaṇmai oṉṟilēṉ eṇmaiyiṉ antō varuntu kiṉṟaṉaṉ vāḻvaṭai vēṉō oṇmai ampalat toḷiceyum cuṭarē oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: You taught me that the bliss of your grace is the only truth and everything else is false. Yet my weak heart turns pale and still clings to worldly madness. I possess no goodness. Alas, I suffer in my weakness. Will I ever attain true life? O flame shining brightly in the beautiful hall! O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur!
commentary: Knowing the truth is not the same as being free. The divine taught Vallalar that the bliss of grace is the only reality and the material world is false. Despite this, his weak heart still clings to worldly madness. He suffers in the gap between understanding the truth and experiencing it.

translit: naiyu māṟeṉaik kāmamā tikaḷtām naṇuki vañcakam nāṭṭukiṉ ṟatunāṉ ceyyu māṟitaṟ kaṟintilaṉ entāy tikaikkiṉ ṟēṉ aruḷ tiṟampeṟu vēṉē vaiyu māṟilā vaṇkaiyar uḷattiṉ maṉṉi vāḻkiṉṟa māmaṇik kuṉṟē uyyu māṟaruḷ ampalat tamutē oṟṟi ōṅkiya uttamap poruḷē.
translation: Lust and other desires approach to wear me down and plant deceit within me. My father, I do not know how to overcome this. I stand bewildered. Will I ever attain the power of your grace? You are the great mountain of gems dwelling permanently in the hearts of generous people who never speak a word of blame. O nectar of the hall granting grace for salvation! O Supreme Reality towering in Otriyur!
commentary: Base desires do not just distract the mind; they wear the soul down and plant deceit within it. Vallalar confesses his bewilderment, not knowing how to defeat these inner enemies. He observes that the divine dwells in the hearts of generous people who never speak ill of others. Recognizing his helplessness, he pleads for the power of grace to save him.

note: Editor's note: a general poem (potu, பொது), not tied to one temple.
translit: āṇṭa tuṇṭunī eṉṟaṉai aṭiyēṉ ākkai oṉṟumē acaimaṭaṟ paṉaipōl nīṇṭa tuṇṭumaṟ ṟuṉṉaṭik kaṉpē nīṇṭa tillaival neṟicelum oḻukkam pūṇṭa tuṇṭuniṉ puṉitanal oḻukkē pūṇṭa tillai-eṉ puṉmaiyai nōkki īṇṭa vantaru ḷāyeṉil antō eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: You have taken me and ruled me. My body alone has grown tall like a palmyra tree with swaying fronds. But love for your feet has not grown. I have taken up conduct that treads harsh paths. I have not taken up your pure and good conduct. Seeing my baseness, if you do not come here to bestow your grace upon me, alas, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Physical maturity does not equal spiritual growth. Without love for the divine, a person wanders into harsh, destructive ways of living. Vallalar asks for grace to rescue him from the painful consequences of wasted time.

translit: ūḻai yēmika nontiṭu vēṉō uḷattai nōvaṉō ulakiṭai mayakkum pāḻai yēpalaṉ taruvateṉ ṟeṇṇip pāvi yēṉperum paṭaruḻak kiṉṟēṉ māḻai yērtiru mēṉi-em perumāṉ maṉami raṅki-eṉ valviṉai keṭavan tēḻai yēṟkaru ḷāyeṉil antō eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: Shall I deeply lament my fate? Shall I blame my mind? Thinking this delusive barren wasteland of the world yields fruit, I, a sinner, suffer great sorrow. O our Lord whose sacred form has the beauty of gold! If you do not take pity in your heart, come to destroy my strong karma, and bestow your grace upon this poor wretch, alas, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Worldly life is a barren wasteland. Chasing its illusions only creates strong karma (the bound consequences of past actions) and brings sorrow. Only divine pity and grace can break this cycle and prevent ruin.

translit: īṉṟu koṇṭa-eṉ tantaiyum tāyum yāvum nī-eṉa eṇṇiya nāyēṉ māṉṟu koṇṭa-iv vañcaka vāḻviṉ mayakki ṉālmika vaṉmaikaḷ ceytēṉ cāṉṟu koṇṭatu kaṇṭaṉai yēṉum tamiya ṉēṉmicait tayavukoṇ ṭeṉṉai ēṉṟu koṇṭaru ḷāyeṉil antō eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: I, a dog, considered you to be my mother and father who bore me, and everything else. Confused by the delusion of this deceptive worldly life, I committed many cruel deeds. Even though you have witnessed this yourself, if you do not take pity on me in my loneliness and accept me with grace, alas, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Delusion leads people to commit cruel acts and forget their spiritual foundation. The divine sees all these failures clearly. Yet even knowing the depth of his mistakes, Vallalar relies on God, trusting that divine compassion is greater than human error.

translit: ammai appaṉeṉ āruyirt tuṇaivaṉ aracaṉ tēcikaṉ aṉpuṭait tēvaṉ immai yiṟpayaṉ ammaiyiṟ payaṉmaṟ ṟiyāvu nī-eṉa eṇṇiniṟ kiṉṟēṉ cemmai yiṟpeṟum aṉparuḷ ḷakañcēr celva mē-eṉaic cērttaru ḷāyēl emmai yiṟpeṟu vēṉciṟu nāyēṉ eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: I stand considering you to be my Mother, Father, the companion of my precious life, King, Guru, loving God, the fruit of this life, the fruit of the next, and all else. O wealth abiding in the hearts of perfect devotees! If you do not gather me and bestow your grace, what refuge will I, a little dog, attain? What will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: God replaces every worldly bond as mother, father, teacher, and companion. When a person realizes this, the divine becomes their only wealth. Without the refuge of grace, there is nowhere else to turn for safety.

translit: tāya rātiyar calippuṟu kiṟpār tamarum eṉṟaṉait taḻuvutal oḻivār nēya rātiyar nēyamviṭ ṭakalvār niṉṉai nampi-eṉ neñcuvak kiṉṟēṉ tīya rātiyil tīyaṉeṉ ṟeṉainiṉ tiruvu ḷattiṭaic cērttiṭā toḻittāl ēyar kōṉukkaṉ ṟaruḷumem perumāṉ eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: Mothers and others grow weary of me. Relatives cease to embrace me. Friends and others abandon their affection and depart. Trusting you, my heart rejoices. If you reject me from your sacred mind by concluding I am the most wicked among the wicked, O our Lord who once bestowed grace upon Eyarkon, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Human relationships are fragile and conditional. Family and friends eventually lose patience, withdraw their affection, or pass away. Trusting the divine brings lasting joy, because God is a constant refuge who can accept and transform even those who feel they are the most wicked.

translit: muṉṉai nāṉceyta valviṉaic cimiḻppāṉ mōka vāriyiṉ mūḻkiṉa ṉēṉum aṉṉai pōlumeṉ āruyirt tuṇaiyām appa niṉaruḷ ampiyai nampi taṉṉai nērciva ñāṉameṉ karaiyaic cārku vēmeṉum tarukkuṭaṉ uḻaṉṟēṉ iṉṉum niṉaruḷ īntilai antō eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: Though I drowned in the ocean of delusion, bound by the hard karma I accumulated in the past, I wandered with the arrogant thought that I would reach the unparalleled shore of divine wisdom by trusting the boat of your grace. O Father, my dear life's companion who is like a mother to me, you still have not granted your grace. Alas, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: It is easy to turn trust in God into an excuse for arrogance. Vallalar admits that even while drowning in his karma and worldly delusion, he casually assumed God would ferry him to safety. He realizes this pride is dangerous and worries it will leave him abandoned to a terrible fate.

translit: uṇṇu kiṉṟatum uṟaṅkukiṉ ṟatummēl uṭuttu kiṉṟatum ulavukiṉ ṟatummāl naṇṇu kiṉṟatum naṅkaiyar vāḻkkai nāṭu kiṉṟatum navaiyuṭait toḻilkaḷ paṇṇu kiṉṟatum āṉapiṉ uṭalaip pāṭai mēluṟap paṭuttukiṉ ṟatumeṉ ṟeṇṇu kiṉṟatō ṟuḷampataik kiṉṟēṉ eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: Eating, sleeping, dressing, wandering around in illusion, seeking out life with women, committing sinful acts, and after all this, laying the body on a bier: every time I think of this sequence, my heart shudders. What will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Ordinary human existence can look empty. Vallalar strips life down to its bare facts: we eat, sleep, dress, chase desires, make mistakes, and finally die. Looking at life as an endless cycle of habits ending in a funeral fills him with dread and drives his desperate cry for a higher purpose.

translit: kallai vellavum valla-eṉ maṉantāṉ kaṭavuḷ niṉaṭik kamalaṅkaḷ niṉaittal illai nallainiṉ aruḷeṉak kataṉāl illai illainī irakkamil lātāṉ allai illaiyāl aruḷtarā tiruttal aṭiya ṉēṉaḷa vāyiṉiṅ kiṭarkkē ellai illai-eṉ ṟuḷampataik kiṉṟēṉ eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: O God, my heart, hard enough to conquer a stone, does not think of your lotus feet. You are perfectly good, and because of this, there is no grace for me. You are not without compassion. Yet if your withholding of grace applies only to me your servant, my heart trembles knowing my suffering here will have no end. What will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Spiritual dryness is a failure of the human heart, not a lack of divine mercy. Vallalar describes his mind as harder than stone because it refuses to turn toward the divine. He knows God is compassionate, meaning that if grace is missing, the fault lies in his own stubborn resistance.

translit: poṅku māyaiyiṉ puṇarppiṉuk kuḷḷam pōkki niṉṟatum pulappakai varkaḷāl iṅku mālari ēṟṟiṉmuṉ karipōl ēṅku kiṉṟatum iṭarpperuṅ kaṭalil taṅkum ācaiyaṅ karāppiṭit tīrkkat tavippil niṉṟatum tamiyaṉēṉ taṉaiyum eṅkum ākiniṉ ṟāyaṟin tilaiyō eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: I surrender my mind to the attachments of surging illusion. I languish here, tormented by my hostile senses, like an elephant standing before a fierce lion. I stand in agony as the crocodile of desire, dwelling in the vast ocean of sorrow, grabs and drags me. You who exist everywhere as everything, do you not know the state of this lonely soul? What will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Worldly distractions pull at the mind with violent force. Vallalar feels his physical senses attacking his peace like a fierce lion hunting an elephant, while his desires drag him under like a crocodile. Since God exists everywhere and in everything, he wonders how the divine could overlook his lonely struggle against these powerful forces.

translit: arakkaṉ allaṉyāṉ arakkaṉē eṉiṉum arakka ṉukkummuṉ aruḷaḷit taṉaiyē purakka eṉṉainiṉ aruṭkaṭaṉ eṉṟē pōṟṟu kiṉṟaṉaṉ pulaiyariṟ pulaiyēṉ urakka iṅkiḻait tiṭumpiḻai ellām uṉṉal aiyanī uṉṉi-eṉ aḷavil irakkam niṉtiru uḷattilai yāṉāl eṉcey kēṉnara kiṭai-iṭum pōtē.
translation: I am not a demon. Yet even if I were, you granted your grace to a demon in the past. The lowest of the low, I praise you, declaring that it is the duty of your grace to protect me. O Lord, do not dwell on all the glaring wrongs I commit here. If you think of them and hold no compassion for me in your divine heart, what will I do when cast into hell?
commentary: Divine mercy must bypass strict justice. Vallalar reminds God that grace has historically been granted even to literal demons. He asks the Lord to act out of pure pity rather than judging his flaws, knowing that if his mistakes are weighed against him, he has no hope of salvation.

note: Editor's note: a general poem (potu, பொது), not tied to one temple.
translit: tampi rāṉtaya virukka-iṅ keṉakkōr tāḻvuṇ ṭō-eṉat tarukkoṭum iruntēṉ empi rāṉniṉak kēḻaiyēṉ aḷavil irakkam oṉṟilai eṉeṉpa tiṉṉum nampi rāṉeṉa nampiniṟ kiṉṟēṉ nampum eṉṟaṉai vempiṭac ceyiṉum cempi rāṉaruḷ aḷikkiṉum uṉatu cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: I remained arrogant, thinking, "While the Lord's compassion exists, can there be any lowliness for me here?" My Lord, you have absolutely no pity on this poor soul. What can I say? Yet I stand trusting, saying "He is our Lord." Whether you make me, who trusts you, wilt in sorrow, or whether you grant your grace, O radiant Lord, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Vallalar confesses he once took God's compassion for granted. Now, even feeling ignored and left to suffer, he realizes he has no power of his own. Whether he receives grace or sorrow, every outcome belongs to the divine will.

translit: tuṭṭa neñcaka vañcakak koṭiyēṉ colva teṉṉai-eṉ tolviṉai vacattāl iṭṭa nalvaḻi alvaḻi eṉavē eṇṇum ivvaḻi iraṇṭiṭai eṉainī viṭṭa tevvaḻi avvaḻi akaṉṟē vēṟum ōrvaḻi mēviṭap paṭumō ciṭṭar uḷḷuṟum civaperu māṉniṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: What can I say, a cruel one with a wicked, deceitful heart? Driven by my ancient karma, between the two paths considered good and bad, whichever path you leave me on, can I stray from it and reach another? O Lord Siva who dwells in the hearts of the virtuous, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Past actions, or karma, pull the mind toward good or bad choices. Vallalar admits he cannot steer his life or stray from the path God sets. Total surrender means accepting that human beings are directed by the divine hand.

translit: ūṭṭu kiṉṟaṉai uṇṇukiṉ ṟaṉaṉmēl uṟakku kiṉṟaṉai uṟaṅkukiṉ ṟaṉaṉpiṉ kāṭṭu kiṉṟaṉai kāṇukiṉ ṟaṉaṉnī kaḷippik kiṉṟaṉai kaḷippuṟu kiṉṟēṉ āṭṭu kiṉṟaṉai āṭukiṉ ṟaṉaṉiv akila kōṭiyum avvakai yāṉāl tīṭṭum aṉparuk kaṉpaniṉ taṉatu cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: You feed me, and I eat. You put me to rest, and I sleep. Then you show things, and I see. You make me rejoice, and I rejoice. You make me dance, and I dance. If millions of universes behave in this very way, O Lover of the devotees who cherish you, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Every ordinary action, from eating and sleeping to seeing and rejoicing, is moved by God. Vallalar sees he is directed by the divine, just like millions of universes. Human beings depend on the Lord for every motion and breath.

translit: kaṇṇi lāṉcuṭar kāṇa-uṉ ṉutalpōl karutti lēṉumniṉ karuṇaiyai viḻaintēṉ eṇṇi lā-iṭai yūṟaṭut tataṉāl iḷaikkiṉ ṟēṉeṉai ēṉṟukoḷ vataṟkeṉ uṇṇi lāviya uyirkkuyir aṉaiyāy uṉṉai ottatōr muṉṉavar ilaikāṇ teṇṇi lāmuṭic civaparam poruḷniṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: Like a blind man wishing to see the light, I desired your grace even though I lack understanding. I grow weary as countless obstacles beset me. To accept me, O You who are the life of the life dwelling within me, there is no primal being equal to you. O Supreme Reality, Siva with the clear moon upon your crown, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Wanting divine grace without understanding is like a blind person wishing to see the light. Exhausted by obstacles, Vallalar appeals to the Lord dwelling within him as the life of his life. He casts himself on God, his only rescue.

translit: meccu kiṉṟavar vēṇṭiya ellām viḻi-i maikkumuṉ mēvalkaṇ ṭuṉaināṉ naccu kiṉṟaṉaṉ nacciṉum koṭiyēṉ naṉmai eytavō vaṉmaiyuṟ ṟiṭavō iccai naṉṟaṟi vāyaruḷ ceyyā tirukkiṉ ṟāy uṉak kiyāṉceyta teṉṉē ceccai mēṉi-em civaparañ cuṭarniṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: Seeing those who praise you attain everything they desire before an eye can blink, I yearn for you. Even though I yearn, I am cruel. Whether I am to attain goodness or suffer hardship, you know my desire well. Yet you remain without granting grace. What have I done to you? O Supreme Jothi of Siva with a form red like the Ixora flower, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Vallalar watches others receive divine blessings in the blink of an eye and aches for the same grace. He knows he is flawed, yet questions why the Lord leaves him waiting in hardship. He accepts he can do nothing except submit to God's decision.

translit: nāṭun tāyiṉum nallavaṉ namatu nātaṉ eṉṟuṉai nāṭumap poḻutē vāṭu neñcam taḷirkkiṉṟēṉ maṟṟai vaikaṟ pōtelām vāṭukiṉ ṟaṉaṉkāṇ pāṭun toṇṭarkaḷ iṭarppaṭil tariyāp paṇpeṉ maṭṭumniṉ pālilai pōlum tēṭum pattartam uḷattamar vōyniṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: The moment I seek you, thinking, "Our Lord is better than a caring mother," my withered heart blossoms. At all other times of the day, see, I wither. It seems your nature of being unable to bear it when your singing servants suffer is absent only in my case. O you who abide in the hearts of seeking devotees, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: The mere thought of God's maternal love is enough to revive a despairing heart. Yet Vallalar feels this comfort slip away, leaving him to wonder why God rushes to help others but seems to ignore his suffering.

translit: maruḷa ḷitteṉai mayakki-iv ulakil varuttu kiṉṟaṉai maṟṟeṉak kuṉṟaṉ aruḷa ḷikkilai āyiṉum niṉakkē aṭimai yākkilai āyiṉum vēṟṟup poruḷa ḷikkilai āyiṉum oruniṉ poṉmu kattai-ōr pōtu kaṇ ṭiṭavē teruḷa ḷittiṭil pōtum iṅ kuṉatu cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: You have given me delusion, bewildered me, and you afflict me in this world. Even if you do not grant me your grace, even if you do not make me your slave, even if you do not grant me any other wealth, it is enough if you grant me the clarity to see your golden face just once. Here, apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Vallalar asks for nothing but a single moment of clear vision. God can withhold grace, refuse his service, and deny him all wealth. None of that matters if he can just pierce through his worldly delusion to see the divine face even once.

translit: māṟu kiṉṟaṉaṉ neñcakam añci vaḷḷal ittuṇai vantilaṉ iṉimēl kūṟu kiṉṟateṉ eṉṟayar kiṉṟēṉ kulavit tēṟṟumak koḷkaiyar iṉṟi ēṟu kiṉṟaṉaṉ irakkamuḷ ḷavaṉnam iṟaivaṉ iṉṟaruḷ īkuvaṉ eṉṟē tēṟu kiṉṟaṉaṉ eṉceykēṉ niṉatu cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: I falter, my heart fears, and I languish, thinking, "The generous Lord has not come for so long, what is there to say anymore?" Without anyone to affectionately console me, I lift myself up and find clarity, thinking, "Our Lord is compassionate, He will grant grace today." What can I do? Apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: The spiritual path often swings between fear and sudden hope. Left alone with no one to comfort him, Vallalar falls into despair over God's absence. He then has to pull himself back up, clinging to the thought that a compassionate God must eventually bring relief.

translit: tāyi ṉumperun tayavuṭai yavaṉnan talaivaṉ eṉṟunāṉ tarukkoṭum tirintēṉ nāyi ṉumkaṭai yēṉpaṭum iṭarai nāḷum kaṇṭaṉai nalaruḷ ceyyāy āyi ṉumtiru mukaṅkaṇṭu makiḻum aṉpar tampaṇi āṟṟimaṟ ṟuṭalam tēyi ṉummika naṉṟeṉak karuḷuṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: I wandered with pride, thinking, "Our Lord possesses greater compassion than a mother." You see daily the sufferings experienced by me, who am lower than a dog, yet you do not grant your good grace. Even so, grant me grace to feel it is very good even if my body wears away performing service for the devotees who rejoice upon seeing your sacred face. Apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: If a direct connection with God seems blocked, the next best thing is serving those who have found it. Vallalar feels ignored by the divine despite his suffering. In his surrender, he asks only for the strength to wear his body out serving the devotees who have already seen God's face.

translit: vāṉum vaiyamum aḷikkiṉum uṉpāl maṉamvait tōṅkuvar vaḷḷalniṉ aṭiyār nāṉum avvakai ulakiyal oḻukkil nāṭi niṉṉaruḷ nalampeṟa viḻaital kūṉum ōrmuṭak kaṇṇili vāṉil kulavum oṇcuṭar kuṟittiṭal pōlum tēṉum kaikkumniṉ aruḷuṇṭēl uṇṭuṉ cittam aṉṟiyāṉ ceyvatoṉ ṟilaiyē.
translation: Even if given heaven and earth, your devotees, O generous Lord, keep their minds fixed on you and flourish. My desiring to attain the goodness of your grace while pursuing the worldly path is like a hunchbacked, crippled, and blind person aiming for the radiant sun glowing in the sky. If I have your grace, even honey will taste bitter. Apart from your will, I do nothing.
commentary: Worldly desires and divine grace cannot be pursued at the same time. Vallalar compares himself to a blind and crippled person trying to reach the sun, feeling it impossible to catch hold of God while clinging to worldly habits. He knows that once grace is given, even the sweetest things in life will lose their taste.

note: Editor's note: sung at Chidambaram, which Saiva tradition calls simply “the Temple” (kōyil, கோயில்).
translit: tuṟaiyiṭum kaṅkaic ceḻuñcaṭaik kaṉiyē cuyampira kācamē amutil kaṟaiyiṭum kaṇṭat toruperuṅ karuṇaik kaṭavuḷē kaṇṇutaṟ karumpē kuṟaiyiṭum kuṇattāl koṭiyaṉēṉ eṉiṉum koṭuntuya rālalain taiyā muṟaiyiṭu kiṉṟēṉ aruḷtarā teṉṉai mūṭaṉeṉ ṟikaḻvatu muṟaiyō.
translation: O Fruit on the lush matted hair that holds the Ganga! O self-luminous Light! O God of immense compassion whose throat bears the dark stain! O Sugarcane with an eye on your forehead! Even if I am cruel and flawed in character, I am tossed about by terrible sorrow, O Lord, and I cry out to you. Is it proper for you to despise me as a fool and deny me your grace?
commentary: Vallalar asks God not to turn him away because he is flawed. He invokes the traditional imagery of Siva: bearing the sacred river Ganga in his matted hair, a third eye of wisdom, and a dark throat from swallowing poison to save the world. His suffering should earn God's compassion, regardless of his ignorance.

translit: ikaḻntiṭēl eḷiyēṉ taṉṉainī aṉṟi ēṉṟukoḷ pavarilai antō akaḻnteṉa tuḷattaic cūṟaikoṇ ṭalaikkum añarelām aṟuttaruḷ purivāy pukaḻntiṭum toṇṭar uḷattiṉum veḷḷip poruppiṉum potuviṉum niṟaintu tikaḻntaruḷ paḻukkum teyvatat taruvē celvamē civaparam poruḷē.
translation: Do not despise this poor wretch. Alas, there is no one but you to accept me. Sever all the sorrows that dig into my heart, ravage it, and toss me about, and grant me your grace. O divine tree that fills the hearts of praising devotees, the silver mountain, and the public hall, shining and ripening with grace! O Wealth! O Supreme Reality of Siva!
commentary: God is the only refuge left to quiet his ravaged heart. Vallalar describes the divine presence filling three sacred spaces: a devotee's inner heart, the legendary silver mountain of Mount Kailash, and the public hall of the temple at Chidambaram. He views God as a divine tree offering the sweet fruit of grace to anyone seeking shelter.

translit: poruḷelām puṇarkkum puṇṇiyap poruḷē puttamu tēkuṇap poruppē iruḷelām aṟukkum pēroḷip piḻampē iṉpamē eṉperun tuṇaiyē aruḷelām tiraṇṭa oruciva mūrtti aṇṇalē niṉaṭik kapayam maruḷelām koṇṭa maṉattiṉēṉ tuṉpa mayakkelām māṟṟi-āṇ ṭaruḷē.
translation: O holy Reality that joins all things together! O fresh nectar! O mountain of good qualities! O blazing mass of great light that severs all darkness! O Bliss! O my great companion! O unique embodiment of Siva formed of concentrated grace! O Lord, I seek refuge at your feet. Remove all the sorrowful confusion of my delusion-filled mind and rule over me.
commentary: God is a blazing mass of light that destroys the darkness of ignorance. Vallalar sees the divine not as a distant ruler, but as a great companion and pure, concentrated grace. Seeking refuge in this light, he asks God to clear away the mental confusion and delusion causing his suffering.

translit: āṇṭaniṉ karuṇaik kaṭaliṭai oruciṟ ṟaṇuttuṇait tivalaiyē eṉiṉum īṇṭa-eṉ ṟaṉmēl teṟittiyēl uyvēṉ illaiyēl eṉceykēṉ eḷiyēṉ nīṇṭavaṉ ayaṉmaṟ ṟēṉaivā ṉavarkaḷ niṉaipparum nilaimaiyai aṉpar vēṇṭiṉum vēṇṭā viṭiṉumāṅ kaḷikkum vimalaṉē viṭaipperu māṉē.
translation: Even if you splash just an atom-sized drop from your ruling ocean of compassion upon me, I will be saved. If not, what can I, a poor wretch, do? The tall Vishnu, Brahma, and the other celestials find your state hard to even conceive. Yet you grant that state to your devotees whether they ask for it or not. O immaculate one! O Lord mounted on the bull!
commentary: Even a single microscopic drop from the vast ocean of divine compassion is enough to save a life. Vallalar points out a contrast: the creator and preserver gods, Brahma and Vishnu, struggle even to comprehend this grace. Yet it is given freely and intimately to true devotees, sometimes before they even ask.

translit: perumaiyil piṟaṅkum periyanaṟ kuṇattōr peṟṟatōr peruntaṉip poruḷē arumaiyil piramaṉ ātiya tēvar aṭaintanaṟ celvamē amutē irumaiyiṟ payaṉum niṉtiru aruḷē eṉṟuniṉ aṭaikkalam āṉēṉ karumaiyiṟ poliyum viṭanikar tuṉpak kaḷaikaḷain teṉaiviḷait taruḷē.
translation: O great and matchless Reality attained by those of great and radiant virtues! O good wealth and nectar attained with difficulty by Brahma and the other gods! Realizing that the fruit of both this world and the next is your holy grace, I have taken refuge in you. Weed out my sorrows that resemble dark poison, and cultivate me with your grace.
commentary: Divine grace is the only true reward in this life and the next. Using an agricultural metaphor for spiritual growth, Vallalar asks God to act as a farmer, weeding out his dark, poisonous sorrows so his soul can be cultivated and ripened by grace.

translit: viḷaittaṉaṉ pavanōyk kētuvām viṭaya viruppiṉai neruppuṟaḻ tuṉpiṉ iḷaittaṉaṉ antō ēḻaimai ataṉāl eṉceykēṉ eṉpiḻai poṟuttut taḷaittavaṉ tuyarnīt tāḷaval lavarniṉ taṉai-aṉṟi aṟintilaṉ tamiyēṉ kiḷaittavāṉ kaṅkai naticcaṭai yavaṉē kiḷartarum ciṟpara civaṉē.
translation: I cultivated desires for worldly objects that cause the disease of birth. I grew weary in sorrow fierce as fire. Alas, what can I do in my ignorance? I stand alone. I know no one else but You who can forgive my faults, remove my binding sorrow, and rule me. O Lord with the branching celestial river Ganges in Your matted hair, O shining Supreme Siva of pure consciousness.
commentary: Worldly desires act as a disease that traps the soul in endless cycles of birth and suffering. The resulting sorrow burns like fierce fire. Recognizing his helplessness, Vallalar turns to God as the only presence capable of forgiving his mistakes and breaking his chains.

translit: ciṟpara civaṉē tēvartam talaimait tēvaṉē tillai-am palattē taṟpara naṭañcey tāṇuvē akila carācara kāraṇap poruḷē aṟpartam iṭañcel paṟpala tuyarāl alaitaru kiṉṟaṉaṉ eḷiyēṉ kaṟpakam aṉaiyaniṉ tiruvaruṭ kaṭalil kaḷippuṭaṉ āṭuva teṉṟō.
translation: O Supreme Siva of pure consciousness. O Chief of the gods. O Pillar of reality who performs the supreme dance in the hall of Thillai. O Source of all moving and unmoving things in the universe. I wander tossed by endless sorrows, approaching petty people for help. I am poor and helpless. When will I bathe with joy in the ocean of Your divine grace, which grants boons like the heavenly wish-fulfilling tree?
commentary: There is a stark contrast between the supreme majesty of God and the desperate human condition. Driven by hardship, people often waste time begging ordinary, flawed individuals for help. Vallalar's longing is to stop wandering and plunge into the limitless, wish-fulfilling ocean of divine grace.

translit: eṉṟuniṉ aruḷnīr uṇṭuvan tiṭumnāḷ eṉṟuniṉ uruvukaṇ ṭiṭumnāḷ eṉṟuniṉ aṭiyark kēvalcey tiṭumnāḷ eṉṟeṉa takattuyar aṟumnāḷ maṉṟuḷniṉ ṟāṭum parañcuṭark kuṉṟē vāṉavar kaṉaviṉum tōṉṟā toṉṟuṟum oṉṟē aruṇmaya māṉa uttama vittaka maṇiyē.
translation: When will the day come for me to drink the waters of Your grace? When will the day come for me to see Your form? When will the day come for me to serve Your devotees? When will the day come for my inner sorrow to be severed? O Mountain of supreme light dancing in the hall. O Ancient One who remains unseen even in the dreams of the celestial beings. O excellent, wondrous Gem made of pure grace.
commentary: Deep spiritual longing breaks down into four essential desires. Vallalar yearns to taste divine grace, see God's true form, serve other devoted seekers, and end all inner grief. God is addressed as a mountain of supreme light, a presence so vast that even the gods cannot glimpse it in their dreams.

translit: vittakam aṟiyēṉ viṉaiyiṉēṉ tuṉpa virikaṭal āḻntaṉaṉ antō attaka vēṉai eṭuppavar niṉṉai aṉṟi-eṅ kaṇumilai aiyā mattakak kariyiṉ uripuṉai pavaḷa vaṇṇaṉē viṇṇavar aracē puttaka niṟaiviṉ aṭiyavar vēṇṭum poruḷelām purintaruḷ pavaṉē.
translation: I possess no wisdom. I am bound by past actions. I have sunk into the vast ocean of sorrow. Alas. O Lord, I have no one anywhere to lift me up from this state except You. O coral-hued Lord who wears the flayed skin of the mighty elephant. O King of the celestials. O Lord who grants every desire of devotees filled with the perfect knowledge of scriptures.
commentary: Past actions bind the soul and pull it into a deep ocean of sorrow. Acknowledging a lack of wisdom, Vallalar admits he is powerless to save himself. He appeals to divine grace as the only force capable of reaching down and pulling him to safety.

translit: aruḷpavaṉ niṉṉai allatai iṅkum aṅkummaṟ ṟeṅkumiṉ ṟatupōl maruḷpavaṉ eṉṉai allatai maṇṇum vāṉamum tēṭiṉum iṉṟē iruḷpavam uṭaiyēṉ eṉceykēṉ niṉtāḷ iṇaituṇai eṉaniṉain tuṟṟēṉ maruḷpavat toṭumeṉ tuyaraṟut tāḷvāy vāḻiya aruṭperun tuṟaiyē.
translation: Just as there is no one to bestow grace except You, here, there, or anywhere else, there is no one as deluded as me, even if one searches the earth and the heavens. I possess this dark worldly birth. What can I do? I approached You, trusting Your twin feet as my only support. Destroy my sorrow and this deluding birth, and rule over me. Long live the great harbor of grace.
commentary: There is a humble symmetry between the creator and the soul. Just as there is no source of grace anywhere in the universe other than God, there is no one as lost in dark delusion as Vallalar. Helpless, he casts himself at God's feet, asking for his worldly confusion to be destroyed forever.

translit: kēḷaṉan tāṉoru pōtuṇ ṭaṉaimaṉak kētamaṟa nīḷaṉam tēṭu muṭiyāṉ etuniṉak kīntateṉṟē vēḷaṉam pōlnaṭai miṉṉārum maintarum vēṭikkaiyāy ēḷaṉam ceykuvar nī-aru ḷāviṭil eṉappaṉē.
translation: My Father! If you do not bestow grace, young women with swan-like gaits and young men will mock me for sport, saying: "Listen, you ate only one meal a day to rid your mind of sorrow. What did the Lord, whose crown the great swan sought, give you?"
commentary: Intense spiritual discipline looks foolish to ordinary people without visible divine grace. Vallalar worries carefree youth will mock his strict fasting, a practice meant to clear the mind of worldly sorrow. The "great swan" refers to the creator deity Brahma taking the form of a bird to search in vain for the top of the Lord's infinite pillar of light.

translit: appāniṉ poṉṉaruḷ eṉmēl tayaicey taḷittilaiyēl tuppā ṉavumoru pōtutuv vātu cuḻaṉṟaṉaiyē ippāril īcaṉ tiruvaruḷ nīpeṟṟa teṅṅaṉamō ceppāy eṉavarip pārcirip pāric cekattavarē.
translation: Father! If you do not mercifully bestow your golden grace upon me, the people of this world will taunt and laugh at me, saying: "You wandered around without eating good food even once a day. Tell us, how did you attain the Lord's holy grace on this earth?"
commentary: Society measures every effort by visible results. Wandering and refusing the comfort of good food are standard marks of a seeker, yet people will quickly point out the futility of such hardship if it brings no blessing. Vallalar feels exposed to public ridicule while waiting on God's mercy.

translit: tītucey tēṟkaruḷ ceyvāṉniṉ cittam tirumpilaiyēl tātucey tēkattu ṇā-oru pōtu tavirntaniṉak kētucey tāṉcivaṉ eṉṟē ulakar iḻivuraittāl yātucey vēṉteyva mē-eḷi yēṉuyirk kiṉṉamutē.
translation: O God! Sweet nectar of this poor one's life! If your heart does not turn to bestow grace upon me who has done wrong, the people of the world will insult me, asking: "You gave up eating even once a day for this physical body. What did Siva do for you?" If they speak so, what will I do?
commentary: The pain of public insult is amplified by a sense of unworthiness. Ordinary people cannot understand starving the physical body unless God intervenes. By calling the Lord the sweet nectar of his life, Vallalar shows the real heartbreak is the prospect of being abandoned by his only sustenance.

translit: teriyāmai yālciṟi yēṉceykuṟ ṟattainiṉ cittamatil piriyāmai vaittaruḷ ceytilai yēleṉaip peṟṟavaḷum periyācai koṇṭapiḷ ḷāyaraṉ eṉtarap peṟṟateṉṟē pariyācai ceykuva ḷālaya lāreṉ pakaruvatē.
translation: If you keep the faults this little one committed out of ignorance in your mind and do not grant grace, even the mother who bore me will mock me, saying: "O child who harbored great desires! What did Hara give you?" What then will strangers say?
commentary: The fear of ridicule peaks when Vallalar imagines his own mother scoffing at his spiritual desires. If the person who gave him life mocks his devotion to Hara (a name for God as the remover of illusions), the judgment of strangers will be unbearable. He begs God to overlook the faults born of human ignorance and offer protection from this intimate shame.

translit: eṇṇāmal nāyaṭi yēṉceyta kuṟṟaṅkaḷ yāvumeṇṇi aṇṇāniṉ cittam iraṅkāy eṉiliṅ kayalavartām peṇār iṭattavaṉ pēraruḷ caṟṟum peṟātaniṉak koṇṇātiv vaṇmai viratameṉ ṟāleṉ uraippatuvē.
translation: O Lord! If you count all the faults committed by this dog-like servant instead of ignoring them, and if your heart does not show pity, outsiders here will say to me: "You received none of the great grace of the Lord who holds a woman on His left side. This severe vow is unfit for you." If they say this, what will I reply?
commentary: Vallalar fears the harsh verdict of society declaring him unfit for his vows if he fails to attain grace. He begs God not to weigh his past mistakes but to respond with pity. The description of the Lord holding a woman on His left side refers to Ardhanarishvara, representing the balance of divine justice and mercy.

translit: poyyāṉa vañcaka ṉēṉpiḻai yāvum poṟuttuṉaruḷ ceyyāy eṉiletu ceykuvaṉ yāṉic cekatalattōr eyyā viratattil yātupeṟ ṟāyeṉ ṟikaḻvarkaṇṭāy ayyā-eṉ iṉṉamu tē-ara cē-eṉa tāṇṭavaṉē.
translation: If you do not forgive all the mistakes of this false deceiver and grant your grace, what will I do? The people of this world will mock me, asking, "What did you gain from your tireless vows?" O Lord, my sweet nectar, my King, my Ruler.
commentary: Strict spiritual vows mean nothing to the outside world unless the soul experiences God's presence. Vallalar feels flawed and fears public ridicule if his efforts end in failure.

translit: uṉuḷḷam koṇṭēṟ karuḷāy eṉiliv ulakarpoyyām eṉuḷḷam koṇṭa kaḷavaṟi yātuniṉ ṟēṭaviṅkē niṉuḷḷam koḷvira tappayaṉ yātu nikaḻtteṉavē muṉuḷḷam koṇṭu moḻivarkaṇ ṭāyem mutalavaṉē.
translation: If you do not accept me in your heart and grant your grace, these worldly people, unaware of the deceit in my false heart, will step forward and say, "Tell us the fruit of the vows you held in your heart." See, they will boldly speak this way, O our Primal Lord.
commentary: Society often judges a spiritual life by its visible rewards. Vallalar admits his heart holds secret deceit that others cannot see, knowing they will gladly mock his outward religious vows if God remains silent.

translit: muntōkai koṇṭuniṉ taṇṇaruḷ vāriyiṉ mūḻkutaṟkiṅ kantō-eṉ tuṉpam tuṭaittaru ḷāyeṉil āṅkulakar vantō civavira tā-etu peṟṟaṉai vāytiṟa-eṉ ṟintōr tarucaṭai yāyviṭai yāyeṉṉai ēcuvarē.
translation: Alas, if you do not wipe away my sorrow and grant your grace so I can bathe in the ocean of your cool grace with supreme longing, the people of the world will come and demand, "O follower of Siva's vows, what did you gain? Open your mouth!" O Lord with the crescent moon in your matted hair, O rider of the bull, they will mock me.
commentary: The poem imagines the painful ridicule directed at someone who follows traditional religious practices but remains spiritually empty. Without the direct experience of divine grace, the outward signs of a devotee only invite the world's laughter.

translit: ācum paṭiyil akaṅkā ramumuṭai yāṉeṉṟeṇṇip pēcum paṭiyil eṉakkaru ḷāyeṉil pērulakōr ēcum paṭivarum poyvēṭaṉ eṉṟatai eṇṇi-eṇṇik kūcum paṭivaru mē-eṉcey kēṉeṉ kulateyvamē.
translation: If you see me as a flawed and arrogant person on this earth and refuse to grant me your grace, I will become known as a false ascetic facing the mockery of the vast world. Thinking about this constantly, I shrink in shame. What will I do, O deity of my lineage?
commentary: A spiritual life lived without inner transformation feels like pretending. Vallalar dreads being exposed as a false ascetic and shrinks in shame at the thought of the world discovering his lingering pride.

translit: aitaṭ ṭiṭumneñ cakattēṉ piḻaikaḷai āyntuveṟum poytaṭ ṭikaluṭai yēṟkuṉ karuṇai purintilaiyēl veytaṭṭi uṇṭa viratāniṉ nōṉpu viruttameṉṟē kaitaṭṭi veṇṇakai ceyvarkaṇ ṭāyaruṭ kaṟpakamē.
translation: If you examine the mistakes of my weak heart and refuse your compassion to me, a man filled with sheer falsehood and hostility, people will clap their hands and laugh mockingly, saying, "O ascetic who secretly feasted, your penance is useless!" See this, O wish-fulfilling tree of grace.
commentary: The deepest humiliation for a seeker is being exposed as a hypocrite. Vallalar fears performing public acts of penance while secretly indulging earthly desires, a failure that reduces the spiritual path to a joke.

sections.title: Lamenting the Failure to Receive Grace

note: Editor's note: a general poem (potu, பொது), not tied to one temple.
translit: naṉṟi oṉṟiya niṉṉaṭi yavarkkē nāṉum iṅkoru nāyaṭi yavaṉkāṇ kuṉṟiṉ oṉṟiya iṭarmika uṭaiyēṉ kuṟṟam nīkkumnal kuṇamilēṉ eṉiṉum eṉṟiṉ oṉṟiya civaparañ cuṭarē iṉpa vāriyē eṉṉuyirt tuṇaiyē oṉṟiṉ oṉṟiya uttamap poruḷē uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: I am a dog-like servant to your devotees who abound in goodness. My sorrows are huge like a mountain. Even though I lack the good qualities that eradicate faults, O Supreme Light of Siva that shines eternally! O ocean of bliss! O companion of my soul! O Supreme Reality united in the One! Who else claims me but You?
commentary: Placing himself at the very bottom, Vallalar calls himself a dog serving God's true devotees. Lacking the good qualities to fix his faults, and bearing huge sorrows, he appeals directly to the Supreme Light. He asks how anyone but God could take ownership of such a flawed soul.

translit: tītu ceytaṉaṉ ceykiṉṟēṉ ceyvēṉ tīya ṉēṉkoṭun tīkkuṇa iyalpē ētu ceytaṉa ṉēṉumeṉ taṉṉai ēṉṟu koḷvatem iṟaivaniṉ iyalpē ītu ceytaṉai eṉṉaiviṭ ṭulakil iṭarkoṇ ṭēṅkeṉa iyampiṭil aṭiyēṉ ōtu ceyvatoṉ ṟeṉṉuyirt tuṇaiyē uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: I did evil, I do evil, and I will do evil. I am wicked, and cruel, bad qualities form my nature. Whatever I have done, accepting me is your nature, my Lord. If you tell me to leave because of what I have done, leaving me to suffer and languish in the world, I have only one thing to say, O companion of my soul. Who else claims me but You?
commentary: Vallalar admits he has done wrong in the past, does it now, and will do it again. He contrasts his wicked nature with God's nature of pure acceptance. If God turns him away for his actions, he has nowhere else to go. His only defense is that he belongs to the divine.

translit: ceṉṟa nāḷiṉum celkiṉṟa nāḷil ciṟiya ṉēṉmikat tiyaṅkuṟu kiṉṟēṉ maṉṟa nāṉivaṇ ivvakai āṉāl vaḷḷa lēniṉai vaḻuttumā ṟetuvō eṉṟa ṉāliṉi āvatoṉ ṟilai-uṉ eṇṇam eppaṭi appaṭi icaika uṉṟa ṉālkaḷit tuvakaikoḷ kiṉṟēṉ uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: I, a lowly man, am bewildered even more today than in the days past. O Lord of the Hall! O Generous One! If I remain in this state here, how can I praise you? There is nothing more I can do. Let your will be done. I rejoice and delight only through You. Who else claims me but You?
commentary: With the confusion of worldly life growing worse, Vallalar admits he has reached the limit of his efforts. Calling out to the Lord of the Hall (the space of divine presence and cosmic dance), he surrenders his will. He finds joy trusting God to handle what he cannot.

translit: maiyal vāḻkkaiyil nāḷtoṟum aṭiyēṉ varunti neñcakam māḻkuva tellām aiya aiyavō kaṇṭiṭā tavarpōl aṭampi ṭippatuṉ aruḷiṉuk kaḻakō ceyya mēloṉṟum aṟintilaṉ civaṉē tillai maṉṟiṭait teṉmuka nōkki uyya vaittatāḷ nampiniṟ kiṉṟēṉ uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: Every day in this deluded life, this servant suffers and my heart faints. O Lord! Alas! Is it fitting for your grace to stubbornly ignore my suffering like someone who cannot see? O Siva, I know nothing else to do. I stand trusting the feet that saved me, looking south in the Hall of Thillai. Who else claims me but You?
commentary: The pain of worldly delusion breaks Vallalar's heart. He asks God if it is right to act blind and ignore this suffering. Having no other solution, he stands fixed in trust, looking south in the Hall of Thillai (Chidambaram), waiting for the grace that once saved him to act again.

translit: maṇṇa kacciṟu vāḻkkaiyiṉ poruṭṭāl varunti maṟṟataṉ vaṉmaikaḷ ellām eṇṇa eṇṇa-eṉ neñcakam pataippuṟ ṟēṅki ēṅkināṉ iḷaippuṟu kiṉṟēṉ aṇṇal niṉtiru aruṭṭuṇai aṭaintāl amaintu vāḻkuvaṉ aṭaivakai aṟiyēṉ uṇṇa nalamu taṉaiya-em perumāṉ uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: Suffering for the sake of this petty earthly life, my heart shudders the more I think of all its cruelties. I languish and grow weary. O Supreme Lord, if I reach the support of your holy grace, I will live in peace. Yet I do not know how to reach it. O my Lord, you are like sweet ambrosia to consume. Who else claims me but You?
commentary: The triviality of earthly survival fills Vallalar with dread and exhaustion. Knowing true peace comes only from divine grace, he confesses he does not know how to reach it. He compares God to life-giving nectar (ambrosia), asking to be claimed because he cannot make the journey alone.

translit: aṉṉai appaṉum nī-eṉa makiḻntē akaṅku ḷirntunāṉ ātarit tiruntēṉ eṉṉai ippaṭi iṭarkoḷa viṭuttāl eṉcey kēṉ itai yāroṭu pukalkēṉ poṉṉai ottaniṉ aṭittuṇai malaraip pōṟṟu vārkkunī purikuva tituvō uṉṉai eppaṭi āyiṉum maṟavēṉ uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: Rejoicing that you are my mother and father, my heart cooled and I sought your refuge. If you abandon me to suffer like this, what will I do? To whom will I tell this? Is this what you do to those who praise your twin flower-like feet that shine like gold? Whatever happens, I will never forget you. Who else claims me but You?
commentary: Questioning God's treatment of those who trust him, Vallalar approaches the divine as a child approaches its parents, finding comfort in that bond. Even feeling abandoned to suffering, he refuses to seek help anywhere else.

translit: nīlam iṭṭakaṇ maṭaviyar mayakkāl neñcam ōrvaḻi nāṉoru vaḻiyāy ñālam iṭṭa iv vāḻkkaiyil aṭiyēṉ naṭuṅki uḷḷakam naliyumeṉ taṉmai ālam iṭṭaruḷ kaḷattanī aṟintum aruḷa ḷittilai ākamaṟ ṟitaṉai ōlam iṭṭaḻu taraṟṟi-eṅ kuraippēṉ uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: Deluded by women with collyrium-lined eyes, my heart went one way and I went another. I tremble and wither within in this worldly life. You hold the poison in your graceful throat. Even knowing my nature, you have not granted your grace. Where can I weep, wail, and cry out about this? Who else claims me but You?
commentary: Worldly desires pull Vallalar in opposite directions, dividing mind from action. He reminds God of the ancient story where Lord Siva drank cosmic poison to save the universe, asking why such a merciful God ignores his current suffering. With nowhere else to turn, he brings his tears directly to the divine.

translit: koṭiya pāviyēṉ paṭumpari tāpam kuṟittuk kaṇṭumeṉ kuṟai-akaṟ ṟātu neṭiya kālamum tāḻttaṉai niṉatu neñcum vañcakam nērntatuṇ ṭēyō aṭiyar tantuyar kaṇṭiṭil tariyār aiyar eṉpareṉ aḷavaḵ tilaiyō oṭiya mātuyar nīkkiṭāy eṉṉil uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: You clearly see the suffering of this cruel sinner, yet you have not removed my flaws. You have delayed for a long time. Has your heart taken up deceit? People say the Lord cannot bear to see the sorrow of his devotees. Does that not apply to me? If you do not remove this crushing sorrow, who else claims me but You?
commentary: Vallalar challenges God's reputation for mercy. Since tradition says the divine cannot bear to see a devotee suffer, Vallalar asks if God is deceiving him by delaying help. This questioning comes from an intimacy where a devotee feels close enough to demand answers from his master.

translit: eṉeṉ ṟēḻaiyēṉ nāṇamviṭ ṭuraippēṉ iṟaiva niṉṟaṉai iṟaippoḻu tēṉum uṉeṉ ṟāleṉa turaimaṟut tetirāy ulaka māyaiyil tilakameṉ ṟuraikkum miṉeṉ ṟāliṭai maṭaviyar mayakkil vīḻnteṉ neñcakam āḻntuviṭ ṭataṉāl uṉaṉ peṉpateṉ ṉiṭattilai yēṉum uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: What can this poor wretch say after abandoning all shame? O Lord, if I tell my heart to think of you for even a fleeting moment, it refuses my word and opposes me. My heart has fallen and sunk into the delusion of women with lightning-like waists, those called the very pinnacle of worldly illusion. Because of this, there is no love for you within me. Even so, who else claims me but You?
commentary: Vallalar admits his mind rebels against him, refusing to focus on the divine for even a second. Swallowed by physical attraction and worldly illusions, he confesses he currently feels no love for God. Yet he still asks to be saved, relying on God's unchanging nature instead of his own merit.

translit: aṭiya ṉēṉmicai āṇṭava niṉakkōr aṉpi runtateṉ ṟakaṅkarit tiruntēṉ koṭiya ṉēṉpaṭum iṭarmuḻu taṟintum kūli yāḷaṉaip pōleṉai niṉaittē neṭiya ittuṇaip pōtumōr ciṟitum neñci raṅkilai cañcalat taṟivum oṭiya niṉṟaṉaṉ eṉceykēṉ civaṉē uṉai-a lāleṉai uṭaiyavar evarē.
translation: O Lord, I was proud in thinking you held some love for your servant. Though you fully know the troubles this cruel sinner suffers, you regard me as a mere hired laborer. For all this long time, your heart has not pitied me in the slightest. I stand here with my mind broken by sorrow. What will I do, O Lord Siva? Who else claims me but You?
commentary: Vallalar feels God is treating him with cold distance, like a master ignoring a hired laborer. His earlier pride in thinking he was specially loved has been shattered by this long silence. Standing with a broken mind, he repeats his core realization: he has no refuge but Lord Siva.

tamil: வளங்கிளர் சடையும் விளங்கிய இதழி மாலையும் மால்அயன் வழுத்தும்
குளங்கிளர் நுதலும் களங்கிளர் மணியும் குலவுதிண் புயமும்அம் புயத்தின்
தளங்கிளர் பதமும் இளங்கதிர் வடிவும் தழைக்கநீ இருத்தல்கண் டுவத்தல்
உளங்கிளர் அமுதே துளங்குநெஞ் சகனேன் உற்றரு ணையில்பெற அருளே.
translit: vaḷaṅkiḷar caṭaiyum viḷaṅkiya itaḻi mālaiyum mālayaṉ vaḻuttum kuḷaṅkiḷar nutalum kaḷaṅkiḷar maṇiyum kulavutiṇ puyamumam puyattiṉ taḷaṅkiḷar patamum iḷaṅkatir vaṭivum taḻaikkanī iruttalkaṇ ṭuvattal uḷaṅkiḷar amutē tuḷaṅkuneñ cakaṉēṉ uṟṟaru ṇaiyilpeṟa aruḷē.
translation: O nectar surging in the heart, grant your grace so that I, possessing a trembling heart, may reach Arunai and rejoice at the sight of your majestic presence. You sit there flourishing with fertile matted hair, a bright konrai flower garland, a radiant forehead praised by Vishnu and Brahma, a throat shining like a sapphire, strong rounded shoulders, feet like lotus petals, and a form like the morning sun.
commentary: Vallalar longs to see God's physical presence at the holy city of Arunai. He asks for the grace to stand before Lord Siva's majestic, radiant form—praised even by the creator and preserver gods—hoping it will finally calm his restless heart.

tamil: அன்பர்தம் மனத்தே இன்பமுற் றவைகள் அளித்தவர் களித்திடப் புரியும்
பொன்பொலி மேனிக் கருணையங் கடலே பொய்யனேன் பொய்மைகண் டின்னும்
துன்பமுற் றலையச் செய்திடேல் அருணைத் தொல்நக ரிடத்துன தெழில்கண்
டென்புளம் உருகத் துதித்திடல் வேண்டும் இவ்வரம் எனக்கிவண் அருளே.
translit: aṉpartam maṉattē iṉpamuṟ ṟavaikaḷ aḷittavar kaḷittiṭap puriyum poṉpoli mēṉik karuṇaiyaṅ kaṭalē poyyaṉēṉ poymaikaṇ ṭiṉṉum tuṉpamuṟ ṟalaiyac ceytiṭēl aruṇait tolnaka riṭattuṉa teḻilkaṇ ṭeṉpuḷam urukat tutittiṭal vēṇṭum ivvaram eṉakkivaṇ aruḷē.
translation: O beautiful ocean of compassion with a golden body, you grant joyous things to the minds of your devotees and make them rejoice. I am a false one. Do not look at my falsehood and make me wander in suffering anymore. I must praise you with my very bones and heart melting as I behold your beauty in the ancient city of Arunai. Grant me this boon right here.
commentary: God is an ocean of compassion who brings pure joy to the minds of true devotees. Vallalar contrasts this divine perfection with his own sense of falsehood and inner turmoil. He asks God to overlook his flaws and end his wandering. His only request is the chance to stand in the ancient city of Arunai, praising the Lord with a melting heart.

tamil: பூத்திடும் அவனும் காத்திடு பவனும் புள்விலங் குருக்கொடு நேடி
ஏத்திடும் முடியும் கூத்திடும் அடியும் இன்னமும் காண்கிலர் என்றும்
கோத்திடும் அடியர் மாலையின் அளவில் குலவினை என்றுநல் லோர்கள்
சாற்றிடும் அதுகேட் டுவந்தனன் நினது சந்நிதி உறஎனக் கருளே.
translit: pūttiṭum avaṉum kāttiṭu pavaṉum puḷvilaṅ kurukkoṭu nēṭi ēttiṭum muṭiyum kūttiṭum aṭiyum iṉṉamum kāṇkilar eṉṟum kōttiṭum aṭiyar mālaiyiṉ aḷavil kulaviṉai eṉṟunal lōrkaḷ cāṟṟiṭum atukēṭ ṭuvantaṉaṉ niṉatu canniti uṟa-eṉak karuḷē.
translation: The creator and the protector took the forms of a bird and a beast to search for your head and your dancing feet. They praise you, yet they still cannot see them. The good people declare that you joyfully abide within the garland of devotees strung together forever. Hearing this, I rejoiced. Grant me the grace to reach your sacred presence.
commentary: Vallalar recalls an ancient story where the creator and protector gods took the forms of a bird and a boar to find the top and bottom of a massive pillar of divine light. They failed to measure God's full extent. Yet, the wise say God happily makes a home among humble devotees. This gives Vallalar immense hope to join that sacred presence.

tamil: அருள்பழுத் தோங்கும் ஆனந்தத் தருவே அற்புத அமலநித் தியமே
தெருள்பழுத் தோங்கும் சித்தர்தம் உரிமைச் செல்வமே அருணையந் தேவே
இருள்பழுத் தோங்கும் நெஞ்சினேன் எனினும் என்பிழை பொறுத்துநின் கோயில்
translit: aruḷpaḻut tōṅkum āṉantat taruvē aṟputa amalanit tiyamē teruḷpaḻut tōṅkum cittartam urimaic celvamē aruṇaiyan tēvē iruḷpaḻut tōṅkum neñciṉēṉ eṉiṉum eṉpiḻai poṟuttuniṉ kōyil poruḷpaḻuttōṅkum canniti muṉṉarppōntuṉaip pōṟṟumāṟaruḷē.
translation: O tree of bliss ripening with grace. O wonderful, pure, eternal one. O rightful wealth of the Siddhars who flourish with mature clarity. O beautiful Lord of Arunai. Even though I possess a heart overgrown with darkness, forgive my faults. Grant me the grace to stand before the rich and sacred presence of your temple and praise you.
commentary: God is the ultimate treasure for the Siddhars (perfected beings who have attained spiritual clarity). Feeling his own heart is thick with darkness, Vallalar asks for forgiveness. He seeks the simple grace of standing before the temple's rich presence to offer his praise.

tamil: மறையும் அம் மறையின் வாய்மையும் ஆகி மன்னிய வள்ளலே மலர்மேல்
இறையும்மா தவனும் இறையும்இன் னவன்என் றெய்திடா இறைவனே அடியேன்
பொறையும்நன் னிறையும் அறிவும்நற் செறிவும் பொருந்திடாப் பொய்யனேன் எனினும்
அறையும்நற் புகழ்சேர் அருணையை விழைந்தேன் அங்கெனை அடைகுவித் தருளே.
translit: maṟaiyum am maṟaiyiṉ vāymaiyum āki maṉṉiya vaḷḷalē malarmēl iṟaiyummā tavaṉum iṟaiyumiṉ ṉavaṉeṉ ṟeytiṭā iṟaivaṉē aṭiyēṉ poṟaiyumnaṉ ṉiṟaiyum aṟivumnaṟ ceṟivum poruntiṭāp poyyaṉēṉ eṉiṉum aṟaiyumnaṟ pukaḻcēr aruṇaiyai viḻaintēṉ aṅkeṉai aṭaikuvit taruḷē.
translation: O eternal benefactor, you became the scriptures and the truth of those scriptures. O Lord, the god on the lotus and the great ascetic cannot reach you and measure your greatness. I am a false one lacking patience, complete perfection, knowledge, and good composure. Even so, I long for Arunai of resounding good fame. Grant me your grace and bring me to that place.
commentary: God is both the sacred scriptures and the living truth they contain. Vallalar admits his personal shortcomings, yet his longing for Arunai remains powerful. He asks the ultimate benefactor to guide him safely to that sacred destination.

tamil: தேடுவார் தேடும் செல்வமே சிவமே திருஅரு ணாபுரித் தேவே
ஏடுவார் இதழிக் கண்ணிஎங் கோவே எந்தையே எம்பெரு மானே
பாடுவார்க் களிக்கும் பரம்பரப் பொருளே பாவியேன் பொய்யெலாம் பொறுத்து
நாடுவார் புகழும் நின்திருக் கோயில் நண்ணுமா எனக்கிவண் அருளே.
translit: tēṭuvār tēṭum celvamē civamē tiru-aru ṇāpurit tēvē ēṭuvār itaḻik kaṇṇi-eṅ kōvē entaiyē emperu māṉē pāṭuvārk kaḷikkum paramparap poruḷē pāviyēṉ poyyelām poṟuttu nāṭuvār pukaḻum niṉtiruk kōyil naṇṇumā eṉakkivaṇ aruḷē.
translation: O wealth sought by seekers! O Siva! O Lord of holy Arunapuri! O our King wearing a garland of blooming cassia flowers! O my Father! O my Lord! O Supreme Reality who grants to those who sing! Forgiving all the lies of this sinner, grant me the grace to reach your holy temple praised by those who seek you.
commentary: The highest spiritual wealth belongs to those who seek the divine with devotion and song. Standing in God's presence requires a cleansing of past falsehoods. Vallalar trusts in God's nature as a forgiving father, asking only for the grace to reach the holy temple.

tamil: உலகுயிர் தொறும்நின் றூட்டுவித் தாட்டும் ஒருவனே உத்தம னேநின்
இலகுமுக் கண்ணும் காளகண் டமும்மெய் இலங்குவெண்ணீற்றணி எழிலும்
திலகஒள் நுதல்உண் ணாமுலை உமையாள் சேரிடப் பாலுங்கண் டடியேன்
கலகஐம் புலன்செய் துயரமும் மற்றைக் கலக்கமும் நீக்குமா அருளே.
translit: ulakuyir toṟumniṉ ṟūṭṭuvit tāṭṭum oruvaṉē uttama ṉēniṉ ilakumuk kaṇṇum kāḷakaṇ ṭamummey ilaṅkuveṇṇīṟṟaṇi eḻilum tilaka-oḷ nutaluṇ ṇāmulai umaiyāḷ cēriṭap pāluṅkaṇ ṭaṭiyēṉ kalaka-aim pulaṉcey tuyaramum maṟṟaik kalakkamum nīkkumā aruḷē.
translation: O Peerless One who abides in every soul in the world, making them experience life and directing them! O Supreme One! Grant me the grace to see your shining three eyes, your dark throat, the beauty of the bright white ash adorning your body, and the Goddess with a radiant forehead wearing a tilaka and unweaned breasts residing on your left side. Through this sight, remove the sorrow and confusion caused by my tumultuous five senses.
commentary: God is the inner engine of life, dwelling in every soul and directing its path. Vallalar longs for a direct vision of Siva alongside the Goddess, who wears a tilaka (a traditional auspicious mark on the forehead). Witnessing this divine reality is the only cure for the endless agitation and sorrow caused by the five senses.

tamil: அருட்பெருங் கடலே ஆனந்த நறவே அடிநடு அந்தமுங் கடந்த
தெருட்பெரு மலையே திருஅணா மலையில் திகழ்சுயஞ் சோதியே சிவனே
மருட்பெருங் கடலின் மயங்குகின் றேன்என் மயக்கெலாம் ஒழிந்துவன் பிறவி
இருட்பெருங் கடல்விட் டேறநின் கோயிற் கெளியனேன் வரவரம் அருளே.
translit: aruṭperuṅ kaṭalē āṉanta naṟavē aṭinaṭu antamuṅ kaṭanta teruṭperu malaiyē tiru-aṇā malaiyil tikaḻcuyañ cōtiyē civaṉē maruṭperuṅ kaṭaliṉ mayaṅkukiṉ ṟēṉeṉ mayakkelām oḻintuvaṉ piṟavi iruṭperuṅ kaṭalviṭ ṭēṟaniṉ kōyiṟ keḷiyaṉēṉ varavaram aruḷē.
translation: O great ocean of grace! O honey of bliss! O great mountain of wisdom transcending beginning, middle, and end! O self-luminous Jothi shining in holy Tiruvannamalai! O Siva! I am confused in the great ocean of delusion. Let all my confusion cease, and to cross and escape the great dark ocean of harsh birth, grant this poor one the boon to come to your temple.
commentary: God is a self-luminous light (Jothi) and a mountain of wisdom without beginning or end. Human life often feels like a dark, confusing ocean of harsh births and delusions. Divine grace is the only rescue from this turbulent water, pulling the soul safely to the shores of spiritual clarity.

tamil: கருணையங் கடலே கண்கள்மூன் றுடைய கடவுளே கமலன்மால் அறியா
அருணைஎங் கோவே பரசிவா னந்த அமுதமே அற்புத நிலையே
இருள்நிலம் புகுதா தெனைஎடுத் தாண்ட இன்பமே அன்பர்தம் அன்பே
பொருள்நலம் பெறநின் சந்நிதிக் கெளியேன் போந்துனைப் போற்றும்வா றருளே.
translit: karuṇaiyaṅ kaṭalē kaṇkaḷmūṉ ṟuṭaiya kaṭavuḷē kamalaṉmāl aṟiyā aruṇai-eṅ kōvē paracivā ṉanta amutamē aṟputa nilaiyē iruḷnilam pukutā teṉai-eṭut tāṇṭa iṉpamē aṉpartam aṉpē poruḷnalam peṟaniṉ cannitik keḷiyēṉ pōntuṉaip pōṟṟumvā ṟaruḷē.
translation: O beautiful ocean of compassion! O God with three eyes! O our King of Arunai, unknown to Brahma and Vishnu! O nectar of supreme Siva-bliss! O wondrous state! O Bliss who uplifted and ruled me so I do not enter the land of darkness! O love of your devotees! Grant grace so that I, a poor one, may come to your presence to attain true wealth and praise you.
commentary: Divine compassion lifts the soul completely out of ignorance and darkness. In traditional poetry, Siva is often praised as the ultimate reality whose true nature remains hidden even from major deities like Brahma and Vishnu. The greatest wealth a person can achieve is simply standing in this divine presence and experiencing the pure nectar of spiritual bliss.

tamil: ஏதுசெய் திடினும் பொறுத்தருள் புரியும் என்உயிர்க் கொருபெருந் துணையே
தீதுசெய் மனத்தார் தம்முடன் சேராச் செயல்எனக் களித்தஎன் தேவே
வாதுசெய் புலனால் வருந்தல்செய் கின்றேன் வருந்துறா வண்ணம்எற் கருளித்
தாதுசெய் பவன்ஏத் தருணையங் கோயில் சந்நிதிக் கியான்வர அருளே.
translit: ētucey tiṭiṉum poṟuttaruḷ puriyum eṉuyirk koruperun tuṇaiyē tītucey maṉattār tammuṭaṉ cērāc ceyaleṉak kaḷitta-eṉ tēvē vātucey pulaṉāl varuntalcey kiṉṟēṉ varuntuṟā vaṇṇameṟ karuḷit tātucey pavaṉēt taruṇaiyaṅ kōyil cannitik kiyāṉvara aruḷē.
translation: O one great companion to my soul who forgives and grants grace whatever I do! My God who gave me the resolve not to associate with those of evil minds! I suffer because of the troublesome senses. Grant me grace so I do not suffer, and allow me to come to your presence in the beautiful temple of Arunai praised by Brahma.
commentary: God is the soul's intimate companion, offering forgiveness no matter what mistakes a person makes. This divine friendship provides the inner strength to avoid harmful company and cruel intentions. When the physical senses cause pain and distraction, taking refuge in grace restores peace to the mind.

sections.title: The Decad of the Divine Offering

note: Editor's note: sung at Pullirukkuvelur (puḷḷirukkuvēḷūr, புள்ளிருக்குவேளூர்), today Vaitheeswaran Koil, where Siva is worshipped as the divine physician.
translit: caratat tālaṉpar cārntiṭum niṉtiru viratat tālaṉṟi vēṟoṉṟil tīrumō paratat tāṇṭava ṉēpari tippuri varatat tāṇṭava ṉē-ivva ruttamē.
translation: O Lord who performs the cosmic dance! O dancing Lord who grants boons in Parithippuri! Will this suffering end by anything other than your divine vow, which devotees approach with truth?
commentary: Parithippuri is Vaitheeswaran Koil. Human suffering cannot be cured by earthly means; it is resolved only through God's vow to protect those who approach Him with a truthful heart.

translit: vēta ṉēṉumvi lakkutaṟ pālaṉō tīta ṉēṉtuyar tīrkkumva yittiya nāta ṉē-uṉṟaṉ nallaruḷ illaiyēl nōtal nērumvaṉ nōyilci ṟitumē.
translation: O Vaithiyanatha who ends the sorrow of this wicked one! If your good grace is absent, is even Brahma capable of removing even a slight part of this painful and harsh disease?
commentary: Vaithiyanatha is the divine physician. Without this healing grace from the Supreme, no other deity, not even Brahma the creator, has the power to relieve even a fraction of life's afflictions.

translit: arunti ṉālaṉpa kaṅkuḷir āṉanta virunti ṉālmakiḻ vittaruḷ aṇṇalē varunti nāṭava rumpiṇi niṉaruḷ marunti ṉālaṉṟi maṟṟoṉṟil tīrumō.
translation: O Lord who delights devotees with a feast of bliss that cools their hearts when they consume it! Will this afflicting disease that seeks us out be cured by anything other than the medicine of your grace?
commentary: Worldly suffering is contrasted with the joy God provides. The deep-seated disease of worldly affliction can only be cured by the medicine of divine grace.

translit: mālum nāṉkuva taṉaṉum māmaṟai nālum nāṭaru nampara ṉē-eva rālum nīkka-a ritivva ruttamniṉ ēlum nallaruḷ iṉṟeṉil caṟṟumē.
translation: O Supreme Lord whom Vishnu, the four-faced Brahma, and the four great Vedas seek but cannot comprehend! Without your fitting good grace, it is impossible for anyone to remove even a fraction of this suffering.
commentary: The Supreme Lord is beyond the comprehension of great gods like Vishnu and Brahma, and even the sacred scriptures. Because of this supremacy, only His direct grace has the power to lift away our suffering.

translit: tēvar āyiṉum tēvarva ṇaṅkumōr mūvar āyiṉum mukkaṇa niṉaruḷ mēvu ṟātuvi lakkiṭaṟ pālarō ōvu ṟāta-u ṭaṟpiṇi taṉṉaiyē.
translation: O three-eyed Lord! Without the presence of your grace, are even the celestials, or the unique Trinity worshipped by the celestials, capable of dispelling this unceasing disease of the body?
commentary: The absolute necessity of God's grace becomes clear when looking at the highest beings in traditional religion. Neither the celestial beings nor the great Trinity of gods can heal the unceasing ailments of life unless the Supreme Lord's grace is present.

translit: vaiya nāyaka vāṉavar nāyaka taiyal nāyaki cārntiṭum nāyaka uyya niṉṉaruḷ oṉṟuva tillaiyēl veyya nōykaḷvi lakuva tillaiyē.
translation: Lord of the earth! Lord of the celestials! Lord embraced by the beautiful Goddess! If Your grace does not unite with me to save me, these cruel diseases will not depart.
commentary: God is the ruler of all realms, from the physical earth to the celestial heavens. The core message is that human effort alone cannot cure deep suffering. Only a direct union with divine grace can drive cruel diseases away.

translit: kallai villilka ṇittaruḷ ceytatōr ellai iṉṟi-e ḻumiṉpa veḷḷamē illai illainiṉ iṉṉaruḷ illaiyēl tollai nōyiṉto ṭakkatu nīṅkalē.
translation: You who graciously made a bow of the great mountain! O boundless rising flood of bliss! No, no, if Your sweet grace is absent, the grip of ancient disease will never release me.
commentary: The mountain bow refers to the traditional story of Siva using Mount Meru as a weapon. The divine flood of bliss contrasts with the ancient, deeply rooted diseases of the human condition, which only grace can wash away.

translit: nīti mātavar neñciṭai niṉṟoḷir cōti yēmutto ḻiluṭai mūvarkkum āti yēniṉa ruḷ oṉṟum illaiyēl vāti yāniṟkum vaṉpiṇi yāvumē.
translation: O Jothi shining in the hearts of great and righteous sages! O primal source of the three gods who perform the three cosmic functions! If Your grace is absent, all these severe diseases will endlessly torment me.
commentary: The divine is the ultimate Jothi (light) shining within pure minds. As the original source of the three deities who create, sustain, and destroy the universe, only His grace shields against physical and spiritual torment.

translit: pattar nittampa yilpari tippuri utta mapporu ḷē-uṉa ruḷtaṉaip pettam aṟṟiṭap peṟṟavark kallatu nittam uṟṟane ṭumpiṇi nīṅkumō.
translation: O supreme reality in Parithippuri where devotees gather daily! Will this enduring daily disease ever depart for anyone except those who have received Your grace and severed all bonds?
commentary: True healing is tied directly to spiritual liberation. Enduring suffering only leaves those who have received divine grace and severed the worldly attachments that bind the soul.

translit: caiva ciṟkuṇar tammuḷam maṉṉiya teyva taṟpara ṉēciva ṉē-iṅku uyva taṟkuṉa ruḷoṉṟum illaiyēl naiva taṟkuna ṇukuva nōykaḷē.
translation: O divine Supreme abiding in the hearts of virtuous Saivites! O Siva! If Your grace is absent for my salvation here, diseases will approach and make me waste away.
commentary: God dwells directly in the hearts of pure devotees. Without this saving divine presence, human life is reduced to a gradual, unavoidable wasting away from illness.

note: Editor's note: sung at Otriyur and at Thillai (Chidambaram) (tiruvoṟṟiyūrum tiruttillaiyum, திருவொற்றியூரும் திருத்தில்லையும்).
translit: appār malarccaṭai āramu tē-eṉ aruṭṭuṇaiyē tuppār pavaḷa maṇikkuṉṟa mēciṟ cukakkaṭalē veppār tarutuya rālmeli kiṉṟaṉaṉ veṟṟaṭiyēṉ ippār taṉileṉṉai appā-añ cēleṉa ēṉṟukoḷḷē.
translation: O rare nectar with flower-entwined matted hair bearing the river! My companion of grace! O hill of pure coral gems! O ocean of supreme bliss! I, this empty devotee, languish from the heat of sorrow. O father, accept me in this world and tell me to fear not.
commentary: Vallalar begs God for shelter from the suffering of worldly life, waiting for reassurance not to fear. The river carried in matted hair is a traditional reference to Siva, invoked here as an ocean of supreme bliss.

translit: ēṉṟukoḷ vāṉnama tiṉṉuyir pōlmukkaṇ entai-eṉṟē cāṉṟukoḷ vāyniṉai nampiniṉ ṟēṉit tami-aṭiyēṉ māṉṟukoḷ vāṉvarum tuṉpaṅkaḷ nīkka matittilaiyēl ñāṉṟukoḷ vēṉaṉṟi yātucey vēṉinta nāṉilattē.
translation: Believing my three-eyed father will accept me like his own sweet life, I stood trusting you completely. I am a lonely devotee. If you do not resolve to remove the approaching sorrows that bewilder me, I will hang myself. What else can I do in this vast world?
commentary: Vallalar's desperation is absolute: he threatens to take his own life if God does not intervene. This reveals his total dependence on divine grace. Without his three-eyed father to remove his sorrows, he is isolated with no other refuge.

translit: nilattē ciṟuvarcey kuṟṟaṅkaḷ yāvum niṉaittaṟavōr calattē uḷattai viṭāreṉpar ātaliṉ tātaiyeṉṟē kulattēvar pōṟṟum kuṇakkuṉṟa mē-eṅ kulateyvamē pulattē iḻitakai yēṉpiḻai yāvum poṟuttaruḷē.
translation: They say the righteous do not let their hearts succumb to anger when they consider all the faults committed by little children in this world. Therefore I call you father. O hill of virtues praised by the celestial gods! O our family deity! Please forgive all the errors of this lowly one caught in the senses.
commentary: Vallalar asks for forgiveness by comparing God to an adult dealing with a child. Just as the righteous do not hold onto anger when children make mistakes, he trusts God will overlook his earthly faults. Caught in the physical senses, he appeals to God's boundless patience.

translit: aruḷār amutap peruṅkaṭa lētillai ampalattil poruḷār naṭampuri puṇṇiya ṉēniṉaip pōṟṟukilēṉ iruḷār maṉattiṉ iṭaruḻan tēṉiṉi yātuceykēṉ maruḷār malakkuṭil māyntiṭil uṉaruḷ vāyppataṟkē.
translation: O great ocean of graceful nectar! O holy one performing the meaningful dance in the hall of Thillai! I do not praise you. I suffer the afflictions of a dark heart. What will I do now? When this deluded hut of impurities perishes, how will I attain your grace?
commentary: Fear of dying before achieving spiritual freedom haunts Vallalar. Describing the physical body as a fragile hut of impurities destined to perish, he worries his distracted mind keeps him from praising the divine dance at Thillai, the sacred shrine of Chidambaram. He remains anxious about securing grace before his time runs out.

translit: vāyāra niṉpoṉ malarttāḷ tuṇaiyē vaḻuttukilēṉ ōyā iṭaruḻan tuḷnali kiṉṟaṉaṉ ōkeṭuvēṉ pēyāyp piṟantilaṉ pēyumov vēṉpulaip pēṟuvakkum nāyāyp piṟantilaṉ nāykkum kaṭaippaṭṭa nāṉiṅṅaṉē.
translation: I do not praise your golden flower-feet with a full voice. I suffer ceaseless afflictions and wither within. Alas, I am ruined. I was not born as a demon, yet I do not even equal a demon. I was not born as a dog that rejoices in foul meat, yet here I am, worse than a dog.
commentary: Vallalar uses severe self-criticism to express his spiritual inadequacy. Feeling he has fallen lower than demons or scavenging dogs, he employs this traditional self-deprecation to strip away all personal pride and demonstrate an absolute need for divine mercy.

translit: nāṉceyta kuṟṟaṅkaḷ ellām poṟuttuniṉ nallaruḷnī tāṉcey taṉai-eṉil aiyāmuk kaṭperuñ cāmi-avaṟ kēṉcey taṉai-eṉa niṟṟaṭup pārilai eṉaracē vāṉceyta naṉṟiyai yārtaṭut tārinta vaiyakattē.
translation: O Lord, great three-eyed God. My King. If you forgive all my faults and bestow your good grace upon me, no one will stand in your way and ask, "Why did you grant this to him?" Who in this world has ever stopped the goodness bestowed by the sky?
commentary: God is absolutely free to forgive faults and grant grace. Vallalar asks the Divine to choose to save him, since no one can question God's choices. He compares this freedom to the sky pouring rain: no earthly power can stop the weather, and no one can stop God from showing mercy.

translit: vaiyakat tē-iṭar mākkaṭal mūḻki varuntukiṉṟa poyyakat tēṉaip purantaru ḷāmal puṟampoḻittāl naiyakat tēṉetu ceyvēṉan tō-uḷ nalikuvaṉkāṇ meyyakat tēniṉ ṟoḷirtarum ñāṉa viricuṭarē.
translation: O vast flame of wisdom shining within the truth. I possess a false heart and suffer, drowning in the great ocean of sorrow in this world. If you cast me aside without protecting and blessing me, what will I do with my broken heart? Alas, see how I suffer within.
commentary: Without divine protection, the suffering soul has nowhere to turn. Drowning in worldly sorrow, Vallalar cries out to the vast flame of wisdom. Casting him aside would leave him destroyed. He begs the Divine to look directly at his inner pain and offer shelter.

translit: virituya rāltaṭu māṟukiṉ ṟēṉinta vevviṉaiyēṉ perituya rāniṉṟa nallōr aṭaiyumniṉ pēraruḷtāṉ aritukaṇ ṭāyaṭai vēṉeṉal āyiṉum aiyamaṇip purituvar vārcaṭai yāynī uvappil puriyiluṇṭē.
translation: I falter in vast sorrow, burdened by cruel karma. Your great grace, attained by highly exalted and virtuous people, is truly rare. Though I say I will attain it, O Lord with beautiful long matted hair like red coral, it is possible only if you gladly bestow it.
commentary: Divine grace cannot be earned or demanded. Vallalar acknowledges this grace is rare, typically reserved for the virtuous. Suffering under his cruel karma (the accumulated effects of past deeds), he admits he cannot reach God through his own effort. His only hope is that God decides to bestow it out of gladness.

translit: uṇṭō-eṉ pōltuya rālalai kiṉṟavar uttamanī kaṇṭōr ciṟitum iraṅkuki lāyik kaṭaiyavaṉēṉ paṇṭōr tuṇai-aṟi yēṉniṉṉai yaṉṟiniṟ paṟṟiniṉṟēṉ eṇṭōḷ maṇimiṭaṟ ṟentāy karuṇai iruṅkaṭalē.
translation: Is there anyone who wanders in sorrow like me? O Supreme One, seeing this, you show no pity at all. I am the lowest of the low. I know no companion but you since ancient times. I hold onto you alone. O my Father with eight shoulders and a sapphire-hued throat. O vast ocean of compassion.
commentary: True devotion allows the worshipper to question God's apparent silence. Feeling abandoned, Vallalar wonders how an ocean of compassion can look at his sorrow and feel no pity. Though the lowest of the low, he has clung to this single divine companion since ancient times. He invokes Siva's blue throat—stained from swallowing the world's poison—reminding God of his historic role as a savior.

translit: kaṭalē aṉaiya tuyarmikai yāluṭ kalaṅkumeṉṉai viṭalē aruḷaṉ ṟeṭuttāḷal vēṇṭumeṉ viṇṇappamī taṭalē ṟuvanta aruṭkaṭa lē-aṇi ampalattuḷ uṭalē maruvum uyirpōl niṟai-oṟṟi yūrappaṉē.
translation: O Lord of Otriyur, who fills the beautiful hall just as life pervades the body. O ocean of grace who gladly rides the mighty bull. It is not the way of grace to abandon me while I am troubled within by sorrow as vast as the sea. You must uplift and claim me. This is my petition.
commentary: Leaving a suffering soul behind defies the nature of divine grace. Vallalar submits a formal petition to be uplifted from his sea of sorrow. He compares God's presence in the temple hall to the soul filling a physical body. Since God is the very life of the world, the Divine must act on its compassionate nature and claim him.

translit: vēkamuṟu neñca melivum eḷiyēṉṟaṉ tēka melivum terintum iraṅkāyēl māka natiyum matiyum vaḷarcaṭai-em ēka iṉimaṟ ṟeṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: Our One Lord with growing matted hair bearing the celestial river and the moon. Even knowing the fatigue of my agitated heart and the frailty of my poor body, if you do not show mercy, who else will pity me now?
commentary: The image of the Lord wearing the celestial river and the moon shows his vast, cosmic nature. Yet Vallalar approaches him with personal exhaustion. If the supreme source of life ignores his worn-out body and troubled mind, he has nowhere else to turn.

translit: kaḷḷa maṉattuk kaṭaiyōrpāl nāṇuṟumeṉ uḷḷa melivum uṭalmelivum kaṇṭiruntum eḷḷiṉ aḷavum iraṅki aruḷāyēl eḷḷum ulakil eṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: Even seeing the frailty of my body and the shrinking of my heart, which feels ashamed to approach the lowest men of deceitful minds, if you do not grant mercy even the size of a sesame seed, who else will pity me in this mocking world?
commentary: Worldly survival often demands begging from deceitful people, a prospect that fills Vallalar with shame. He asks the divine for the smallest measure of grace, because without it he remains unprotected in a cynical world.

translit: poṉṉai vaḷarppāraip pōṟṟāmal emperumāṉ uṉṉaimatit tuṉṉuṟumeṉ uḷḷam aṟintiruntum aṉṉaiyiṉum cāla aruḷvōy aruḷāyēl eṉṉai mukampārt teṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: My Lord, even knowing my heart that respects and contemplates only you without praising those who hoard gold, if you, who are more gracious than a mother, do not grant me grace, who will look at my face and pity me?
commentary: Relying on maternal divine love, Vallalar chooses to focus on God rather than wasting breath flattering wealthy people who hoard gold.

translit: tuṉṉuṭaiya viyākkiramat tōluṭaiyāṉ tāṉirukkap poṉṉuṭaiyār pakkam pukuvāṉēṉ eṉṟiruppēṉ taṉṉuṭaiya tuṉpam tavirttiṅ karuḷāyēl eṉṉuṭaiyāy maṟṟiṅ keṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: I tell myself there is no need to seek out those who possess gold when the Lord wearing the stitched tiger skin is here. My master, if you do not remove my sorrow and grant me grace here, who else will pity me?
commentary: The stitched tiger skin represents detachment from worldly wealth and status. Vallalar finds comfort in this, realizing he has no need to chase rich patrons when he can seek refuge with a master who values nothing material.

translit: vaṉkaṇṇar tammai matiyātuṉ poṉṉaṭiyiṉ taṉkaṇ aṭiyēṉtaṉ cañcalavaṉ neñcakattiṉ puṉkaṇ uḻalvaip pukalkiṉṟēṉ kāttilaiyēl eṉkaṇ aṉaiyāy eṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: Disregarding the hard-hearted ones, I lay the miserable suffering of my restless and stubborn heart at your golden feet. O Lord who are like my own eyes, if you do not protect me, who will pity me?
commentary: Calling the Lord his own eyes shows how Vallalar relies on the divine presence for survival and clarity. He ignores the hard-hearted people around him, choosing instead to bring the stubborn struggles of his mind directly to the feet of God.

translit: tōṉṟuvatum māyvatumām cūḻcciyiṭaip paṭṭalaintu māṉṟukoḷum tēvar marapai matiyāmē cāṉṟukoḷum niṉṉaic caraṇaṭaintēṉ nāyēṉai ēṉṟukoḷāy eṉṉil eṉakkār iraṅkuvarē.
translation: Disregarding the lineage of gods who wander bewildered, caught in the snare of appearing and vanishing, I took refuge in you, the perfect Lord. If you do not accept me, a dog, who else will show me mercy?
commentary: Vallalar distinguishes between the absolute divine and traditional gods of mythology. These lesser gods are bound by the same cycle of birth and death that traps humans.
