commentary: When grace opens this space to a true devotee, the ultimate truth becomes as obvious as a gooseberry in the palm of the hand. This clarity washes away fear and the darkness of ignorance.

translit: petta muñcatā mutti yumperum pēta māyatōr pōta vātamum cutta munteṟā vitta muntarum corūpa iṉpamē tuykkum vāḻkkaiyum nitta munterin tuṟṟa yōkartam nimala mākimeyn niṟaivu koṇṭaciṟ citta muñcelāp parama rāciyam civaci tamparam civaci tamparam.
translation: There is bondage, eternal liberation, and philosophical debate full of great divisions. There is purity, unceasing wealth, and the life of enjoying the bliss of one's true nature. Yet this is the supreme secret beyond the reach of even the pure consciousness of the flawless yogis who have realized the eternal and attained true fulfillment. It is Siva Chidambaram, Siva Chidambaram.
commentary: Religious philosophy is full of endless debates over bondage and liberation, purity and spiritual wealth. The supreme secret of Chidambaram rests far above these divided arguments, remaining entirely beyond the reach of even the most accomplished yogis.

sections.title: The Holy Decad on the Mother

translit: ulakiṉuyir vakai-uvakai yuṟa-iṉiya aruḷamutam utavumā ṉanta civaiyē uvamaicola ariya-oru periyaciva neṟitaṉai uṇarttupē riṉpa nitiyē ilakupara aparanilai icaiyumava ravarparuvam iyaluṟa uḷaṅkoḷ paraiyē irumaineṟi orumaiyuṟa arumaipeṟu perumaitaṉai īnteṉai aḷitta aṟivē kalakamuṟu cakacamala iruḷakala veḷiyāṉa kāṭciyē karuṇai niṟaivē kaṭakaraṭa vimalakaya muka-amutum aṟumukak kana-amutum utavu kaṭalē alakilvaḷam niṟaiyumoru tillaiyam patimēvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: O blissful Goddess Sivai who grants the sweet nectar of grace so all lifeforms in the world may rejoice! O treasure of supreme bliss who reveals the great path of Siva, which defies all comparison! O supreme Goddess Parai who holds in your heart the maturity of each being as they attain the shining higher and lower states! O supreme intelligence who gave me the rare greatness where the dual paths become one, and thus saved me! O open vision that dispels the darkness of turbulent inherent impurity! O fullness of compassion! O ocean who brought forth the nectar-like pure elephant-faced Lord and the nectar-like six-faced Lord! O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, which brims with infinite wealth! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: Vallalar praises the Divine Mother, Sivai or Umai, as the source of all life and grace. As the feminine aspect of the divine, she births the universe and guides souls toward maturity. He credits her with the vision that cleared his inherent impurities, uniting the world's dualities into a single spiritual path.

translit: kaṟpavai-e lāṅkaṟṟuḷ uṇarpavai-e lāmaṉak karicaṟa uṇarntu kēṭṭuk kāṇpavai-e lāṅkaṇṭu ceypavai-e lāñceytu karuneṟi akaṉṟa periyōr poṟpavai-e lāñceṉṟu pukalpavai-e lāṅkoṇṭu puripavai elāmpu rintuṉ pukaḻavai-e lāmpukaḻn tuṟumavai-e lāmuṟum pōtavai elāma ruḷuvāy niṟpavai-e lāmniṟpa acaipavai-e lāmacaiya niṟaipavai elāñcey nilaiyē niṉaipavai-e lāmnekiḻa neṟi-avai-e lāmōṅkum nittiyā ṉanta vaṭivē aṟpuṭaiya aṭiyarpukaḻ tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: The great ones learn all there is to learn, inwardly realize all there is to realize without mental blemish, listen, see all there is to see, do all there is to do, and transcend the cycle of birth. As they visit all beautiful places, accept all teachings, perform all deeds, sing all your praises, and attain all there is to attain, you grant them all wisdom. O state of being who makes all stationary things stand, all moving things move, and all full things full! O form of eternal bliss where all thoughts dissolve and all true paths flourish! O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, praised by loving devotees! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: When learning turns into living wisdom, spiritual masters escape the cycle of birth. Vallalar praises the Divine Mother as the silent power behind this realization. She is the active force making stationary things stand and moving things move, guiding sincere seekers to eternal bliss where worldly thoughts dissolve.

translit: ikkaṇami runta-im meyyeṉṟa poykkūrai iṉivaru kaṇappō tilē iṭiyāti rukkumō iṭiyumō eṉceykōm eṉceykōm iṭiyum eṉilyām tekkaṇam naṭakkavarum akkaṇam pollāta tīkkaṇam iruppa teṉṟē cintainain tayarāta vaṇṇamnal aruḷtanta tikaḻ parama civacattiyē ekkaṇamum ēttumoru mukkaṇi paramparai imācala kumāri vimalai iṟaivipai ravi-amalai eṉamaṟaikaḷ ēttiṭa irunta ruḷtarun tēviyē akkaṇutal empirāṉ tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: "Will this false roof called the body, which exists in this moment, remain standing or will it collapse in the very next moment? What shall we do? What shall we do if it collapses? When the time comes to walk south toward death, a wicked host of evils will await us." As my mind withered with such thoughts, you granted your good grace so I would not despair, O radiant supreme Siva-Sakti! O Goddess who abides and bestows grace while the Vedas constantly praise you as the three-eyed Goddess, the Supreme One, the Daughter of the Himalayas, the Pure One, the Sovereign, Bhairavi, and the Immaculate One! O gem who rejoices with our Lord bearing an eye on his forehead, dwelling in the holy city of Thillai! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: The physical body is fragile, and the fear of sudden death haunts the human mind. Vallalar compares the body to a false roof that could cave in at any second, leaving the soul vulnerable to the dark forces waiting at the end of life. His mind withered under this anxiety until the Divine Mother gave him her grace, replacing his fear with spiritual security.

translit: poyyāta moḻiyummayal ceyyāta ceyalumvīṇ pōkāta nāḷum viṭayam puriyāta maṉamumuṭ piriyāta cāntamum puntitaḷa rāta nilaiyum eyyāta vāḻvumvē ṟeṇṇāta niṟaivumniṉai eṉṟummaṟa vāta neṟiyum iṟavāta takavummēṟ piṟavāta katiyumiv ēḻaiyēṟ karuḷcey kaṇṭāy koyyātu kuviyātu kumaiyātu maṇamvīcu kōmaḷat teyva malarē kōvāta muttamē kuṟaiyāta matiyamē kōṭāta maṇivi ḷakkē aiyāṉa ṉamkoṇṭa tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: Grant to this poor soul words that never lie, actions that cause no delusion, days that are never wasted, a mind that does not pursue sensory objects, inner peace that never departs, a state of unfaltering intellect, a life free from fatigue, a fullness that contemplates nothing else, a path that never forgets you, the quality of deathlessness, and the state of freedom from future birth. O tender divine flower that emits fragrance without being plucked, without closing, and without fading! O unstrung pearl! O unwaning moon! O unswerving jeweled lamp! O gem who rejoices with the five-faced Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: Vallalar asks for the total integrity needed to live a spiritual life: truthful words, a mind detached from distractions, unbroken inner peace, and days that are never wasted. He asks the Divine Mother for the highest goals: a life without fatigue, a deathless body, and freedom from rebirth.

translit: pavamāṉa eḻukaṭal kaṭantumēṟ katiyāṉa patinilai aṇaintu vāḻap pakalāṉa cakalamuṭaṉ iravāṉa kēvalap pakaiyun taṭāta paṭi-ōr tavamāṉa kalaṉilaruḷ mīkāma ṉālalatu tamiyēṉ naṭatta varumō tāṉā naṭakkumō eṉceykēṉ niṉtiruc caraṇamē caraṇam aruḷvāy uvamāṉa maṟṟapara civamāṉa cuttaveḷi uṟavāṉa muttar uṟavē uruvāṉa aruvāṉa oruvāṉa ñāṉamē uyirāṉa oḷiyiṉ uṇarvē avamāṉa nīkki-aruḷ tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: To cross the seven oceans of birth and attain the supreme state of the Lord, I must avoid the enmity of the day-like active state and the night-like inert state. Can I, a lonely soul, steer the ship of penance unless guided by the captain of grace? Will the ship sail on its own? What shall I do? Your holy feet are my only refuge. Grant me your grace. O kinship of the liberated souls who relate to the pure space of the incomparable supreme Siva! O wisdom that is with form, without form, and the ultimate One! O awareness of the light that is the life of all! O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who removes our disgrace and grants grace! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: The cycle of repeated birth is an ocean no human being can cross alone. Vallalar compares his spiritual practice to a ship, but admits his own efforts cannot steer it. He needs the Divine Mother's grace to act as captain, guiding him safely past the extremes of worldly distraction and mental dullness until he reaches the pure space of the supreme divine.

translit: cūriṭṭa naṭaiyileṉ pōriṭṭa maṉataināṉ colliṭṭa muṭaṉa ṇaittut tuṉṟiṭṭa mōṉameṉum naṉṟiṭṭa amutuṇṭu cummā irutti eṉṟāl kāriṭṭi taṟkumuṉ yāriṭṭa cāpamō kaṇṭilēṉ ammam ma-ōr kaṇamēṉum nillātu pollātu puviyil kaṟaṅke ṉaccuḻal kiṉṟatē tāriṭṭa nī-aruḷ cīriṭṭi ṭāyeṉil tāḻpiṟavi taṉṉil atutāṉ taṉṉaivīḻt tuvataṉṟi eṉṉaiyum vīḻttumit tamiya ṉēṉeṉ ceykuvēṉ āṟiṭṭa caṭaiyāḷar tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: I embraced my battling mind, which walks a cruel path, with gentle words. I told it to consume the excellent nectar of deep silence and just remain still. Alas, I do not know whose dark curse from the past causes this. It does not stay still for even a moment. This wicked mind spins like a top in this world. If you, wearing a garland, do not grant your grace, this mind will drag itself into a lowly birth and it will drag me down as well. What can I, a lonely one, do? O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who bears the river on his matted hair! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: The mind is restless and cannot be tamed by sheer willpower. Vallalar describes his own mind spinning out of control like a top, unable to rest in silence despite his gentle words. He warns that without divine grace, this relentless mental spinning will drag a person down into lower states of existence.

translit: māyai-eṉum iravileṉ maṉaiyakat tēviṭaya vātaṉai-e ṉuṅkaḷ vartām vantumaṉa aṭimaiyai eḻuppi-ava ṉaittamatu vacamāka uḷavu kaṇṭu mēyamati eṉumoru viḷakkiṉai avitteṉatu meynnilaic cāḷi kai-elām vēṟuṟa uṭaittuḷḷa poruḷelām koḷḷaikoḷa mikanaṭuk kuṟṟu niṉaiyē nēyamuṟa ōvātu kūvukiṉ ṟēṉcaṟṟum niṉcevik kēṟa ilaiyō nīti-ilai yōtaruma neṟiyumilai yō-aruḷiṉ niṟaivumilai yō-eṉ ceykēṉ āyamaṟai muṭiniṉṟa tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: In the night of illusion, the thieves of sensory desires entered my house. They woke up the servant of my mind, brought him under their control through cunning, and extinguished the lamp of my intellect. They broke open the chests of my true state and looted all the wealth within. Trembling intensely, I call out to you unceasingly with love. Does my cry not reach your ears at all? Is there no justice? Is there no path of dharma? Is there no fullness of grace? What shall I do? O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who stands at the crown of the studied Vedas! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: Sensory desires act like thieves in the dark, sneaking in to rob a person of their spiritual awareness. They corrupt the mind, extinguish the light of the intellect, and steal one's inner wealth. Vallalar cries out for divine help, asking if grace and justice have abandoned him to these worldly cravings.

translit: vevviṉaik kīṭāṉa kāyamitu māyameṉa vēta mutalā kamamelām mikupaṟai-a ṟaintumitu veyilmañcaḷ niṟameṉum vivēkar coṟkēṭ ṭaṟintum kavvaipeṟu kaṭalulakil vairamalai ottavar kaṇattiṭai iṟattal palakāl kaṇṇuṟak kaṇṭumip pulai-uṭaliṉ māṉamōr kaṭu-aḷavum viṭuva taṟiyēṉ evvamuṟu ciṟiyaṉēṉ ēḻaimati eṉṉamati iṉṉamati eṉṟu ṇarkilēṉ intamati koṇṭunāṉ entavakai aḻiyāta iṉpanilai kaṇṭu makiḻvēṉ avviyama kaṟṟi-aruḷ tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: The Vedas and Agamas beat loudly like drums, declaring that this body born of cruel karma is an illusion. I have listened and learned from the wise who describe it as the fleeting yellow of turmeric dried in the sun. In this world surrounded by the roaring ocean, I have seen with my own eyes how people as strong as diamond mountains die in a single moment. Even so, I do not know how to discard my pride in this wretched physical body, even by the measure of a mustard seed. I am a flawed and lowly person. What kind of poor mind is this? I do not understand it. With this mind, how can I ever discover and rejoice in the imperishable state of bliss? O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who removes malice and grants grace! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: Even when we see the physical body is fragile and temporary, letting go of our attachment to it is difficult. Vallalar observes people as strong as mountains dying in an instant. Yet he confesses he still clings to bodily pride, asking how a flawed mind can ever reach a state of imperishable joy.

translit: oḷimaruvum uṉatutiru varuḷaṇut tuṇaiyēṉum uṟṟiṭil ciṟutu rumpum ulakam paṭaittalmutal muttoḻil iyaṟṟumeṉa uyarmaṟaikaḷ ōra ṉantam teḷivuṟamu ḻakka-atu kēṭṭuniṉ tiruvaṭit tiyāṉam illā malavamē ciṟuteyva neṟicellum māṉiṭap pēykaḷpāl cērāmai eṟka ruḷuvāy kaḷimaruvum imayavarai araiyaṉmakaḷ eṉavaru karuṇaitaru kalāpa mayilē karutumaṭi yavaritaya kamalamalar micai-aruṭ kalaiki ḷaravaḷar aṉṉamē aḷinaṟaikoḷ itaḻivaṉai tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: The countless exalted Vedas roar clearly that if one attains even an atom of your luminous divine grace, even a small piece of straw can perform the three cosmic functions beginning with the creation of the world. Hearing this, human ghosts waste their lives following the paths of petty deities without meditating on your holy feet. Grant me the grace to never join them. O peacock with beautiful plumage who grants compassion, arriving as the daughter of the king of the joyous Himalayas! O swan who grows and stirs the arts of grace upon the lotus hearts of meditating devotees! O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who wears a garland of honey-filled konrai flowers swarming with bees! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: A single drop of divine grace holds limitless power. Vallalar says even a piece of straw could create worlds if it possessed this grace. Yet people waste their lives chasing petty deities for small worldly favors. He asks for the strength to stay away from these misguided paths.

translit: nīṟaṇin toḷirakka maṇitarit tuyarcaiva neṟiniṉṟu ṉakku riya-ōr nimalamuṟum ainteḻut tuḷnilaiyu ṟakkoṇṭu niṉṉaṭip pūcai ceytu vīṟaṇin teṉṟumoru taṉmaipeṟu civañāṉa vittakarpa tampara vumōr meyccelva vāḻkkaiyil viruppamuṭai yēṉitu viraintaruḷa vēṇṭum amutē pēṟaṇin tayaṉmālum intiraṉum aṟivariya perumaiyai aṇinta amutē piracamalar makaḷkalaicol makaḷvicaya makaḷmutal peṇkaḷciram mēvum maṇiyē āṟaṇin tiṭucaṭaiyar tillaiyam patimaruvum aṇṇalār makiḻum maṇiyē akilāṇṭa mumcarā caramumīṉ ṟaruḷparaci vāṉanta valli umaiyē.
translation: I long for a life of true wealth. In this life, I wish to smear sacred ash, wear shining rudraksha beads, stand firmly in the exalted Saiva path, and hold deeply within myself the pristine five-syllable mantra belonging to you. I wish to worship your feet and praise the feet of the wise masters of divine wisdom, who are adorned with greatness and maintain a single unchanging nature forever. You must grant this to me swiftly, O nectar! O nectar adorned with excellence, bearing a greatness difficult for Brahma, Vishnu, and Indra to comprehend! O gem resting upon the heads of goddesses like Lakshmi of the honey-filled lotus flower, Saraswati of arts and speech, and the victorious Durga! O gem who rejoices with the Lord dwelling in the holy city of Thillai, who wears the river on his matted hair! O Paracivananta Valli! O Umai, you birthed and graced the entire universe and all moving and unmoving things!
commentary: True wealth is a life of steady spiritual dedication. Vallalar longs to immerse himself in the traditional path of worship, wearing sacred ash, holding the five-syllable mantra within, and praising the masters of divine wisdom. He prays for this devoted life to be granted swiftly.

sections.title: The Sacred Decad on the Goddess of Arts

tamil: தவளமலர்க் கமலமிசை வீற்றிருக்கும் அம்மனையைச் சாந்தம் பூத்த
குவளைமலர்க் கண்ணாளைப் பெண்ணாளும் பெண்ணமுதைக் கோதி லாத
பவளஇதழ்ப் பசுங்கொடியை நான்முகனார் நாஓங்கும் பாவை தன்னைக்
கவளமத கயக்கொம்பின் முலையாளைக் கலைமாதைக் கருது வோமே.
translit: tavaḷamalark kamalamicai vīṟṟirukkum ammaṉaiyaic cāntam pūtta kuvaḷaimalark kaṇṇāḷaip peṇṇāḷum peṇṇamutaik kōti lāta pavaḷa-itaḻp pacuṅkoṭiyai nāṉmukaṉār nā-ōṅkum pāvai taṉṉaik kavaḷamata kayakkompiṉ mulaiyāḷaik kalaimātaik karutu vōmē.
translation: Let us meditate upon the Goddess of Arts. She is the Mother seated majestically upon a white lotus flower. Her eyes are blue water lilies blossoming with peace. She is the feminine nectar. She is a tender green creeper with flawless coral lips. She is the maiden who rises upon the tongue of the four-faced Brahma. Her breasts are like the tusks of an elephant in rut.
commentary: Saraswati, the Goddess of Arts and Learning, is traditionally seated on a white lotus to symbolize purity. Dwelling upon the tongue of Brahma (the creator god), she is the source of all knowledge, speech, and creative power in the universe.

tamil: சங்கம்வளர்ந் திடவளர்ந்த தமிழ்க்கொடியைச் சரச்சுவதி தன்னை அன்பர்
துங்கமுறக் கலைபயிற்றி உணர்வளிக்கும் கலைஞானத் தோகை தன்னைத்
திங்கணுதல் திருவைஅருட் குருவைமலர் ஓங்கியபெண் தெய்வந் தன்னைத்
தங்கமலை முலையாளைக் கலையாளைத் தொழுதுபுகழ் சாற்று கிற்பாம்.
translit: caṅkamvaḷarn tiṭavaḷarnta tamiḻkkoṭiyaic caraccuvati taṉṉai aṉpar tuṅkamuṟak kalaipayiṟṟi uṇarvaḷikkum kalaiñāṉat tōkai taṉṉait tiṅkaṇutal tiruvai-aruṭ kuruvaimalar ōṅkiyapeṇ teyvan taṉṉait taṅkamalai mulaiyāḷaik kalaiyāḷait toḻutupukaḻ cāṟṟu kiṟpām.
translation: Let us worship and proclaim the praise of Saraswati, the Goddess of Arts. She is the Tamil creeper who flourished as the Sangam flourished. She is the peacock of true knowledge who imparts the arts to her devotees to elevate them and grants them inner realization. She is the beautiful one with a crescent-moon forehead. She is the Guru of grace. She is the lofty Goddess of the lotus. Her breasts are like mountains of gold.
commentary: The Goddess is the patron of the Tamil language. The Sangam refers to the ancient academies of Tamil poets and scholars. She acts as both a teacher of worldly arts and a spiritual guide leading devotees to inner realization.

tamil: கலைபயின்ற உளத்தினிக்குங் கரும்பினைமுக் கனியைஅருட் கடலை ஓங்கும்
நிலைபயின்ற முனிவரரும் தொழுதேத்த நான்முகனார் நீண்ட நாவின்
தலைபயின்ற மறைபயின்று மூவுலகும் காக்கின்ற தாயை வாகைச்
சிலைபயின்ற நுதலாளைக் கலைவாணி அம்மையைநாம் சிந்திப் போமே.
translit: kalaipayiṉṟa uḷattiṉikkuṅ karumpiṉaimuk kaṉiyai-aruṭ kaṭalai ōṅkum nilaipayiṉṟa muṉivararum toḻutētta nāṉmukaṉār nīṇṭa nāviṉ talaipayiṉṟa maṟaipayiṉṟu mūvulakum kākkiṉṟa tāyai vākaic cilaipayiṉṟa nutalāḷaik kalaivāṇi ammaiyainām cintip pōmē.
translation: Let us meditate upon Mother Kalaivani. She is the sugarcane sweetening the hearts of those steeped in the arts. She is the triad of sweet fruits. She is the ocean of grace. She is worshipped and praised by ascetics firmly established in exalted states. She abides on the tip of the long tongue of the four-faced Brahma, chanting the Vedas and protecting the three worlds. Her forehead is shaped like a victorious bow.
commentary: Kalaivani is another name for Saraswati, meaning the Goddess of Speech and Arts. The triad of sweet fruits (mango, jackfruit, and banana) represents the ultimate sweetness in Tamil culture. Chanting the Vedas (ancient sacred scriptures), she uses the power of sacred sound to protect the worlds.

note: Editor's note: sung at Pullirukkuvelur (puḷḷirukkuvēḷūr, புள்ளிருக்குவேளூர்), today Vaitheeswaran Koil, where Siva is worshipped as the divine physician.

translit: nalla maruntim maruntu - cukam nalkum vaittiya nāta maruntu.
translation: This medicine is a good medicine. It is the medicine of the Lord of Healing that grants bliss.
commentary: The divine is the ultimate healer, and grace itself is the perfect medicine that brings lasting happiness.

translit: aruḷvaṭi vāṉa maruntu - nammuḷ aṟputa māka amarnta maruntu iruḷaṟa vōṅkum maruntu - aṉpark kiṉpuru vāka irunta maruntu. - nalla
translation: It is the medicine formed of grace. It is the medicine seated wondrously within us. It is the medicine that rises to dispel darkness. It is the medicine that stands as the very form of joy for devotees. This is the good medicine.
commentary: God is not a distant object of worship. This healing presence is seated within the human heart. It clears away the darkness of ignorance and becomes joy for those who love the divine.

translit: cañcalan tīrkkum maruntu - eṅkun tāṉōtā ṉākit taḻaikkum maruntu añcaleṉ ṟāḷum maruntu - cacci tāṉanta māka amarnta maruntu. - nalla
translation: It is the medicine that cures sorrow. It is the medicine that flourishes everywhere as itself. It is the medicine that governs us by saying fear not. It is the medicine seated as pure existence, consciousness, and bliss. This is the good medicine.
commentary: This divine presence cures worldly anxieties and tells the soul to have no fear. Vallalar calls it existence, consciousness, and bliss (caccitāṉanta). Though it lives within the heart, it flourishes everywhere as the living fabric of the universe.

translit: vittaka māṉa maruntu - catur vēta muṭivil viḷaṅku maruntu tattuvā tīta maruntu - eṉṉait tāṉākkik koṇṭa tayāḷa maruntu. - nalla
translation: It is the miraculous medicine. It is the medicine shining at the pinnacle of the four Vedas. It is the medicine beyond all elemental principles. It is the compassionate medicine that transformed me into itself. This is the good medicine.
commentary: Vallalar says this grace exists beyond the teachings of scripture and the physical and mental building blocks of the universe (tattvas). Through compassion, this divine cure absorbs the soul and transforms the devotee into its own nature.

translit: piṟappai yoḻikku maruntu - yārkkum pēcap paṭāta periya maruntu iṟappait tavirkkum maruntu - eṉṉuḷ eṉṟu maturit tiṉikku maruntu. - nalla
translation: It is the medicine that abolishes birth. It is the great medicine beyond anyone's words. It is the medicine that wards off death. It is the medicine that remains eternally sweet and delightful within me. This is the good medicine.
commentary: The ultimate cure provides freedom from the endless cycle of birth and physical death. Vallalar describes this immortal state as beyond human language, leaving only a feeling of eternal sweetness within him.

translit: nāṉatu vāku maruntu - para ñāṉa veḷiyil naṭikku maruntu mōna vaṭivā maruntu - cīvaṉ mutta ruḷattē muṭikku maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that makes me become That. The medicine that dances in the space of supreme wisdom. The medicine whose form is silence. The medicine that fulfills the hearts of liberated souls.
commentary: The divine acts as a healing medicine that transforms the soul, merging human awareness into the supreme reality of God. It exists as inner silence and brings fulfillment to those who have reached spiritual liberation.

translit: puttamu tāku maruntu - pārtta pōtē piṇikaḷaip pōkku maruntu patta raruntu maruntu - anu pāṉamun tāṉām parama maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that is fresh nectar. The medicine that dispels diseases the very moment it is seen. The medicine consumed by devotees. The supreme medicine that is itself the carrier.
commentary: In traditional healing, a remedy is often taken with a liquid carrier (anupanam) like honey or milk. Vallalar says this divine medicine is self-sufficient: it is both the cure and the sweet nectar that delivers it. Seeing this supreme light is enough to cure all ailments of the soul.

translit: mālayaṉ tēṭu maruntu - muṉṉa mārkkaṇṭa raikkākka vanta maruntu kālaṉaic cāytta maruntu - tēvar kāṇuṅ kaṉaviṉuṅ kāṇā maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine sought by Vishnu and Brahma. The medicine that came long ago to protect Markandeya. The medicine that struck down the god of death. The medicine unseen even in the dreams of the celestial gods.
commentary: This divine medicine conquers the human affliction of death itself. Vallalar recalls the story of Markandeya, a young boy saved from the god of death by this very grace. The highest celestial gods search for this supreme healing in vain and cannot grasp it even in their dreams.

translit: taṟpara yōka maruntu - upa cānta ruḷattiṭaic cārnta maruntu ciṟpara yōka maruntu - uyar tēvarel lāntoḻun teyva maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine of supreme yoga. The medicine that resides in the hearts of the deeply peaceful. The medicine of absolute conscious yoga. The divine medicine worshipped by all the exalted gods.
commentary: This medicine is found only in the hearts of those who have reached inner peace. It represents the highest state of conscious union with the divine, a supreme reality worshipped by exalted gods of the heavens.

translit: ampalat tāṭu maruntu - para mānanta veḷḷat taḻuttu maruntu empala māku maruntu - vēḷūr eṉṉun talatti lirukku maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that dances in the hall. The medicine that immerses one in the flood of supreme bliss. The medicine that becomes my strength. The medicine that resides in the sacred place called Velur.
commentary: The divine medicine dances as light in the open space of the soul, flooding human awareness with supreme bliss. Vallalar identifies this source of spiritual strength with the divine presence enshrined at Velur, a sacred temple town famous for its healing deity.

translit: cētappa ṭāta maruntu - uṇṭāl tēṉpō liṉikkun teviṭṭā maruntu pētappa ṭāta maruntu - malaip peṇṇiṭaṅ koṇṭa periya maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine that cannot be destroyed. If consumed, it tastes sweet like honey and never cloys. The medicine without divisions. The great medicine that holds the mountain's daughter on its left side. This is the good medicine.
commentary: The divine is an eternal medicine that heals the soul. Unlike earthly cures, it never spoils and tastes sweet. The imagery of the mountain's daughter on the left side points to the traditional form of Siva, representing a divinity where masculine and feminine are united.

translit: ārkku maritā maruntu - tāṉē āti yanātiyu māṉa maruntu cērkkum punita maruntu - taṉṉait tēṭuvōr taṅkaḷai nāṭu maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine that is hard for anyone to obtain. The medicine that is itself both the beginning and the beginningless. The holy medicine that unites us. The medicine that seeks those who seek it. This is the good medicine.
commentary: This sacred medicine is the source of all things, existing before time. Although it is rare and hard to grasp, it searches for those who search for it. Sincere spiritual effort draws the divine to the seeker.

translit: puṇṇiyark kāṉa maruntu - pari pūraṇa mākap poruntu maruntu eṇṇiya viṉpa maruntu - ema teṇṇamel lāmuṭit tiṭṭa maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine meant for the virtuous. The medicine that exists as absolute fullness. The blissful medicine of our thoughts. The medicine that fulfilled all our intentions. This is the good medicine.
commentary: The divine presence acts as an all-encompassing cure for those who live virtuously. It is an absolute fullness that brings spiritual bliss. Connecting with this reality fulfills all genuine intentions.

translit: pālvaṇṇa māku maruntu - atil paccai niṟamum paṭarnta maruntu nūlvaṇṇa nāṭu maruntu - uḷḷē nōkkukiṉ ṟōrkaḷai nōkku maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine of milk-white hue. The medicine over which the color green also spreads. The medicine sought by the scriptures. The medicine that looks at those who look inward. This is the good medicine.
commentary: The colors of milk-white and green represent the union of masculine and feminine aspects of the divine. While sacred scriptures try to locate this truth in words, it is found through inner experience. When a person looks within themselves, the divine looks back at them.

translit: pārkkap pacipō maruntu - taṉṉaip pārāta varkaḷaic cērā maruntu kūrkkat terinta maruntu - anu kūla marunteṉṟu koṇṭa maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine that dispels hunger when looked upon. The medicine that will not approach those who refuse to look at it. The medicine known with sharp clarity. The medicine embraced as a favorable cure. This is the good medicine.
commentary: Beholding this divine medicine is enough to erase the hunger of the soul. It requires a conscious choice, however: the divine will not approach those who refuse to turn their attention toward it. When embraced willingly, it becomes a clear cure for all suffering.

translit: kōtilā tōṅku maruntu - aṉpar koḷḷaikoṇ ṭuṇṇak kulāvu maruntu mātoru pāka maruntu - eṉṉai vāḻvitta eṉkaṇ maṇiyā maruntu. - nalla
translation: The flawless, rising medicine. The medicine that rejoices as devotees plunder and consume it. The medicine with a woman on one side. The medicine that is the pupil of my eye which made me flourish. This is the good medicine.
commentary: Divine grace is an infinite cure that devotees can drink up without depleting it. This medicine is highly personal. It lives within the pupil of Vallalar's eye, bringing his spiritual life into full bloom.

translit: ēka vuruvā maruntu - mikka ēḻaika ḷukkum iraṅku maruntu cōkan tavirkku maruntu - parañ cōtiyeṉ ṟaṉpar tutikku maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine of a single form. The medicine that shows mercy even to the most impoverished. The medicine that dispels sorrow. The medicine that devotees praise as the supreme Jothi. This is the good medicine.
commentary: Grace is the single, undivided reality that devotees praise as the supreme Jothi (divine light). It does not demand wealth or status to work its cure. Instead, this medicine pours out its mercy on the poor and the sorrowful, healing their grief with light.

translit: kōmaḷaṅ kūṭu maruntu - nalaṅ koṭukkat tucaṅkaṭṭik koṇṭa maruntu nāmaḷa vāta maruntu - nammai nāmaṟi yumpaṭi naṇṇu maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine united with the tender one. The medicine that raised its flag to bestow goodness. The medicine we cannot measure. The medicine that approaches us so we may know ourselves. This is the good medicine.
commentary: The divine is beyond human measurement, yet it reaches out to us out of tender love. It raises a flag of victory over ignorance to bring us goodness. By approaching us, this medicine cures our blindness, allowing us to see and know our spiritual selves.

translit: celvan taḻaikku maruntu - eṉṟun tīrā viṉaiyelān tīrtta maruntu nalvan taṉaikoḷ maruntu - para nātānta vīṭṭiṉuḷ naṇṇu maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine that makes wealth flourish. The medicine that cured all endless, lingering karma. The medicine that accepts good reverence. The medicine that resides in the supreme home at the end of sound. This is the good medicine.
commentary: This divine medicine wipes out the lingering effects of karma, the cycle of past actions and their consequences that keeps souls bound. It resides in the supreme home at the end of sound, a state of spiritual stillness. From that high silence, it brings spiritual wealth to anyone who offers reverence.

translit: vāypiṭi yāta maruntu - mata vātamum pittamu māykku maruntu nōypoṭi yākku maruntu - aṉpar nōkkiya nōkkiṉuḷ nōkku maruntu. - nalla
translation: The medicine that does not restrict the mouth. The medicine that destroys fierce wind and bile. The medicine that turns disease to dust. The medicine that looks into the very gaze of the devotees. This is the good medicine.
commentary: Worldly medicines often come with strict dietary rules and bitter tastes, but this divine cure places no limits on the mouth. It destroys the root causes of physical illness, described here through the traditional bodily humors of fierce wind and bile. Above all, it is a responsive medicine: when a devotee looks for it, the divine light looks back into their eyes.

translit: peṇṇācai tīrkku maruntu - poruṭ pērācai yellām piḷakku maruntu maṇṇācai tīrkku maruntu - ellām valla marunteṉṟu vāḻttu maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that cures the desire for women. The medicine that shatters all immense greed for wealth. The medicine that cures the desire for land. The medicine praised as the all-powerful medicine.
commentary: God's grace frees the mind from worldly attachments. Traditional thought identifies three main human cravings: lust, greed for wealth, and greed for land. This divine medicine removes all three.

translit: eṉṟuṅ keṭāta maruntu - varum ellāp piṇikku mituvē maruntu tuṉṟuñ civōka maruntu - nammaic cūḻntiru maikkun tuṇaiyā maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that never spoils. This alone is the medicine for all diseases that afflict us. The medicine of the abundant unitive experience. The medicine that surrounds us and serves as our companion in both worlds.
commentary: Physical medicines expire and only treat the body. The divine medicine is eternal and heals every physical and spiritual affliction. It merges the soul into the divine experience and remains our companion in this life and the next.

translit: kaṇṇoḷi kāṭṭu maruntu - ammai kaṇṭu kalantu kaḷikku maruntu viṇṇoḷi yāru maruntu - para vīṭu taruṅkaṅkai vēṇi maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that reveals the light of the eyes. The medicine that the Mother sees, unites with, and rejoices in. The medicine brimming with celestial light. The medicine with the Ganges river in its matted hair, which grants the supreme state of liberation.
commentary: Vallalar uses the traditional features of Lord Siva, who holds the river Ganges in his matted hair and shares his joy with the divine Mother. This grace opens our inner spiritual vision, flooding the seeker with heavenly light and granting liberation.

translit: kāyāmpū vaṇṇa maruntu - oru kañca malarmicaik kāṇu maruntu tāyāṅ karuṇai maruntu - ciṟ catāciva māṉameñ ñāna maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine with the hue of the dark kaya flower. The medicine seen upon a lotus flower. The medicine of maternal compassion. The medicine of true knowledge that stands as the supreme Sadasiva.
commentary: The supreme medicine unites the traditional forms of the major deities: the dark blue flower of Vishnu, the lotus seat of Brahma, and the truth of Siva. All these resolve into one supreme reality made of pure knowledge and a mother's limitless compassion.

translit: aḷavaik kaṭanta maruntu - yārkkum arumai yarumai yarumai maruntu uḷaviṟ kiṭaikku maruntu - oṉṟum oppuyar villā tuyarnta maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that transcends all measure. The medicine that is exceedingly rare for anyone to attain. The medicine obtained through subtle inner understanding. The exalted medicine that has absolutely no equal or superior.
commentary: God's absolute grace cannot be measured or won through external actions. It is rare to secure in the outward world, yet can always be found by those who turn inward and seek it quietly through their own understanding.

translit: taṉmaya māku maruntu - civa cātaṉar neñcil taḻaikku maruntu ciṉmaya jōti maruntu - aṭṭa cittiyu muttiyuñ cērkku maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that transforms you into its very nature. It flourishes in the hearts of Siva's practitioners. This good medicine is the Jothi of pure consciousness. It grants the eight mystic powers and supreme liberation.
commentary: The divine light acts as a medicine that transforms the seeker into its own nature. It is pure consciousness in the form of Jothi, granting earthly spiritual powers and freedom, and thriving in the hearts of sincere practitioners.

translit: maṟantā loḷikku maruntu - taṉṉai maṟavā tavaruḷ vaḻaṅku maruntu iṟantā leḻuppu maruntu - eṉak keṉṟun tuṇaiyā yirukku maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that hides if you forget it. It bestows grace upon those who never forget it. This good medicine resurrects the dead. It remains my companion forever.
commentary: The divine presence requires constant mindfulness. If you forget it, it hides from your awareness; if you keep it in your thoughts, it pours out grace. Vallalar says this medicine can raise the dead and serve as an eternal companion.

translit: karumpi liṉikku maruntu - kaṭuṅ kaṇṭakark kellāṅ kacakku maruntu irumpaik kuḻaikku maruntu - pē riṉpa veḷḷattē yiḻukku maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that is sweeter than sugarcane. It tastes bitter to all the cruel and wicked. This good medicine softens iron. It pulls you into the flood of supreme bliss.
commentary: The experience of grace is sweet, yet bitter to those with cruel hearts. This divine medicine softens a mind as hard as iron and draws the soul into a boundless flood of supreme joy.

translit: aṇimaṇi kaṇṭa maruntu - aruḷ ānanta cutta vakaṇṭa maruntu piṇitavi riṉpa maruntu - yārkkum pēcā marunteṉṟu pēcu maruntu. - nalla
translation: This is the good medicine that has a beautiful jewel-like throat. It is the pure and boundless medicine of grace and bliss. This joyful medicine eradicates disease. It is proclaimed by all as the medicine beyond speech.
commentary: The jewel-like throat points to Siva, who swallowed deadly poison to save the world. Vallalar describes this divine medicine as pure, boundless grace that cures all diseases. Though universally praised, the experience of this joy remains beyond the reach of words.

translit: mūvark kariya maruntu - celva muttuk kumāraṉai yīṉṟa maruntu nāviṟ kiṉiya maruntu - taiyal nāyaki kaṇṭu taḻuvu maruntu.
translation: This medicine is rare for the three chief gods to attain. It gave birth to the treasured Lord Muthukumaran. This medicine is sweet to the tongue. It is the medicine that Goddess Thaiyal Nayagi looks upon and embraces.
commentary: This supreme medicine is so elevated that even the traditional trinity of gods cannot reach it. Vallalar identifies it as the source of Murugan, here called Muthukumaran, and the beloved of the goddess Thaiyal Nayagi. These deities are enshrined at Vaitheeswaran Koil, a temple of healing, rooting the metaphor of divine medicine in familiar sacred geography.

translit: nalla maruntim maruntu - cukam nalkum vaittiya nāta maruntu.
translation: This medicine is a good medicine. It is the medicine of the Lord of Healing that grants well-being.
commentary: Grace is the perfect medicine for the soul. The divine is called the Lord of Healing because this supreme light cures the root disease of human suffering. While ordinary medicine treats the physical body, this spiritual medicine brings lasting well-being.

translit: ampalattil āṭukiṉṟār pāṅkimā rē - avar āṭṭaṅkaṇṭu nāṭṭaṅkoṇṭēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, He dances in the Hall. Seeing His dance, I fixed my desire upon Him, O friends.
commentary: Vallalar speaks as a young woman who has fallen in love with the dancing Lord. The Hall (Ambalam) represents both the great physical temple at Chidambaram and the boundless space of spiritual consciousness. Once the soul witnesses the movement of divine grace within that space, it is captivated.

translit: āṭukiṉṟa cēvaṭimēṟ pāṅkimā rē - mika ācaikoṇṭu vāṭukiṉṟēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, I conceived a deep longing for His dancing red feet and I languish, O friends.
commentary: In Tamil poetry, the Lord's feet are often described as red like lotus petals. These feet represent divine grace stepping into the world to uplift living beings. The physical wasting away is a traditional metaphor for the soul's intense spiritual hunger.

translit: iṉpavaṭi vāyccapaiyiṟ pāṅkimā rē - naṭa miṭṭavarmē liṭṭamvaittēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, He takes the form of bliss in the Hall. I placed my love upon Him who dances there, O friends.
commentary: The Lord's very form is bliss. The soul is naturally drawn to this joy, pouring out its own love in response to His presence.

translit: īṉavuṭaṟ kiccaivaiyēṉ pāṅkimā rē - naṭa ṉēcartamai yeytumvaṇṇam pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, I hold no desire for this lowly body. I seek only to attain the Lord of the Dance, O friends.
commentary: Vallalar rejects physical existence and worldly attachments. Compared to the divine dancer, the body and its comforts hold no appeal. His single goal is union with God.

translit: uttamarpoṉ ṉampalattē pāṅkimā rē - iṉpa uruvāki ōṅkukiṉṟār pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, the supreme Lord in the Golden Hall stands exalted as the very form of bliss, O friends.
commentary: The Golden Hall (Pon Ambalam) is the supreme space of light where grace operates in perfect clarity. Vallalar teaches that within this high state of spiritual awareness, God is experienced as an exalted, living joy.

translit: ūṉavula kaikkarutēṉ pāṅkimā rē - maṉṟil uttamaruk kuṟavāvēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, I do not think of this fleshy world. O friends, I will become the beloved of the supreme one in the hall.
commentary: The soul's single desire is to unite with the supreme Lord in the hall of light, leaving all worldly concerns behind.

translit: kaṟpaṉaiyel lāṅkaṭantār pāṅkimā rē - eṉṟaṉ kaṟpaṉaikkuṭ paṭuvārō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, he has transcended all imagination. O friends, will he be bound by my imagination?
commentary: God exists far beyond the limits of the human mind. How could limited thoughts ever hold or comprehend a Lord who transcends imagination?

translit: kaṇṭilarnāṉ paṭumpāṭu pāṅkimā rē - mūṉṟu kaṇṇuṭaiyā reṉpāraiyō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, he does not see the suffering I endure. O friends, alas, they say he possesses three eyes.
commentary: Vallalar points out a painful irony. Tradition claims the Lord has three eyes and sees everything, yet he seems blind to the sorrow the soul endures.

translit: kaṉmaṉamel lāṅkaraippār pāṅkimā rē - maṉaṅ karaiyāreṉ ṉaḷavilē pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, he melts all stony hearts. O friends, his own heart does not melt for me.
commentary: There is a bitter contrast in how the Lord acts. He is famous for melting the most stubborn hearts with his grace, but his own heart remains cold to the soul's longing.

translit: kaḷḷamoṉṟu maṟiyēṉāṉ pāṅkimā rē - eṉṉaik kaiviṭavun tuṇivārō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, I know no deceit at all. O friends, will he dare to abandon me?
commentary: Because the soul's devotion is pure and innocent, she trusts that the Lord will never abandon her.

translit: kaṟpaḻittuk kalantārē pāṅkimā rē - iṉṟu kainaḻuva viṭuvārō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He ruined my chastity and united with me, O friends. Will he let me slip from his hands today, O friends?
commentary: In the tradition of Tamil love poetry, the soul speaks as a woman whose lover has taken everything from her. Here, losing her chastity means surrendering her worldly identity and ego to the divine. After tasting such union, the soul wonders how the Lord could abandon her now.

translit: kaṇṭavarel lāmpaḻikkap pāṅkimā rē - eṉṟaṉ kaṉṉiyaḻit tēyoḷittār pāṅkimā rē.
translation: While everyone who sees me casts blame, O friends, he ruined my maidenhood and then hid himself, O friends.
commentary: The soul feels the sting of worldly society, which often mocks intense spiritual devotion. The Lord granted her an experience of his presence and then vanished. This withdrawal leaves the soul exposed to the world's judgment while she waits in pain for his return.

translit: kāmaṉaikkaṇ ṇālerittār pāṅkimā rē - eṉṟaṉ kātalaikkaṇ ṭaṟivārō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He burned the god of love with his eye, O friends. Will he look upon my love and understand it, O friends?
commentary: Tradition says the Lord burned Kama, the god of physical desire, to ashes with a single glance from his fiery eye. The soul worries about this detachment, wondering if the Lord who destroys all worldly lust will still recognize and accept her spiritual love.

translit: kāvalaiyel lāṅkaṭantu pāṅkimā rē - eṉṉaik kaikalanta kaḷḷaravar pāṅkimā rē.
translation: Crossing all defenses, O friends, he is the thief who joined hands with me, O friends.
commentary: The Lord acts as a divine thief who sneaks past every barrier the human mind puts up. He bypasses all the ego's defenses to steal the heart and unite with the soul.

translit: kāṇaviḻain tēṉavaraip pāṅkimā rē - koṇṭu kāṭṭuvārai yaṟintilēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: I yearn to see him, O friends. I know no one who can take me and show him to me, O friends.
commentary: The pain of separation reaches its peak. The soul wants to experience the Lord's presence again, yet feels helpless because she cannot find a guide to lead her back to him.

translit: kiṭṭavara vēṇṭumeṉṟār pāṅkimā rē - nāṉ kiṭṭumuṉṉē yeṭṭaniṉṟār pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He told me to come near, my friends. Before I could approach, he stood far away, my friends.
commentary: The divine presence is often elusive. The Lord invites the soul closer, but then withdraws just out of reach. This playful retreat deepens the soul's longing and keeps her seeking him.

translit: kiṉṉaraṅkē ḷeṉṟicaittār pāṅkimā rē - nāṉ kēṭpataṉmuṉ cēṭpaṭuttār pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He told me to listen to the kinnaram lute and played its music, my friends. Before I could hear it, he moved far away, my friends.
commentary: The Lord promises the sound of the kinnaram (a traditional stringed lute) but vanishes before she can listen. Spiritual glimpses often fade quickly like this, leaving the seeker hungry for a lasting connection.

translit: kiḷḷaiyaittū tāviṭuttēṉ pāṅkimā rē - atu kēṭṭuvarak kāṇēṉaiyō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: I sent a parrot as my messenger, my friends. Alas, I do not see it returning with his reply, my friends.
commentary: Following the Tamil poetic tradition of love, the longing soul sends a bird to carry her message to God. The silence that follows shows her desperation and the agonizing wait for a divine response.

translit: kītavakai pāṭiniṉṟār pāṅkimā rē - atu kēṭṭumati mayaṅkiṉēṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He stood singing various melodies, my friends. Hearing that music, my mind was completely entranced, my friends.
commentary: The divine music finally reaches her and sweeps away her thoughts. When God reveals himself, the sheer beauty of that experience overtakes the mind.

translit: kīḻmaikuṟi yāmaleṉṉaip pāṅkimā rē - maṉak kēṇmaikuṟit tārēyaṉṟu pāṅkimā rē.
translation: He did not look at my lowliness, my friends. On that day he sought only the intimacy of my heart, my friends.
commentary: God's grace operates on compassion. The Lord does not care about a person's flaws, social status, or perceived lowliness. He looks past all worldly judgments and seeks only a loving connection with the human heart.

translit: kīṭamaṉai yēṉeṉaiyum pāṅkimā rē - aṭik kēyaṭimai koṇṭāraṉṟu pāṅkimā rē.
translation: Though I am like a worm, O friends, He took me as a slave to His feet on that day, O friends.
commentary: Vallalar marvels at the scale of divine grace. He feels as worthless as a worm, yet the Lord claims him completely.

translit: kuṟṟamellāṅ kuṇamākap pāṅkimā rē - koḷḷuṅ koṟṟavareṉ koḻunarkāṇ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: See that the King who accepts all flaws as virtues is my husband, O friends.
commentary: True love goes beyond forgiveness. God loves the soul so much that he embraces her faults as virtues.

translit: kuṟṟamoṉṟuñ ceytaṟiyēṉ pāṅkimā rē - eṉṉaik koṇṭukulam pēcuvārō pāṅkimā rē.
translation: I have not committed a single fault, O friends. Will He accept me and then question my lineage, O friends?
commentary: Will God, having claimed the soul, question her lineage (kulam)? God accepts the soul for her pure intent, not for her birth.

translit: kuñcitappoṟ pātaṅkaṇṭāṟ pāṅkimā rē - uḷḷa kuṟaiyellān tīruṅkaṇṭīr pāṅkimā rē.
translation: If you see His raised golden foot, O friends, know that all your inner grievances will be resolved, O friends.
commentary: The raised golden foot is a traditional symbol of the Lord's dancing grace offering shelter to the world. Beholding this grace erases every sorrow and feeling of lack.

translit: kūṟṟutaitta pātaṅkaṇṭīr pāṅkimā rē - naṅkaḷ kuṭikkellāṅ kulateyvam pāṅkimā rē.
translation: Behold the feet that kicked Death, O friends. He is the family deity for our entire lineage, O friends.
commentary: Kicking Death recalls the story of the Lord saving a young devotee from Yama, the god of death. Taking the Lord as the supreme guardian means seeking protection from mortality itself.

translit: kūṟariya pataṅkaṇṭu pāṅkimā rē - kaḷi koṇṭuniṟka viḻaintēṉāṉ pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, having seen those indescribable feet, I longed to stand filled with joy, O friends.
commentary: Seeing the divine feet means experiencing God's grace directly. Vallalar desires only to remain in this state of pure, lasting joy forever.

translit: kūṭalviḻain tēṉavaraip pāṅkimā rē - atu kūṭumvaṇṇam kūṭṭiṭuvīr pāṅkimā rē.
translation: O friends, I desired union with him. Please bring us together so that this union takes place, O friends.
commentary: The soul's highest desire is union with the divine. In this poetic tradition, these friends represent the supportive company of other seekers or the guiding presence of grace, leading the soul to its ultimate destination.

translit: taṉṉaiyaṟin tiṉpamuṟa veṇṇilā vē - oru tantiranī collavēṇṭum veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon, you must tell me a method to know myself and attain bliss, O white moon.
commentary: The spiritual path begins with self-knowledge. Recognizing the soul is the only way to experience lasting bliss.

translit: nātamuṭi mēlirunta veṇṇilā vē - aṅkē nāṉumvara vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon resting upon the crown of primal sound, I beg to come there too, O white moon.
commentary: The divine light rests beyond the highest reaches of creation. The crown of primal sound (nātam) is the very first vibration of the universe. Vallalar longs to rise past all earthly and cosmic levels to join it.

translit: caccitāṉan takkaṭalil veṇṇilā vē - nāṉun tāḻntuviḻa vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon, I beg to plunge deep into the ocean of existence, consciousness, and bliss, O white moon.
commentary: The ultimate reality is a boundless ocean of pure existence, consciousness, and bliss (saccitāṉantam). Vallalar longs to lose his individual identity within it.

translit: irāppakalil lāviṭattē veṇṇilā vē - nāṉum irukkaveṇṇi vāṭukiṉṟēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon, I languish with the thought of being in that place where there is neither night nor day, O white moon.
commentary: Day and night represent the passage of time and the endless cycle of opposites, like joy and sorrow or birth and death. Vallalar longs for a timeless state of continuous light where these earthly divisions no longer exist.

translit: tēcuniṟa māyniṟainta veṇṇilā vē - nāṉuñ civamayama tāyviḻaintēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon who abounds as the hue of radiant light, I yearned to become the very nature of Siva, O white moon.
commentary: The goal of this spiritual longing is transformation. Becoming the very nature of the divine (civamayam) means shedding a limited human identity to become radiant light.

translit: pōtanaṭu vūṭirunta veṇṇilā vē - malap pōtamaṟa vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon dwelling in the center of true knowledge, I pray for the consciousness of impurities to be completely severed, O white moon.
commentary: The moon here stands for the light of true knowledge. Impurities are the illusions that bind and confuse the mind.

translit: ārumaṟi yāmaliṅkē veṇṇilā vē - aru ḷāḷarvaru vārōcollāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon, tell me if the gracious Lord will come here without anyone knowing, O white moon.
commentary: Vallalar longs for the Lord of grace to arrive in secret, seeking a quiet union meant only for the soul and God.

translit: antaraṅka cēvaiceyya veṇṇilā vē - yeṅkaḷ aiyarvaru vārōcollāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon, tell me if our Lord will come so I may perform intimate service, O white moon.
commentary: True devotion is expressed as a desire for direct, personal service to God. Vallalar waits for the Lord to offer this inner dedication away from any public display.

translit: vētamuṭi mēlirunta veṇṇilā vē - mala vētaiyuḷa vētucollāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon resting upon the crown of the Vedas, tell me the cause of the affliction of impurities, O white moon.
commentary: Resting high above the Vedas means this divine light is greater than all ancient scriptures. Vallalar looks to this supreme light for answers to why the soul must suffer the pain of worldly impurities.

translit: kuṇṭalippāl niṉṟilaṅkum veṇṇilā vē - antak kuṇṭalippāl vēṇṭukiṉṟēṉ veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon shining in the realm of Kundalini, I beg for the milk of that Kundalini, O white moon.
commentary: Kundalini is the latent spiritual energy within the human body. Its milk is the blissful nourishment that flows when this inner power awakens.

translit: ātiyanta meṉṟuraittār veṇṇilā vē - anta ātiyanta māvateṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: They spoke of the beginning and the end, O white moon. What is that beginning and end, O white moon?
commentary: Spiritual traditions often describe the divine as the original source where everything starts and the final destination where everything returns. Vallalar questions the actual reality behind these common descriptions.

translit: vittilāma lēviḷainta veṇṇilā vē - nītāṉ viḷaintavaṇṇa mētucollāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: You arose without a seed, O white moon. Tell me how you came to be, O white moon.
commentary: In the natural world, every plant grows from a seed, but divine grace appears without any physical cause or origin. Vallalar wonders how something so perfect can arise from nothing at all.

translit: mupporuḷu moṉṟateṉpār veṇṇilā vē - anta mūṉṟumoṉṟāy muṭintateṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: They say the three entities are one, O white moon. How did those three culminate as one, O white moon?
commentary: Traditional teachings often divide reality into three entities: God, the individual soul, and the world of matter. Vallalar wants to understand how these separate elements eventually dissolve into a single, unified truth.

translit: nāṉatuvāy niṟkumvaṇṇam veṇṇilā vē - oru ñāṉaneṟi collukaṇṭāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: So that I may stand as That, O white moon, tell me a path of wisdom, O white moon.
commentary: The plea to 'stand as That' points to a spiritual state where the boundary between the self and God vanishes. Vallalar asks for practical guidance to allow the individual soul to become one with the ultimate reality.

translit: ñāṉamaya māyviḷaṅkum veṇṇilā vē - eṉṉai nāṉaṟiyac collukaṇṭāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: O white moon shining as pure wisdom, tell me how I may know myself, O white moon.
commentary: True spiritual life depends on knowing one's own nature. Vallalar asks for the secret of self-realization: to understand who he really is, stripped of all worldly illusion.

translit: vācivāci yeṉṟuraittār veṇṇilā vē - anta vāciyeṉṉa pēcukaṇṭāy veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He said, "Vasi, vasi," O white moon! Speak and tell me what that "vasi" is, O white moon!
commentary: The master teaches the word "Vasi." Vāci means breath in spiritual practice, and when its syllables are reversed they form "Siva," the name of God. Vallalar asks to reveal the secret behind this instruction on breath and divine union.

translit: aintalaippām pāṭṭukiṉṟār veṇṇilā vē - avar ampalattil niṉṟateṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He makes the five-headed serpent dance, O white moon! Why does he stand in the hall, O white moon!
commentary: The five-headed serpent represents the human mind with its five turbulent senses. God makes this creature dance to his tune, mastering what usually masters us. Vallalar wonders why the divine chooses to stand in the open hall of the soul to perform this feat.

translit: ōreḻutti laintuṇṭeṉpār veṇṇilā vē - atu ūmaiyeḻut tāvateṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He says there are five within a single letter, O white moon! Why does it become the silent letter, O white moon!
commentary: The single letter holding five things refers to a sacred syllable containing the five divine actions or the five sounds of God's name. Yet this sound becomes a "silent letter." Spiritual truth is found in quiet inner experience rather than spoken chants.

translit: ampalattil āṭukiṉṟār veṇṇilā vē - avar āṭukiṉṟa vaṇṇameṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He dances in the hall, O white moon! What is the manner of his dancing, O white moon!
commentary: The dance in the hall represents the continuous movement of divine grace sustaining all creation. Vallalar asks to describe the exact beauty and nature of this cosmic performance.

translit: antarattil āṭukiṉṟār veṇṇilā vē - avar āṭumvakai eppaṭiyō veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He dances in the open space, O white moon! How does he perform this dance, O white moon!
commentary: The open space refers to the vast expanse of the inner mind and the cosmos itself. Vallalar wants to know how God dances in a place with no boundaries and no solid ground. This pictures the divine presence moving freely through the infinite space of pure awareness.

translit: aṇuvilaṇu vāyiruntār veṇṇilā vē - eṅkum ākiniṉṟa vaṇṇameṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He exists as the atom within the atom, O white moon. What is this nature of His, standing as all things everywhere, O white moon?
commentary: God is both the smallest particle imaginable and the vastness of everything that exists. The speaker marvels at how the divine can be entirely hidden inside a single atom while simultaneously being the entire universe.

translit: aṇṭapaki raṇṭamellām veṇṇilā vē - aiyar āṭṭameṉṟu colvateṉṉa veṇṇilā vē.
translation: They say that all the universes and the outer realms are the dance of the Lord, O white moon. What does this mean, O white moon?
commentary: Vallalar asks the moon to explain the mystery of the divine dance. Every expanding galaxy and realm is the continuous motion of God at play.

translit: amparatti lāṭukiṉṟār veṇṇilā vē - eṉṉai āṭṭukiṉṟār imparattē veṇṇilā vē.
translation: He dances in the cosmic space, O white moon. He makes me dance in this world, O white moon.
commentary: God moves the stars above and directs the steps of a soul below. Both the vast universe and the individual are swept up in the same divine dance.

sections.title: The Kommi Dance of Lord Natesar

translit: kommiya ṭippeṇkaḷ kommi yaṭi - iru koṅkaiku luṅkavē kommi yaṭi.
translation: Clap the Kommi, girls, clap the Kommi. Clap the Kommi so your breasts shake.
commentary: Women in Tamil villages traditionally perform the kommi by gathering in a circle and clapping their hands to a shared, joyful beat.

translit: nammai yāḷumpoṉ ṉampala vāṇaṉai nāṭik kommiya ṭiyuṅka ṭi - patam pāṭik kommiya ṭiyuṅka ṭi. - kommi
translation: Seek the Lord of the Golden Hall who rules us and clap the Kommi, girls. Sing his hymns and clap the Kommi, girls.
commentary: The dancers direct their celebration toward Nataraja, who dances in the golden temple of Chidambaram. Singing and clapping are an active, joyful way of seeking the divine.

translit: kāma makaṟṟiya tūya ṉaṭi - civa kāma cavuntari nēya ṉaṭi māmaṟai yōtucev vāya ṉaṭi - maṇi maṉṟeṉu ñāṉavā kāya ṉaṭi. - kommi
translation: He is the pure one who banished lust. He is the lover of beautiful Sivakami. His red mouth chants the great Vedas. His form is the sky of wisdom known as the ruby hall.
commentary: God is pure and free from worldly lust, yet devoted to his companion, the goddess Sivakami. His very body is the vast, open sky of spiritual wisdom, while his voice chants the ancient scriptures known as the Vedas.

translit: āṉantat tāṇṭava rāja ṉaṭi - namai āṭkoṇ ṭaruḷiya tēja ṉaṭi vāṉanta māmalai maṅkai makiḻ - vaṭi vāḷaṉa ṭimaṇa vāḷa ṉaṭi. - kommi
translation: He is the king of the blissful dance. He is the radiant light who claimed and graced us. He is the handsome one, the husband who delights the daughter of the great towering mountain.
commentary: Nataraja is the king of the blissful dance, a cosmic motion that creates and sustains the universe. He is a radiant light that claims devotees personally, and the beloved husband to the goddess born of the towering mountains.

translit: kallaik kaṉivikkuñ cutta ṉaṭi - muṭi kaṅkaik karuḷiya kartta ṉaṭi tillaicci tampara citta ṉaṭi - tēva ciṅkama ṭiyuyar taṅka maṭi. - kommi
translation: He is the pure one who melts even stone. He is the Lord who granted grace to the river Ganga on his head. He is the Siddha of Thillai Chidambaram. He is the divine lion, the exalted gold.
commentary: God's grace can soften the hardest hearts. He is a Siddha, a master of spiritual perfection residing in Thillai Chidambaram, who wears the mighty river Ganges in his hair to protect the world from its crashing force.

translit: peṇṇoru pālvaitta matta ṉaṭi - ciṟu piḷḷaik kaṟikoṇṭa pitta ṉaṭi naṇṇi namakkaru ḷatta ṉaṭi - mika nallaṉa ṭiyellām valla ṉaṭi.. - kommi
translation: He is the wild one who keeps a woman on one half of his body, oh friend. He is the madman who accepted the curry made of a little child, oh friend. He is the Father who draws near to bestow grace upon us, oh friend. He is the exceedingly good one, the all-powerful one, oh friend. Dance the kommi!
commentary: In one form, Lord Siva shares half his body with the goddess. In an ancient legend, he tested a devotee by demanding a meal made from the devotee's own child. Vallalar affectionately calls the divine a madman for these acts. Yet this unpredictable god is the loving Father who approaches us to give his grace.

translit: ampalat tāṭalcey aiya ṉaṭi - aṉpar aṉpuk keḷitaru meyya ṉaṭi tumpai muṭikkaṇi tūya ṉaṭi - cuyañ cōtiya ṭiparañ cōti yaṭi. - kommi
translation: He is the Master who dances in the Hall, oh friend. He is the truthful one who easily yields to the love of his devotees, oh friend. He is the pure one who wears the thumba flower on his crown, oh friend. He is the self-radiant Jothi, the supreme Jothi, oh friend. Dance the kommi!
commentary: The divine Master wears simple white thumba flowers in his hair. Won over easily by the pure love of his devotees, this dancing god is the supreme, self-radiant light of ArutPerunJothi.

translit: kommiya ṭippeṇkaḷ kommi yaṭi - iru koṅkaiku luṅkavē kommi yaṭi.
translation: Dance the kommi, oh women, dance the kommi! Dance the kommi so that your two breasts sway, oh friend!
commentary: The poem ends with a joyful call to the women to dance the kommi, a traditional folk dance performed in a circle with rhythmic clapping. The energetic swaying of the dance captures the physical ecstasy of praising the divine.

translit: taṇmati yoṇmukap peṇmaṇi yē - uṉṉait tāṉkoṇṭa nāyaka rārē ṭi aṇmaiyiṟ poṉṉaṇi yampalat tāṭalcey aiya ramuta raḻaka raṭi.
translation: O jewel among women with a bright face like the cool moon, who is the lord that took you for himself? He is the Lord, the sweet nectar, the beautiful one who dances in the nearby golden hall, my friend.
commentary: The poem takes the form of a dialogue. A friend notices a change in the young woman—representing the soul—and asks who has claimed her.

translit: ceṅkayaṟ kaṇmaṭa maṅkainal lāy - uṉṟaṉ ceṅkai piṭittava rārē ṭi aṅkaya lāraṉṟu poṉṉampa latteṅkaḷ āṉantat tāṇṭava rāja ṉaṭi.
translation: O good and innocent girl with eyes like red carp, who grasped your fair hand? He is no stranger. He is our King of the dance of bliss in the golden hall, my friend.
commentary: In Tamil tradition, grasping the hand signifies a formal vow or marriage. The young woman proudly declares she is bound to the divine King.

translit: kaṉṉaṟ cuvaimoḻi miṉṉiṭai yāy - uṉṉaik kaṉṉi yaḻittava rārē ṭi uṉṉaṟ kariyapoṉ ṉampalat tāṭalcey uttama rāṉanta citta raṭi.
translation: O girl with a waist like lightning and words as sweet as sugarcane, who took your virginity? He is the supreme one, the blissful Siddha who dances in the golden hall that defies human thought, my friend.
commentary: The loss of virginity represents the soul's intimate, total union with the divine. The Lord is described as a Siddha, a perfected spiritual being, whose dance lies beyond ordinary human thought.

translit: tīmaiyi lātapeṇ māmayi lē - uṉṉaic cērntu kalantava rārē ṭi tāmamu ṭikkaṇin tampalat tēyiṉpat tāṇṭavañ ceyyuñ catura raṭi.
translation: O flawless girl like a great peacock, who joined and united with you? He is the skillful one who wears a garland on his crown and performs the dance of bliss in the hall, my friend.
commentary: The friend continues to ask about this deep, transforming relationship. The reply describes God not as an abstract force, but as an intimate, masterful dancer adorned with a garland, bringing absolute joy to the soul.

translit: aṉṉana ṭaippeṇka ḷāramu tē - uṉṉai aṉpiṟ puṇarntava rārē ṭi tuṉṉa luṭaiyiṉa rampalat tēniṉṟa tūya tirunaṭa rāya raṭi.
translation: O precious nectar among women with the graceful gait of a swan, who embraced you in love? He is the pure King of the holy dance who wears a patched garment and stands in the hall, my friend.
commentary: The supreme majesty of the Lord is contrasted with his humble appearance. The soul recognizes the great King of the holy dance even in the patched garment of a wandering ascetic.

translit: kāraḷa kappeṇ cikāmaṇi yē - uṉṟaṉ kaṟpai yaḻittava rārē ṭi pēraḷa vaikkaṭan tampalat tēniṉṟa pittar parāṉanta nitta raṭi.
translation: O crest-jewel among women with dark hair, who ruined your chastity, girl? It was the madman who stands in the Ambalam transcending all vast measures, the eternal one of supreme bliss, girl.
commentary: The soul's complete surrender to the divine is pictured as a young woman losing her honor to a wild lover. Vallalar calls the divine a madman because supreme grace operates outside human logic and social rules. This mad lover stands in the Ambalam, the hall of true consciousness, a space far too vast for the mind to measure. By giving herself up to this eternal bliss, the soul leaves behind worldly ego and conventional attachments.

sections.title: Song for the Lord of the Dance

tamil: தெண்டனிட்டே னென்று சொல்ல டி - சு வாமிக்குநான்
translit: teṇṭaṉiṭṭē ṉeṉṟu colla ṭi - cu vāmikkunāṉ teṇṭaṉiṭṭē ṉeṉṟu colla ṭi.
translation: Tell Him I bowed down, my friend. Tell the Lord that I bowed down.
commentary: Vallalar adopts the persona of a woman asking her companion to act as a messenger and deliver a humble greeting to the Lord.

translit: taṇṭalai viḷaṅkun tillait talattiṟpoṉ ṉampalattē kaṇṭavar mayaṅkavēṭaṅ kaṭṭiyāṭu kiṉṟavarkku teṇṭa
translation: To Him who dances in the Golden Hall in the sacred town of Thillai surrounded by lush gardens, taking on an appearance that mesmerizes all who see Him, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: Thillai is the ancient name for Chidambaram, the temple town where Siva is worshipped as Nataraja, the Lord of the Dance. The Golden Hall is where He performs His cosmic dance, taking on a form that captivates the mind.

translit: kaṟpūra vācamvīcum poṟpānti rumukattē kaṉintapuṉ ṉakaiyāṭak karuṇaikka ṭaikkaṇāṭa aṟpārpoṉ ṉampalattē āṉantat tāṇṭavam āṭikkoṇ ṭēyeṉṉai āṭṭaṅkaṇ ṭārukku teṇṭa
translation: To Him whose beautiful divine face radiates the fragrance of camphor, where a gentle smile plays and eyes cast graceful side glances. To Him who performs the dance of bliss in the splendid Golden Hall and watches me dance in His play, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: Vallalar visualizes the divine face and the sacred scent of camphor used in temple worship. He recognizes a connection between God and the soul: while the Lord performs His dance of bliss, He simultaneously watches Vallalar move through the dance of his own life.

translit: iḻintālu nammaiyiṅkē yēṟṟuvā reṉṟaṭaintāl ēṟṟuvār pōlēpiṉṉu miḻiyavaip pārukkup paḻantāṉ naḻuvimellap pālil viḻuntateṉṉap pacappip pacappiyaṉpar paṇṭam paṟippavarkkuteṇṭa
translation: To Him who, when we approach Him trusting He will uplift us even if we fall, acts as though He will accept us but casts us down again. To Him who speaks sweetly like a fruit slipping softly into milk, only to steal the belongings of His devotees, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: Vallalar praises God through playful complaint. He teases the Lord for being unpredictable, drawing devotees in only to steal their hearts and strip them of earthly attachments.

translit: cuṭṭatiru nīṟupūcit tontōmeṉ ṟāṭuvārkkut tōṉṟutalai mālaiyaṇi tōḷviḷaṅka varuvārkkup piṭṭukkācaip paṭṭumāṟaṉ pirampaṭi paṭṭavarkkup piḷḷaikkaṟik kācaikoṇṭa kaḷḷattava vēṭarukku teṇṭa
translation: To Him who smears burnt holy ash and dances chanting rhythmic syllables. To Him who arrives with radiant shoulders wearing a garland of skulls. To Him who longed for sweet rice flour and took blows from the Pandya king's cane. To the deceptive ascetic who craved a meal of a child's flesh, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: Vallalar recalls famous Tamil stories of God playfully testing His saints. Once, He carried mud for a poor woman in exchange for sweet rice flour, taking a beating from a king's cane for neglecting the work. He also tested another devoted saint by appearing as a fierce ascetic, demanding a meal made from the saint's own child to prove his absolute surrender.

translit: vāḻntārai mēṉmēlum vāḻaccey pavarukku mācupaṟit tavarkaiyiṟ kācupaṟik kiṉṟavarkkut tāḻntārai yaṭikkaṭi tāḻakkāṇ pavarukkut tāṉāki nāṉākit taṉiyēniṉ ṟavarukkuteṇṭa
translation: To Him who makes the prosperous prosper even more, to Him who snatches coins from the hands of those who have stripped away their impurities, to Him who constantly watches the lowly fall even lower, to Him who became Himself, became me, and stands all alone, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: When God makes the prosperous prosper or watches the lowly fall, He is actually enriching those already filled with devotion and breaking down the ego of the humble. Snatching coins from the pure means stripping away their last worldly attachments so He can merge with them.

translit: ātiyanta naṭuvillā āṉanta nāṭarukku aṇṭaruyir kāttamaṇi kaṇṭacaci kaṇṭarukkuc cōtimaya māyviḷaṅkun tūyavaṭi vāḷarukkut toṇṭarkuṭi keṭukkavē tujaṅkaṭṭik koṇṭavarkku teṇṭa
translation: To Him of the blissful realm that has no beginning, middle, or end, to Him who protected the lives of the celestials, who has a sapphire-dark neck and wears the moon, to Him of pure form who shines radiantly as Jothi, to Him who has hoisted a flag specifically to ruin the households of His devotees, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: The ruin of the devotees' households is actually the destruction of their worldly attachments, freeing them for a higher spiritual life. The Lord, who in traditional stories saved the celestial beings by holding deadly poison in His dark throat, is shown here shining as pure, radiant Jothi.

translit: pāṭṭukkācaip paṭṭumuṉṉam paravaitaṉ vāyiliṟpōyp paṇpuraittut tūtaṉeṉṟē paṭṭaṅkaṭṭik koṇṭavarkku vīṭṭukkācaip paṭuvārai vīṭṭaiviṭṭut turattiyē vēṭṭāṇṭi yāyulakil ōṭṭāṇṭi yākkuvārkku teṇṭa
translation: To Him who desired songs in the past and went to the doorstep of Paravaiyar, speaking sweet words and earning the title of messenger, to Him who chases out of their worldly homes those who desire the ultimate home, making them destitute wanderers holding begging bowls in this world, tell Him I bowed down.
commentary: God loves devotion so much that He once acted as a romantic messenger to the woman Paravaiyar for a saint who sang beautiful songs. Now, making seekers destitute wanderers is His way of chasing them out of earthly homes to ensure they rely entirely on divine grace rather than physical wealth.

translit: tāyvaṟiṟṟiṟ piṟavātu tāṉē muḷaittavarkkuc cātikula maṟiyātu tāṇṭavañcey kiṉṟavarkku ēya toḻilaruḷu meṉpirāṇa nāyakarkku ēmānta varaiyellām ēmāttu mīcarukku
translation: To Him who sprouted on His own without being born from a mother's womb, to Him who performs the cosmic dance knowing nothing of caste or clan, to the Lord of my life who assigns fitting tasks, to the Lord who deceives all the gullible ones,
commentary: God dances knowing nothing of caste or clan: such human divisions have no place before him. Vallalar lovingly calls the Lord a deceiver because He playfully tricks people into giving up their worldly illusions in exchange for true spiritual life.

tamil: தெண்டனிட்டே னென்று சொல்ல டி - சு வாமிக்குநான்
translit: teṇṭaṉiṭṭē ṉeṉṟu colla ṭi - cu vāmikkunāṉ teṇṭaṉiṭṭē ṉeṉṟu colla ṭi.
translation: tell Him I bowed down, girl. Tell the Lord I bowed down, girl.
commentary: Vallalar completes the message, asking the companion to carry the news of total surrender to the Lord who playfully disrupts the world.

translit: iṉṉan tayavuvara vilaiyā - uṉakkeṉmītil eṉṉa varmañ colaiyā.
translation: Has mercy not yet come? Tell me what grudge you hold against me.
commentary: The poem opens with a remarkably direct and conversational question to the divine. The speaker asks God plainly why grace is being withheld, wondering aloud if God holds a personal grudge against him.

translit: aṉṉam pālikkuntillaip poṉṉam palattilāṭum aracē - aracē - aracēyeṉ ṟalaṟavum iṉṉan
translation: Even as I cry out, "O King, O King, O King who dances in the golden hall of Thillai that grants nourishment!" has mercy still not come?
commentary: Vallalar addresses God as the sovereign dancer in Thillai (Chidambaram), a sacred temple space of both spiritual and physical nourishment. Repeating his plea three times captures the raw desperation of a cry for a response that never arrives.

translit: ciṉṉañ ciṟuvayati leṉṉai yaṭimaikoṇṭa civamē - civamē - civamēyeṉ ṟalaṟavum iṉṉan
translation: Even as I cry out, "O Sivam, O Sivam, O Sivam who took me as your servant at a very tender age!" has mercy still not come?
commentary: God claimed Vallalar as a devotee when he was only a young child. This lifelong bond makes the current silence feel especially painful and confusing.

translit: muṉṉam piḻaipoṟuttā yiṉṉam poṟātuviṭṭāl muṟaiyō - muṟaiyō - muṟaiyōveṉ ṟalaṟavum iṉṉan
translation: Even as I cry out, "You forgave my faults before. If you do not forgive them now, is it just, is it just, is it just?" has mercy still not come?
commentary: Vallalar demands divine justice. Since God has already established a pattern of forgiving past mistakes, it would be unfair to withhold that forgiveness now.

translit: taṉṉai yaṟiyāveṉṉai yiṉṉa luṟacceytāyē takumō - takumō - takumōveṉ ṟalaṟavum iṉṉan
translation: Even as I cry out, "You have caused me, one who does not even know himself, to suffer in affliction. Is this fair, is this fair, is this fair?" has mercy still not come?
commentary: Vallalar points to his helpless ignorance, confessing he does not even understand his own nature. He questions how a compassionate God can let such a vulnerable soul endure continued suffering.

translit: paṇṭu makiḻnteṉaiyāṭ koṇṭu karuṇaiceyta paramē - paramē - paramēyeṉ ṟalaṟavum iṉṉan
translation: Even as I cry out, "O Supreme One, O Supreme One, O Supreme One who joyfully made me your own and granted me grace in the past,"
commentary: Vallalar grounds his plea in the past, reminding the Supreme that God has already joyfully accepted him and shown him grace before.

translit: koṇṭu kulampēcuvā ruṇṭō vulakileṅkaḷ kuruvē - kuruvē - kuruvēyeṉ ṟalaṟavum
translation: and even as I cry out, "O our Guru, O Guru, O Guru, is there anyone in this world who takes someone in and then criticizes their lineage,"
commentary: A true master (Guru) does not accept a disciple only to later judge them based on their family background or worldly lineage. Vallalar asks God to show that same unconditional acceptance now.

translit: iṉṉan tayavuvara vilaiyā - uṉakkeṉmītil eṉṉa varmañ colaiyā.
translation: do you still feel no compassion? Tell me, what grievance do you hold against me?
commentary: Despite these desperate cries, divine compassion is still withheld. Vallalar asks God if a hidden fault or grudge stands between them.

translit: ākamamu māraṇamu marumporuḷeṉ ṟoruṅkuraitta ēkavuru vākiniṉṟā rivarārcol tōḻi mākanati muṭikkaṇintu maṇimaṉṟu ḷaṉavarata nākamaṇi miḷiranaṭa navilvārkāṇ peṇṇē.
translation: "Friend, tell me, who is this standing as the single form, whom the Agamas and Vedas unanimously proclaim as the rare reality?" "O girl, see, He wears the celestial river on His crown and dances unceasingly in the hall of gems while the serpent's jewel gleams."
commentary: The single, supreme truth described by ancient scriptures is not an abstract concept, but the active, dancing Lord. A girl asks her companion to identify the ultimate reality praised by both the Agamas (scriptures of temple worship and theology) and the Vedas (ancient root texts). The friend answers by describing God as a cosmic dancer wearing a celestial river on his head, showing that the highest truth is a living, continuous presence.

translit: aruḷālē aruḷiṟai aruḷkiṉṟa poḻutaṅ kaṉupava mākiṉṟa teṉṉaṭi tāyē teruḷālē maruḷālē teriyātu teriyum tirunaṭa iṉpameṉ ṟaṟiyāyō makaḷē.
translation: "Mother, what is experienced there when the Lord of Grace grants grace through grace?" "Daughter, do you not know it is the bliss of the divine dance, unknowable through clarity or delusion, yet known?"
commentary: The experience of pure grace cannot be grasped by ordinary thinking. When God grants grace to a soul, the result is spiritual bliss. This joy of the divine dance exists beyond the mind's normal states of clarity or confusion, revealing itself in a way the intellect cannot capture.

translit: aṟivālē aṟiviṉai aṟikiṉṟa poḻutaṅ kaṉupava mākiṉṟa teṉṉaṭi tāyē ceṟivālē piṟivālē teriyātu teriyum tiruvaruḷ uruvameṉ ṟaṟiyāyō makaḷē.
translation: "Mother, what is experienced there when knowledge is known through knowledge?" "Daughter, do you not know it is the form of divine grace, unknowable through union or separation, yet known?"
commentary: True spiritual understanding reveals the actual form of divine grace. The daughter asks what happens when the soul's pure awareness directly knows the ultimate reality.
