The mother replies that this experience transcends all earthly ideas of coming together or breaking apart. It is a direct encounter with grace that cannot be measured by ordinary human feelings of physical union or separation.

tamil: திருவருட் புனிதை மகிழநின் றாடும் தில்லைமன் றழகனே என்பாள்
மருவருட் கடலே மாணிக்க மலையே மதிச்சடை வள்ளலே என்பாள்
இருவருக் கரிய ஒருவனே எனக்கிங் கியார்துணை நின்னலா தென்பாள்
வெருவிஉட் குழைவாள் விழிகணீர் துளிப்பாள் வெய்துயிர்ப் பாள்என்றன் மின்னே.
translit: tiruvaruṭ puṉitai makiḻaniṉ ṟāṭum tillaimaṉ ṟaḻakaṉē eṉpāḷ maruvaruṭ kaṭalē māṇikka malaiyē maticcaṭai vaḷḷalē eṉpāḷ iruvaruk kariya oruvaṉē eṉakkiṅ kiyārtuṇai niṉṉalā teṉpāḷ veruvi-uṭ kuḻaivāḷ viḻikaṇīr tuḷippāḷ veytuyirp pāḷeṉṟaṉ miṉṉē.
translation: "O beautiful Lord of the Thillai hall who dances to the delight of the holy Goddess of grace," she cries. "O fragrant ocean of grace, mountain of rubies, generous Lord with the moon in your matted hair," she cries. "O unique Lord, rare even for the two great gods to reach, who is my companion here but you?" she cries. Startled, her heart melts, her eyes shed tears, and she breathes heavy sighs, my lightning-bright daughter.
commentary: The young woman is overwhelmed by longing. She praises the Lord of Thillai (Chidambaram, the sacred city of the dancing Siva). Her physical reactions show a love that has taken over her body and mind.

tamil: ஓடுவாள் தில்லைத் திருச்சிற்றம் பலம்என் றுருகுவாள் உணர்விலள் ஆகித்
தேடுவாள் திகைப்பாள் தியங்குவாள் ஐயோ தெய்வமே தெய்வமே என்பாள்
வாடுவாள் மயங்கி வருந்துவாள் இருந்து வல்வினை யேன்பெற்ற மகளே.
translit: ōṭuvāḷ tillait tirucciṟṟam palameṉ ṟurukuvāḷ uṇarvilaḷ ākit tēṭuvāḷ tikaippāḷ tiyaṅkuvāḷ aiyō teyvamē teyvamē eṉpāḷ pāṭuvāḷpataippāḷ pataṟuvāḷnāṉpeṇpāvikāṇpāvikāṇeṉpāḷ vāṭuvāḷ mayaṅki varuntuvāḷ iruntu valviṉai yēṉpeṟṟa makaḷē.
translation: She runs. Crying "Thillai's holy little hall," she melts and loses her senses. She searches, stands bewildered, and swoons. "Alas, O God, O God!" she cries. She sings, trembles, and panics. "Look, I am a sinful woman, look, a sinner!" she cries. She withers, faints, and suffers, this daughter born to me, a woman of cruel karma.
commentary: The daughter's spiritual longing causes panic and physical collapse. She feels unworthy of the God she seeks. Watching this agony, the mother blames her own karma (the accumulated result of past actions) for bringing such suffering upon her child.

tamil: இலகுபே ரின்ப வாரிஎன் கின்றாள் என்னுயிர்க் கிறைவன்என் கின்றாள்
அலகிலாக் கருணை அமுதன்என் கின்றாள் அன்பர்கட்கன்பன்என் கின்றாள்
திலகவா ணுதலாள் இவ்வணம் புலம்பித் தியக்கமுற் றழுங்குகின் றாளே.
translit: ulakelān taḻaippappotuviṉil ōṅkum orutaṉit teyvameṉkiṉṟāḷ ilakupē riṉpa vāri-eṉ kiṉṟāḷ eṉṉuyirk kiṟaivaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ alakilāk karuṇai amutaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ aṉparkaṭkaṉpaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ tilakavā ṇutalāḷ ivvaṇam pulampit tiyakkamuṟ ṟaḻuṅkukiṉ ṟāḷē.
translation: "He is the one supreme God who rises high in the common hall so that all the worlds may flourish," she cries. "He is the shining ocean of immense bliss," she cries. "He is the Lord of my life," she cries. "He is the nectar of boundless grace," she cries. "He is the lover of His devotees," she cries. Lamenting like this, the girl with the bright marked forehead sinks into bewilderment and grief.
commentary: Even in her bewilderment, the young woman recognizes the divine. God is a personal protector who loves those who turn to Him, and her inability to reach Him leaves her consumed by grief.

tamil: உருஎலாம் உடைய ஒருவன்என் கின்றாள் உச்சிமேல் கரங்குவிக் கின்றாள்
கருஎலாங் கடந்தாங் கவன்திரு மேனி காண்பதெந் நாள்கொல்என் கின்றாள்
translit: tiru-elāmaḷikkumteyvameṉ kiṉṟāḷ tirucciṟṟampalavaṉeṉkiṉṟāḷ uru-elām uṭaiya oruvaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ uccimēl karaṅkuvik kiṉṟāḷ karu-elāṅ kaṭantāṅ kavaṉtiru mēṉi kāṇpaten nāḷkoleṉ kiṉṟāḷ maru-elāmmayaṅkum malarkkuḻal muṭiyāḷ varuntukiṉṟāḷeṉṟaṉ makaḷē.
translation: "He is the God who grants all blessings," she cries. "He is the Lord of the holy little hall," she cries. "He is the unique one who takes all forms," she cries, folding her hands in prayer above her head. "When will I cross beyond all cycles of birth to see His holy form?" she cries. She suffers so much, my daughter with flowers braided into her fragrant hair.
commentary: The goal of the daughter's intense love is liberation. She wants to break free from the cycle of birth and death to see God face to face. Folding her hands above her head is a traditional gesture of surrender, showing she holds nothing back in her spiritual quest.

tamil: மின்இணைச் சடில விடங்கன்என் கின்றாள் விடைக்கொடி விமலன்என் கின்றாள்
பொன்இணை மலர்த்தாள் புனிதன்என் கின்றாள் பொதுவிலே நடிப்பன்என் கின்றாள்
என்இணை விழிகள் அவன்திரு அழகை என்றுகொல் காண்பதென் கின்றாள்
துன்இணை முலைகள் விம்முற இடைபோல் துவள்கின்றாள் பசியபொற் றொடியே.
translit: miṉiṇaic caṭila viṭaṅkaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ viṭaikkoṭi vimalaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ poṉiṇai malarttāḷ puṉitaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ potuvilē naṭippaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ eṉiṇai viḻikaḷ avaṉtiru aḻakai eṉṟukol kāṇpateṉ kiṉṟāḷ tuṉiṇai mulaikaḷ vimmuṟa iṭaipōl tuvaḷkiṉṟāḷ paciyapoṟ ṟoṭiyē.
translation: "He is the beautiful Lord with lightning-like matted hair," she cries. "He is the pure one with the bull banner," she cries. "He is the holy one with feet like a pair of golden flowers," she cries. "He dances in the common hall," she cries. "When will my two eyes see His holy beauty?" she cries. As her closely set breasts heave, she wilts just like her slender waist, this girl wearing fresh golden bracelets.
commentary: The young woman visualizes the traditional features of Siva. Her devotion is so intense that it exhausts her physical body. Her wilting frame shows that longing for God drains away worldly strength until only love remains.

tamil: கருங்களிற் றுரிபோர்த் தம்பலத் தாடும் கருணைஎங் கடவுள்என் கின்றாள்
பெருங்களி துளும்ப வடவனத் தோங்கும் பித்தரில் பித்தன்என் கின்றாள்
ஒருங்களி மிழற்றும் குழலினார் என்போல் உறுவரோ அவனைஎன்கின்றாள்
தருங்களி உண்டாள் போல்கின்றாள் நாணும் தவிர்க்கின்றாள் என்அருந் தவளே.
translit: karuṅkaḷiṟ ṟuripōrt tampalat tāṭum karuṇai-eṅ kaṭavuḷeṉ kiṉṟāḷ peruṅkaḷi tuḷumpa vaṭavaṉat tōṅkum pittaril pittaṉeṉ kiṉṟāḷ oruṅkaḷi miḻaṟṟum kuḻaliṉār eṉpōl uṟuvarō avaṉai-eṉkiṉṟāḷ taruṅkaḷi uṇṭāḷ pōlkiṉṟāḷ nāṇum tavirkkiṉṟāḷ eṉarun tavaḷē.
translation: She says, "He is our God of grace who dances in the Hall wearing the flayed skin of a black elephant." She says, "Brimming with great joy, He stands high in the banyan forest, the maddest of the mad." She says, "Will women with hair humming with bees ever attain Him like I do?" My girl of rare penance acts like one who has drunk intoxicating toddy, casting aside her modesty.
commentary: The soul's love for God sweeps away ordinary social manners. The young woman acts as if drunk on divine grace, boldly claiming her unique bond with the dancing Lord over all others.

tamil: மன்றிடை நடிக்கும் மணாளனை அல்லால் மதிப்பனோ பிறரைஎன்கின்றாள்
வன்துயர் நீக்கும் அவன்திரு வடிவை மறப்பனோ கணமும்என் கின்றாள்
translit: maṉṟiṭai naṭikkum maṇāḷaṉai allāl matippaṉō piṟarai-eṉkiṉṟāḷ vaṉtuyar nīkkum avaṉtiru vaṭivai maṟappaṉō kaṇamumeṉ kiṉṟāḷ oṉṟumil lavaṉeṉ ṟuraikkiṉum ellām uṭaiyavaṉākumeṉkiṉṟāḷ poṉṟutal piṟaḻtal iṉiyuṟēṉ eṉṟēpoṟṟoṭipoṅkukiṉṟāḷē.
translation: She says, "Will I value anyone other than the Bridegroom who dances in the Hall?" She says, "Will I forget even for a moment His sacred form that removes harsh sorrow?" She says, "Even if people say He has nothing, He is the Lord of everything." The girl with golden bracelets surges with emotion, declaring, "I will no longer suffer death or deviation."
commentary: Devotion fixes the mind on the divine, bypassing worldly logic. Though others might see the Lord as a wandering ascetic with nothing, she knows He is the master of all things, and her faith frees her from death itself.

tamil: பெருத்தகுங் குமப்பொற் கலசவாண் முலையார் பேசுக பலபல என்பாள்
மருத்தகு குழலாள் மனமொழி உடலம் மற்றவும் அவன்கழற் கென்பாள்
குருத்தகு குவளைக் கண்ணின்நீர் கொழிப்பாள் குதுகுலிப் பாள்பசுங் கொடியே.
translit: tiruttaku tillait tirucciṟṟampalattē teyvamoṉ ṟuṇṭemakkeṉpāḷ peruttakuṅ kumappoṟ kalacavāṇ mulaiyār pēcuka palapala eṉpāḷ maruttaku kuḻalāḷ maṉamoḻi uṭalam maṟṟavum avaṉkaḻaṟ keṉpāḷ kuruttaku kuvaḷaik kaṇṇiṉnīr koḻippāḷ kutukulip pāḷpacuṅ koṭiyē.
translation: She says, "I have one God in the sacred little Hall of beautiful Thillai." She says, "Let the women with bright breasts like great golden pots smeared with vermilion gossip and say many things." The girl with fragrant hair says, "My mind, speech, body, and all else belong to His feet." The tender creeper of a girl sheds copious tears from her fresh blue lotus eyes and rejoices.
commentary: The young woman offers her being to God, dedicating her physical body, words, and thoughts to His feet. She remains unaffected by the mocking gossip of her peers, weeping only tears of joy for her one Lord in Thillai.

tamil: அம்பலத் தாடும் அழகனைக் காணா தருந்தவும் பொருந்துமோ என்பாள்
கம்பமுற் றிடுவாள் கண்கள்நீர் உகுப்பாள் கைகுவிப் பாள்உளங் கனிவாள்
வம்பணி முலைகள் இரண்டும்நோக் கிடுவாள் வள்ளலைப்பரிகிலீர் என்பாள்
உம்பரன் தவஞ்செய் திடுமினீர் என்பாள் உயங்குவாள் மயங்குவாள் உணர்வே.
translit: ampalat tāṭum aḻakaṉaik kāṇā taruntavum poruntumō eṉpāḷ kampamuṟ ṟiṭuvāḷ kaṇkaḷnīr ukuppāḷ kaikuvip pāḷuḷaṅ kaṉivāḷ vampaṇi mulaikaḷ iraṇṭumnōk kiṭuvāḷ vaḷḷalaipparikilīr eṉpāḷ umparaṉ tavañcey tiṭumiṉīr eṉpāḷ uyaṅkuvāḷ mayaṅkuvāḷ uṇarvē.
translation: She says, "Is it right to eat without seeing the beautiful One who dances in the Hall?" She trembles, sheds tears, joins her hands in reverence, and melts in her heart. Looking at her two adorned breasts, she says, "You do not embrace the generous Lord. Perform exalted penance." She suffers and swoons in her awareness.
commentary: The desire for God becomes an overwhelming physical ache that interrupts the basic routine of eating. Every part of her body yearns for divine union; she even tells her own form to perform penance for failing to reach Him, fainting from the force of her love.

translit: cuntara nīṟaṇi cuntarar naṭaṉat toḻilvallār vantaṉar iṅkē vantaṉam eṉṟēṉ mātēnī mantaṇam itukēḷ antaṉam ilanam vāḻvellām antaram eṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā avarcūtē.
translation: The beautiful Lord who wears beautiful ash, the master of the art of dance, came here. I said, "Welcome." He replied, "Oh woman, listen to this secret. All our boundless life is the vast sky." What is his trickery, my friend!
commentary: The soul welcomes the divine into her inner life. He reveals that their true life has no physical limits or worldly bounds, existing in the vast sky of pure spiritual awareness.

translit: nampala māmeṉa naṉmaṉai pukkār naṭarājar empala māvīr emperu māṉī rē-eṉṟēṉ vampala maṭavāy emmuṭai iṉpa vāḻvellām ampalam eṉṟār eṉṉaṭi ammā avarcūtē.
translation: Lord Nataraja entered our good house, saying, "This is our place." I said, "You are my strength, You are my great Lord." He replied, "Oh innocent woman, our entire life of bliss is the open hall." What is his trickery, my friend!
commentary: The divine dancer claims the soul's inner being as his rightful home. Through wordplay, he reveals that their life of perfect bliss unfolds in the open hall of grace. True union with the divine happens in this boundless space of consciousness.

note: Editor's note: theme (turai): the heroine speaks to her companion (talaimakaḷ pāṅkiyoṭu kūṟal, தலைமகள் பாங்கியொடு கூறல்). Verse 1: in a letter of 26 November 1866 to Irukkam Rathina Mudaliar, Vallalar corrected the opening to viṇpaṭaitta poḻiṟṟillai (விண்படைத்த பொழிற்றில்லை); the first edition (1867) and the 1896 edition print viṇpaṭaitta pukaḻttillai (விண்படைத்த புகழ்த்தில்லை). This book follows his correction.
translit: viṇpaṭaitta poḻiṟṟillai ampalattāṉ evarkkum mēlāṉāṉ aṉparuḷam mēvunaṭa rājaṉ paṇpaṭaitta eṉai-aṟiyā iḷamparuvan taṉilē parintuvantu mālaiyiṭṭāṉ pārttaṟiyāṉ mīṭṭum peṇpaṭaitta peṇkaḷellām avamatittē valatu pēcukiṉṟār kūcukiṉṟēṉ picci-eṉal āṉēṉ kaṇpaṭaittum kuḻiyilviḻak kaṇakkumuṇṭō avaṉṟaṉ kaṇakkaṟintum viṭuvēṉō kaṇṭāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: The Lord of the Hall in Thillai with its sky-touching groves stands above all others. He is Nataraja, the King of Dance who dwells in the hearts of His devotees. In my tender youth when I did not yet know myself, He came with compassion and placed a marriage garland on me. He has never looked back at me since. All the women despise me and speak harshly. I shrink in shame and am called a madwoman. Is it right to fall into a pit when one has eyes? Knowing His true nature, will I ever let Him go? See this, my friend.
commentary: Vallalar pictures his soul as a young bride claimed by God before she was mature enough to understand what it meant. Left waiting for His return, she faces the mockery of ordinary society. Even when the world calls her devotion madness, she refuses to abandon the truth she has seen.

translit: cīttamaṇi ampalattāṉ eṉpirāṇa nātaṉ civaperumāṉ emperumāṉ celvanaṭa rājaṉ vāytta-eṉṉai aṟiyāta iḷamparuvan taṉilē makiḻntuvantu mālaiyiṭṭāṉ maṟittummukam pārāṉ āyttakalai kaṟṟuṇarnta aṇaṅkaṉaiyār tamakkuḷ ārceyta pōtaṉaiyō āṉālum itukēḷ kāyttamaram vaḷaiyāta kaṇakkumuṇṭō avaṉṟaṉ kaṇakkaṟintum viṭuvēṉō kaṇṭāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: The Lord of the gem-studded Hall is the Lord of my life. He is Lord Siva, our master, the wealthy King of Dance. In my tender youth when I did not know myself, He came with joy and placed a marriage garland on me. He refuses to turn and look at my face. I wonder who among the beautiful women well-versed in the arts poisoned His mind. Even so, listen to this. Is there a rule that a tree heavy with fruit will not bend? Knowing His true nature, will I ever let Him go? See this, my friend.
commentary: Vallalar wonders if his Lord has been distracted by others, yet knows His nature is generous. He compares God to a tree heavy with ripe fruit, trusting that just as a burdened branch naturally bends to offer its harvest, His abundant grace must eventually reach him.

translit: eṉṉuyiril kalantukalan tiṉikkiṉṟa perumāṉ eṉiṟaivaṉ potuvilnaṭam iyaṟṟumnaṭa rājaṉ taṉṉai-aṟi yāpparuvat teṉṉaimaṇam purintāṉ taṉai-aṟinta paruvattē eṉai-aṟiya virumpāṉ piṉṉai-aṉṟi muṉṉumoru piḻaipurintēṉ illai peṇparitā paṅkāṇal peruntakaikkum aḻakō kaṉṉaleṉṟāl kaikkiṉṟa kaṇakkumuṇṭō avaṉṟaṉ kaṇakkaṟintum viṭuvēṉō kaṇṭāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: The great Lord mingles endlessly in my life and tastes so sweet. My Lord is Nataraja, the King of Dance who performs in the common Hall. He married me at an age when I did not know myself. Now that I have reached the age of knowing myself, He does not wish to know me. I have committed no fault in the past or the present. Is it beautiful for this noble Lord to watch a woman suffer in sorrow? Is there a rule that sugarcane tastes bitter? Knowing His true nature, will I ever let Him go? See this, my friend.
commentary: The soul feels the painful irony of spiritual timing. When she was ignorant, God sought her out, but now that she is fully awake and longing for Him, He remains hidden. Despite this pain, she knows God cannot be cruel, just as sugarcane cannot taste bitter.

translit: teruḷamutat taṉiyōkar cintaiyilum ñāṉac celvaraṟi viṭattumnaṭañ ceyyumnaṭa rājaṉ aruḷamutam aḷippaṉeṉṟē aṉṟumaṇam puṇarntāṉ aḷittaṟiyāṉ aṇuttuṇaiyum aṉupavittum aṟiyēṉ maruḷuṭaiyāṉ allaṉoru vañcakaṉum allaṉ maṉamirakkam mika-uṭaiyāṉ valviṉaiyēṉ aḷavil iruḷuṭaiyār pōlirukkum iyalpeṉṉai avaṉṟaṉ iyalpaṟintum viṭuvēṉō iṉittāṉeṉ tōḻī.
translation: Nataraja is the King of Dance who dances in the minds of matchless yogis possessing nectar-like clarity and in the awareness of those rich in wisdom. He married me that day and promised to give me the nectar of His grace. He has given me nothing, and I have not experienced even an atom of it. He is not confused, and He is no deceiver. He possesses immense compassion in His heart. Why does He act like someone trapped in darkness toward me, a soul burdened by harsh karma? Knowing His true nature, will I let Him go now, my friend?
commentary: Vallalar knows God does not deceive anyone and that His heart is full of compassion. If He seems distant, the barrier is not His cruelty. The soul wonders if her own heavy past actions have created a darkness that makes Him appear hidden.

translit: ciṉmayamām potuviṉilē taṉmayamāy niṉṟu tirunaṭañcey peruṅkaruṇaic celvanaṭa rājaṉ eṉmayamnāṉ aṟiyāta iḷamparuvan taṉilē eṉṉaimaṇam purintaṉaṉī tellārum aṟivār iṉmayamil lātavarpōl iṉṟumaṇan taruḷāṉ iṟai-aḷavum piḻaipurintēṉ illai-avaṉ itayam kaṉmayamō aṉṟucuvaik kaṉimayamē eṉṉum kaṇakkaṟintum viṭuvēṉō kaṇṭāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He stands as His true self in the Hall of pure consciousness. He is the wealthy King of Dance of great compassion who performs the sacred dance. In my tender youth when I did not know my own nature, He married me. Everyone knows this. Today He refuses to grant me union and acts as if He lacks all sweetness. I have not committed even the slightest fault. Is His heart made of stone? No, it is made of sweet fruit. Knowing this truth, will I ever let Him go? See this, my friend.
commentary: God performs His sacred dance in a space of pure consciousness. Though He keeps His distance, the soul refuses to believe His heart is made of stone. She is certain His core is as sweet as ripe fruit, and this trust makes it impossible for her to give up on Him.

translit: eṉkuṇattāṉ ellārkkum iṟaivaṉellām vallāṉ eṉakattum puṟattumuḷāṉ iṉpanaṭa rājaṉ peṇkuṇattai aṟiyāta iḷamparuvan taṉilē piccēṟṟi maṇampurintāṉ peritukaḷit tiruntēṉ vaṇkuṇattāl aṉupavamnāṉ aṟiyaniṉṟa poḻutil vantaṟiyāṉ iṉpamoṉṟum tantaṟiyāṉ avaṉum veṇkuṇattāṉ allaṉmiku nallaṉeṉap palakāl viḻittaṟintum viṭuvēṉō viḷampāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He shares my nature. He is the Lord of everyone and the all-powerful one. He exists both inside me and outside me. He is the joyful Nataraja. During my tender youth, before I knew the nature of womanhood, He made me mad with love and married me. I rejoiced greatly. Yet, when I stood ready to understand the experience through mature nature, He does not come. He gives no pleasure at all. Still, He is not a hollow-natured man. He is exceedingly good. Having realized this many times with awakened eyes, will I ever let Him go? Tell me, my friend.
commentary: Speaking as a bride to her friend, Vallalar says God claimed his soul in its innocent youth, filling it with a joyful madness. Now that the soul is spiritually mature and ready for union, God withholds His presence. Yet, knowing the Lord's absolute goodness, the soul refuses to abandon Him.

translit: poyyāta pukaḻuṭaiyāṉ potuvilnaṭam purivāṉ puṇṇiyarpāl naṇṇiyanaṟ puṉitanaṭa rājaṉ koyyāta arumpaṉaiya iḷamparuvan taṉilē kuṟittumaṇam purintaṉaṉnāṉ maṟittumvarak kāṇēṉ ceyyāta ceykai-oṉṟum ceytaṟiyēṉ ciṟitum tiruvuḷamē aṟiyummaṟṟeṉ oru-uḷattiṉ ceyalkaḷ naiyāta eṉṟaṉuyir nātaṉaruṭ perumai nāṉaṟintum viṭuvēṉō navilāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He possesses unfailing fame. He dances in the common hall. He is the pure Nataraja who approaches the virtuous. During my tender youth, when I was like an unplucked bud, He chose me and married me. Yet now I do not see Him returning. I have not committed any wrong deed, not even slightly. His divine heart alone knows the actions of my solitary heart. Knowing the glorious grace of the Lord of my uncrushed soul, will I ever let Him go? Tell me, my friend.
commentary: The soul remembers being chosen by God when it was as innocent as an unplucked flower bud. Even though she has committed no wrong, the Divine delays His return. Because God alone knows the purity of her heart, the bride waits with steady trust and refuses to walk away.

translit: kaṇṇaṉaiyāṉ eṉṉuyiril kalantuniṉṟa kaṇavaṉ kaṇakkaṟivāṉ piṇakkaṟiyāṉ karuṇainaṭa rājaṉ taṇṇaṉaiyām iḷamparuvan taṉṉileṉait taṉittut tāṉēvan taruḷpurintu taṉimālai puṉaintāṉ peṇṇaṉaiyār kaṇṭapaṭi pēcavumnāṉ kūcāp perumaiyoṭum iruntēṉeṉ arumai-elām aṟintāṉ uṇṇaṉaiyā vakaivaravu tāḻttaṉaṉiṉ ṟavaṉṟaṉ uḷamaṟintum viṭuvēṉō uraiyāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He is like my own eye. He is the husband who remains mingled in my life. He understands justice but knows no conflict. He is the compassionate Nataraja. During my cool, tender youth, He set me apart. He came of His own accord, bestowed His grace upon me, and adorned me with an unparalleled garland. Even when other women spoke whatever they wished, I remained unashamed and filled with pride. He knew all my precious worth. Today, He delays His arrival, keeping me from experiencing union. Knowing His heart, will I ever let Him go? Speak, my friend.
commentary: When God first bestowed His grace, the soul proudly wore it like a wedding garland, unbothered by the gossip of the world. Now, even as the Lord delays their final union, the soul remains steadfast. Having known His compassionate heart, the bride knows she can never abandon Him.

translit: ūṉmaṟanta uyirakattē oḷiniṟainta oruvaṉ ulakamelām uṭaiyavaṉeṉ ṉuṭaiyanaṭa rājaṉ pāṉmaṟanta ciṟiya-iṉam paruvamatiṉ mālaip parintaṇintāṉ terintataṉip paruvamitiṟ pariyāṉ tāṉmaṟantāṉ eṉiṉumiṅku nāṉmaṟakka māṭṭēṉ tavattēṟi avattiḻiyac cammatamum varumō kōṉmaṟanta kuṭiyēpōl miṭiyēṉnāṉ avaṉṟaṉ kuṇamaṟintum viṭuvēṉō kūṟāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He is the unique One filled with light within the soul that has transcended the flesh. He owns all the worlds. He is my Nataraja. During my tender youth, when I was a small child just leaving behind milk, He affectionately adorned me with a garland. Yet in this ripe age of awareness, He shows no affection. Even if He has forgotten me, I will never forget Him here. Having ascended through penance, would I consent to descend into ruin? I do not languish in poverty like a subject forgotten by their king. Knowing His nature, will I ever let Him go? Speak, my friend.
commentary: Vallalar describes God as the pure light within a soul that has risen above bodily attachments. Even if the Lord appears to forget her now that she is spiritually mature, the bride insists she will never forget Him. Having climbed so high through devoted practice, the soul refuses to slide backward into worldly life.

translit: taṉittapara nātamuṭit talattiṉmicait talattē talaivarelām vaṇaṅkaniṉṟa talaivaṉnaṭa rācaṉ iṉittacukam aṟintukoḷā iḷamparuvan taṉilē eṉpuruva naṭu-iruntāṉ piṉpukaṇṭēṉ illai aṉittamilā iccaritam yārkkuraippēṉ antō avaṉaṟivāṉ nāṉaṟivēṉ ayalaṟivār uḷarō tuṉittanilai viṭuttorukāl cuttanilai ataṉil cukaṅkaṇṭum viṭuvēṉō collāyeṉ tōḻī.
translation: He is the Supreme Lord who stands upon the highest peak of the ultimate primal sound, worshipped by all other leaders. He is Nataraja. During my tender youth, before I learned of sweet pleasure, He resided in the center of my eyebrows. Since then, I have not seen Him. Alas, to whom will I recount this eternal history? He knows it, and I know it. Does any stranger know it? Having once abandoned the state of suffering and experienced the joy of the pure state, will I ever let Him go? Tell me, my friend.
commentary: Spiritual awakening began at the center of the eyebrows, the focal point of inner vision where God first appeared in her youth. The Lord who revealed Himself there is the Supreme Being, standing above all creation and primal sound. Having tasted this pure, sorrowless state, the soul is bound to God forever, sharing a secret history the outside world cannot understand.

translit: veṟutturaittēṉ piḻaikaḷelām poṟuttaruḷal vēṇṭum viḷaṅkaṟivuk kaṟivāki meyppotuvil naṭippōy kaṟutturaittār tamakkumaruḷ kaṉinturaikkum periya karuṇaineṭuṅ kaṭalēmuk kaṇṇōṅku karumpē maṟutturaippa tevaṉaruḷnī vaḻaṅkukiṉum aṉṟi maṟuttiṭiṉum uṉṉaiyalāl maṟṟorucār paṟiyēṉ ceṟutturaitta uraikaḷelām tiruvaruḷē eṉṟu cintippa tallāmal ceyvakai-oṉ ṟilaṉē.
translation: I spoke out of frustration. You must forgive all my faults and bestow grace, O Lord who dances in the true public hall as the intelligence within bright intelligence. O great vast ocean of compassion who speaks sweetly with grace even to those who speak angrily to You. O towering sugarcane with three eyes. What is the use of arguing further? Whether You grant Your grace or deny it, I know no refuge other than You. I have no choice but to consider all harsh words as divine grace itself.
commentary: The soul, speaking as a bride, apologizes for lashing out in anger. Arguing is useless because she has nowhere else to turn, whether God grants her wish or remains silent.

translit: mikutturaittēṉ piḻaikaḷelām cakittaruḷal vēṇṭum meyyaṟiviṉ puruvāki viyaṉpotuvil naṭippōy tokutturaitta maṟaikaḷumpiṉ viritturaittum kāṇāt turiyanaṭu vē-irunta periyaparam poruḷē pakutturaitta payaṉuraikkōr poruḷāki viḷaṅkum parañcuṭarē paramparaṉē pacupatiyē aṭiyēṉ vakutturaippa tevaṉaruḷnī vaḻaṅkukiṉum aṉṟi maṟuttiṭiṉum uṉṉaiyalāl maṟṟorucār pilaṉē.
translation: I spoke excessively. You must bear with all my faults and grant grace, O Lord who takes the form of true knowledge and dances in the vast public hall. O great supreme reality dwelling in the center of the transcendent state, unseen even by the compiled Vedas despite their elaborate expositions. O supreme flame, O supreme Lord, O master of souls, who shines as the ultimate meaning of all analyzed truths. What is the use of my explaining things to You? Whether You grant Your grace or deny it, I have no refuge other than You.
commentary: Human speech fails when trying to capture the divine. Because God dwells beyond the reach of ancient scriptures, the bride sees that explaining or justifying herself is pointless.

translit: muṉṉavaṉē ciṟiyēṉnāṉ ciṟitumaṟi yātē muṉinturaitta piḻaipoṟuttuk kaṉintaruḷal vēṇṭum eṉṉavaṉē eṉtuṇaiyē eṉuṟavē eṉṉai īṉṟavaṉē eṉtāyē eṉkuruvē eṉatu maṉṉavaṉē eṉṉuṭaiya vāḻmutalē eṉkaṇ māmaṇiyē maṇimiṭaṟṟōr māṇikka malaiyē aṉṉavaṉē ampalattuḷ āṭukiṉṟa amutē āṟaṇinta caṭaiyāyyāṉ vēṟutuṇai ilaṉē.
translation: O primal Lord. I am a lowly one. Knowing nothing at all, I spoke in anger. You must forgive my faults and sweetly bestow Your grace. O my Lord. O my companion. O my kin. O my creator. O my mother. O my guru. O my king. O the very source of my life. O great gem of my eye. O ruby mountain with a jewel-like blue throat. O Lord of such greatness. O nectar dancing in the hall. O Lord wearing the river in Your matted hair. I have no other companion.
commentary: The bride claims God as her mother, her companion, her teacher, and the very source of her life. Stripping away her previous frustration, she admits her own ignorance and throws herself entirely on his mercy.

translit: ciṉanturaittēṉ piḻaikaḷelām maṉampoṟuttal vēṇṭum tīṉatayā nitiyēmeyñ ñāṉacapā patiyē puṉainturaippār akattoṉṟum puṟattoṉṟum niṉaittē poyyulakar āṅkavarpōl puṉainturaittēṉ alaṉnāṉ iṉantirunti eṉaiyāṭkoṇ ṭeṉṉuḷamarn teṉaittāṉ evvulakum toḻanilaimēl ēṟṟiyacaṟ kuruvē kaṉantaruciṟ cuka-amutam kaḷittaḷitta niṟaivē karuṇainaṭat taracē-eṉ kaṇṇilaṅku maṇiyē.
translation: I spoke in anger. You must find it in Your heart to forgive all my faults. O treasure of compassion for the destitute. O Lord of the true hall of wisdom. I did not speak deceitfully like the false people of the world who say one thing while thinking another. You corrected my nature, took me as Your own, sat within me, and lifted me to a state worshipped by all worlds, O true guru. O fullness who joyfully offered the profound nectar of spiritual bliss. O king of the dance of compassion. O shining gem of my eye.
commentary: Even in anger, the bride's outburst was honest. Her raw, vulnerable frustration contrasts with the polite, empty words of worldly people who say one thing while thinking another.

translit: ūṭutaṟkōr iṭaṅkāṇēṉ uvakkumiṭam uḷatō uṉṉiṭamum eṉṉiṭamum ōriṭamā taliṉāl vāṭutaṟku nērntiṭilō māṭṭāmai yālum maṉampiṭiyā maiyiṉālum ciṉanturaittēṉ cilavē kūṭutaṟku vallavaṉnī kūṭṭi-eṉaik koṇṭē kulampēca vēṇṭāmeṉ kuṟippaṉaittum aṟintāy nāṭutaṟkiṅ keṉṉālē muṭiyātu nīyē nāṭuvittuk koṇṭaruḷvāy ñāṉacapā patiyē.
translation: I see no room for a lover's quarrel. Is there even a place for it? Your place and my place are one and the same. When driven to despair, I spoke a few words in anger out of helplessness and an unruly mind. You have the power to unite us. Take me in union and do not speak of lineage. You know all my intentions. I cannot seek You out on my own. You Yourself must make me seek You and bestow Your grace, O Lord of the hall of wisdom.
commentary: A traditional lover's quarrel requires distance between partners, but the bride realizes no such distance exists. Because the soul and God share the same space, her anger was a desperate cry of helplessness, and only God has the power to draw her into union.

translit: eṉṉuḷamnī kalantukoṇṭāy uṉṉuḷamnāṉ kalantēṉ eṉceyaluṉ ceyaluṉṟaṉ iruñceyaleṉ ceyalē piṉṉuḷanāṉ pitaṟṟalelām vēṟukuṟit teṉainī piḻai-ēṟṟa niṉaittiṭilō peruvaḻakkiṭ ṭiṭuvēṉ aṉṉaiyiṉum tayavuṭaiyāy appaṉeṉak kāṉāy aṉṟiyumeṉ āruyiruk kāruyirāy niṟaintāy maṉṉumaṇip potunaṭañcey maṉṉavaṉē karuṇai mānitiyē eṉakkaruḷvāy maṉakkalakkan tavirttē.
translation: You merged into my heart, and I merged into your heart. My actions are your actions, and your great actions are my actions. If you interpret my recent babblings differently and try to impute faults to me, I will raise a huge dispute against you. You possess more compassion than a mother. You became my father. Furthermore, you pervade my precious life as its innermost life. O King who dances in the enduring ruby hall. O great treasure of grace. Dispel my mind's confusion and bless me.
commentary: The speaker claims a complete, inseparable union with God, where human action and divine action become exactly the same. Because of this deep intimacy, he feels safe enough to argue, warning that he will raise a dispute if the Lord tries to find fault with his recent emotional outbursts. He trusts that God, who is more compassionate than a mother, will understand the confusion in his heart.

translit: eṇaṅkuṟiyēṉ iyalkuṟiyēṉ ētuniṉai yātē eṉpāṭṭuk kiruntēṉiṅ keṉaivalintu nīyē maṇaṅkuṟittuk koṇṭāynī koṇṭatutoṭ ṭeṉatu maṉamvēṟu paṭṭatilai māṭṭāmai yālē kaṇaṅkuṟittuc cilapukaṉṟēṉ pukaṉṟamoḻi eṉatu karuttililai uṉṉuṭaiya karuttiluṇṭō uṇṭēl kuṇaṅkuṟippāṉ kuṟṟamoṉṟuṅ kuṟiyāṉeṉ ṟaṟavōr kūṟiṭumav vārttai-iṉṟu māṟiṭumē aracē.
translation: I made no calculations and noted no worldly ways. I thought of nothing and kept entirely to myself. You forcefully decided to marry me here. From the moment you claimed me, my mind has never wavered. Out of sheer weakness, counting the heavy moments, I blurted out a few things. The words I spoke are not held in my heart. Are they held in yours? If they are, the saying of the righteous that you note only good qualities and ignore all faults will be proven false today, O King.
commentary: Vallalar speaks as a bride whom God claimed by force. Because God initiated this union, she argues that frustrated words spoken in a moment of weakness should not be held against her. She reminds God of His reputation for ignoring faults, warning that holding a grudge now would prove the saints wrong.

translit: maṉampiṭiyā maiyiṉālō māṭṭāmai yālō maṟatiyiṉā lō-eṉatu varuttamata ṉālō tiṉampiṭiyā mayakkālō tikaippālō piṟarmēl ciṉattālō etaṉālō cilapukaṉṟēṉ itaṉaic ciṉampiṭiyāt tēvartiru vuḷampiṭiyā teṉavē cintaikaḷit tirukkiṉṟēṉ tiruvuḷattai aṟiyēṉ iṉampiṭiyā maiyumuṇṭō uṇṭeṉilaṉ puṭaiyār ēcalpukaḻ pēcaleṉa iyamputaleṉ ulakē.
translation: Whether my mind lost its grasp, or I felt too weak, or I forgot myself, or I suffered in sorrow, or I fell into a daily delusion, or I was bewildered, or I felt angry at others, or for some other reason, I blurted out a few things. My mind rejoices with the thought that you, the Divine who harbors no anger, will not hold this against me in your divine heart. Yet I do not truly know your divine will. Would you fail to embrace your own kin? If you would, why does the world declare that the scoldings of those who love are taken as praise?
commentary: Vallalar asks for divine patience, appealing to the intimate bond between them. When people who love each other argue, even their scolding is a form of praise because it comes from a place of absolute trust.

translit: nāyakarē umatuvacam nāṉirukkiṉ ṟatupōl nāṭiyatat tuvattōḻi naṅkaiyareṉ vacattē mēyavarā kāmaiyiṉāl avarmēlaṅ keḻunta vekuḷiyiṉāl cilapukaṉṟēṉ vēṟuniṉait taṟiyēṉ tūyavarē veṟuppuvaril vitiveṟukka eṉṟār cūḻavitit tāraiveṟut tiṭutalavar tuṇivē tīyavarā yiṉumkuṟṟam kuṟiyātu pukaṉṟāl tīmoḻi-aṉ ṟeṉattēvar ceppiyatum uḷatē.
translation: O Lord! Just as I remain under your control, the young women who serve as my companions, representing the governing principles, did not submit to my control. Out of the anger I felt toward them, I blurted out a few things. I know no other intention. O Pure One! The wise advise that if hatred arises, one should hate fate. Their conclusion is to hate the one who ordained that fate. You, the Divine, have also declared that when even wicked people speak without intending offense, their words are not considered evil.
commentary: Vallalar personifies his physical and mental faculties as disobedient companions. His frustration was directed at his inability to control these inner forces, not at God. He admits that being angry at earthly struggles sometimes looks like anger toward the one who designed his fate, but he trusts the Lord will forgive words spoken without malice.

translit: kuṟṟamoru ciṟiteṉiṉum kuṟittaṟiyēṉ vēṟōr kuṟai-ataṉāl cilapukaṉṟēṉ kuṟittaṟiyēṉ mīṭṭum caṟṟumaṉam vēṟupaṭṭa tillaikaṇṭīr eṉatu cāmi-ummēl āṇai-oru caturumniṉait taṟiyēṉ peṟṟavaḷum uṟṟavarum cuṟṟamumnīr eṉṟē piṭittirukkiṉ ṟēṉpiṟitōr veṭippumurait taṟiyēṉ iṟṟaitoṭut teṉaḷavil vēṟuniṉai yātīr eṉṉuṭaiya nāyakarē eṉācai ituvē.
translation: I have never intended even the slightest fault. Because of some other flaw, I blurted out a few things without intent. See that my mind has not wavered even slightly since. My Lord, I swear upon you. I harbor no cunning thoughts. I hold fast to the truth that you are my mother, my relatives, and my kin. I know not how to voice any other outburst. From this day forward, do not think differently of me. O my Lord, this is my desire.
commentary: Vallalar swears directly upon God that he meant no disrespect. Stripping away all defenses, he declares that the divine is his only family and support. His only desire is for God to accept his complete dependence and never doubt his devotion again.

glossary.def: Agamas: the scriptures of temple worship and doctrine. Vallalar says their truth is known by grace, not by reading.
Ambalam: the hall or open stage where God dances. It is the hall at Chidambaram and, within, the space of consciousness where God is known.
Ananda: supreme spiritual bliss. For Vallalar this bliss is the true form of the divine, revealed once a person steps away from worldly delusion.
Appar: a highly revered ancient Tamil saint. Vallalar deeply admired his intense, humble devotion and recalls stories of God serving Appar as an ordinary travel companion.
Hari: another name for Vishnu, the Hindu god of preservation. Vallalar mentions him to show the supremacy of the ultimate Lord.
Arunai: the holy city of Tiruvannamalai. Vallalar yearns to stand in the physical presence of God here to finally calm his restless heart.
Arur: a major temple town in Tamil Nadu dedicated to Siva. Vallalar addresses the deity of this shrine intimately as his father and absolute master.
ArutPerunJothi: the Vast Grace-Light. Vallalar's name for God, the one infinite Light of grace from which everything comes, open to every living being.
Ayan: a traditional name for Brahma, the creator deity. Vallalar invokes this name to emphasize that even the highest celestial beings must humbly worship the supreme divine light.
Sakkiyar, one of the Saiva saints, who worshipped God each day by throwing a stone at the Siva lingam. Vallalar recalls him to show that God accepts any offering made with a true heart.

Jains. Vallalar recalls the old stories of the Saiva saints and the Jain monks, and names the quarrelling Jains among those his heart turns away from. In his later songs he says that the Grace Light taught him from the beginning that caste, creed and religion are false.
Sambandar: a highly revered child saint of the Tamil devotional tradition. Vallalar references him to illustrate how intimately God responds to a devotee.
Sambhu: a traditional name for Siva meaning the source of peace. Vallalar invokes this title to emphasize God as the ultimate, self-created sanctuary for the living soul.
Shanmuka: the six-faced Lord, commonly known as Murugan. Vallalar invokes this traditional deity as an inner divine presence on which the mind should meditate.
Sangam: the ancient academies of Tamil poets and scholars. Vallalar reveres these legendary literary assemblies as the historical foundation of Tamil heritage.
Sankara: a name for Siva meaning the bringer of peace. Vallalar invokes this title to contrast God's peaceful protection with the terrifying nature of worldly conflict.
Sanmarkkam: the true path. Vallalar's name for the way of grace, compassion, and direct knowledge of God, open to every living being.
Satguru: the true spiritual master. For Vallalar, God alone is the ultimate teacher who dwells within the soul and guides it toward enlightenment.
Saraswati: the Goddess of Speech, Arts, and Learning. Vallalar praises her as the source of all sacred sound and creative power.
Sadasiva: the eternal and supreme form of Siva. Vallalar invokes this name to emphasize a divine nature that remains completely beyond the grasp of traditional deities.
Sakti: divine energy. In traditional philosophy, this represents the active, creative power of the universe which Vallalar sees as an expression of supreme grace.
Chera: the saint-king Cheraman Perumal, who famously rode a horse to heaven. Vallalar uses his legendary journey to prove that steadfast devotion makes impossible spiritual goals attainable.
Chidambaram: the supreme space of pure consciousness. Vallalar identifies this as the ultimate spiritual arena where the divine performs the eternal dance of grace.
Chit Sabhai: the hall of wisdom or divine consciousness. Vallalar identifies this both as the sacred dancing space of the Lord and the inner sanctum of the human heart.
Chitrambalam: the little hall or the innermost sanctum. Vallalar points to this as both the physical shrine in Thillai and the private space within the human heart where conscious bliss occurs.
Siddhar: perfected beings or mystics who possess supernatural powers. Vallalar points out that even these highly advanced masters cannot fully comprehend the supreme nature of God.
Siva: the supreme Lord. Vallalar uses this name to address the ultimate reality that rules the universe and guides the soul toward supreme light.
Sivakama Valli: the goddess embodying the dynamic energy of divine grace. Vallalar invokes her to represent the deep joy that accompanies the supreme Lord's dance.
Sivakami: the goddess of divine grace and bliss, the consort of Nataraja. She represents the compassionate energy that accompanies the cosmic dance.
Sivam: the supreme divine reality. In Vallalar's poetry this represents the ultimate state of grace and truth, often equated directly with pure spiritual light.
Jothi: light or flame. Vallalar identifies the ultimate divine reality as the supreme Jothi, a self-luminous presence that dispels the deep darkness of human delusion.
Sundarar: the eighth-century Tamil saint. Vallalar references the traditional story where the divine Lord appeared at Sundarar's wedding with a legal contract to claim him as a bonded servant.
Swayambhu: a self-manifested or uncreated being. Vallalar uses this term to describe the ultimate Divine that exists independently, providing an eternal refuge.
Ezhuthariyum Peruman: the Lord who knows the written destiny. A specific title for the presiding deity at the Otriyur temple, emphasizing that God sees past human ignorance.
Lakshmi: the goddess of wealth. Vallalar uses her to symbolize the supreme spiritual wealth granted to those who possess true devotion.
Himalayas: the great mountain range. Vallalar uses it as a symbol of towering, unshakeable divine majesty and ancient spiritual heritage.
Indra: the king of the gods in traditional Hindu mythology. Vallalar completely rejects his heavenly paradise, insisting that receiving God's compassion is infinitely better.
Ravana: the mythical demon king. Vallalar refers to his story to show that even the most powerful and arrogant rulers are humbled in the end by divine might.
Yama: the Hindu god of death and cosmic justice. Vallalar vividly describes his terrifying arrival to underscore the extreme urgency of spiritual awakening.
Jeevakarunyam: active compassion for all living beings. For Vallalar, relieving the suffering of others is the primary requirement for experiencing true spiritual liberation.
Kailash: the sacred silver mountain abode of Lord Siva. Vallalar points out that pure chanting unlocks this supreme spiritual realm easily.
Kalahasti: an ancient temple town where the legendary hunter-saint Kannappar offered his eyes to God, representing the pinnacle of unlettered devotion.
Kaman: the Hindu god of physical desire. Vallalar references the traditional story where the Lord burned this deity to ashes to show that divine focus burns away worldly lust.
Ganges: the sacred river. Vallalar invokes the image of the Lord holding this river in his hair to symbolize the cooling grace that washes away the heat of worldly suffering.
Kanchi: a historic temple city in Tamil Nadu. Vallalar mentions it as one of the sacred earthly sites where the divine presence actively grants grace.
Kannappar: a legendary hunter-saint who offered chewed meat and his own eyes to God. Vallalar invokes his story to prove that raw devotion matters far more than formal ritual purity.
Kandan: the warrior-god Murugan. Vallalar refers to God as the tender source that brings forth Kandan to protect and guide devotees.
Karma: the accumulated weight of past actions. Vallalar describes it as a force that turns the human heart into stone, which only divine grace can break.
Murder. Vallalar means the murder of any living being, not only of humans, and condemns it absolutely as a barrier to spiritual life.
The golden shower flower. Vallalar frequently mentions this traditional floral garland of the Lord to invoke a familiar, approachable form of the divine.
Guhan: a sacred name for the deity Murugan. Vallalar appeals to Siva as the father of Guhan to highlight the Lord's protective and paternal nature.
Kumaran: the god Murugan, son of Siva. Vallalar invokes this youthful deity to highlight the protective and accessible nature of the divine family.
Kundalini: the latent spiritual energy located within the human body. Vallalar seeks the pure nourishment that flows when this inner power is awakened.
Guru: spiritual teacher. Vallalar identifies the supreme divine light as the ultimate guide who dispels human ignorance.
Malam: filth or spiritual impurity. In Vallalar's poetry, this represents the accumulated ignorance and worldly attachments blocking the soul's path to divine light.

Manikkavasagar: a celebrated saint and poet in the Tamil tradition. Vallalar frequently recalls how God personally intervened to rescue this devotee to demonstrate divine readiness to save a beloved soul.
Maraikkadu: a sacred temple town. Vallalar references the legendary opening of its locked doors by the songs of Appar and Sambandar as proof of the power of sincere devotion.
Markandeyar: an ancient sage. Vallalar invokes the story of God saving this devoted youth from the god of death to prove that divine grace can conquer mortality itself.
Madurai: an ancient temple city in southern India. Vallalar references this location as the famous earthly stage where God personally appeared to perform astonishing wonders.
Mayai: illusion or the deceptive nature of material existence. Vallalar identifies this as the force that traps human consciousness in physical desires and blinds it to the divine reality.
Meru: a massive mythical mountain. Vallalar refers to the story of God effortlessly bending this huge stone mountain into a bow to show that divine grace can conquer anything.
Murugan: the warrior-god, considered the son of Siva. Vallalar frequently addresses the supreme divine presence through this specific form in his early devotional phase.
Namasivaya: the sacred five-syllable mantra meaning adoration to Siva. Clinging to this name is the ultimate refuge for a soul completely devoid of merit.
Nandi: the sacred white bull. Vallalar invokes this traditional mount of Lord Siva to represent supreme divine majesty.
Nataraja: the supreme dancing Lord of the cosmic hall. Vallalar views this form as the ultimate expression of divine grace and the true destination for the wandering soul.
Ghee, clarified butter, the usual fuel of temple lamps. Vallalar recalls the lamp that burned with water as with ghee (096).
Sacred ash worn on the body. Vallalar views this ash as a powerful spiritual shield that secures basic worldly needs and symbolizes the complete burning away of all earthly ignorance.
Om: the primordial sacred sound of the universe. Vallalar cries out this syllable as an intimate plea for relief from the poison of earthly sorrow.

Otriyur, also called Otri: the holy temple town by the sea at the northern edge of Chennai. Vallalar walked there to worship day after day in his early years; most poems of this book are sung there. The word otri also means a pledge or mortgage, a pun the verses play on.
Pasupati: the Lord of all souls. Vallalar invokes this traditional title to describe God as the supreme caretaker and guide for all bound, struggling individuals.
Padambakkanathar: the Lord of Padampakkam, a local name for the deity at the Otriyur temple. Vallalar addresses God by this title to express an intimate and grounded devotion.
Parvati: the goddess who serves as the consort of the supreme Lord. Vallalar envisions her as the cosmic witness to God's endless dance of existence.
Bhava: worldly bondage or the cycle of physical birth. Vallalar warns that without divine grace, the soul remains hopelessly trapped in this cycle.
Brahma: the creator deity in classical Hindu theology. Vallalar emphasizes that even major cosmic gods like him are unable to fully comprehend the supreme divine flame.
Baseness, moral impurity: living without truth, charity or love for other beings. Vallalar calls himself pulaiyēṉ, a base one; the word describes conduct, never birth.
Puliyur: an ancient name for the sacred town of Chidambaram. Vallalar reveres this town as the earthly location of the golden hall where the divine dances.
Pullirukkuvelur: a sacred temple town in Tamil Nadu renowned for its healing deity, Vaithiyanatha. Vallalar identifies the divine presence enshrined here as the ultimate spiritual medicine.
Rudraksha: sacred prayer beads. Vallalar compares these beads to precious gems to show that true spiritual wealth replaces the need for worldly ornaments.
Tamil: the language. Vallalar views it as a refined, sacred medium through which God grants grace to sincere devotees.
Dharma: righteousness or moral duty. Vallalar identifies this universal moral order as the solid foundation upon which the divine presence rests.
Tattvas: the physical and mental building blocks of the universe. Vallalar teaches that supreme divine grace transcends every natural law and elemental category.
Devas: celestial beings or gods living in heavenly realms. Vallalar emphasizes the supreme power of divine grace by noting its unstoppable nature, outranking all celestials.

Thillai: the sacred temple town of Chidambaram where Siva performs his cosmic dance. Vallalar views this location as a symbol of the ultimate spiritual space where the divine connects with the pure soul.
Thirumullaivayil: a sacred temple town near Chennai. Vallalar frequently visited its shrine and addressed the resident deity directly in his early devotional verses.

Thirunavukkarasar: a celebrated poet-saint whose desperate songs opened physically locked temple doors. Vallalar points to his life as proof that a sincere cry from the heart overpowers religious authority.
Thiruvalithayam: a sacred site near Chennai, now called Padi. Vallalar sang intimate verses here, marveling at the contrast between the temple deity's supreme power and humble appearance.
Thiruvarur: a major temple town in Tamil Nadu dedicated to Siva. Vallalar addresses the deity of this shrine intimately as his father and absolute master.
Thiruvasagam: the sacred collection of Tamil hymns composed by the saint Manikkavasagar, revered for their intense devotional outpouring.
Thyagar: the Great Giver, a famous title for the presiding deity at Otriyur. Vallalar playfully challenges this title by asking why a supposedly generous God refuses to speak a comforting word.

Turiya: the transcendent fourth state of consciousness beyond waking, dreaming, and deep sleep. Vallalar views this as the pure spiritual realm where the soul directly perceives and merges with the supreme Jothi.
Durga: a powerful aspect of the Goddess. Vallalar references her to invoke the divine feminine energy that protects the universe and dispels ignorance.
Umai: the goddess Uma, representing divine feminine energy. Vallalar invokes her alongside Siva to emphasize the maternal compassion that must always accompany divine power.
The Upanishads. Ancient philosophical scriptures. Vallalar points to the divine light as the ultimate truth shining at the very peak of these sacred texts.
Vaitheeswaran Koil: a famous temple of healing in Tamil Nadu. Vallalar identifies its presiding deity as the ultimate spiritual medicine for the soul.
Valli: the divine consort of Murugan. She represents the approachable and sweet nature of divine grace.
Vallalar: the author of the Thiru Arutpa. This honorific name meaning 'the supremely generous one' was given to Ramalinga Adigal by his followers.
Vanni: a sacred tree whose leaves and flowers are traditionally offered in worship. Vallalar visualizes the Lord wearing these flowers to evoke his role as the ultimate healer.
Vadavur: the birthplace of the saint Manikkavasagar, often used as a traditional name for him.
Bhairava: a fierce manifestation of the divine. Vallalar mentions this terrifying form to illustrate God's ultimate authority over arrogant creator deities.
Vaithiyanatha: the supreme divine physician. Vallalar uses this name to emphasize that God alone dispenses the ultimate medicine of grace to heal the spiritual diseases of worldly existence.
The Vedas. The ancient spiritual scriptures. Vallalar teaches that the ultimate divine reality is so deep it escapes the understanding of even these foundational texts.
Vinayakar: the elephant-headed Lord, commonly known as Vinayakar. Vallalar points to this form as a focal point for inward meditation to anchor the restless mind.

Vishnu: the preserver deity in Hindu tradition. Vallalar references him to establish the absolute supremacy of the ultimate Lord, whose pure grace remains beyond the comprehension of even the highest traditional gods.
